en: The *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra. Homage to the Omniscient One!
1. The Legend of Prabhāsa:
His mind is as stainless as crystal and does not grasp at passion;
with a heart moistened by compassion, he has dried up all faults.
May he who has himself struck down the enemy of cyclic existence through non-anger become omniscient for your unwavering welfare.
Possessing deep shade, with the circle of stable Dharma as its roots, established in the watering trench of merit,

it is endowed with wide-spreading branches shimmering with the waters of wisdom, learning, and compassion; it has the brilliance of contentment for its leaves, pure fame for its flowers, and always bears excellent fruit.
Victorious is the glorious Buddha, the wish-fulfilling tree that fulfills all hopes.
The resolve of those of great majesty arises to rescue the world from this ocean of saṃsāra, which is a mine of sea-monsters; how this is heard here [in tradition] is as follows.
There is a city named Prabhāvatī, surrounded by golden palatial mansions,
like the sky filled with the celestial chariots of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Inhabited by Vidyādharas and frequented by hosts of Siddhas and Gandharvas,
it rested upon the earth like the city of Śakra, attained by the virtuous through their good deeds.
Constantly frequented by those whose nature consists of truth, vows, charity, and compassion,
it was like the capital city of Dharma, abounding in meritorious dwellings.
In that city there was a king named Prabhāsa, an ornament of the earth,
whose splendorous fame is reverently honored by the gods.
If the clusters of flowers that are his fame—the abundant fragrance of whose virtues has reached all the fawn-eyed women—have become ear-ornaments for them; KAvk_1.8.
The kings placed his command— which was radiant with golden flowers— upon the circles of their crowns like a garland, for he was one who knew the proper means.
Once, as the Lord of the World was seated,
the lord of the Naga forest approached him and, placing his knees upon the ground, spoke.
"O King, we have captured this wondrous elephant of divine splendor;
having heard of your fame, he has come to earth like Airāvaṇa."
"Let this elephant, worthy of the gods, be seen standing at the gate;
for the exertion of masters toward their servants is indeed fruitful when it is witnessed."
Having heard this, the king went out accompanied by his ministers and beheld at the gate an elephant, like Mount Kailāsa in motion.
It was like the spring season itself, attended by bees drawn by its unrestrained fragrance who acted as the drummers for its cheeks,
and which was noble with the ornaments of love.
With his hand resting upon the edge of his tusk and his eyes closed,
he was recollecting the splendor of the Vindhya forests of plantain, sallakī, and kānana trees.
By the command of Agastya, he went to earth to assume the sovereignty of elephants—
tall as the Vindhya mountain and wafting the fragrance of blooming saptacchada trees.
Beholding that palace, adorned with ivory pillars and serving as an abode for the play of Fortune, the lord of the earth reflected thus out of amazement: KAvk_1.17 //
Oh, how uninterrupted is the succession of world-creations, arising from the deeds of those who possess the wonder of manifold emanations and ever-new excellences!
By whom was this elephant produced— without churning the ocean of nectar, without the labor of Vāsuki,
and without the extraction of the mountain?
Then the king,
whose commands were honored, gave an order to the elephant-keeper named Saṃyāta, saying, "Let this elephant be tamed."
When the protector of the earth had departed for his inner apartments after giving those instructions,
he went forth and captured a serpent capable of bearing the weight of all training.
Like a wise and true disciple, constrained by the practice of his previous birth,
he was led by that effort to complete proficiency in all branches of learning.
Free from anxiety regarding his many gifts, endowed with power and energy, and patient, he—
who found a favorable outcome even in the destruction of his enemies— attained equality with the king.
Then,
having fulfilled his task, he returned and reported to the lord of men that the king of elephants had successfully completed its training.
Seeing him under the control of the goad,
with the power of his transformation arisen and having ascended to the peak of enthusiasm, the king considered him to be the very goddess of victory.
With his enthusiasm aroused by a desire to witness the training in dexterity and other skills that had arisen from his great joy,
he ascended him with vigor, like the thousand-rayed sun ascending the mountain of sunrise.
Then, like the minister of a lordly elephant under his control,
Saṃyāta displayed his skill in traversing the entire circle of the mandala.
In the course of observing elephants, the king, longing for the sport of hunting,
plunged into the great forest as if entering his own valor.
He went forth as if summoning the elephants of the quarters with the rays of his jeweled armlets,
which extended far away like the finest shoots of the *sallakī* tree.
There in the forest, the forest deities beheld him as he was walking,
their eyes filled with ears of joy and wonder.
The winds from the Vindhya mountains, filled with the fragrance of the flowers from the tresses of Śabarī’s braid,
served that lord of the earth.
Then, in the vicinity of the Vindhya mountains, where the trees provided pleasure according to one's own will,
the elephant fell into a state of longing as he recalled the events of his former life of luxury.
Having smelled the scent of the female elephant bound by love, that elephant,
like a king intoxicated with pride, abandoned the restraint of the goad.
As he ran with great haste, drawn by passion like a staff-bearer,
there was no cessation for him anywhere, as if he were utterly deluded within saṃsāra.
Seeing the elephant, which possessed the speed of a wind, advancing as he went, the king of elephants, seized by doubt, spoke these words to Saṃyāta: KAvk_1.35 //
"Aha! This elephant, who once turned his back upon this master’s goad, has now been seen by you to have been brought under discipline."
The circle of the quarters seems to whirl, the trees seem to follow him;
by the weight of his footsteps, the earth reels as if intoxicated.
Since fate has turned adverse at this untimely hour like a god,
all efforts toward human exertion have become fruitless.
Having heard these words, he approached the Lord with trepidation;
out of embarrassment caused by the reproach of his instruction, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, this elephant was made by me entirely dependent on all his activities;
having caught the scent of a female elephant, why has he now fallen into such agitation?"
Living beings who have fallen under the sway of desire do not remember instruction, nor restraint, nor courtesy, nor goodness; they remember only desire.
By what means can the mind, overflowing with the delight of passion and directed toward sense objects, be restrained—
like a stream of water that has fallen into a vast chasm?
We are skilled trainers in the training of physical exertion;
even sages are not experts in the training of mental discipline.
Disregarding all fatigue due to passion, with every restraint shattered,
this fool runs headlong like a rogue elephant driven by a goad.
"O Lord of the Earth, grasp a branch of the tree and let go of this man;
for it is true that a wicked person, having fallen into calamity, brings down even those who support him."
Having heard Saṃyāta’s words, which were appropriate for the occasion, the king,
accompanied by him alone, climbed onto the branch of a great tree.
When the king had descended from the tree, mounted his horse, and departed,
the elephant plunged into the thicket, reached a female elephant, and embraced her.
Then, after seven days had passed, the elephant Śāntasmara returned;
having eaten at his pleasure, he remained there, having bound himself to the hitching post by his own will.
Seeing him arrive in person, restrained by the discipline of his training,
he went forth and announced it to the king out of joy at the excellence of his skill.
Drawn by the snare of passion, he who had set out afflicted by love—
that very elephant, unswerving in his training, has now arrived of his own accord.
Restrained by signals, submissive, and a connoisseur of flavors, the elephant born of the *sallakī* breed,
remaining firm in discipline, accepts a mouthful of glowing-hot iron.
Drawn by the savor of sensual desire, he fell into a miserable transformation;
now, having returned to his natural state, the fever of passion has been stilled.
O Lord, lions, tigers, elephants, and the like can be subdued;
but the mind, intoxicated by the liquor of passion and directed toward sense objects, cannot.
Having heard this, the king, reflecting that it was indeed so, said:
"O Saṃyāta, what you have spoken is true and appropriate."
Is there anyone in this world by whom the elephant of a mind-intoxicated [being] has been brought,
through the nature of tranquility, to be bound by the tether of self-restraint?
When this was said, he, possessed by the deity, approached him and spoke: "O Lord, there exist those who are intent on uprooting the afflictions of the world without remainder. (KAvk 1.56)
Those who perceive the world through discernment, whose intense grasp is born of dispassion,
and who are purified by tranquility and contentment— they alone are the awakened ones, truly enlightened.
Having thus heard the designation "Buddha," a vow born of the practice of previous lives arose in the king, whose mind was set upon perfect enlightenment.
When this world is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
which is like a sea of crocodiles, may I, liberated through perfect enlightenment, ferry it across by means of the bridge of virtue.
Then the deities of the Śuddhāvāsa realm spoke from the sky:
"O Great-Minded One, you shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha."
Having heard those words, the king, the best among those free from passion,
possessing the memory of his former births and divine vision, proceeded toward the state of a Bodhisattva.
Then that being of vast magnitude, whose eyes were fixed upon reality, compassionate toward all beings sinking in the ocean of existence,
became [so] through his union with the desire for awakening newly arising.
He was a bridge of skill for the lowly, for the purpose of ferrying sentient beings across.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Legend of Prabhāsa," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
2. The Legend of Śrīsena.
Victorious are those Jinas in this world, who are like sandalwood trees of merit;
for even when subjected to cutting, rubbing, or burning, they remain unperturbed for the sake of others.
There exists a city named Ariṣṭā, which is to be reckoned by its multitude of virtues;
in rivalry with it, even the city of Śakra would not be more exalted.
In that city there was a king renowned as Śrīsena,
who was like a mine for the jewels of all virtues, a veritable ocean of gems.
By the power of that clever man, who was capable of benefiting others,
all the directions became devoted to him, just as they are by the power of the sun.
He was adorned with glories fragrant through the giving of wealth,
and with elephants white as ashes, like the wish-fulfilling trees of the world.
He was simple-hearted though a repository of arts, high-minded though simple,
and free from deceit though possessed of great intelligence— this was due to the merit of his subjects.
As long as the sun blazes and as long as the wind blows,
so long did his command and his fame remain unimpeded.
He, whom twelve thousand ministers— who are skilled in tranquility and exertion and possess the eye of knowledge regarding the six political measures— wait upon.
While that king was devoted to righteousness, the people became virtuous;
for subjects become equal to their lord in qualities, just as wives do.
By the power of his merit, people traveling to the third heaven proceeded without obstruction through the celestial chariots toward the city of Śakra.
Having seen the human world enveloped by the world of the gods,
Śatakratu, conceiving enmity toward the lord of the earth, reflected:
By that very [conduct], Fortune was bestowed upon the kings, and it performed wonders for the world;
and by his auspicious character, he caused the cessation of the pride of all conscious beings, including ourselves.
I, a practitioner of illusion, must test the fortitude of that man whose mind is unbroken by the power of the burning forest fire.
Having reflected thus for a very long time, Śakra, followed by all the gods,
transformed his form and descended into the world of mortals.
In the meantime,
the high-minded minister, the preceptor of the kingdom’s protection and devoted to deliberating upon the affairs of the subjects, spoke to the king.
O King,
the Lord of the Thirty-three gods is put to shame by you, who shine as a sovereign through a kingdom free from passion and by your sincere acts of giving.
Seeing another’s possession of perfect virtues and one’s own lack thereof,
who indeed would not fall under the sway of envy?
People who are envious and who delight in rivalry with the excellence of others generally experience agitation even at the virtuous deeds of the great.

May you be devoted to the practice of giving away all your possessions and to the discipline of giving with restraint; for indeed, the resolve to give away one's children, wife, and even oneself is an act of extreme recklessness.
Those dreadful dreams, which cause such terror, are seen;
by them, the violent shattering of the crest-jewel of the world is foretold.
And the report of the astrologers, who speak the truth, is heard:
"The protector of the earth will give his body [in sacrifice]," which is most difficult to endure.
The gift of one's body is the cause for making the assembly of all supplicants' desires fruitless;
yet, remaining as a wish-fulfilling tree, he becomes the giver of everything.
Therefore, O protector of the earth, desist from this reckless act of giving;
for your body is the jewel of protection for the world, dependent upon your offspring.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the minister, the lord of the earth,
the luster of whose lower lip was washed by a smile as white as his own goodness, addressed him.
"O great minister, you have spoken what is beneficial and worthy of a counselor;
however, I cannot endure the anguish of turning my back on those who seek my favor."
Those in whose mouths the words "Give!
uttered by beggars flash forth as harsh syllables of refusal, they are living beings who have already lost their lives.
"What can be gained from one who, having set in his heart the thought, 'I shall obtain this from him,' turns away when the petitioner arrives? What is the use of such a man living? (KAvk 2.27)
Fie on the birth of that meritless and pitiless soul, whose mind remains cool even upon hearing of the suffering of afflicted people! (KAvk 2.28)
For this reason, even though it is fraught with danger, this body is dear to the virtuous,
because at some time, in some place, it may become of service to someone.
Having heard these words of the courageous king, the minister said nothing at all, reflecting upon the immutability of what was destined to be.
Then, on one occasion, while that lord of the earth was sporting in his pastimes,
there was a wife named Jayaprabhā, who was like Rati to the Lord of Love.
From afar, with unblinking eyes, the sage-teacher beheld a beautiful woman who had arrived by chance, like a snare of mental attachment.
Seeing her, as if she were someone familiar from affection born of association with his practice in a previous life,
that heap of fortitude lost his self-command.
Although he was free from desire, his mind, stirred by latent impressions,
abandoned its aversion to worldly existence and returned to the realm of longing.
For this latent impression from the practice of previous births does not depart from all living beings; it is constantly woven together by the threads of continuous affection.
Having reached that hermitage, the young student, who had completed his studies and vows, said, "Please accept the teacher's fee."
He said to him: "My child, I have no need for a livelihood in the forest;
nevertheless, if you are insistent, hear what it is that I desire."
"O King Śrīsena,
if Queen Jayaprabhā can be given by you to me, then she shall be my fee."
Having heard what was thus spoken by the teacher, the disciple, his mind trembling,
became overwhelmed with doubt regarding the attainment of a request that was impossible to fulfill.

Having gone there, he entered the palace of the lord of kings— a dwelling where the doors were perpetually open at the will of supplicants, and which was filled with the confidence of those entering at their own ease.
His mind deeply distressed by the wretchedness of begging for what cannot be obtained,
his face bowed down from extreme embarrassment, he seemed to gaze at the earth.
Seeing that petitioner arrive, the lord of the earth became overjoyed,
like the ocean whose swelling has been aroused by the gift of nectar.

Having been asked by the king, "What is your desire? and being thus honored, he spoke with syllables faltering from embarrassment at recounting an unworthy tale: "Your Majesty, there is a certain man in this city who is a friend of mine. He is a merchant’s son, handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. Yet, though he possesses such qualities, he is not happy; for he has no wife. Therefore, O King, please grant me a favor: give him a wife. The king, having heard these words, was filled with wonder and said: "I shall do so. Then, having summoned the merchant’s son, he gave him a maiden of noble lineage as a wife. Having obtained her, the youth lived happily, like a god in heaven. But after some time, that wife became pregnant. When she had reached her time, she gave birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks. As the days passed, the boy grew up, and when he had attained the age of youth, he was sent by his father to another land to acquire wealth. After many years had passed, he returned home, bringing with him great riches. Seeing his son returned from abroad, the merchant was delighted and embraced him. Then, having performed the rites of hospitality, the merchant said to his son: "My son, you have acquired much wealth; now, let us go to the king and inform him of our success. Thus instructed by his father, the merchant’s son went to the palace with his parents. There, having approached the king, he bowed and said: "O King, this is my father, and this is my mother. We have returned from abroad with abundant wealth. Now, please grant us leave to depart. The king, having heard this, was pleased and said: "Go, and may prosperity attend you. Then, having taken leave of the king, the merchant’s son departed with his parents. On the way, they saw a great forest. It was dense with various trees, filled with lions, tigers, and elephants, and infested by robbers. Seeing that terrible forest, the merchant was terrified and said to his son: "My son, we have entered a dangerous forest full of dangers. How shall we escape it? Alas, what misfortune! Hearing his father's lamentation, the son reflected: "This is surely the result of my own karma; for I did not perform meritorious deeds in a previous life. Thus reflecting, he comforted his parents and said: "Do not fear, father and mother. I shall protect you both from this danger. Having spoken thus, the merchant’s son took up a sword and shield and stood ready to fight. Then a band of robbers, seeing them, surrounded them on all sides. The robbers said: "Who are you? Where are you going? Give us your wealth! The merchant’s son replied: "I am a merchant’s son traveling with my parents. I have come here seeking refuge; why do you wish to harm us? The robbers laughed and said: "We are robbers who live by plunder. We will not release you unless you give us your wealth. The merchant’s son said: "If you must have my wealth, take it. But first, please listen to my story. And so, out of compassion, the merchant’s son began to tell his tale, his voice faltering with shame at the recital of his unworthy past. [The rest of the story follows the narrative of the merchant’s son.]
O you who were formerly a wish-fulfilling tree for those seeking their goals,
I— though previously indifferent to others' needs— have now come to beg for my own pride, even at a station that is very difficult to attain.
"O King, when my vow of learning is complete, let Queen Jayaprabhā be given as the desired fee for my preceptor, if it is possible."
When the disciple of the sage had spoken thus, O Lord of the Earth, the king's mind—
pierced by the impulse of affection and generosity— was suddenly split in two.
He spoke to the bird with the light of his teeth spreading from the tips, as if covering it with a clean garment: "Let my beloved be taken."
"O Guru, without deliberation I shall give you whatever you desire;
truly, my heart, startled by the thought of separation from you, no longer takes account of the truth."
Having spoken thus, the king summoned his lotus-eyed beloved,
who was ever clung to his heart like a second manifestation of his own life-force.
Though restrained by his father with the fire of the calamity of separation, and though forbidden by his excessive affection, the kinsman of Love; || KAvk_2.50 ||
He suddenly gave her, who was like a doe with eyes trembling from exhaustion and terror as she wondered, "What is this?", to the disciple of the sage.
When his beloved was given away by the king with a nature inclined toward renunciation, the earth,
girdled by the restless oceans, trembled as if terrified of his generosity.
For whose sake even Indra, Candra, and the other gods endured an unbearable misfortune in their bodies— who would not hold those beloved women dear?
For the sake of women, some abandon their virtue, some their wealth, some their dharma, others their asceticism; some abandon their modesty, and some even their very bodies.
That which is the very essence of passion for men, the very life of their lives,
that same thing becomes like a mere blade of grass when given as a gift by those of noble character.
When he had departed taking her with him, the king,
distressed by separation and hating happiness because of that separation, became like the god of love himself.
Seeing the king’s beloved brought by his disciple—
deprived of life as if she had gone to the realm of the next world— the sage [was moved].
Tormented by deep-seated remorse and utterly shamed,
he reflected upon his own unseemly deed, which had arisen from the surging tide of his karma.
"Alas! Like a mere child, out of nothing but frivolity, I have myself fallen without hesitation into the mire of infamy."
This wife of the one who honors the castes and stages of life, the mother of progeny for those who perform their duties— she has been cast by me into the fire of suffering.
But I did not grasp moral conduct, nor did I remember self-restraint;
I did not even calculate dispassion, and I did not contemplate discernment.
Alas! Here, the minds of those devoid of discernment turn away from the true path;
intoxicated by the wine of lack of restraint, they run only along wrong paths.
Having reflected thus, that sage, his luster diminished by embarrassment,
approached the king’s beloved and spoke with a downcast face.
"Take heart, O mother; you ought not to grieve.
This affliction and this misconduct of mine have come about solely through the power of destiny."
Having abandoned the fatigue and heat beneath this tree on the bank,
you shall now go to your own abode along with us.
When the sage had spoken thus, the goddess, like one sprinkled by showers of nectar,
regained her vitality and resolve, and abandoned her fear and agitation.
Having heard this wonderful deed of the donor, which pervaded the three heavens,
Vāsava approached in order to test the king’s courage and compassion.
In a desolate forest, a man in the form of a Brahmin, whose lower half of the body had been devoured by a tiger,
was seized by four sons who were crying out in distress.
With profuse blood flowing and his circle of entrails hanging down,
his life-force departed amidst agonies as if he were firmly bound by his own sins.
He was closely pursued by flesh-eating beasts due to the scent of fresh raw meat,
like a man of wealth followed by calamities arising from greedy kings and thieves.
Having reached another city, he became the cause of wonder and amazement for the city-dwellers,
who were themselves afflicted by compassion, wretchedness, and sorrow.
Like sorrow personified, like unbearable terror,
he suddenly caused distress and agitation among the women of the city.
Then, while the king was seated in the hall for receiving petitioners,
he was placed before him by those four sons in the form of small stools set upon a bench.
Seeing him overwhelmed by the uneven afflictions of the onset of slaughter,
the people closed their eyes, with their faces contorted.
Raising his right arm, which had been released from his chest that was trembling with agitation,
he addressed the king with words faltering due to distress.
"Hail to you, O lord of the earth! I am a brahmin who has reached this state, like one burdened by grave sin at dawn; behold me, O treasury of compassion."
Devoured by a tiger in the dense forest of the terrible cycle of existence,
I live on only because this heavy suffering must inevitably be experienced.
Even in this heat of calamity,
my life-breaths— enduring intense suffering— do not abandon me, like virtuous friends who remain steadfast.
"If someone were to give you half of their own body after cutting it off,
then your life would be saved"— thus did the deity of the sky speak to me.
O treasury of compassion, who in this world gives life?
For generally, people seek their own happiness and are averse to the welfare of others.
I have come to you for refuge— you who are the giver of all at all times, the kinsman of the wretched and the distressed, and who never turns away even when asked for the gift of your own body.
You alone are born in this world as a tree of merit,
for whom the emergence of the fruit is the noble gift of sincere and respectful generosity.
What need is there for you to mention other virtues of yours, O generous one?
For in this world, the drum of your good deeds is struck solely by your giving.
Those like you, whose vows consist of pure conduct in rescuing those fallen into distress,
are obtained through the merchandise of merit during times of calamity.
Like gentle southern breezes, the virtuous— who are friends of abundant bliss and as cooling as yellow sandalwood— dispel the heat of suffering.
From this face of yours, which is as beautiful as the full moon,
speech that rains down nectar rises up, reviving all beings like moonlight.
Having been addressed thus by him, the king, his heart suddenly pierced by that same pain, spoke these agitated words to him who was fainting in a swoon: *Kāvyamālā 2.87*
"Take heart and cast off this external grief born of the loss of life;
O twice-born one, I shall give you half of my body without any hesitation."
For the fortunate one, the body undergoes injury for the sake of helping others;
indeed, this body, perishing in an instant, cannot be preserved even if it is guarded.
When the king had spoken thus, the high-minded great minister, his mind trembling as if struck by a thunderbolt, said:
"Alas! Through the habit of rashness, this lord has become addicted to exertion;
he no longer considers what is beneficial at all, due to the exhaustion of his subjects' merit."
Who else besides you, O virtuous one, is capable of the welfare of the subjects,
such that the servant is eloquent with devotion, while the king is both listener and doer?
The master, with eyes closed in the manner of an elephant, does not perform what is beneficial;
how many such riches of enjoyment can be counted for good servants?
The speech of those who speak with humility shines for a very long time in the ear of those by whom it has been made into a honey-cluster, strewn with the auspicious whorls of virtue.
This is a Rākṣasa and a Piśāca, assuming the deceptive form of a Brāhmaṇa;
he has become a seeker of the jewels that protect the worlds by means of [their] bodies.
Even if this great illusion were not created by him,
how could there be life for even a moment for one whose body has been cut to pieces?
Whatever good deed is performed with a wicked grasp, without due reflection,
results in self-inflicted pain in this life and brings no happiness in the next world.
One should always give only what is possible; how can that which is impossible be given?
Only the proclamation of giving away one's entire possessions, one's body, and so forth, is truly magnificent.
Today, this nectar for the ears has arrived from afar for those who have come seeking it; yet for other seekers present there, he is now a bestower of jewels of great value.
O King, you must protect the lives of your subjects with every effort— even at the cost of your own life— for you are a wish-fulfilling gem to those who seek their welfare.
Be gracious, have mercy on us, O Lord; do not commit such a rash act!
One does not sell oneself for the sake of a mere fragment of glass.
Having spoken thus, the preeminent minister fell at the feet of his lord;
yet the king did not rise from his resolve to offer his own body.
With the radiance of his teeth gleaming like a smile of affection, he spoke,
as if dispelling the darkness of delusion caused by attachment to life.
"O great minister, although this has been clearly stated by you with pure devotion,
I cannot endure the life-threatening danger facing this brahmin."
The internal torment born from the pain of being rejected by suppliants cannot be dispelled even by necklaces, snow, lotuses, lotus-stalks, the moon, or sandalwood paste.
O Sumati, you whose mind is entirely intent on removing the suffering and pain of all beings,
you ought not to create an obstacle for my awakening.
Even in another birth, when I gave away my body, no pain arose in me;
I remember that past event with a mind set on perfect enlightenment.
Long ago, seeing a tigress emaciated by hunger and intent on devouring her cubs,
I gave my own body, unhesitatingly, for their protection.
In my birth as Śibi, I gave a pair of eyes to a blind man, and I protected a pigeon from the fear of a hawk by means of my own body. (KAvk 2.109)
In the *Candraprabhāvatāra*, his head was offered to Raudrākṣa,
and in other births, all his possessions, sons, wives, and so forth were given away.
When this was said by the Bodhisattva, that preeminent minister of the king was neither alive nor as if lifeless, his senses overwhelmed with distress.
Then, by the king whose command was inviolable,
two men named Palagaṇḍa were appointed to the task of dismembering his body with a saw-edged blade.
Overwhelmed by intense grief and deluded by Śakra’s illusory power,
the two of them somehow prepared themselves for the severing of the lord of the earth’s body.
As half the body of the king, who remained free from agitation, was being split by the edge of a cruel saw,
the earth trembled.
With fallen meteors, crimson garments, and stars dropped by the destruction,
the sky wept aloud, its continuous stream of tear-drops being the scattered fragments of stars.
Unable to endure the intense suffering arising from the sight of that slaughter,
he quickly covered his face as the sun covers itself with a veil of dust.
While that protector of subjects had his body mangled by saws,
the people wailed, their cries filling the quarters of the sky with echoes.
Beholding the king’s unperturbed composure, Śakra, appearing in his double form,
his mind overcome by wonder and lingering regret, reflected for a long time:
Oh, how the mind of this one of great intelligence is tender with compassion,
yet has attained a hardness even greater than a diamond when it comes to the sufferings of others!
Deeper even than the ocean, loftier even than Mount Meru,
and more wondrous even than the third heaven— oh, how marvelous is the conduct of the great-souled!
Even when his life-breath departs, the essence of a being from the great ocean of beings does not diminish,
just as the greatness of a virtuous man is not lost even when calamity falls upon him.
While the thousand-eyed Indra was thus reflecting,
the lower half of the body of the lord of the earth was severed and fell swiftly to the ground.
Although his body was split in two, he remained filled with joy and vigor,
his life sustained by the resolve to protect all living beings.
Then, by his command, with half of his body joined together so that his form was complete,
the Brahmin rose from his injury and spoke to him.
"O King, you shine forth; this honor belongs to you who are free from passion.
Indeed, through the sincere gift of your body, your already great fame has become even more distinguished."
Alas, for the deluded Creator, who did nothing more than make [the world] equal to the purity of the jewel of your mind, what poverty of comparison! KAvk 2.126.
Cut down, yet well-rounded and straight, you are sweet-natured for the sake of others;
like a stalk of sugarcane, you endure unbearable pain while remaining lofty.
Having spoken thus, Śakra, in the form of a brahmin,
filled [the earth] with the nectar-dripping juices born from the *saṃjīvana* plants that arise at the moment of recollection.
Then, his form revealed out of satisfaction, Purandara praised the lord of the earth for having so perfectly joined together half of his own body.
Then a heap of white flowers fell from the sky,
appearing like the laughter of joy of the earth as it was suddenly uplifted at that moment.
In the meantime, the sage, having returned bringing his beloved wife Jayaprabhā,
was filled with wonder and related that entire account to them.
United with his pure wife, who was like his own stainless glory,
he— remaining unshaken even in the face of humiliation— spoke when questioned by Śakra.
Then, in Jambudvīpa, that lord of the earth sat upon a divine throne fashioned by Viśvakarman, strewn with a rain of jewels.
Having been consecrated by the Lord of the Gods, he propitiated him along with his beloved wife;
his subjects were pervaded by the merit arising from the power of his generosity.
Having fulfilled his vow to ferry all sentient beings across the ocean of saṃsāra,
he became joyful, his mind fully awakened to perfect enlightenment.

Seeing that the king’s mind was filled with friendliness and fresh compassion, perfected through his being a true being, pure, and manifesting the fruit of pacifying the suffering of those in distress by the sacrifice of himself, Śakra— his eyes washed by tears of joy and feeling ashamed—
departed for the city of the immortals, which was filled with the king's glory.
Thus, his majesty being worshipped by hosts of gods, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and lords of Nāgas, whose hair stood on end with joy, the Bodhisattva—
capable of protecting the earth and fashioning it so that it shone with the splendor of the celestial realm— attained [the state of] a world-protector.

In order to instruct the monks, the Blessed One, the Victor, spoke as follows, illustrating the excellence of giving through a discourse on a previous incarnation: pūrvāvatārasaṃvāde dānotkarṣam udāharan / upadeśāya bhikṣūṇām ity āha bhagavān jinaḥ // KAvk_2.138 //
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Legend of Śrīsena," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
3. The Legend of Maṇicūḍa.
In this wondrous creation, amidst the whirlpools of jewels produced from the ocean, some fortunate jewel among men is born who has manifested a noble rebirth.
There is a city named Sāketa, the very ornament of the earth’s fortune, white as camphor and filled with the radiance of the moon.
Where he dwelt with those worthy of service, who were embodiments of radiant goodness and possessed minds as pure as the Ganges—
like sacred fords inhabited by performers of meritorious deeds.
In that city, the inhabitants delight in the Nandana-like garden of their good deeds, which is in full bloom with fame and filled with the fragrance of merit.
There was a king there, known as Mehacūḍa, a great ocean of the jewels of abundant virtues and the enemy of the moon of his fame.
By him— who was worthy of being a constant refuge and who dispelled the age of strife—
the people were made to uphold the Dharma, as if by the Kṛta Yuga itself.
The lord of the earth, capable of forgiveness, endowed with prosperity, and devoted to compassion,
was beloved by his subjects— he who was renowned and had conquered his senses.
Initiated into the sacrifice of non-violence, he bestowed upon all living beings the holy gift of fearlessness, which was filled with the nectar of immortality.
He who was free from pride despite his power and wealth, who spoke kindly,
who was characterized by forgiveness even in his lordship, and who had conquered his senses even in his youth.
By that mountain-king, who was profound yet lofty, heroic, moon-like in luster, and possessed of noble wings,
wonder was spread abroad.
That king, who was without equal, possessed two ornaments:
a compassion full of self-sacrifice, and the youthfulness of the splendor of his meritorious deeds.
Padmākara had a beloved queen named Kāntimatī, who,
like the splendor of dawn, was always free from blemish and a festival of rising glory.
Like prosperity shining through the virtue of a master,
or like beauty through good character, that policy shone brightly through the moon among kings by means of his renunciation.
With her, whose widespread fame was celebrated as "Ever-Blissful," that best of kings shone like Mount Meru with the splendor of the triple heaven.
In due time, she conceived a fetus that was the abode of auspiciousness for her husband,
just as Aditi bore the sun for the prosperity of the world-lotus.
She shone like the fire-drill with the sacred fire, like the shore with the ocean, like the moon with its nectar,
and like the navel of Govinda with the lotus-born Brahmā within its womb.
Due to the power of her pregnancy,
the king bestowed upon all the multitudes of supplicants wealth exceeding their desires, according to whatever they wished for.
When questioned again by the king regarding her pregnancy-longing,
that auspiciously pregnant woman herself delivered a discourse on the True Dharma, like the goddess Sarasvatī.
A treasure-trove of Dharma, containing jewels of perfect merit and extracted by ritual means,
it always protects those who are protected from vast misfortunes and sufferings.
For those who have fallen into the perils of the wilderness and are afflicted by suffering on the path to the next world,
there is no other like the Dharma— a tree of shade that is affectionate, ever-growing, and fulfilling all hopes with its fruit.

Light in darkness, an incomparable jewel in calamity, a supporting hand when falling, a wish-fulfilling tree for those who beg, a chariot for victory over the world, provisions on the path of wandering,
a great medicine for the disease of suffering, and a consolation for minds bewildered by the fear of existence— [this is the Dharma].
In the heat, a grove of sandalwood trees is a steadfast friend; for the virtuous, righteousness is their kinsman.
Having heard these and other words of the queen, which were pure with righteousness,
the illustrious people in the world became solely devoted to the Dharma as their refuge.
Then, in due time, the queen gave birth to a son who was like the sky giving birth to the moon, the dispeller of the world's darkness.
A gem was born with him as an ornament for his topknot,
adhering from a previous life like stainless discernment.
That auspicious jewel, composed of merit, shone upon his head;
by the power of its radiance, the nights became like days.
The drops of nectar flowing from that crest-jewel cause base metal to turn into gold and pacify all misfortune.
Then, at the word of that infant who remembered his former births,
the king gave all the gold produced from the jewel-mine to the supplicants along with his wife.
At his birth, the deities filled the sky and the city with flowers, jewels, banners, parasols, flags, fans, and silken garments.
The king bestowed upon him the name Maṇicūḍa, for his soul was illuminated by all branches of knowledge that had arisen with perfect clarity.
That noble son, born like the *pārijāta* tree from the ocean, stirred his father’s heart with an overflowing nectar of joy.
Like Paulomī with Jayanta,
or Pārvatī with Kumāra, his mother shone because of that son of noble birth.
Then, in the course of time, when the lord of the earth had ascended to the celestial abode by means of the stairs of his well-performed deeds, Maṇicūḍa became king.
When the world had been completely filled by the gift of that wish-fulfilling gem of his,
there was neither one who suffered nor any beggar, as it shone with the light of merit and happiness.
He had an excellent elephant named Bhadragiri,
whose trunk-tips were moist with the flow of ichor, as if imitating his master.
Once, while he was staying in that great abode as the leader of the world,
the sage Bhavabhūti, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, approached him.
Taking hold of a divine maiden whose face was charming with loveliness,
she was like the personified splendor and fortune of the inexhaustible lord of the night.
She was exceedingly ashamed in this world, as if due to the lack of restraint of her breasts, the passion for her lotus-feet, and the fickleness of her eyes.
The lord of subjects honored that sage, who was accompanied by his daughter and possessed the splendor of asceticism,
once he had accepted a seat.
The maiden also, beholding the king— steadfast, profound, and beautiful, who,
out of compassion for the suffering of others, seemed like the God of Love (Smara) having laid aside his bow— KAvk_3.39.
With the rays of his crest-jewel, which cause the destruction of misfortune,
he seemed to write, as if with saffron, a protective string of syllables across the quarters of the sky.
It was adorned with a chowrie whose wind was scattered by its tossing,
as if it were a living being breathing out, though devoid of the means to ferry the world across [to liberation].
He was adorned with a magnificent jewel necklace that captivated the heart,
as if it were the very offspring of Śeṣa for the purpose of pacifying the calamities of the netherworld.
Carrying the earth with his great arm and patience with his mind,
he fell under the sway of a longing wonder.
Taking that life-giver of the bodiless god (Kāma), whose eyes were as tremulous as a young deer's, onto his lap, the sage spoke to the lord of the earth.
With you risen, who causes the lotuses that are the eyes of the world to bloom,
this world shines like it does with the divine Vivasvat.
"Alas! Does not this pride of yours, accumulated through delusion, arise from the abundance of your power—like a hatred of virtues found in a virtuous man?"
O King, for you, the protector of the world whose mind is filled with compassion for the world and who delights in loving-kindness,
fame is enduring and the supreme perfection.
You are a donor who is tireless and straightforward, performing virtuous deeds without artifice;
for this very reason, you are especially worthy of honor by the wise.
This lotus-eyed maiden was born from the heart of a lotus;
she was reared by me in my hermitage with the water remaining after the fire oblations.
"O King, O Supreme Person, let this woman be accepted by you as your chief queen; she is as worthy of you as Śrī is of Viṣṇu. (KAvk 3.50)
"You shall give me the full fruit of the merit of this sacrifice in due time";
having spoken thus and bestowed the maiden upon the king according to the prescribed rites, the sage departed.
Like the god of love having attained Rati, the king took delight with his beloved Padmāvatī in the beautiful garden,
like a meritorious person in a well-constructed pleasure grove.
Then, in the course of time, she gave birth to a son named Padmacūḍa, who was like a pearl upon the creeper of his lineage and a mirror reflecting the virtues of his father.
His great prosperity was unassailable even by Śakra and the other world-protectors,
and his deeds were praised by the Lotus-born One himself.
He filled the quarters of space with the abundance of the fragrance of his fame;
he was a wish-fulfilling tree for the auspicious attainment of all the needs of the multitude of seekers.
Remembering the words of the Sage at the proper time, the lord of the earth brought forth a great sacrificial gift,
fully endowed with the wealth of non-violence.
At that sacrifice, where all desires were unimpeded,
sages headed by Bhārgava and kings such as Duṣprasaha gathered together.
While that sacrifice, which was showering down countless riches,
was proceeding, the Lord of the Gods arose from the midst of the fire in the form of a Rākṣasa.
Approaching the king, emaciated and with a deformed body,
he begged for food and drink, saying, "I am afflicted by hunger and thirst."
Then, at the command of the king, his familiar attendants brought him various kinds of food and drink.
Then, laughing slightly, the Rākṣasa said to the king:
"O King, this is not pleasing to us, for we are eaters of flesh."
"Great satisfaction arises for us from the flesh and abundant blood of one recently slain;
let that which you desire be given."
"Since you are the granter of all desires, I have come to you;
having promised 'I shall give,' it is not fitting for you to refuse."
Having heard these words of the guardian, the king was overcome with compassion;
though bound by his vow of non-violence, he became distressed by the refusal of his supplicants.
Then he thought: "By fate, this doubt regarding dharma has arisen;
for I cannot endure this unbearable violence, nor the fruitlessness of one who seeks [merit]."
And flesh cannot be obtained from bodies without slaughter;
I would not endure even a fraction of the suffering of a body for the sake of a single ant.
"Having bestowed upon all beings the meritorious gift of fearlessness, how can I give him flesh produced by the slaughter of living creatures? (KAvk 3.67)
Having reflected thus, the king, overwhelmed with compassion, said to him:
"I give you my own flesh and blood, cut from my own body."
When the lord of the earth had spoken thus, the world became agitated;
yet his ministers could not endure his resolve to sacrifice his body.
Although he was being restrained by kings and likewise by sages out of affection,
he cut his own body and gave him flesh, blood, and fat.
O Lord of the Earth, as the flesh of the king was being devoured by a rakshasa whose blood reached up to his throat, the earth trembled for a moment.
Then Queen Padmāvatī, seeing her husband in such a state,
fell down lamenting and became overwhelmed by a swoon of delusion.
Seeing that powerful courage of the lord of men, the lord of gods abandoned his form as a rākṣasa and spoke to him with palms joined in reverence: KAvk_3.73.
"O King, by this difficult deed of yours, whose body would not become covered with the armor of bristling hair? (KAvk 3.74)
Oh, how extraordinary is your merit! Oh, how supreme is your courage!
Oh, how boundless is the endurance of you, O King, who are free from passion!
They feel sorrow at the sorrows of others, are free from greed for things difficult to obtain,
are patient toward their adversaries, and are virtuous people who serve as bridges of merit.
A certain surge of vigor in beings arises within these great-souled ones,
by which the three worlds, moistened with compassion, become objects of their pity.
Having spoken thus, and having restored his body to health with divine herbs,
Śakra, bowing in shame, propitiated him and departed for his own abode.
Then, when the sacrifice had been completed according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the earth,
who is honored by the gods, performed worship for the kings and the best of sages.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, having bestowed villages, maidens, and cities along with a rain of jewels,
he was joined by Hari, who was worthy of the gods and adorned with a golden garland.
He gave the royal elephant named Brahmaratha to his domestic priest,
which could travel a hundred yojanas swiftly in a single day.
Seeing that the elephant Bṛhadgiri had been surrendered to him by the king,
King Duṣprasaha’s mind was drawn toward it by his longing for it.
Then, while the kings were departing in wonder at the splendor of the sacrifice,
the fruit of the sacrifice was offered by the monarch to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having approached him, preceded by words of greeting,
the Vāhīka, a pupil of Marīci, who had received honor and a seat from the sage, spoke to him.
"O King, at the conclusion of my studies, my teacher,
seeking service, desires a preceptor’s fee that is difficult for ordinary people to obtain."
You alone have been created by Fate as the bestower of what is difficult to obtain;
for indeed, many wish-fulfilling trees are never born in this world.
"Let Queen Padmāvatī, together with her son, be given as an attendant to my guru,
who is aged and emaciated by asceticism."
When the sage had spoken thus, the king, a mountain of fortitude, steadied his mind against the pain born of separation from his beloved and replied to him:
"O Sage, I bestow upon you this desired teacher’s fee:
my beloved wife, who is dearer to me than life itself, together with a young lover."
Having said this, the king gave Padmāvatī along with her son to him;
for those whose souls consist of courage, renunciation is more dear than their own lives.
Taking the king’s beloved wife, who was distressed by the suffering of separation,
along with her son, the sage went to his hermitage and presented them to his preceptor.
In the meantime, the arrogant Duṣprasaha, king of the Kurus,
requested through a messenger the elephant Bhadragiri from the lord of the earth for his own prosperity.
When the king did not give up the elephant that had been offered by the domestic priest,
he then came forward himself to fight with great ferocity.
When the city gates were blocked by the powerful King of the Kurus,
the army of the protector of the earth became fierce with the passion for battle.
Although that lion among heroic elephants was capable of tearing his enemies asunder, he,
agitated by fear for the destruction of living beings, reflected out of compassion:
"Alas! My supreme ally, King Duṣprasaha, has suddenly become my enemy through his greed for and delusion regarding Mātaṅga."
Affections end in affection with good people; with those of middling character, they end in a lack of affection;
but with wicked people, they end in terrible enmity and become life-destroying.
Alas! While life perishes in an instant, we—who possess such great power—make this effort solely for the purpose of destroying the lives of others.
This effort for the sake of food belongs to those who are unpeaceful due to violence, who are attached to the activities of the Kali age,
and who are consecrated by their passion for battle.
For those who sell their lives through service and seek the morsels of food from the fierce,
this quarrel of cruel and malicious people is as unbearable as that of dogs.
Alas! The minds of those greedy for wealth, characterized by cruel conduct, rush toward their own pleasure alone, cooled only by the suffering of others.
For those who, prepared for victory in battle, enjoy sovereignty with its borders stained red—
how could there be even a single drop of compassion in their hearts, which are more cruel than the cruel?
"This king is difficult to subdue, greedy, and greatly deluded; though he has committed an offense, he must not be slain, for he is an object of my compassion. (KAvk 3.103)
As he was thinking thus, out of compassion for him who sought the forest,
four Pratyekabuddhas arrived of their own accord through the sky.
Having heard that desire of King Praśamaśīla, the omniscient ones, who were seated upon their thrones after having been worshipped, were pleased and spoke the truth.
O protector of the earth, your compassion for those wandering in saṃsāra, blinded by the veil of delusion,
is truly fitting for one who discerns the world of sentient beings.
O King, let that which you desire be done; let your mind be fixed upon awakening.
Now, while this obstruction remains, one must simply plunge into the forest.
The secluded forest regions, which are strewn with the spray of contentment arising from the spontaneous realization of the self, are dear only to those who have attained tranquility.
Having spoken thus and, with a mind intent on bestowing grace, having granted him passage through the sky,
they departed together with him, illuminating the quarters with their radiance.
When they had departed for their own abodes, the protector of the earth, having reached the forest on the slopes of the Himalayas,
became disciplined and tranquil.
The forest lands, filled with the bliss of liberation, shone as if they were dear to his intellect, which was pure through discernment like that of the virtuous.
When that sun-like king had suddenly been hidden by the mountain,
the subjects, having fallen into the darkness of delusion, lamented in their grief.
Then his ministers went to the sage Marīci in his hermitage and requested the prince,
who was capable of protecting the kingdom.
Having received what was given by the Sage, who is free from change,
the ministers made preparations with their armies and established the prince in his own city.
Having received from the Sage that which was singularly free from change, the minister,
leading the foremost of brave warriors, reached the King of the Kurus on the field of battle.
With his chariot, elephants, and horses struck down, destroyed, and broken by him,
he fled toward Hastināpura to seek protection from pursuit.
When Duṣprasaha had been defeated in battle by the powerful prince,
the earth, resting upon his arms, regained its remaining stability through the ministers.
Then, in the course of time, in the city of King Duṣprasaha, who was of a corrupt soul,
there occurred drought, famine, pestilence, and violent conflict.
Reflecting thus, afflicted by remorse at the severe calamity that had befallen the country,
he found no protection, his rites for auspiciousness having become fruitless.
When asked for a remedy against this calamity, his ministers said to him:
"O Great King, this arising of misfortune among the subjects is difficult to endure."
O Lord, if the crest-jewel of King Maṇicūḍa,
which distills nectar, can be obtained, then this calamity will be overcome by it.
"We have heard from our spies that the king is staying on the slopes of the Himalayas,
his mind pure through discernment and turned away from the cycle of existence."
When entreated, that wish-fulfilling jewel of the universe surely grants its gem;
there is nothing—not even son, wife, or body—that it will not give away.
Having heard these words of the minister and having resolved "so be it" in his heart,
he dispatched the brahmins to his presence in order to beg for the jewel.
At this juncture, King Maṇicūṣa, wandering in the forest,
reached the extensive hermitage precinct of the sage Marīci.
There, Queen Padmāvatī, observing a vow of subsisting on fruits and roots,
was traveling through the lonely forest in fear, in accordance with the sage’s command.
Seeing her fallen into such a miserable state, some Śabaras who had come out hunting,
desiring to seize her as she trembled, cried out in a piteous voice.
Having heard that most unbearable cry of compassion, "Alas, King Maṇicūḍa! Save me! which resembled the wailing of ospreys, KAvk_3.128.
Suddenly overtaken by fear, the king beheld his own beloved wife,
like the splendor of the moon fallen when terrified by Rāhu.
Clad in the garments of dispassion and embracing the stainless state,
she seemed to proclaim the impermanence of all enjoyments and unions.
Beholding that Sugata, who was like a royal swan, whose breast was the circle of her vihāra,
whose eyes were reddened by tears and saffron, and who was full of compassion;
Even when reflecting upon the wonders of the conduct of worldly existence,
the king’s mind was as if severed by the sword of compassion, though it had been previously hardened.
Seeing the Lord of the World, the Tathāgata, alone in the forest, deprived of his parasol and fly-whisk, the goddess felt as if she were herself without a protector.
Overcome by the poison of separation from him, agitated by the flavor of the sight of him,
and filled with both grief and joy, she became utterly distraught.
Once she had been led away by the king, the Śabaras fled in all directions, terrified of the curse;
for darkness, even when accompanied by lightning, is never seen at the rising of the sun.
In the meantime, Māra, who harbors hatred toward tranquility and dwells within the hearts of all beings, approached the king in human form and spoke to him.
O King, you ought not to abandon this beloved and devoted wife of yours, whose eyes are like lotuses,
in the desolate forest, O lotus-eyed one!
For this [city] of yours, O King of Kings, having become devoid of happiness like a mental state that has lost its joy,
does not shine, being deprived of royal enjoyment.
Having heard this and recognizing him to be the god of love— an obstacle to his discernment— the king replied with a smile:
I know you, O Desire, who are desireless toward tranquility and self-restraint;
for who indeed has not been deluded by you, the one possessed of such contentment?
When the king had thus spoken and suddenly vanished like the god of love,
the queen became distraught, tormented by the fire of separation.
The king, who had conquered the god of love, spoke to his wife— who was suffering, afflicted by grief, and deprived of her husband's company— consoling her.
O Queen, being devoted to the practice of dharma, you ought not to grieve;
this entire delusion of worldly enjoyment is bitter and ends in sorrow.
For embodied beings whose lives are as flickering as waves,
these [days] are filled with water droplets slipping from the tips of trembling lotus petals.
These female dancers of a moment, like streaks of lightning from the clouds of time,
are the tongues of the serpent of saṃsāra— fortunes as fickle as a playful flirtation.
The disease of separation occurs at the very moment of enjoyment; worldly prosperities are like a wedding in a dream;
the splendor of happiness is like the flame of a lamp struck by the wind; and the conduct of existence is like the dancing of a madman—such is the nature of saṃsāra.
Compassion is that upon which all depend, not wealth; Dharma is ever-luminous, not lamps;
fame is truly delightful, not youth; and merits are enduring, not lives.
Having thus consoled his wife and dismissed her to the dwelling of the great seer, Satyavrata wandered through the penance groves,
which were holy with contentment and turned away from the cycle of worldly existence.
Then those five brahmins, dispatched with haste by King Duṣprasaha,
beheld in the edge of the forest that being of pure essence, who was a friend to the needy and a kinsman at an unseasonable time.
Having offered a benediction slowly, as if their fortitude had been pierced by trepidation,
they addressed him with a breath of long, hot sighs that revealed the intensity of their ascetic heat.
O King, in the city of King Duṣprasaha, the people were deprived of their peaceful community by cruel calamities;
with all their desires cut short, they were reduced to nothing but the sound of intense lamentation.

O King, this crest-jewel bestowed by Your Majesty— the sole cause for pacifying the affliction of drought and whose power is renowned for protecting the three worlds— brings about the cessation of its calamity.

Those like you alone become the refuge for people in this world during times of distress— possessing a life of compassion, moist with the sprouts of sandalwood, pure in intention, and radiant as moonstones.
Thus entreated by them, his courage undiminished and his heart being filled with the essence of compassion,
he reflected and spoke, as if the distress of the people had entered within him through the path of his ears.
Aha! How indeed can that king endure the cries of distress arising from the suffering of separation, which rend the hearts of his subjects who are oppressed by the calamity of the gods?
"Let this jewel, born from the base of my head, be quickly cut off and accepted by me;
I shall be blessed if I can become a cause, even for a moment, for the destruction of the suffering of those who seek my help."
As soon as these words were spoken by the lord of the earth, the earth— with its mountains, oceans, and great mountain ranges—
trembled for a long time, as if terrified by the intense agony of having its very summit torn away.
Then, by the king’s words— which were like extremely sharp weapons to one whose mental disposition was tender with compassion— he,
whose mind was sharper even than a sharp weapon, proceeded to cut off his own head.

That was a difficult task for the lord of men; for the gods, led by Brahmā (Nalināsana), along with the Vidyādharas and those known as Siddhas, arrived in celestial chariots in the sky to behold him whose courage was undiminished.
While his head was being forcibly split open, he— his body drenched by streams of blood that produced the shimmering illusion of jewels—
endured the agony, being intent upon the happiness of the supplicant.
Beholding that being who maintained his fortitude despite the closing of his eyes from the force of intense agony,
the brahmins— who had attained the state of Rākṣasas— did not cease their cruel conduct for even a moment.

Reflecting upon the suffering of his father-in-law’s body— the body of worldly beings consisting of affliction and overwhelmed by hundreds of thousands of such miseries— the king became even more deeply distressed.
He reflected: "Whatever fruit of merit I have obtained by giving jewels bound to my body, may that [merit] ward off the intense suffering of men in hell when their demerit ripens."
When that jewel was extracted and sprinkled with blood, it became fixed at the root of his palate;
though he was bewildered by fainting, he felt joy because of the fulfillment of the supplicant’s desire.

Having given the jewel with his own hand, its sprout-like fingers trembling, he fell— closing the world in total darkness like the intensely red sun— just as the sun sets when it has bestowed its light upon the twice-born.
When he, whose vitality was unimpaired, had fallen upon the earth, those twice-born ones took the jewel along with showers of flowers from the gods and quickly went to the city of King Duṣprasaha.
Having been freed from calamities by him and having attained a multitude of enjoyments worthy of heaven,
he praised that bodhisattva’s courage, which was fit for delivering all sentient beings.
In the meantime, while the lord of men had regained some consciousness,
the sages headed by Marīci, such as Bhārgava and Gautama, arrived from the forests, having heard of his gift of jewels.
And Queen Padmāvatī, following after Marīci, seeing him wounded,
was struck by a surge of fainting and fell for a moment to the ground like a young creeper that has been cut down.
Then, amidst the praise of the king that spread to the ends of the earth from the celestial bards moving through the sky,
the subjects, together with the princes and the chief ministers, approached the lord of the people.
Beholding the lord of the earth fallen upon the ground, his limbs drenched in blood yet his courage undiminished,
and suffering the affliction of great pain, there arose among the people a chatter of false imaginings regarding what had not occurred.

Alas! This tree of shade—compassionate, worthy of service by all seekers, straightforward, and of virtuous conduct—has been cut down by certain wicked-souled men, intent on their own meager self-interest; what a tragedy! (KAvk 3.172)
Aha! This mango tree, having renounced its life for the sake of others, has reached a state of supreme wonder;
though its body is severed yet remains fragrant, it becomes noble even when its soul has departed.
For a greedy creature, even his own kin are not his own; for one who pursues desire, there is no regard for wealth.
But for the compassionate one who strives for the welfare of beings with all his soul, even his body is not an object of attachment.
Those for whose sake the multitude of supplicants undergoes a state of wretchedness with their whole being, becoming beggars themselves—
those very people are but as straw to those who have taken the vow of uplifting the miserable, when their lives are staked upon the act of protection.

While such various exclamations were thus resounding from the circle of sages, the sage Marīci, his eyes filled with tears, approached the king and spoke out of affection: *iti pravāde vividhānubhāve vijṛmbhamāṇe munimaṇḍalasya / bhūpālamabhyetya sabāṣpacakṣurmunirmarīciḥ praṇayāduvāca //* KAvk_3.176 //
"O King, having adopted the state of a friend without cause, out of compassion for the people, this body of yours—
the very ground for providing protection to your subjects— has been surrendered by you as if it were a blade of grass."
A destruction has begun for you, who act without regard even for your own life, O friend of the needy;
for this body, which is a mass of lotuses, has been employed by you in a place of ruin according to your desire.
O King, is there even the slightest desire for reward in this vow of virtuous conduct, even at the risk of one’s life?
For the sake of this petitioner, your mind does not undergo any change, despite the pain of splitting open your own flesh.
Thus questioned by the sage among sages with a mind manifesting wonder, he,
having steadied his pain with effort and wiped his blood-smeared face, spoke.
O Sage, I have no other desire for fruit; rather, I have but one great longing:
that in birth after birth, I may exist solely for the sake of ferrying across those beings who are submerged in the terrible cycle of existence.
"In this tearing apart of my body for the sake of my benefactor's pleasure, there is not even a trace of agitation in me.
If this vow I have spoken is true, then let this body of mine become whole again."
As soon as these words were spoken regarding the innate power appropriate for a being of such virtue by King Satyadhana,
his body— by the force of truth— had its wounds healed and was instantly covered with jewels.
Then, although entreated by the gods led by Śakra and Viriñci, and by all the sages filled with great joy,
the king did not become desirous of enjoyments for the sake of protecting the earth.
Having regained her consciousness through the sage’s words, Padmāvatī went together with the prince to her husband for the sake of ending their separation,
[just as] the happiness of subjects comes from the occupation of the lion throne.

Then, having approached him, those Pratyekabuddhas, filled with compassion for the welfare of the world and filling the quarters of the sky with the radiance of their bodies, spoke as if pouring forth joy.

The prince does not endure the unbearable state of being abandoned again after the long-awaited end of their separation; nor does the queen, for a continuous succession of sorrows is indeed a calamity that has no remedy.

How could he who gives his own body to one who asks for it—the sole cause for pacifying the suffering of those in distress—how could he show indifference even toward his own kin? For this is the very nature of Dharma, whose purpose is solely the welfare of others.

Having heard what was thus said, the lord of men, having somehow resolved with his intellect that "so be it," reached his own city by means of celestial chariots through the sky and, together with his sons, took possession of his royal station.
Thus that Bodhisattva Satyavān, a being of vast virtue who had long governed his kingdom, attained the state of a Sugata;
having manifested manifold splendors through the jewel-studded caityas, parasols, and precious lamps of the Victor’s city, he realized enlightenment through the cultivation of the primary marks.
Thus spoke the Blessed Buddha, illustrating his own life story as an instruction on giving to the monks for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Avadāna of Maṇicūḍa," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
4. The Legend of Māndhātṛ:
The riches of those with noble minds shine throughout the worlds, smiling with the white parasols and the gracefully raised, beautiful chowries that serve as the handmaidens of the celestial realms;
and their fame, which satisfies the ears as it rises upward, is radiant like a mass of camphor.
Oh, how great is the fruit of even a tiny grain of that gift; indeed, generosity is the primary cause of prosperity!
There was a king named Upoṣadha,
by whose splendor fame, cherished by the gods, arose like nectar from the ocean of milk.
Before that lord of the earth, who possessed the entire earth, whose name did not cause the heads of kings to bow when they prostrated themselves? (KAvk 4.3)
By him the earth was adorned, just as pure intelligence is by righteousness, compassion by generosity,
and prosperity by humility.
The abode of the moon-like splendor, possessing virtues and a lofty lineage,
stood at the summit of all monarchs, with every other royal umbrella beneath him.
He whose auspicious fame, radiant as the waters of the Gaṅgā, rests upon the head of the Lord,
wanders extensively through the worlds as an ornament for the universe.
He who performed thousands upon thousands of sacrifices and whose splendor surpassed that of the thousand-eyed Indra,
had sixty thousand wives of beautiful appearance.
Once, for the sake of protecting the sages and finding an opportunity to destroy the rākṣasas,
he mounted his horse and roamed through the lands of asceticism.
There, some royal sages were carrying a jar for a son-securing sacrifice;
scorched by the fatigue of the long journey, he drank from it as it was filled with water.
Having drunk the milk from the mantra-empowered jar in a secluded place,
that lord of the earth reached the capital and conceived a child.
Victorious is that destiny, the ground of a multitude of wonders, for whom dreams, illusions, magic tricks, and the like are but mere trifles.
Who is capable of delimiting the arrangement of the wondrous lines of Fate, which performs the variegated work of manifold diversity?
In time, having burst through his head like the sun breaking through a cloud,
he suddenly emerged with divine radiance once his wound had healed.
The king’s wives took him, who bore the marks of universal sovereignty over the world,
as if he were an embodiment of merit that had taken refuge there, their breasts flowing with milk out of maternal affection.
"This praiseworthy infant will sustain me in the place of a mother"—
by such words spoken among themselves, the prince became known as Māndhātṛ.
As he grew up, indulging in the sports of childhood,
six Indras passed away during the time of his meritorious play until his lifespan was exhausted.
Having reached the prime of youth and mastered all branches of knowledge, he,
upon his father’s departure to heaven, assumed the kingdom that had descended to him by succession.
A yakṣa named Divaukas, who had become a servant of Sukṛti,
brought him divine materials for the consecration.
With his crown bound with gold and his turban-crest fashioned,
he attained the splendor of Mount Meru adorned with abundant garlands.
Then, at that very moment, the seven jewels appeared for him:
the wheel, the horse, the gem, the elephant, the queen, the householder, and the general.
And he had a thousand sons, equal in form, strength, and vigor,
like the thousand arms of a king who has conquered his enemies.
He placed the entire earth, whose girdle is the shore of the ocean, upon his arm,
making it rest peacefully upon Śeṣa.
Devoted to the protection of the world and the abode of ever-fresh lotuses,
that universal emperor shone like the hand of Viṣṇu, the performer of good deeds.
His fame is the Gaṅgā of the three worlds, his fortunes are adorned with majesty;
he is the first blossoming of the creeper of well-performed deeds.
Once, he wandered gracefully through the forest edges with his ministers, beholding the beauty of the blossoming flowers.
There he saw wingless birds moving on foot,
appearing as if they had grown emaciated after remembering their former course through the path of the sky.
Seeing them like the poor—deprived of wings, without refuge, their livelihood exhausted, and naked—the king spoke out of compassion: KAvk_4.27.
"Alas! What evil deed have these wretched birds committed, that they are deprived of wings and move with such difficulty?"
When the lord of the earth had spoken thus, his soul overwhelmed with compassion, the great minister Satyasena, standing before him, said to him: KAvk_4.29.
"O Lord, I have heard this being told by the forest-dwellers regarding the cause that led to the falling of the wings of the birds here."
In this penance grove, a sanctuary of merit, there dwell five hundred sages of radiant splendor,
devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas.
"These birds have always caused a great disturbance in the forest of trees, creating obstacles for their study, meditation, and recitation. KAvk_4.32.
The circle of sages grew exceedingly enraged at that flock of birds, which was causing the extreme impairment of their hearing.
In an instant, by the nourishment of the heat of that great curse which had become manifest, the wings of the birds who had committed offenses were shattered on all sides.
These birds, deprived of their wings and wandering in distress,
move with weary steps through the forest like your enemies.
Having heard this from the great minister, the lord of the earth,
overcome with compassion and tormented by the curse of the birds, spoke.
Oh, how the splendor of even those who are peaceful has matured in the forest!
The embers and the sages alike burn without restraint.
Of what use are those false ascetics who, for their own pleasure,
have not performed the sprinkling of water— namely forgiveness— upon their minds scorched by anger?
For those whose intellect is serene, whose minds are friendly, and who possess compassion, generosity, self-control, and patience—their austerity is praiseworthy;
for others, it is merely the emaciation of the body.

What is the use of austerities for those filled with anger? What is the use of the forest for those who have abandoned their vows? What is the use of wealth for those possessed by greed? And what is the use of sacred learning for those of wicked conduct?
Thus, with their minds turbid and devoted to intense anger,
let those sages, who are indeed difficult to endure, depart from my domain.
Having spoken thus, the king dispatched a message to them by means of messengers, saying:
"Let as much land as is under my dominion be abandoned."
Having heard the message of the king, who was enraged by the bird's partiality,
the sages were embarrassed and reflected deeply.
"This lord of men is the master of the earth, which has the four oceans as its moat and girdle;
where shall we go? What land is there that is not under his command?"
Having reflected thus, O sages, they went to the side of the Golden Mountain,
which was crowded with gods and siddhas and situated near the region of Jambūdvīpa.
Then, by the immense power of that lord of the earth,
the earth became one where crops were never seen, yet which yielded jewels and garments.
By his command,
which caused even Indra, the subduer of Pāka, to feel abashed, the clouds rained down gold for seven days with a continuous downpour.
Moving through the sky with his great power and his armies,
he brought under his control the continent named Pūrvavideha, inhabited by divine beings.
At the outset, eighteen crores of warriors, possessing abundant heroism, strength, and vigor, became capable of traveling through the sky.
Then he, whose command was unassailable, ruled over the continent of Godānīya,
as well as Uttarakuru and the slopes of Mount Sumeru.
As he dwelt happily on the golden peaks of Mount Meru,
much time passed for that lord of the four continents, who was like Śakra himself.
Once, while traveling through the sky to see the gods,
he who resembled a god made the quarters of the sky appear as if covered by dark clouds, like by elephants.
Then, as those sages were performing austerities on the side of Mount Meru after having been expelled,
the dung of elephants and horses fell from the sky upon their heads.
Then, looking toward the sky with eyes inflamed by anger,
they made the directions tawny, like a mass of flickering flames of reddish-brown light.
Saying "What is this? out of anger, as he was about to discharge the fire of a curse, the divine messenger approached them and spoke, agitated with great joy.
This is King Māndhātṛ, whose commands rest upon the crowns of all sovereigns without exception,
and whose glory is equal to that of Indra, the subduer of Pāka.
"O Queen, this man is advancing through the sky with his armies—he whose speech, which takes pride in its own merit, is blessed by the chanting of his praises. (KAvk 4.57)
In him, for whom all the splendors of worldly happiness had been revealed,
neither delusion was seen, nor the pride born of power, as if he were composed of pure consciousness.
He is Kaubera by virtue of his manifestation as the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), Kaumāra through his possession of power (Śakti),
Aiśvara due to his union with the Bull (Vṛṣa), and Vaiṣṇava because of his association with Śrī.
Through the expansion of his majesty he bears the splendor of the sun; through his delighting of the people, that of the moon;
through the crushing of the arrogant forces, that of Indra; and thus he possesses a divine form.
Bali departed for the netherworld and Dadhīca was reduced to nothing but bones;
yet even today, the ocean does not cease its agitation because of his sacrifice.
Having heard these words of the divine messenger,
the sage named Durmukha, standing in the midst of the other sages, released a stream of curse-water toward the sky.
Then, laughing, the leader of the armies said to him:
"O great seer, restrain your anger; do not bring about the destruction of your ascetic merit."
"Furthermore, O King, this curse shall go before the monarch, bringing shame for its fruitlessness:
'Alas, these are not birds, against whom you were capable of destroying their wings!'"
When the husband of Śauntī had spoken thus, the king, seeing his army paralyzed by the curse before him, said in astonishment: "What is this? (KAvk 4.65)
Then, approaching him in a state of agitation, the commander-in-chief said to him:
"O King, because of the curse of those great seers, the army does not advance."
And this wheel-treasure of yours, reeling in the sky due to the curse,
bears a resemblance to the sun whose sharp rays are obstructed by clouds.
Having heard this, and seeing it exactly as described before him, the king instantly rendered the curse—
along with its fierce and futile fury— ineffectual by his mere glance.
Protecting the bodies of the great seers and filled with compassion,
