he whose commands are effortless in play cast his matted locks upon the ground.
"Since we have become a mere burden for those whose anger and delusion remain unsubdued, our lives are in vain"—
as if out of such shame, their matted locks sank down upon the surface of the earth.
Then, having reached the summit of Meru, the abode of the gods,
the king beheld the city named Sudarśana, which was pleasant to behold.
There, the Nāgas provide protection;
the Yakṣas known as Karoṭapāṇis have emerged from the famous waters, and there are the gods called Mālādharas.
Likewise, the Sadāmatta gods, whose soldiers are emboldened by their wrath,
known as the Mahārājakāyikas, are the most powerful among the thirty [gods].
And the four great kings, clad in armor and bearing weapons,
having been conquered by the power of the king, were made the leaders of his own army.
Then he beheld the tree known as Pārijāta, which was as magnificent as a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), exceedingly beautiful with its blossoms, and the refuge of the inhabitants of heaven.
Then, upon the summit of Mount Meru, he reached the assembly hall named Sudharmā, which was like a pure, bright garland, illuminating the sky with its own radiance.
There shines the palace known as Vaijayanta, renowned and radiant with a multitude of pillars made of gold, coral, and lapis lazuli.
Where the lotus ponds attained a likeness to the celestial women through their faces as lotuses and their curls as bees;
and the celestial women attained a likeness to the lotus ponds through their faces as lotuses and their curls as bees.
There, through the reflections of the gods of the Thirty-three upon the jeweled floors, pillars, and walls,
even this single world of the gods assumes the character of many worlds of the gods.
There, the quarters of the sky, adorned with clusters of palaces featuring jeweled archways,
shone as if pervaded by hundreds of Indra’s rainbows.
There, the Nandini cows, possessing the splendor of the Nandana grove, appear as if dancing with their hands— their sprouts— shaken by the gentle breeze.
And there is the delightful celestial garden named Caitraratha,
which maintains a perpetual festival for Love and Spring, filled with passion and desire.
Having beheld the abode of the gods, which fulfills all desires, possesses every happiness, is radiant with flowers of every season, and surpasses all others, the king [was struck with wonder].
With eyes moist with the bliss of a momentary, steady tremor, he thought:
"These are indeed the fruit-bearing stages for those of virtuous deeds."
There she beheld Airāvaṇa, the elephant of the Lord of the Gods, surrounded by circles of hovering bees; fragrant and full of life, he was like the Nandana grove incarnate.
Then Purandara, having learned that the destroyer of cities had arrived,
went out to meet him joyfully along with all the hosts of Maruts.
Honored by the king of the gods,
the king of kings, the best among those free from passion, took his place upon the assembly floor resplendent with rows of jewels.
While the thirty gods were seated in rows upon jeweled couches,
the illustrious king sat upon half the seat of Śatakratu.
There, as the lord of gods and the lord of men sat together upon a single seat,
their forms were seen to be indistinguishable, both noble with a multitude of virtues.
Then Hari spoke to the king, whose lotus-face was being drunk by the bees that were the clear eyes of all the gods.
Oh, how praiseworthy is your rising, O treasury of splendors!
The earth and the heavens have been graced by you, just as they are by the radiant sun.
This banner of victory for your imperial sovereignty shines throughout the three worlds, its majesty exalted and its white cloth of fame resplendent.
The goddess Sarasvatī is impelled by my ears and eyes to proclaim the bliss of drinking the nectar of your stories and the flavor of beholding you.
By you alone— having attained prosperity through well-performed deeds—
this certainty regarding the doctrine of the fruit of actions has been firmly established, with all doubt severed.
For this very reason, among the collection of sense-faculties, the eye alone is the object of longing,
since those like you, whose conduct is worthy of merit, are seen through the power of merits.
When this was said by the Lord of the Thirty-three, Māndhātṛ, the treasury of glory, spoke with his face bowed: "This is the power of your grace."
Thus, as he dwelt in the triple heaven being constantly honored with reverence by the gods,
six Indras passed away during his time there.
With the entire host of asuras destroyed by his prowess,
the victory of the king of the gods became one whose rise was free from all danger.
In the blazing battle with the Dānavas,
the gods, subsisting on the shade of his arms, found their rest beneath that great tree of his heroism.
For him who partakes of that which was purchased with the coin of merit, there is inexhaustible happiness;
yet, within the great flow of time, six Indras have passed away.
A pure mind is the hallmark of one who enjoys the fruits of virtuous deeds;
through turbidity, its near destruction arises.
Then, in the course of time, the desire of that being— who was seized by turbidity,
overcome by greed, and possessed of great pride— arose.
"This is the sovereignty of the thirty gods, protected by the strength of my arms;
therefore, I cannot endure this mockery of sharing half the throne."
"Am I not the sole lord of the gods by virtue of my power?
This arm of mine is capable of bearing the weight of the entire world."
Having displaced the Lord of the Gods from his sovereign wealth of the celestial empire—
a glory marked by the single royal umbrella— he seized it for himself, as was his due.
As he was thinking thus, desiring to commit treachery against Śakra,
his splendor of power, which possessed a brilliant radiance, became withered like a garland.
The river of fortune, surging with the rising of clouds and falling upon the shore of benevolence,
surely agitates the restless mind.
Heedlessness is the messenger of calamities, unbearable even for the great;
it is a mind agitated by sin, intended solely for the uprooting of virtue.
Merely by the thought of evil, the lord of the earth instantly fell to the ground like a tree whose roots have been severed and whose fruit has fallen away.
Lack of practice destroys knowledge; the onset of pride destroys fortune;
malice destroys goodness; and greed destroys prosperity.
Alas! The great rise of the intoxication of pride, which brings such immense prosperity, causes those intoxicated by the emergence of wealth to fall downward all at once.
In a previous birth, he worshipped the one named Sarvavibhu;
as a result of that, he obtained a kingdom desirable even to the Lord of the Maruts.
A certain extraordinary power, more than that of the lord of the gods and truly wondrous, arose from him;
it was no small mass produced from the portion of his gift to the worthy recipient.
In a previous birth, he was a pure merchant named Utkarika who lived in the city called Bandhumatī.
The one named Vipaśyin, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, intent on delivering all sentient beings, went for alms and entered that house.
With a serene mind, he threw a handful of mung beans into his bowl;
four of them fell therein, while the remainder fell upon the ground.
By the power of that gift, Māndhātṛ, the lord of the earth,
having become the sovereign of all continents, attained half of Śakra’s throne.
Because he had fallen from his focus on the earth with his mind elsewhere,
leaving only the bean behind, he fell from the abode of the gods at the conclusion of that fruit.
Where the garland of mental constructs rolls about like a fragmented dream, never flickering within the midst of dreams and illusions—
that [state] becomes possessed of the vast enjoyment of worldly prosperity for those who possess good fortune.
That row of jackfruit trees was like a wish-fulfilling tree for those who give.
Thus spoke the Blessed Buddha, out of affection, regarding the glory that is the fruit of giving,
while instructing the monks by recounting his own previous births.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Legend of Māndhātṛ," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
5. The Legend of Candraprabha:
The Ocean of Milk, distressed by the request of the gods, churned and trembled for a long time;
indeed, it is said that the wish-fulfilling trees naturally shake when they are about to yield their fruit.
There arises a certain unique individual who, having practiced the state of giving through hundreds of bodies,
remains unshakable and bears his body as a mass of bristling hair during acts of renunciation.
In the northern direction, in the city of Kaulāsahāsinī, there is a city named Bhadraśilā, an ornament of the world, which is unsurpassed.
In that city, the creepers of the gardens of charity— whose flowers were white fame and whose fruit was every prosperity—
brought delight to the inhabitants.
There, the God of Love, terrified by the fire from the eye of the Conqueror of Tripura,
was protected by women solely through their playful, flickering frowns.
There, the row of golden houses, radiant with nets of pearls,
shines like a range of Meru’s peaks adorned with shimmering, vast stars.
In that city there was a glorious king named Candraprabha, the best among rulers,
who, by his splendor, made the moonlight of the day appear as if it were on Mount Kailāsa.
By the floods of light from his body, which surpassed the splendor of the full moon,
there was no depletion of oil or wick in the lamps during the nights.
"By the mere sight of him, even the stars suffer from the fever of love";
thus it was as if the sky were covered by his parasol, which acted like the moon.
"He constantly bestows prosperity resting upon a noble treasury"—
by the mere sight of this, the lotus pond fell into contraction.
Having cast aside the pride of their armies, the splendors of the city-dwellers— manifested by their parasols and crowns— were surpassed by the glory of their pure renunciation.
The splendor of him, who was elevated by the ornament of merit,
shone forth like the string of a bow that is bent yet has ascended to its highest limit.
During the time of that enemy of the Kali age, the lifespan of embodied beings was forty-four thousand years.
That protector of the world, whose splendor was like that of a world-guardian, possessed sixty thousand cities of perfect prosperity.
The performers of sacrifices were the ornaments of his fame, adorned by their own merit;
with the waving tendrils of sacrificial smoke, they shone like the goddess Śrī with her tremulous curls.
His minister, Mahācandra, was ever-risen through the blossoming of his prosperity’s night-lotus,
resplendent like the world of the moon.
By means of that steady aim, which was the banner of the Lord’s wisdom and the helmsman for the ocean of his kingdom,
he crossed to the further shore of fame.
And he became a preeminent minister named Mahīdhara, who,
like the five-faced elephant of the quarters, was capable of bearing the weight of the earth.
For that Bṛhaspati of statesmanship, whose counsel was never divulged,
the neighboring kings were made to abandon their valor, just as serpents are made to relinquish their poison.
That king was adorned by that minister, and he in turn by the king,
just as a virtuous man is adorned by virtue, or a good person by his excellence.
A master who is grateful and upright, and a good servant who is full of devotion,
are obtained only through the conjunction of fortune arising from one's own past merits.
This alone is the repose from long-standing delusion, the source of all prosperity:
that, through the recognition of virtue, one discerns the difference between a master and a true man.
Once, they and the other ministers saw a dream whose fruit was the ruin of the king due to his addiction to gambling.
Seeing those ill omens appear,
they became apprehensive and were constantly preoccupied with rites for peace and prosperity.
Even though Viśvāmitra and the other great sages had gone to the forest of penance, they were agitated by the sight of signs [of his power] and cried out, "He is our master! (Kāvyālaṅkāravṛtti 5.24).
In the meantime, there was a pseudo-Brahmin who had been a Brahma-rākṣasa in a previous birth,
named Raudrākṣa, unbearable for his envy, cruelty, and villainy.
Having heard of the king’s fame arising from his generosity—a fame radiant with every virtue—that man, devoid of merit and hating virtue, was tormented and reflected thus: KAvk_5.26.
"Oh, how wonderful! The fame of this king is sung incessantly in the sky by hosts of Siddhas, Gandharvas, and celestial nymphs."
"Always do needles praising his virtues enter my ear; what can I do? By my very nature, I cannot endure the exaltation of another's qualities. (KAvk 5.28)
"Having gone there, I shall shatter the fame of that Dānaśīla, acquired through his giving, by refusing his request for my head. (KAvk 5.29)
If he does not give his head, the fame arising from my gift will be lost;
but if he gives it, there will be a pacification of my enmity.
Having reflected thus for a very long time, that cruel, hard-hearted, and deceitful man,
a resident of the borderlands of Gandhamādana, went to Bhadraśilā.
Skilled in the practice of sorcery, he assumed an appearance appropriate for a seeker of peace;
yet with defiled intentions, he reached the city of the king.
In this forest of existence, which is perpetually crowded with virtues and faults,
wish-fulfilling trees are born, and poisonous trees are also born.
To whom is distress not inflicted by wicked men, who, like ominous portents, foretell the destruction of all things and cause terrible terror?
What difference is there between a wicked person and darkness— both of whom, by their very nature, harbor faults that obstruct light and are hostile toward those possessed of virtue?

By whom was this wicked serpent created— this one who strikes at his own will, who is unbearable with the poison of hatred toward the virtuous, who has long wings, and who is as formidable as a beast of prey?
When he had entered the city, the personified city-goddess approached the king and spoke, her eyes trembling with fear: KAvk_5.37.
"This seeker of a head, this Brahmin in name only, has come to you;
he who would destroy your life deserves to be put to death, for he would cut short the life of the world."
That man of impure intent was stopped by me at the city gate;
my mind finds no peace, terrified by the sight of him.
To the city deity who was speaking thus,
the king replied with his face bowed down by the shame born from having obstructed a petitioner.
"O Queen, let him enter unhindered, driven by his request;
I cannot endure the failure of the hopes of a suppliant, which is like a long-drawn sigh."
The sacrifice of one's body for the sake of those who beg with affection results in the attainment of merit;
yet embodied beings surely perish even after remaining for a duration equal to the number of world-ages.
This alone is the life of the well-born that is worthy of honor in this world:
that no supplicant with shattered hopes passes before them.
"O lady of virtuous conduct, please show me favor;
let the torment caused by the frustration of my hopes be quickly dispelled."
Having heard these words of the king, whose resolve was unshakable,
the queen, her mind tormented by anxiety, vanished from sight.
Then that crooked rogue arrived, acting like a saw,
himself intent upon the destruction of the upright man, as cruel as a woodcutter’s blade.
When he arrived at the king’s palace, which stood with its doors open for supplicants,
the earth, together with its mountains, trembled out of fear of the king’s destruction.
Having approached the moon-like king, that evil-faced one, like Rāhu,
first uttered a blessing that was as if intended for his own misfortune.

"Hail, O King! For a twice-born man is the achiever of success even in solitude; at dawn, he shall grant you the attainment of your desires, like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for all seekers. (KAvk 5.49)
His vision is like a great rain of nectar; his mind is a friend of goodness; his patience is a broom for sweeping away the dust of anger; his intellect is a mother to those afflicted by suffering;
his fortune is purified by the consecration of the water of generosity; and his speech is employed for the sake of truth.
For you alone, O friend of the world, have been born as that which is eternal.
"For the sake of success, some have said to me, 'Give me the head of a universal monarch (cakravartin)';
but who other than you is able to give it? No one else."
There are wish-fulfilling gems, the kalpa-tree, and the like, which grant manifest objects;
but those like you, who bestow even the most difficult-to-obtain goals, are rare indeed.
When he had spoken thus, the king, whose vast intention was unshakable and who was overflowing with joy at the sight of the supplicant, addressed him:
"I am fortunate, O Brahmin, for whose sake my life is well-lived, as my wealth goes toward the fulfillment of the needs of those who seek it,
becoming a disinterested instrument."
"When will my life-breaths depart for the sake of others?"—this is your heart's desire;
why then do you not seek these merits, if they are indeed desired by you?
"Or rather, let my praiseworthy head be taken for the sake of accomplishing your purpose;
for in this world, whatever is bestowed upon a petitioner remains eternally secure."
When this had been said by the king, who was filled with joy and endowed with courage,
the two great ministers, Mahācandra and Mahīdhara, spoke to him.
"O Lord, the protection of your own life is your foremost duty;
for while you live, all living beings in the world continue to live."
"You ought not to give away your head, for your body is the support of all;
let this head, composed of gold and jewels, be given to this brahmin."
By means of all their resources, they fulfill the heart's desires of those seeking aid;
by protecting them alone, everything becomes protected.
This resolve of this twice-born man is cruel and defiled in mind;
for a wish-granting tree does not survive when its roots are cut away by those who seek its bounty.
Having obtained a head made of gold and jewels, what is the use of this man’s head?
Is the wish-fulfilling gem not to be looked upon and enjoyed by those who are hungry?
When this was said by the two chief ministers, the Brahmin replied, "That head made of gold and jewels is of no use to me. (KAvk 5.63)
Then the king removed his crown, which, with the rays of its pearls,
seemed to shed streams of tears on all sides from the sorrow of separation from his head.
At that moment, the crowns of the city-dwellers fell to the earth along with meteors that resembled flames leaping toward the horizon from a conflagration of the quarters.
When the king had resolved in every way to offer his own head,
those two ministers, unable to bear the sight, prepared to abandon their bodies.
Then, having entered the Ratnagarbha garden,
the lord of the earth prepared to cut off his head beneath a blossoming campaka tree.
Seeing him prepared to cut off his head, the goddess of the garden, overwhelmed with grief, said: "O King, do not commit such a rash act! (KAvk 5.68)
Trembling and lamenting, the young creepers restrained him with the sounds of intoxicated bees and with their hands of swaying sprouts.
With his resolve unwavering, he propitiated the deity of the grove,
and having taken hold of pure awakening, he became possessed of a solemn vow.
In this garden made of jewels, let there be a stūpa for the Teacher, elevated by his mass of merit and worthy of delivering sentient beings.
Whatever merit has been acquired by me through this resolve,
by that may all embodied beings in saṃsāra be free from the cycle of existence.
Having meditated thus, the king tied his head to the branch of a campaka tree with the mass of his hair,
cut it off, and gave it to the brahmin.
Then, O Lord of Men, by virtue of his resolute energy and clear aspiration,
and through certain stainless rays of merit spreading to the ends of the quarters, he—
having dissolved the internal flood of great delusion— attained final nirvana.
In an instant, many people ceased their exertion in the repeated practice of worldly existence.
Thus, by means of this narration of events from a previous birth,
the Blessed Jina provided the monks with a teaching on the true Dharma regarding pure giving.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Avadāna of Candraprabha," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
6. The Avadāna of the Voyage to Badaradvīpa:

Ah! For those who are intent on giving, who possess great heroism, whose natures are pure, who are oceans of courage, and who are filled with great enthusiasm for the sake of others, inconceivable and steadfast [deeds] come to pass.
Whereby mountains, together with their peaks, are scaled as if in play while climbing a palace, reaching the sky;
or where rivers, agitated by the weight of their waters, are treated like the puddles in a cow's hoofprint;
and where the slopes of forests are traversed as if they were the grounds of one’s own residence.
This was the vigorous manifestation of the power of those great-souled ones as they displayed their heroism.
For in the past, the Blessed Buddha, by means of the illumination of his instruction, removed the darkness born of ignorance from the inhabitants of the city of Śrāvastī.
Surrounded by the community of monks and accompanied by a caravan of merchants,
he once departed from Magadha on his own journey.
Seeing him traveling along the forest path, accompanied by a caravan of great purpose, a band of thieves in the Sālā forest reflected thus: KAvk_6.5 //
"Let this Blessed One, who is devoted to the welfare of beings, go ahead;
we shall follow behind with the caravan, filled with heaps of wealth."
Then the Blessed One, the Omniscient, having understood their intention, asked them, "What is this? with a face serene and smiling.
Casting aside their cruelty, they spoke to him with sweet voices, as if the darkness within them had been destroyed by the glances of his gracious smiles: KAvk_6.8.
"O Blessed One, our livelihood is blameworthy and produced by [unwholesome] karma;
it is not through wages, nor agriculture, nor guarding others, nor receiving gifts."
Cruelty is innate to us whose natures are inherently turbid;
O King, what can be done against one's own nature? For the *karṇikā* flower is indeed sharp.
Therefore, you ought not to cause the destruction of our livelihood; please depart.
For once you have gone, we shall seize all the goods of the caravan.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Blessed One, his mind filled with compassion,
for a moment became as unsteady in thought as one swaying on a swing.
Then, having calculated the entire wealth of the caravan,
he gave an equivalent amount to the band of thieves from a treasure he had acquired at that very moment.
In that very same manner,
by going and returning along the road six times, he bestowed wealth upon them for the sake of liberating the caravan.
Furthermore, when he had arrived there with his followers by that path,
the thieves conceived the idea of inviting him to a meal.
The virtuous bestow purity through their gaze and auspiciousness through their conversation;
by the practice of association, they become bridges upon the path of the righteous.

There, with a gaze that was not too intense, the Blessed One, the Victor, brought about for them all— through the destruction of all unwholesome states— a state of meditative concentration and purity.
For those of resolute nature, there are the four means of attraction:
beneficial conduct, common purpose, generosity, and pleasant speech.
For those noble beings, the four divine abodes—
compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and loving-kindness— are their possession.
In the minds of those great-souled ones, three roots of virtue are firmly established:
non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
For those who always delight in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
and whose minds are supported by the powers of skillful means, aspiration, and primordial awareness;
To those who are heroes solely in their protection [of others], who always speak non-duality, who are illuminated by the three sciences, and who possess the fourfold purity; KAvk_6.22 //
To those who are liberated from the five aggregates, who have shattered the six sense-bases,
who are endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment, and who teach the noble eightfold path.
For those who possess the ten powers and are free from the nine bonds,
what thing in the world— be it the conduct of people— is unknown to the Victors?
Then, out of extreme compassion for them as they touched his feet with their heads,
the Blessed One said "So be it" to that invitation to partake of food.
Surrounded by the community of monks whose sins had been exhausted through that vision, he accepted all the food that was offered to him in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Then, by virtue of that aspiration, with the lamp of wisdom as their probe,
they opened their eyes and beheld the radiant state.
Having been ripened by an immediate and intense dispassion and being full of serene faith,
they applied themselves to the practice of renunciation and attained a state of veneration in the world.
Seeing that merit of theirs suddenly manifested before them,
the Blessed One, being questioned by the monks as to what this was, spoke.
Through these acts of protecting a caravan and providing ransoms for it,
he established a connection with Yama even in another birth.
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the birthplace of joy for the excellence of the Kośala people, which is the destination of the extensive path of dharma leading as far as the realms of heaven.
In that city, the river of the gods, carrying its waves of stainless purity,
always gladdens the hearts of embodied beings like compassion itself.
Non-violence alone is to be practiced by the virtuous; it is regarded as true knowledge by the wise;
and it is like forbearance toward all beings—that state which is the abode of the happiness of trust.
While King Brahmadatta— whose name was like that of Brahmā, and who was the abode of blooming lotuses—
was protecting the world as if it were the three realms of existence, during that Brahma-eon.
There lived a caravan leader named Priyaseṇa, who was like Vaiśravaṇa himself;
he was the abode of wealth for caravans of goods, just as the ocean is the receptacle of waters.
He had a son named Supriya, an abode of kindness,
by relying upon whom the caravan of virtues attained its goal.
Endowed with generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom,
he was created by the Creator solely to bewilder the splendor of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
All clear branches of knowledge and vast arts entered that man of noble intent,
just as rivers enter the great ocean with their full and noble currents.
As if longing for the Supreme Person, the Goddess Śrī took refuge in him, who was praiseworthy, whose conduct was adorned with virtues, and whose form was graced with the primary marks.
When his father had gone to the third heaven, the burden of legal affairs, which he had well-performed and acquired in due time,
was established upon the slope of his shoulders.
He thought: "This vast fortune has come down to me through my own lineage;
nevertheless, I believe it is not sufficient for the desires of all who seek wealth."
Of what use is even that very great prosperity residing in a virtuous man,
if it is fruitless toward the remaining supplicants, like wealth already enjoyed by those who arrived first?
The Creator has rendered the vastness of the ocean fruitless,
since even today that submarine fire, though it has filled it, remains no less a seeker of wealth.
Or rather, by whom can one of vast ambition be fully satisfied?
The ocean was reduced to the state of being sipped as a mere mouthful by Agastya.
"What shall I do? This distress is great; there is but one fortune, yet many seekers.
That wealth which is capable of sustaining the burden of all supplicants is not to be found."
"Five and six are thus fulfilled; others are not [fulfilled] by the Śrīkaustubha and the rest.
Even as he spoke thus, the ocean was heated within by the blazing submarine fire (aurvānala).
Therefore, I shall strive with diligence to acquire incalculable wealth;
I cannot endure the sighs of misery from the mouth of a suppliant who has been turned away.
Having reflected thus for a long time, surrounded by a great caravan,
he went to the city of Ratnadvīpa and gathered a collection of jewels.

Then, on the road, the forest-dwelling bandits, who had been released from their struggle for the caravan's wealth, saw him returning against the current of his journey, having accomplished his purpose.
Seeing their reckless attempt to plunder the caravan's wealth,
he protected his followers by giving away his own arrows.
Furthermore, by that same sequence, he traveled back and forth to the Island of Jewels six times and bestowed wealth upon the robbers for the protection of the merchant caravan.
In that very same way, having encountered a multitude of meritorious people,
he likewise beheld those thieves who were intent on plundering the caravan's wealth.
He thought: "Alas! Though these [beings] have been completely filled by me with great wealth, they do not desist from their efforts to seize the property of others."
"Even though I have repeatedly said, 'I shall fill the world with wealth,' alas, these wretched bandits have not been satisfied! (KAvk 6.54)
"Shame on my birth, that of a base-born man, for I am devoid of spirit and enthusiasm, my speech is obstructed by my inability to respond, and my vow has been rendered a mere boast!"
As he reflected thus, tormented by the fire of remorse,
the night passed in solitude like a hundred years.
To him, who was submerged in the mire of grief and as motionless as a lordly elephant,
a deity known as Maheśā spoke in a dream while he was sighing deeply.
O wise one, do not indulge in grief that needlessly withers the body;
for you who have ascended the noble resolve of the virtuous, your desire shall be fulfilled.
There is nothing in this world so difficult to attain through dream or mere imagination that it cannot be accomplished by effort for the wise who are resolute.
Such is the incomparable power of even a single twice-born man,
that by the mere movement of his command, the Vindhya mountain attained equality with the earth.
The uneven becomes level, the distant comes near,
and water turns into dry land at the time of action for the great-souled ones.
This undertaking of yours for the sake of others will surely bear fruit; there is no doubt.
The actions of those possessed of true being are never subject to contradiction or suspicion.
In Badaradvīpa, which is frequented by the gods of the thirty-three,
there are jewels whose power alone is capable of filling the three worlds.
For having transcended the realm of mortals, that most exalted ground,
consisting of merit, is attained neither by those who lack virtuous qualities nor by those of undisciplined self.
"O son, let despair be abandoned; let your mind be made firm;
let enthusiasm be embraced for the journey to Badaradvīpa."
Listen to this brief outline of the sequence for attaining that [state]:
you possess the power of abundant spiritual essence and are capable of crossing over saṃsāra.
In the western quarter,
having crossed over seven hundred vast islands as well as seven great mountains, there exists [a place].
And there is the ocean named Anulomapratiloma, consisting of seven calamities,
across which the meritorious person reaches the further shore by means of favorable winds.
Then there was a mountain bearing the same name, which created a mist of darkness with its winds;
yet upon it, the great medicinal herb named Amogha bestowed health upon the eyes.
Then there is the ocean named Āvarta, where beings are carried across through seven whirlpools by means of plunging and surfacing amidst the Vairambha winds.
Beyond that is the mountain named Āvarta, where dwells the night-stalker Śaṅkhanābha,
who is terrible, life-destroying, and a source of terror to the gods.
Where the great medicinal plant *śaṅkhanābhi*, though entwined by black serpents,
protects one endowed with merit when placed upon the eyes or the head.
Then the ocean named Nīla, where the Rākṣasa Raktākṣa dwelt,
was brought under control by the one who knew the Buddha’s vidyās, after he had overcome the sea-monsters.
Then there was a night-stalker named Nīloda, blue-necked,
with blazing eyes, who dwelt there accompanied by five hundred rākṣasas.
There, a venomous serpent— whose fiery poison it emits through its gaze, breath, touch, and fangs— constantly guards a medicinal herb named Amoghā.
By one who observes the vow of the fast, possessing a mind of loving-kindness and compassion,
that great medicinal herb is obtained after having driven away the black serpent.
Having placed that mountain, which is like a demon’s cart with its fruitless and smooth caves,
upon the crest of his hair, the meritorious man crosses over it as if wading through water.
Now, on the opposite shore of which stands the mountain named Vairambha,
there is a terrible forest called Tāmra, situated within a great grove of *śāla* trees.
There dwelt a great python named Tāmrākṣa, who was unbearable;
by its fierce stench alone, one could not live even with the wind.
For six months while sleeping, his saliva pervades a league;
yet for one tormented by hunger, it does not diminish even when awake for six months.
Having uprooted the earth where bamboo thickets and rocks were fixed,
he [revealed] a cave containing a medicinal herb that blazed day and night, appearing like a mass of collyrium.
Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha-knowledge known as "Non-Enmity," there shall be no fear from that terrible python or from any other being of great power.
Then, those seven great mountains, crowded with bamboo thorns,
were crossed by the hero endowed with valor, using his foot marked with copper plates as a bridge.
Then, having crossed the Śālmalī forest and the seven rivers of caustic brine,
one reaches the mountain named Triśaṅku in the east.
There, thorns called triśaṅkus, which pierce even diamond,
do not enter at all his feet, for they are bound with copper bands.
There is a river named Triśaṅku and there is the mountain Ayaḥśaṅku;
there is the river Upaskīlā, and from that point the river flows in two directions, each further divided in two.
Then there was the mountain named Aṣṭādaśavakra, which was unrestrained;
then a river with a name corresponding to that [mountain], and after that the mountain named Ślakṣṇi.
Then there was a mountain named Adridhūmanetra, its horizons smeared with smoke,
pervaded by circles of cruel venomous serpents whose poison was lethal to both sight and touch.
Within that pond, at its summit, was a great cave secured by stone,
wherein lay the Jyotīrasa gem and the life-restoring Mahauṣadhi herb.
Having split open the cave, with his head, feet, hands, and belly emerging from it,
he who is endowed with the power of the Vajra-mantra is not harmed by cruel serpents.
Then there were seventy-seven mountains of venomous serpents crowded with fierce beings,
and likewise rivers whose abundance of water was shoreless.
Having crossed over all this through his merits, one who is intent on the welfare of others ascends the mountain of nectar,
whose peaks embrace the sky.
Then, on its other side, there appeared the city named Rohitaka, adorned with wish-fulfilling trees and resembling heaven itself.
There lived a caravan leader named Magha, renowned like Indra (Maghavan),
a great being devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
"Being one of faultless intellect and a knower of the land, he will provide you with instructions for the path as you prepare for the journey to Badaradvīpa; he will do everything for you."
Having spoken thus and having encouraged Supriya many times with auspicious and excellent words, the goddess suddenly vanished from sight.
Fully awakened and deeply delighted, reflecting that everything was exactly as it should be,
he set forth, mounted upon his steed and preceded by his own high spirits.
Traveling by the path pointed out by him from Vinitā,
he reached the city of Rphitaka after twelve years of meritorious effort.
In the meantime, due to the ripening of his karma, Magha, the caravan leader,
became physically unwell there, afflicted by a disease that was difficult to cure.
Then, unable to gain entrance into that palace which resembled the residence of a king,
Supriya waited at the door for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
Then, under the pretext of being a physician, he gained entry;
for who does not become a ground for respect through the wisdom of speaking on useful matters?
Knowing the rules of Ayurveda, he,
perceiving through the signs of impending death that only six months of life remained, became filled with anxiety.
Through his attendance upon him with medicines, consisting mostly of what was pleasant and beneficial,
Supriya became so dearly beloved that he attained the status of a favorite in a very short time.
Through his devotion to the science of medicine, he became beloved;
for whatever is brought by one's loved ones, all of that becomes dear to the mind.
Then, through the affectionate attentions of his beloved, his illness reached a state of intensity;
yet mental anguish is pacified by the company of the virtuous, and thus his physical ailment was dissolved.
Then, having gained his confidence, Supriya affectionately made Magha acquainted with the facts of the situation later on, during an occasion for telling his own story.
Having recognized the great-souled one’s unwavering resolve for the sake of others during his journey to Badaradvīpa, Magha spoke to him in wonder: KAvk_6.107.
Ah! In this worthless cycle of existence, there arise certain jewels in the form of essence—those who are solely devoted to the welfare of others.
Fresh youth, a beloved form, a mind inclined toward the welfare of others,
and likewise this accumulation of virtues worthy of merit— this conjunction of qualities is truly fitting.
"Having traversed such a great distance for the sake of another, you have arrived;
I shall assist you, yet I am exceedingly afflicted."
The life-breaths of embodied beings depart only when their allotted time has expired;
let them, even at my end, become the cause for your meditative concentration.
In this very way, that which is expenditure is reckoned as expenditure;
even the loss of one's life for the sake of another is equal to hundreds of gains.
"I have not seen Badaradvīpa myself, but I have heard of it;
I recognize that region in the great ocean by its various characteristic marks."
Having spoken thus to the king, he— who showed no regard even for the words of his friends and kinsmen—
set out upon an auspicious vessel together with Supriya.
Then, mounted upon a ship, those two of vast resolve traveled even hundreds of yojanas,
aided by a favorable wind.
Seeing the water of the great ocean in various colors at every spot, Supriya asked Magha out of curiosity, "What is this? (KAvk 6.116).
Within this ocean there are five mountains of iron in the water;
others consist of copper and silver, while still others are made of gold and jewels.
Due to the particular shadows cast by them, this blazing ocean appears variegated in color at every step, as if medicinal herbs have emerged from within it.
Having spoken thus, Magha, overcome by disease and having reached the limit of his allotted time,
gave up his life, his existence firmly established in his noble fame.
If the lifespan could be broken as easily as the resolve of great-souled beings— which is firmer even than adamantine cement— then what in this world would be impossible to achieve?
Having reached the shore with his ship, Supriya suppressed the grief born of separation from him and performed the funeral rites for his friend.
This alone is the exalted mark of those great-souled ones characterized by courage and vigor:
that their minds remain firm in their sense of duty even at a time when all points of support have been severed.
Once again mounting his carriage and having crossed the ocean,
he entered a formidable forest along the side of the Jewel Mountain.
The intellect of the great is not diminished by separations, nor by anxieties, nor even by the assaults of enemies; it is not impaired by diseases or by the experience of afflictions.
There he saw before him a mountain that had ascended into the sky and blocked all the quarters of the horizon—
an inaccessible peak like an embodied obstacle.
Seeing that mountain devoid of means, like a haughty fool, he lay for a moment upon his bed of leaves below and reflected: KAvk_6.126.
"Alas! How much time has passed since I set out?
Indeed, even the name of Badaradvīpa is not heard anywhere."
He who was my companion in resolve, acquired through the highest price of merit—
he too has been swept away by the surging waves of karma, like a broken boat in an untimely storm.
Even though this means has failed, I shall not indeed turn back from my great resolve;
let there be success or let there be death.
That alone is a birth worthy of honor throughout the three worlds during the course of one's life,
in which the sacrifice of one's life occurs for the sake of benefiting others.
Knowing him to be thus overwhelmed with anxiety there,
the yakṣa named Nīla, who dwells upon a mountain, approached the Ocean of Truth and spoke.
Having gone one yojana to the east, you should ascend the three peaks of the mountain by means of a ladder-like staircase made of cane,
and then proceed.
Thus, following the instruction of the Yakṣa,
he crossed the great mountain and beheld before him a crystal mountain with its lofty peaks.
Upon that single rock, smooth and inaccessible even to birds,
his desire remained inactive for a moment.
Having reflected for a very long time upon that mountain— lofty, without support, and as immovable as his own volition— he became like one depicted in a painting.
Then a yakṣa named Candraprabha, who dwelt in a mountain cave,
approached that one endowed with goodness and spoke to him with a smile.
Having gone a distance of one *krośa* to the east,
there is seen a sandalwood forest of unprecedented splendor, its creepers swaying in the gentle breeze.
There dwells a great medicinal herb named Prasara, hidden within a cave;
it is obtained for the protection of the body by lifting up a massive rock.
Having suddenly ascended the crystal mountain, which is illuminated by its radiance and provided with stairways,
proceed for the attainment of your desired goal.
At that very moment, as if her purpose were accomplished, that great medicinal herb departs;
one should not feel despondency on its account, for the attainment of beloved ones is as flickering as lightning.
Thus, having ascended the mountain according to the ritual prescribed by the Yakṣa,
he beheld before him a city with golden palaces.
Seeing that place, which was as if strewn with the peaks of Mount Meru, as if fashioned from light,
and as if created by wonders themselves, he was filled with amazement.
Seeing that door blocked by two great golden panels,
he sat down at the edge of the forest, where the path was deserted and devoid of people.
In the meantime, at the end of the day, the sun, traveling along the infinite path of the sky,
reached the vicinity of the western mountain as if exhausted.
When the thousand-rayed sun had set, the lovely night slowly set forth like a woman going to meet her lover to seek out the lord of the stars.
Then, with its vast radiance, intent on fulfilling all desires,
the moon, as clear as a Bodhisattva, rose up.
The moonlight, vast and fit for the complete pacification of the mass of darkness,
shone forth like the manifestation of the quality of goodness (*sattva*) that gladdens the mind.
Just as the moon dispels the darkness and delusion of the quarters born from separation from the day,
so indeed is the supreme benefit for others a great ascent for the magnanimous.
For a moment, Supriya, his body being filled by the rays of the moon,
attained sleep— the seal that puts an end to the agitation caused by the waves of the ocean of worldly affairs.
As the night was waning, a goddess named Maheśā, endowed with virtue, courtesy, and respect,
approached him in a dream and spoke.
"O, alas! Great Being, by you, who are intent upon the true nature of reality, vast suffering has been endured for the sake of others, you who are so virtuous."
Since this effort remains but little remaining, you ought not to feel agitation;
for those whose inner being has not yet become exhausted, all accomplishments are within their own control.
This city is made of gold, and beyond it there are three others;
here exist wondrous cities of jewels, each succeeding one more magnificent than the last.
As you opened the door, four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two kinnarīs emerged from them in succession.
For you, who have conquered your senses and are aware of that heedlessness,
what else remains but the attainment of your desire before long?
Thus addressed with affection by the goddess, Supriya then awoke;
having approached three times, he struck the city gate with his hand.
Then four *kiṃnarīs* with tremulous eyes emerged,
like the blossoms of a wondrous tree stirred by the playful breeze.
They cause the mind to rejoice, raining down nectar upon the eyes;
with the radiance of their moon-like faces, they create moonlight even during the day.
Having honored him, those women of lovely appearance, with their affectionate longings and advances toward that noble Smara,
performed for him a kind of hospitality.
Seated upon moonstones,
they assumed their postures like the personified medicinal herbs of Love.
With the radiance of their smiles and playful charms blossoming forth, they spoke to him,
as if offering camphor as a gift of love before him.
"Oh, how fortunate we are, whose home you have come to visit today— even though you are one who can be approached at will— your form adorned with excellent virtues!"
Who has an aversion to nectar? Who has a lack of taste for sandalwood?
Who shows disregard for the moon? Or who is not esteemed by the virtuous?
Although a woman's own affection leads to the destruction of her good fortune, nevertheless,
by the mere sight of you, they have been made to speak.
O virtuous one, this city of the Kinnaras, ourselves surrendered through our affection,
and this jewel as a gift for your speech— all these are already at your disposal.
Having heard these words of theirs, Supriya,
displaying the moonlight of his teeth, spoke in a manner befitting their affection, making the quarters bright with his virtuous nature.
To whom would this nectar of conversation not be an object of great esteem?
It is a source of honor even for oneself, having been honored by many women.
Even this sight alone is praiseworthy, and even that, it is a favor;
how much more so when pearl necklaces, which remove the heat [of summer], are further sprinkled with sandalwood paste?
For such beings, who are as pure as the radiance of the moon,
worldly conduct is appropriately beautiful.
Whose grounds for respect would the mind—not charming in its conduct due to propriety, yet clear through its serenity—and the speech—not harsh, but tender with affection—not be? (KAvk 6.170)
We have adopted the custom appropriate for the materials of worship;

Standing there, she thought: "In my inner apartments dwells this king of peacocks, who knows the nature of character and is skilled in human speech."
"He will certainly tell me of this king's conduct;
meanwhile, a censurable deed has been committed—what shall I do now? (KAvk 8.67)
"Let alone that man of refined intellect who knows the truth and understands the vital points;
even in these inanimate things, suspicion has arisen in me, a woman who has committed a sin."
Having reflected thus, she gave him poisoned food;
for what will women not do when intoxicated by passion and fallen under the sway of the wicked?
As he was being served by her with food and drink containing poison,
the radiant luster of Barhirāja increased and shone forth.
Seeing him restored to health, the queen— fearing the disclosure of her secret,
seized by the malady of grief, and trembling— gradually gave up her life.
Thus, not even by poison did any affliction arise in him;
for the stainlessness of mind of the great renders poison non-poisonous.
Passion is poison, and delusion is a most virulent poison; hatred too is a potent poison.
But the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha, as well as the Truth, are the supreme nectar.
The great ocean of delusion emits a terrible poison, and the great serpent of passion emits a terrible poison;
the forest floor of enmity also emits a terrible poison. There is no other source for this poison than the succession of births.
In another birth, Śrīgupta, desiring unrighteousness, acted in this very same way; she too became his partner in that dharma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, with the waters of his perfectly compassionate gaze,
made Śrīgupta free from passion and oriented toward the Teaching.
Then Śrīgupta, skilled in virtue and possessing pure mindfulness, recollected the three refuges in order to attain the state of illumination;
through his association with the Jina, he acquired merit, for the sight of the virtuous is indeed [meritorious].
It leads to great welfare and to the joy of happiness.
Although Śrīgupta was possessed of the taint of humiliation, the Blessed One— who is intent upon the merit of compassion— removed his ignorance and delusion by necessarily bestowing grace;
for the sake of the monks' destruction of existence, he established the teaching of non-enmity.
By which they do not again become bound in the house of existence for the sake of the knot of becoming.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Legend of Śrīgupta," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
9. The Story of Jyotiṣka:

Fortune brings misfortune to the fortunate, while auspiciousness arising from a noble nature leads to well-being; conversely, the welfare of fools turns into harm—this is the observed order of things.
This light, which bestows extreme brilliance upon the forest of medicinal herbs blinded by the darkness of midnight,
is friendly toward all and serves to destroy the sight of the shore of the Caulukya dynasty.
Formerly, in the city known as Rājagṛha,
there lived a citizen named Subhadra, who was fully established in the life of a householder, during the reign of King Bimbisāra.
Due to his folly, having fallen into delusion and being a hater of all philosophical systems,
he developed an excessive devotion toward the Jain mendicants alone.
To him was born a wife named Satyavatī, distinguished by her noble lineage;
she conceived a fetus, just as the eastern quarter receives the orb of the full moon.
Once, the Blessed Buddha arrived at that house located in the Bamboo Grove known as Kalandakanivāsa for the sake of alms.
Having performed worship together with his wife, he respectfully asked that [deity] about the child situated in the womb: "What will its form be?"
He said: "Having now enjoyed both divine and human pleasures, your son will attain liberation by entering the religious life within my teaching."
When the Blessed One had clearly given these instructions and departed for his own abode,
the mendicant Bhūrika approached the house of the householder.
Having heard that which was spoken by the Blessed One as reported by Subhadra,
the ascetic quickly became overwhelmed by the poison of malice.
Having calculated for a very long time and exerted great effort in the knowledge of the planets,
he saw in the question exactly what had been spoken by the Blessed One.
He thought: "What he has said is true; there is no doubt.
Having taken up a likeness of his power, what shall I say of my own truth?"
If Subhadra understands his omniscience through my words,
then he will abandon his faith in the Kṣapaṇaka out of respect for the Śramaṇa.
Having reflected thus, filled with indignation, he spoke to Subhadra:
"This which has been said by that one who fancies himself omniscient is untrue."
How does a human being attain the divine excellence worthy of the gods?
But since renunciation exists, why was it not considered by him?
For one who is emaciated, tormented by hunger, and has no other recourse,
the vow of a śramaṇa is a refuge worthy of providing excellent nourishment.
"Householder, if you will accept my word as authoritative, behold:
this infant who has been born will bring torment upon our family."
When the mendicant had departed after speaking thus, the householder reflected for a long time and devised various means for causing an abortion.
When, despite the employment of medicinal substances, the fetus was not aborted,
he then had his wife killed in a secluded place by means of violent crushing.
Then, when she had been led by that sinner to the Śītavana cemetery in that city, the mendicants, delighted by the news, sang: KAvk_9.19 //
"Oh, alas! The Omniscient One has spoken the truth regarding this child;
for his mother, born from this very slaughterhouse, has met her death."
This is that divine glory of the child, which is called his state as a "divine human";
and this is his renunciation, in that he met his end within the womb.
Thus, because of their derisive talk on all sides,
a great gathering of people came together solely for the purpose of beholding the cremation ground.
In the meantime, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, having perceived everything with his divine vision,
the Buddha reflected for a moment with a smile.
Alas! Even for those far away, the light of embodied beings is obscured by fools through their persistence in delusion, just as it is by shifting clouds.
By that mendicant, who was destroying his own merit, that foolish-minded man was made to commit even an improper deed out of evil intent. Ah! 9.25.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One himself, surrounded by a multitude of monks and overwhelmed with compassion, went quickly to the Śītavana cemetery.
Having learned that the Blessed One was wandering through the cremation ground,
King Bimbisāra himself, together with his ministers, went to that very place.
Then, when Subhadrā’s wife had been cast into the fire of the funeral pyre,
a child, seated upon a lotus, burst from her womb and rose up like the sun.
When no one could seize him as he stood in the midst of a blazing fire, a great cry of "Alas! arose from the multitude of people.
Then, with a hurried gait,
the pediatrician named Jīvaka took the prince from the Sugata’s command.
By the mere glance of the Victor at the moment the boy was seized,
the fire of his funeral pyre became as cool as yellow sandalwood.
Seeing the beautiful boy released from the fire and still alive,
the mendicants stood for a moment in embarrassment, as if they were dead.
Then the Blessed One, who delights in the welfare of all beings, spoke to Subhadra, who was bewildered by wonder: "Let this son be accepted."
But he, his mind agitated by indecision, out of the doubt "What shall I do?",
for a moment gazed at the faces of the monks themselves for instruction.
They said to him: "This child born from the cremation fire must not be accepted;
wherever he stays, it is certain that that house will surely perish."
When that fool did not accept it because of their words,
the king then took the boy [into his care] according to the teaching of the Jina.
The Blessed One himself gave him the name Jyotiṣka, because he had been obtained from the midst of light and possessed a radiance resembling that of a celestial being.
While that infant was growing up amidst the many retinues of the king,
his maternal uncle, having traveled from another land, arrived there in due course.
Having learned of his sister’s conduct and her death upon the birth of her son,
he approached Subhadra trembling with rage and struck him down.
O fool,
devoted to the mendicant, what good deed indeed have you performed by abandoning your own son through his words and having your wife killed?
Devoid of consciousness by their very nature, yet arisen from the power of another's mantra,
wicked men strike down even those who endure them, like animated corpses (vetālas).
If you do not take the son from Rājagṛha this very moment, then,
having proclaimed the murder of a woman, I shall have you punished for your crime.
Having been addressed thus by him, out of fear of that [curse], the king had his son brought from the palace after a long time,
though he was unwilling to release him, as he had been granted leave by the monarch.
Then, Subhadrā, having passed away in the course of time,
became Jyotiṣka, like the sun among lights, possessing the splendor of the gods.
That wish-fulfilling tree for the needy generally bestowed both divine and human prosperity;
he, moreover, fixed his mind upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, who are the true refuges.
Eager to acquire the jewels of merit, he bestowed that wondrous collection of divine gems, offered out of devotion to him, upon the community of monks.
Marvelous and manifold supernatural powers from the hosts of gods came of their own accord to his house, like rivers flowing into the great ocean.
Maintaining an equal mind toward grass and a jewel, even while dwelling in that house,
he accepted the possession of a jeweled bowl out of consideration for him.
He obtained a pair of divine garments, worthy of comparison with his own fame,
purchased by the price of his merit, as pure as his own home.
Then once, that garment, still damp from bathing, was placed in the sun;
it was carried away by the wind and fell upon the head of the king.
Beholding that unprecedentedly beautiful garment of Jyotiṣka,
the king, amazed by the splendor of his magic, considered his own royal fortune to be as insignificant as a blade of grass.
Having been invited to dine and having reached his jewel-adorned palace,
the king, situated within the abode of Jyotiṣka, thought he had attained heaven.
Then, in the course of time, O protector of the earth, the king, who was devoted to righteousness, was struck down by his son Ajātaśatru,
who, greedy for the kingdom, acted through deceit.
When that king, who possessed excellent virtues and was like the Kṛta age,
had passed away, that son of the best of kings obtained the kingdom as if it were unrighteousness itself.
Seeing that prosperity in the house of Jyotiṣka which was difficult for even kings to obtain, the king approached him and said: "You have been brought up by my father."
"I am your brother by dharma; give me half of your wealth.
If you do not, then from the obstruction of your share, strife alone will arise."
Thus addressed by that cruel-doer out of deceit,
Jyotiṣka gave him a house filled with jewels and departed for his own home.
That prosperity, radiant with divine jewels, abundant, and beneficial to the world,
followed after Hyotiṣka alone, just as splendor follows the sun.
Furthermore, although that prosperity had been abandoned, the virtuous Prabhāvatī returned seven times to King Jyotiṣka,
as if she were unable to bear his absence.
Knowing that [the king] was intent on seizing all his property through various means such as bandits and thieves, Jyotiṣka became despondent and reflected: KAvk_9.60.
Due to the ripening of demerit among the people,
the king— who was as dear to his subjects as a father and tender with affection— has passed away, leaving nothing but his memory behind.
Who else is like him, in whom the subjects,
finding comfort as if in a father, sleep peacefully through the nights, for he is guileless and straightforward?
The wealthy are obtained as easily as blades of grass, while the wise are found as rarely as jewels;
yet a person who is upright and kind is more difficult to find than even nectar.
The birth of such people— who possess guileless cleverness, whose souls are pure and straightforward, and who are neither arrogant nor haughty—
is rare indeed.
Now, due to the ripening of the sins of the people, Kali has arrived out of season— a king of wicked conduct, characterized by hatred and engaged in deceit.
When that sun-like king, a friend to the world, had set,
his son brought about the rise of faults and increased this darkness.
Surely the wicked man is a disinterested friend to the virtuous who have passed away,
since their fame shines forth by means of the latter part of his conduct.
Therefore, this earth, presided over by a king, must be abandoned;
for when the time is one of strife and the ruler of the land is such, how can there be life for people?
For the virtuous, wives are noble through familiarity with excellence; virtues are the true family lineage; prosperity is auspicious and fame is like the moon;
conduct is appropriate for one's station; and wealth is causeless and free from calamity.
When the king is virtuous, the entire family of his subjects becomes free from the dust of sin.

The world indeed enjoys the pleasures that are the fruits of merit— pleasures arising from the root of wealth of the tree of Dharma, radiant with the finest blossoms of faultless desires— if it is not destroyed by the winds of calamity brought about by an evil king.
Kali was the time, the child was the lord, and his prowess was the fire of the funeral pyre;
it was a period crowded with the vetālas of wicked men, swollen by untimely calamities.
Joy is dejected, my intellect is weary, and the glory of happiness has lost its youth;
now I have no desire for the enjoyment of wealth or the pursuit of sensual pleasures.
Wealth, land, home, wife, sons, servants, and attendants—
alas, what an endless acquisition of mental anguish and physical disease for men!
Just as the harsh splendors of the summer heat increase,
so too does the fever of craving blaze within embodied beings.
Even with vast floods of wealth acquired by kings,
the thirst of men is never quenched, just as the waters of the salt ocean do not satisfy it.
If that very same muttering of the wealthy— "it is not, it is not"— which arises from dissatisfaction,
were to become tranquility in a previous birth, who then would there be?

What is the use of wealth accompanied by ill omens and following after strife, delusion, and greed; what is the use of enjoyments that end in separation and are beset by diseases resulting from the habit of falling into hundreds of calamities; or what is the use of false pride consisting of honors and insults received while serving at the palace of a king?
In this time of fear at the end of an eon, only dispassion is the fit object of enjoyment for one who seeks health.
When the time has passed that was stainless from the sight of one's own kin and friends, and when a period of extreme delusion and impurity has arrived;
For men whose minds have bathed in the waters of tranquility and who have abandoned all exertion, dwelling in the solitude of the forest is a source of comfort and a true blessing.
Having reflected thus for a long time, he attained supreme detachment;
for suffering leads to delusion for the foolish, but to discernment for the wise.
Having given everything to those who asked, he departed for the hermitage of the Sugata;
for his mind was drawn by the fetters of prosperity, as one intent upon the happiness of truth does not go forth.
The very moment the royal swan remembered his pure mind, the earth no longer appealed to him, just as a lake does not appeal to one who has reached the ocean.

When the fire of passion for enjoyments— soiled by the smoke of unbearable delusion— has departed, and the mind has gradually attained coolness through the gushing stream of the nectar of contentment,
these women are no longer [attractive], with their limbs as fickle as the waves of drinking-intoxication and their bodies like those of courtesans.
Even for those possessed of tranquility, the momentary meeting with a frown creates an obstacle to prosperity.
Having destroyed the hardships of the path of existence through the teaching of the Omniscient One, he entered the stainless state by means of the life of renunciation;
having attained total equanimity, that sage of incomparable radiance became one who has set out for liberation beyond all marks.
Beholding that accomplishment of enlightenment by Jyotiṣka, the monks, filled with wonder,
questioned the Blessed One, who then related the account of his former life.
Just as seeds sown in hundreds of fields,
so too do people experience the unfailing ripening of the fruits of their karmic actions.
Long ago, in the city of Bandhumatī belonging to King Bandhumat,
there lived a glorious and illustrious householder named Anaṅgana.
Then, on one occasion in the morning, the Teacher, the perfectly enlightened Buddha named Vipaśyin, arrived at that city during his wandering among the people, as is the lot of the virtuous.
Surrounded by sixty-two thousand monks,
he came through the gate of Ānaṅgana with faith, bowed, and was invited [to stay].
He was served for three months with all necessary provisions;
likewise, the king himself, having prostrated, invited him.
Permeated by those two through a persistent rivalry for enjoyments—
enjoyments fit for citizens and fit for kings— he was overcome by the bodiless god of love.
Seeing him honored with the magnificent splendor of an elephant-standard, a jeweled parasol, and chowries, the king, devoid of a wife, became afflicted by love.
Śatakratu, partial toward that being of pure conduct,
rendered assistance with divine splendor for the worship of the Jina.
With that divine splendor, he worshipped the Blessed One,
before whom even the glory of a universal monarch became a vessel for shame.
With rays from jewels that eclipsed the luster of the moon and sun, with fragrant garlands of unfading cloth variegated by the pollen of *kāñkī* flowers, and with fruits of trembling trees;
with chowries being raised and lowered by the playful movements of the heads of those bowing in devotion.
Perceiving that the Sugata had been thus honored by him, the king bowed down in shame.
Thus, in former times, that noble one of merit, free from passion, obtained through devotion a much greater fruit from the Teacher due to the ripening of his auspicious deeds;
yet for him, whose mind was stainless, this [present attainment] arose from a single moment of aspiration.
Just like the sun, he became a source of light, yet he remained dependent upon his feet.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Victor, whose three bodies were illuminated by stainless wisdom, for the purpose of instructing the monks in their vows.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Legend of Jyotiṣka," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
10. The Legend of Sundarīnandā.

There are certain fortunate beings in this world who, possessing compassion directed toward the welfare of sentient beings, endure many fears; with minds tender with affection, they zealously bestow the supreme favor for the sake of the virtue of men. (KAvk 10.1)
In former times, Nanda, the son of the Śākya king, went to Kapilavastu to see the Blessed One, who was delighted by the Nyagrodha grove.
At the conclusion of a discourse on renunciation and mantras, the Blessed One spoke with affection to him who stood before him: "Let the going forth be accepted."
Having propitiated him and presented his request, Nanda replied:
"O Blessed One, although I have obtained merit, I do not desire the life of a renunciant."
Having become an attendant to the entire community of monks,
I shall serve them with all necessary requisites, providing whatever they desire.
Having spoken thus, the prince, whose lotus-feet were touched by those with jeweled crowns,
went to his own palace, longing for his wife.
Having approached his beloved Sundarī, who was as beautiful as Rati, he—
unable to endure even a moment’s separation— revelled in that excellent garden.
Then, on one occasion, the Blessed One, who by his very nature is fond of those possessing virtuous qualities,
went in person to the house of Nanda together with the community of monks.
With a joyful countenance, Nanda performed obeisance at his feet; having honored him as he sat there in great delight, he addressed him with this request: KAvk 10.9.
Of what sprouts of merit is such a ripening as this?
That the Blessed One himself has performed this favor of granting his vision.
Whether it be remembering, hearing of, or even seeing the Great-souled Ones—
this is the great succession of fruits of the creeper of virtue.
Upon seeing this great and friendly radiance,
who indeed would not experience the glorious blossoming of their heart?
The sight of the great is indeed more dear than giving, yields greater fruit than merit, and is more praiseworthy than virtuous conduct. (KAvk 10.13)
While he was speaking thus, words tender with devotion and affection,
the Blessed One, having accepted the worship offered before him, prepared to depart.
Nanda followed after him, carrying in a pure golden vessel excellent offerings,
like his own sweet disposition.
Seeing the Blessed One walking on the road behind her,
Sundarī, unable to endure separation, gazed at him with a devoted side-long glance.
In the presence of her elders, that beloved, casting aside her naturally tremulous gaze out of fear, with her eyes half-closed and her face slightly bowed,
remained for a moment looking away; yet that very act was all the more significant.
"O Lord, you must not go," he said, as if with a voice choked by tears.
Seeing his beloved with her face trembling and breathing a sigh of relief, Nanda said, "I have indeed arrived; it has not been long."
Then, as the Blessed One arrived at his own hermitage, [the king], unable to bear the separation, said with palms joined in reverence: "I shall now go to my own home."
Then, as he sat upon his throne, the Blessed One spoke with a smile to him who stood bowed before him: "What is this haste in your departure now?"

Alas! The minds of those whose reeds of being are tormented by the delusion of affection for the taste of sense-objects are turned away from renunciation and intent only upon the pleasures of the home.
Life itself is adorned by virtues;
virtue is adorned by discernment; and that tranquility which is adorned by dispassion is further adorned by peace.
O wise one, that dullness— which is like an unbearable thorn— placed in the heart of a friend is reckoned by those who know the time of death as the total futility of life;
for these people, whose minds are devoid of detachment and discernment, are just like beasts.
Moments pass and come again like the revolutions of a wheel's rim for those who are devoid of defining characteristics.
Merit is never difficult for those possessed of courage; learning for those possessed of intelligence; moral conduct for those possessed of knowledge;

and happiness for all those possessed of fortune. For those possessed of tranquility, nothing at all is hard to obtain. Yet, even a tiny fraction of a lifespan is difficult to attain from the abode of all things.
Salutations to that [fate] which, through its fruitlessness, brings about the destruction of one who is already pitiable.
In this ocean of sense-objects, which turns counter-clockwise, whose essence is full of beauty, and which is agitated by the emergence of the fierce crocodiles of pride;
in this ocean where the submarine fire of the intensely radiant and powerful passionlessness is ever-present—
for men, intense dispassion alone is the bridge, the means of crossing, and the refuge.
Therefore, O Prince, having conquered your senses, accept the life of renunciation;
for these royal fortunes, though they offer the pleasure of union, are as fleeting as women.
Let the undertaking of the religious life be made solely for the sake of spiritual welfare;
let this miserable grasp of the hollow household and the cycle of existence be abandoned.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, which were an ocean of compassion,
Nanda replied to him, constrained by his former affection.
"O Blessed One, for me renunciation is always only through you;
yet, for the sake of benefiting the community of monks, my supreme devotion shall remain at home."
Having spoken thus, being unable to transgress the word of the Blessed One,
yet being pulled by his love for his beloved, his mind became agitated like a swing.
Again and again, the Blessed One gave him instruction on his vows;
for those intent on helping others do not consider whether one is worthy.
When Nanda, his senses unsubdued, did not desire that renunciation,
then the word of the Blessed One fell of its own accord upon his body.
At that moment, Nanda, clad in saffron robes with bowl in hand,
shone with the radiance of one who inspires fearlessness and with the marks of a Great Man.
By the command of the Jina, he became a forest-dweller and an alms-bowl eater;
through his outward appearance, he entered the state of homelessness as a wearer of rag-robes.
Even though he had become a wandering mendicant, he constantly bore his beloved Śyāmā within his heart,
just as the moon bears the luster of its spot, even when it has been eclipsed.
We do not know by what path some inexplicable passion enters the mind— as if it were made of crystal— so that it does not depart even when washed away.
With a complexion pale from separation and wearing a closely-fitting saffron robe,
he stole away the splendor of the moon, which was itself marred by the stain of evening clouds.
Wandering in the forest, unable to endure his separation and having forgotten his fortitude,
he did not forget Sundarī, the very birthplace of the god of love.
Motionless in his meditation upon her face, which was like the full moon,
he sat for an inconceivably long time upon that rocky surface.
"Aha! Even the Blessed One has exerted such effort to bestow his favor;
yet, because my mind is possessed by passion, I do not attain purity."
I have heard of the conduct of those wandering in saṃsāra who abide by the vow of non-attachment;
nevertheless, my mind does not forget that fawn-eyed woman.
Upon his body, made beautiful by the saffron dye clinging from his beloved, he wore the monastic robe;
with a hand resting upon the curve of her full breasts, he held the alms-bowl.
"This passion of mine increases"—or perhaps it is merely increasing like that of another—yet his constant meditation, which has awakening as its ultimate goal, takes that very state as its object.
"Know, O innocent one, that I have reached you in an instant"—having spoken thus as she was about to depart, he added:
"Alas! I have subsequently taken up this vow of ingratitude, which has become an obstacle to my seeing you."
When she said, "I must not go," her voice trembled with great agitation; yet, even while her elders remained there, she did not set aside the fan but grasped the hem of his garment with her hand—
she who, though drawing a line upon the surface of the earth with her foot, was not noticed by him as he looked elsewhere.
By her, through a command charmingly disguised as an absolute prohibition, my mind has been bound.
Separated from me, that fawn-eyed woman surely does not sleep, lamenting in her grief within the palace like a female ruddy goose on a riverbank.
"Alas, my beloved! Like a gambler obsessed with his dice, I have embraced this false vow solely because my heart has been stolen by you."
"Having abandoned this vow for now, let us go to the presence of our beloved;
for those scorched by the fire of passion, the heat of asceticism is indeed unbearable."
Seeing me, a cruel man, returned after such a long time, I know not what the princess will do, consumed by a fresh surge of wrath.
In every case, an unbearable injury caused by love inevitably leads to transformation;
for a speck of dust clinging to oil is indeed difficult to remove.
"At the very moment I see the forest devoid of the Blessed One, I must go home; this is my firm resolve."
On this very stone slab, with beautiful mountain minerals,
I shall paint that moon-faced woman, having obtained her as the support for my fortitude.
Or rather, how can that beloved enter the domain of a painting—
she whose nectar, blue lotuses, and moons are the very measures of beauty?
Her gaze is like a forest of coral on the shore of an ocean of loveliness, where blue lotuses are swayed by bees moving like startled deer;
and the radiance of her bimba-fruit lips is a path for the multitude of faultless moonbeams— such is that indescribable splendor of her face.
How does the body attain such beauty, which is the very essence of the wonders of the path of art?
Having reflected thus, he slowly drew Sundarī upon the surface of the stone, his fingers trembling and bathed in tears released from his face.
Having placed his beloved before him— she who seemed like a reflection brought forth by his own volition— he spoke with a voice faltering from tears.
Having painted my beloved, whose face is like the autumn moon and who is a rain of every happiness for my eyes, I do not see her for even a moment, choked with tears;
this is surely the fruit of one who has undertaken a vow indifferent to separation from that slender lady.
A curse accompanied by throbbing pain has somehow come upon me because of my own sin.
With the splendor of a forest of blooming lotuses, the water of her tears has been drawn forth by the force of longing;
let this anger born of obstacles encountered at that moment be cast aside.
O beautiful one, give me an answer; why do you maintain this silence?
Truly, this vow of my mind, which consists of waves of passion for you, is my sacred observance.
Seeing him speaking thus from afar, and seeing that [image] painted there,
the monks approached with indignation and addressed the Blessed One.
O Blessed One, this renunciation has been bestowed upon me by you solely out of affection for one so ill-behaved, like a garland of flowers placed around a dog.
Nanda, intent on the muttering of her words and having made the face of the beautiful Ākhilyā his object of meditation, remained at his ease upon the surface of the rock.
Having heard this, the Blessed One summoned Nanda from the forest and asked him, "What is this? as he was bewildered by the separation from his beloved.
He replied, "O Blessed One, it is true that my mind, being intensely attached to my beloved,
finds no delight even in this forest which is approved by the monks."
Having heard these words of Daṇḍa, the Blessed Jina spoke to him,
while with the radiance of his moon-like face he seemed to close the lotus of Rāga’s passion.
"O virtuous one, it is not fitting for your mind to be thus possessed by passion;
the hearts of those intent on what is wholesome are not drawn away by obstacles."

Where is this yoga, which involves the exertion of renouncing enjoyments like blades of thin grass? And where is this censurable pursuit, which merely corresponds to the tasting of a fragment of momentary pleasure?
This path of Māra, difficult to cross, carries away one's merit by its very nature.
For those blinded by passion, that which arises from the yoke becomes suddenly unbearable.
Having thus delivered a long discourse on dispassion to him, the Blessed One said,
"You must remain here," and departed himself for his own task.
