Reflecting that this very moment was suitable for his departure,
Nanda set out for his own home, joyful and eager to behold Sundarī.
As he proceeded, after a long time he somehow reached the road leading toward the city, which was crowded with many monasteries whose doors were closed.
Then the Blessed One, the Omniscient, perceiving that he was preparing to depart out of passion, approached him and said: "Nanda, where are you going so quickly?"
He said: "O Blessed One, for now I have no delight in the forest;
for indeed, no action bears fruit for those whose minds are not at rest."
She is the Goddess Śrī, smiling with her chowries; she is that row of lovely palaces made of jewels;
she is that beautiful young garden-land, where lovely creepers sway in the gentle breeze;
she is that slender, fair-waisted, and beautiful maiden, a creeper-like bow for the God of the Flower-arrows.
My mind does not release its attachment, as if it were the latent impressions from previous births.
"With a mind still possessed of passion, I practice the holy life,
constrained by the cage of my vows like a bird bound in a trap."
"Having abandoned [the world], I shall go forth; let there be for me even an inexhaustible hell.
For a cloth dyed with madder does not attain the state of being free from passion."
To him who was speaking thus repeatedly and preparing to go to his own abode,
the Blessed Jina, with a mind intent on showing favor, stopped him and said:
O Nanda, do not commit such a transgression, for what is censured— whether heard or unheard—
is exactly how an ordinary person proceeds when following the instructions of the wise.
The minds of the wise, who are adorned with virtuous conduct and whose faults have been dispelled by discernment,
do not turn toward unwholesome actions even for the sake of attaining a pleasure devoid of essence.
For one seized by intense passion,
is your attachment to this lowest of acts— not an object of loathing— anything other than a cause for shame?
Born from a womb and attached to a womb, sucking at the breast and rubbing their teats—
alas, they feel no shame, having met their dissolution within this very birth!
Constant avoidance of the virtuous and attachment to the lap of one's mother is seen only in those beasts whose minds are struck by delusion.
"Let this pride in sporting with women be abandoned by you;
for the destruction of serpents along with their enjoyments has been seen within the hole of a termite mound."
Whose pleasure, even when base, does not produce detachment?
For one who finds it even at its conclusion, he is never turned away from it.
Having escaped from the net of the house, why do you rush back to that very place?
For once a deer has gone out, it does not enter the snare again.
Thus, constrained by the command of the Blessed One according to those words,
Nanda returned once more to the hermitage, thinking only of Sundarī.
Then, on one occasion, having instructed Nanda to clean the hermitage,
the Blessed One departed once more, intent upon bestowing his favor by accepting a seat.
As Nanda proceeded to clear the hermitage according to that instruction,
the dust did not rise from the ground, as if passion had departed from his heart.
Then, when he had gone to fetch water from the far bank, the jar—
which had been repeatedly filled and lifted up— became empty once again.
Because of that obstacle to his journey, Nanda’s mind became exceedingly distressed;
yet, abandoning [his hesitation], he departed, eager for the sight of Sundarī.
Then, having perceived with his divine eye that he was departing, the Omniscient One suddenly approached and spoke to him, shattering the pillar of his pride and his desires: KAvk 10.88.
Alas, despite being heated by contact with the vessel and possessing a deep red luster,
your stain of oil does not subside, just like that of a lamp.
Enough of this longing for you; like indigo dye, some inexplicable passion is firmly attached to your heart, since even now you have not become dispassionate.
At its commencement, pleasure blinds one with immediate distress;
once the primary union of limbs has occurred, it embraces one as if with loathing.
Through attachment to the taste of sense objects, as if by evil friends in the form of the senses,
a person is cast into hell, which is a whirlpool of unbearable calamities.
Even by a mere touch, evil association causes distress,
like the putrid stench rising from a rotting fish carcass.
Association with a spiritual friend brings about virtue in every way;
like a pervasive fragrance of sandalwood, it renders one worthy of great honor.
When this was said, the Blessed One, having directly demonstrated the path of the non-existent through the touch of his nose, gave him instruction on that very attachment.
Then, taking Nanda with him, the Blessed One went to Gandhamādana,
fanned by the celestial maidens with yak-tail whisks, like Viriñci himself.

There, having shown him a one-eyed female laborer whose body was afflicted by an undesirable affliction from being scorched by a forest fire, the Jina said: KAvk_10.97: "There, having shown him a one-eyed female laborer whose body was afflicted by an undesirable affliction from being scorched by a forest fire, the Jina said:"
"Do you see this woman, Nanda, whose form is irreproachable in its languor?
To whomsoever she is suitable, this lovely-to-behold woman will be pleasing."
For those who perceive both the existent and the non-existent, passion does not exist; they behold the beauty [of all things].
He for whom a person is dear is the one who finds delight in this world.
"Abandoning all partiality, Nanda, speak the truth:
what is the difference between the beauty of this woman and that of Sundarī?"
Because we do not desire it, we are not at all aware of its other beauty;
yet that which is requested becomes dear to the petitioner, and thus it attains loveliness.
I perceive no distinction whatsoever between her and this [other woman];
the loveliness in this machine of flesh, bone, and sinews is merely a matter of convention.
Thus questioned by the Blessed One, Nanda replied to him, constrained by respect, though the question was entirely inappropriate: "What kind of question is this? (KAvk 10.103).
"What is this that the Blessed One says? What kind of mockery is this grief?
Or where else could the teachers of the universe, the powerful ones, be disciplined?"
Rati was captivated by the superior beauty of Sādhikasundarī,
seeing whom even Smara, the conqueror of the worlds, no longer remembered his own delight.
The bed of night-lotuses does not bloom because of her splendor as if by moonlight;
people who rely solely on fame do not recognize other virtues.
Beholding that mass of flowers— the essence of the fragrance of your face— bound within your thick tresses,
I imagine they have fled to the forest like swans and deer out of fear of those who steal the beauty of your graceful gait and glances.
That gazelle-eyed woman, incomparable and familiar to me, cannot be depicted even with numerous intentions and manifold variations;
for in the balance of comparison, my own face is far lighter than hers.
He is surely the lord of the stars who has ascended into the sky.
If that face of hers— which is charming with the playful dance of her most graceful, creeper-like eyebrows, and which is a true Nandana grove— cannot be obtained,
then this renunciation is my supreme merit; I am her servant, her very servant.
Why do I carry this burden of ascetic observances, which has become like a heavy load?
Having heard these words of Nanda, which were filled with passion, the Blessed One, having cast him aside,
led him by his supernatural power to the abode of the gods.
And there, in the pleasure garden of Śatakratu,
he showed him the lovely celestial women born from the churning of the nectar.
With the spreading streams of crimson luster arising from the groves of his lotus-feet,
he seemed as if followed by the forests of coral on the shores of the ocean.
With her hands, which were like broad-lashed ministers and surpassed the lotus,
she was joined as if with the natural sprouts of the *pārijāta* tree.
With faces as beautiful as the moon, which were like kinsmen to the joy of Love through their loveliness, sweetness, and charm, and which seemed to close lotuses in playful sport; KAvk_10.114.
With their enchanting glances, like those of black antelopes,
they were as if enveloped by floods of nectar touched by the petals of the *kālakūṭa* poison.
Upon suddenly beholding them, whose youthful beauty was at its full bloom,
Nanda’s face became radiant with joy as if bathed in perspiration.
Upon those women with lotus-faces, eyes like broad blue lilies, and breasts as dense clusters of kunda blossoms,
Nanda’s heart fell simultaneously and was made to tremble by the playful swaying of a swing.
Then the Blessed One spoke to Nanda, whose mind was fixed upon her:
"Nanda, your mind delights with affection at the sight of these women."
What difference is there between the beauty of these women and that of Sundarī?
Her excellence is clearly perceived by its very contrast.
If the beauty of the apsarases has been surpassed by yours,
then I shall, in time, make these very women dependent upon you.
"Practice celibacy with a healthy mind and a serene intellect;
then I shall grant you a host of apsarases."
Thus, having gained certainty from the words of the Blessed One, Nanda said,
"So be it," and set his mind upon the vow with the hope of attaining celestial nymphs.
Out of a desire for union with her, he became indifferent toward his own wife;
for there is no constancy in affection when it is overcome by the incomparable power of another's virtues.
Ah! The habitual affection of men, dried up by long separation from those with whom they have lived, suddenly runs toward another.
The loves of embodied beings, though charming with their momentary youth,
are neither true, nor eternal, nor sources of happiness, due to the loss of affection.
Then the Blessed One brought Nanda back to his own hermitage in an instant;
through that resolve, he practiced the holy life with disciplined vows.
With his mind elsewhere, he remembered the perfection of Sundarī’s beauty;
for joy that is momentarily forgotten becomes a stain even upon virtues.
Then, once while wandering about, the wise Nanda beheld somewhere a land inhabited by those condemned to the Karāla hell, filled with large jars.
Upon seeing her, trembling and distressed, wondering "What is this?",
he then questioned those attached to her about the cause of that terrible hell.
They said to him: "This ground, strewn with hundreds of heated cauldrons, has been prepared for Prince Nanda, who is full of joy and passion."
That man of false vows has not yet attained freedom from passion;
he practices celibacy indeed only with the hope of union with celestial nymphs.
For those who have taken false vows, who are greedy, and who are stained by passion, hatred, and the kaṣāyas,
there is an inexhaustible destruction within these eternally boiling cauldrons.
Having heard this, Nanda, his body covered with a cloak of horripilation,
felt as if his very self had fallen away from him due to remorse.
Having approached him, he himself became one who had abandoned the latent tendencies of dwelling with passion,
and who was fully restrained by the supreme holy life.
Then, through the destruction of his dense delusion and the consequent liberation from doubt,
he attained the clarity of great light, just as the water of the ocean attains clarity in autumn.
Free from desire, having attained tranquility and reached the supreme consummation,
that man of pure intellect approached the Blessed One and spoke.
"O Blessed One, I have no need for Apsarases nor for Sundarī;
these glories of the sensory realms are but shadows at their end, accompanied by suffering."
To the very extent that this lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) of phenomena is meditated upon,
to that same extent those whose mental activities are free from obscuration find peace.
Thus, as Daṇḍa spoke, gradually approaching the state of one who is afflicted,
the Blessed One considered him to have attained the purity of Nirvāṇa.
"Of which roots of merit was this fruit obtained by Nanda?
Thus questioned by the monks who had approached him, the Conqueror spoke to them:
Through merits acquired in other births and by one who practiced virtuous deeds,
Nanda attained the perfection of the fruits of his roots of goodness.
Born into a vast and stainless lineage, her body is like that of the god of love; she is a friend to the virtuous, her conduct is ever dear to the good,
her mind is bathed in the waters of tranquility, and her movement is the very embodiment of natural grace.
This is the emergence of vast fruit for men from the flower of virtue.
In former times, in the city of Aruṇāvatī, King Aruṇa showed great reverence toward the stūpa of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Vipaśyin.
While it was being constructed, a twice-born son named Maitra,
who was destined to partake in great enjoyment of merit, became its builder.
Through the power of that merit and his vow, he was born into the family of a householder;
he himself became the provider of the Jantuka-bath festival for the community of monks.
In former times, that man of virtuous conduct, who was an attendant to a Pratyekabuddha,
constructed a magnificent stūpa, radiant with excellent garlands and canopies.
By virtue of that merit and his aspiration, he became the son of Kṛki, the lord of Kāśī,
known by the name Dyutimat, and was marked with divine characteristics.
When the Arhat Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, had passed into final nirvāṇa,
a stūpa made of the seven precious gems was erected by the king of Kāśī.
His son, the radiant Haumacchatra, having ascended to the shining [heaven],
was now born as Nanda in the Śākya clan through that very same meditative application.

Thus, through certain vast merits arising from well-performed deeds acquired through a succession of previous births, Nanda obtained a stainless and noble family, supreme beauty, and enjoyments associated with tranquility; and in the end, he attained the state of the Sugata, the true goal.
"So be it," said the Blessed One; he then gave various instructions on the nature of well-performed deeds to the community of monks regarding the causes of Nanda's auspiciousness.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Legend of Sundarīnandā," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

11. The Legend of Virūḍhaka A person of pure intellect ascends to the highest station by means of the stainless steps of wholesome virtue; one of defiled intellect falls into the abysses of hell, into regions of terrible darkness. (KAvk 11.1)
Formerly, in the prosperous city of Kapilavastu belonging to the Śākyas,
there was a beautiful slave girl belonging to a great Śākya chief.
One named Mālikā, who had exerted herself in the sciences and possessed skill in all the arts,
was as worthy of virtues as a garland is of the God of Love.
At her lord’s command, intent upon gathering flowers in the excellent garden,
she saw the Sugata approaching before her as he wandered about.
Seeing its setting at the end of that [day], her mind became serene;
like the clear autumn season, it gladdened her heart.
Then, her resolve strengthened by the affection of the world, she thought:
"Perhaps even the Blessed One will accept my alms-offering because of my meritorious deeds."
Having understood her intention, the All-Knowing One, overwhelmed with compassion,
extended his bowl and said to her, "O auspicious lady, give."
Having given [the gift] and bowed to him, her desires completely fulfilled,
she made a solemn vow for the cessation of the suffering of servitude.

Then, on one occasion, a twice-born friend of her father’s arrived; having come to that region as an astrologer, he saw her and spoke in amazement: KAvk_11.9: "Then, on one occasion, a twice-born friend of her father’s arrived; having come to that region as an astrologer, he saw her and spoke in amazement:"
"Alas! You are the daughter of that illustrious householder;
yet, deprived of kinsmen and stripped of wealth and enjoyments, you have fallen into servitude."
Ah! Prosperities are as fickle as the flickering play of a serpent’s tongue in this worldly existence, like lightning flashing for a mere moment at the onset of a thick mass of delusion.
"Do not worry about those who are to be approached; I know by the marks on your hands that you will soon become the beloved of the lord of the earth."
"I see upon your hand, which is as delicate as a lotus of Fortune,
the forms of a garland, a discus, and a goad," having said this, the brahmin departed.
Then Mādhava appeared, the friend of spring who is a companion to the god of love, and who is worthy of the good fortune of being embraced by the creepers.
The cluster of blossoms on the Ashoka tree shone like the tongue of that lion-like spring, the enemy of the elephants of pride, as it bent with its crooked arrogance.
The cluster of campaka flowers, a thief of the loveliness of the cheeks of young women,
attained the state of being bound within the tresses of fair-eyed maidens.
Spring brought about the death of the woman separated from her lover by means of the mango trees;
for the powerful, when indifferent to the slaughter of others, are formidable.
The mango creepers became entirely the object of enjoyment for the bees,
just as the charming fortunes of the wicked become the exclusive prey for the greedy.
With his bow made of mango creepers and his arrows fixed upon it, the cuckoo sang as if he were a bard for Kandarpa: "Victory! KAvk_11.19 //
At this juncture, the illustrious Prasenajit, lord of Kosala,
having gone out on a hunt, was carried away by his horse and arrived at that place.
Having dismounted from his horse, that archer, whose form was like the god of love,
beheld a maiden of incomparable beauty, like a second Rati.
As he gazed upon her, the mind of that great-souled one expanded;
through the path of his vision, the god of love entered it out of wonder.
Seeing her with her head bowed in shame, suddenly overcome by trepidation, the lord of men, captivated by the flood of her radiance, thought:
Who is this new young woman with a moon-like face, dark-complexioned and with tremulous pupils,
whose radiance constantly causes the lotuses of our eyes to bloom?
Upon her face, which has lips red as the *pāṭala* flower and is frequented by bees wandering in the fragrance of *bakula* blossoms, I behold the beloved Spring, whose weapon is the moon.
Oh, how unfading is the loveliness of her body, the ornament of youth,
by which even my steadfastness seems to have dissolved like wax upon a conch shell!
Oh, how wonderful is the extraordinary quality of the honey-cluster even at its very beginning,
by which even the six-legged bee is unable to move from one step to the next!
Having reflected thus, King Bhīpa, considering her to be a forest deity,
questioned her and learned the account of those events as it was related by her in due order.
Then, having been offered hospitality there by her with fans of young leaves and pure,
cool waters, the king attained relief.
Exhausted from massaging his lotus-like feet,
he suddenly fell asleep as her hand made contact with them.
Then, in an instant, his fatigue from hunting was allayed;
through that divine touch, he perceived her to be Rati herself, having assumed another form.
Then the great Śākya,
having heard that the Lord of Kosala had arrived, went to that region and honored him who was worthy of worship.
Requested with great respect by him, he gave Mālikā— who was like his own daughter—
to that man worthy of jewels, as a garland of auspiciousness for the god of love.
Taking her— who was like a victory banner for the birth of the Mind-born God (Kāma) and possessed a radiant smile—
the king mounted his elephant and returned to his own city.
On that lap of the mountain-like elephant,
the fresh jasmine creeper shone, joined with King Vasanta, its flickering curls like bees.
Having reached the capital city together with Sundarī,
he sported in a magnificent palace with its jeweled turrets and lofty chambers.
The queen named Varṣākārā was the king’s first beloved;
he regarded her as having an unchanging disposition, just as the earth regards the royal fortune.
She [was amazed] by his divine touch, and he by her perfection of form;
through the excellence of each other's qualities, they both reached a state of supreme wonder.
"The elder sister possesses a divine form, while the other possesses divine touch"—this wonderful report concerning them spread throughout the worlds. (KAvk 11.39)
In the meantime, when the monks in the hermitage asked about the cause of their divine forms and touch, the Blessed One, the Jina, spoke.
Long ago, there were two beloved wives of a householder named the brahmin Śrutavara: they were named Śirīṣikā and Cetī.
Then once, his sister’s husband,
having gradually attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha through renunciation, came to his sister's house.
By her husband's command, she remained there for three months,
invited with devotion, while her two co-wives were left unpresented.
Having honored him with lovely and soft enjoyments in another birth,
they have now been born endowed with beautiful forms and divine touch.
Having first applied discipline to those who were ploughed, he took up the wealth of cattle;
then, in excellent fields where austerity had made the soil supple, he attained a state of extreme sweetness.
At that time, the appropriate seed was sown, which is the supreme power of virtuous action.
The abundance of fruits, radiant with its own ripeness, is enjoyed by those of noble intellect.
Having heard these true words of the Omniscient One, the monks,
having resolved that it was so, took refuge in peace.
Then, in due course, a son was born to the king by his queen Mālikā;
he was named Virūḍhaketi-mukhya and had applied himself diligently to the sciences.
He had a dear friend, the son of his family priest, who was of equal age with him;
he was renowned as Duḥkhamātṛka because he was born through the sorrow of his mother.
Once, accompanied by him, Virūḍhaka, mounted on a horse and having gone out for the hunt,
reached the garden of the best of the Śākyas.
There, the Śākyas, with weapons raised, treated him with contempt, speaking with arrogance: "This is the son of our slave-girl! (KAvk 11.50).
Having returned to his own city, he brooded over their enmity and pride;
for the slander arising from family pride is like the piercing sting of a thorn to embodied beings.
As he was being consumed by that [sorrow], through the thought of a remedy for it,
an intense longing arose in him for the kingdom, even while his father was still alive.
Having brought five hundred ministers, headed by Cārāyaṇa,
under his own control, he sowed dissension among them through strategic means.
Then, at one time, that lord of the earth, having developed discernment,
felt an ever-increasing reverence for hearing the instruction on the Dharma.
Having restrained his horse and mounted his chariot, Prasenajit, self-controlled,
went to see the Blessed One, the Omniscient One.
Having performed the salutation at the feet of the Blessed One while staying in his hermitage, he,
with a mind clarified by His grace, listened to the lineage of the Dharma.
Cārāyaṇa also, having gone quickly by chariot to the city with speed,
performed the consecration of the prince within that very interval.
Then, having addressed the Blessed One, the king prepared to depart;
he saw neither his followers before him, nor the chariot, nor his minister.
The lord of the earth saw from afar Varṣākārā, who was approaching slowly on foot with her painted face.
Having questioned them and learned from their words that Virūḍhaka had been consecrated,
he sent Mālokā away for her son to enjoy his sovereignty.
Taking Varṣākāra with him, he went from Rājagṛha to the city named Ajātaśatru, belonging to his friend,
King Ajātaśatru.
Deprived of his parasol, afflicted by hunger, thirst,
and fatigue, he went along as if vomiting sighs with his long-drawn breaths.
By whom has unerring happiness been attained? Whose life-span is long?
And for whom has the sudden destruction of prosperity not been witnessed following upon its heels?
Having eaten that stale radish, which was as long as the very root of his karma,
and having drunk some water for a moment, he fell down, afflicted by cholera.
Not understanding impermanence, people fall into delusion;
and that [delusion] arises from a thirst for means regarding a body that is itself a collection of misfortunes.
As soon as Ajātaśatru heard that the Lord of Kosala had arrived,
he went out and saw him, his face covered in dust and his life departed.
Having performed the funeral rites for his body after it was followed by his wife,
he went to see the Blessed One, the Sugata, for the sake of quelling his suffering.
Having bowed to him, he said: "O Blessed One, the Lord of Kosala has gone to his death, impoverished, after having sent my friend to the city."
Fie upon this wretched abundance of wealth, a source of infamy, by which this prosperity was not even made a means of service for my friend! (KAvk 11.69)
What is the use of that man who lives, whose friendship becomes fruitless when he reaches a friend in distress, having placed his hope in that friend's heart?
For those for whom fortune is a means to serve friends, wealth is a means to assist the wretched,
and life itself is a means to protect those who are afraid, their existence is truly well-lived.
"O Blessed One, what evil deed was committed by him in a previous birth,
the ripening of which caused him to fall into such a miserable state at the end?"
Thus questioned by the lord of the earth with tearful eyes, the Blessed One spoke to him,
radiating the moonlight of his teeth as he dispensed the cooling balm for his distress.
Do not grieve, O protector of the earth; this is the inherent nature established within existence.
Such indeed is the impermanence of all things that are unreal.
In this vast forest of saṃsāra, the bee of desire, naturally fickle,
incessantly devours the mass of filaments— the life-force of the lotuses that are people born according to their own whims.
Worldly enjoyments flicker like the eyes of a startled doe; fortune is as imperceptible in an instant as lightning flashing from a cloud over the people;
youth possesses a glow as fleeting as the morning sun upon a lotus; and the spark of life quickly perishes on the mountain slope of existence.

The mind is a vessel of loving-kindness, delighting in the welfare of others; it possesses the wealth of the Dharma and is practiced in tranquility and discernment capable of cutting through the breaking of pride.
This is the search for reality for those who find happiness in turning away from the pleasures of sense objects.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, it is a humiliation to be free from all transformation.
People grieve amidst sufferings as if suddenly struck by a stone;
yet they do not perform an immediate remedy for that intense affliction.
What can be done for these people who, though seeing the exertion of existence, are entirely devoid of discernment and,
out of delusion, touch upon what is unwholesome?
Long ago, a brahmin named Suśarman, having obtained some roots from somewhere,
placed them in his mother’s hand and went to the riverbank to bathe.
In that interval, she too, bowing down with the alms-bowl in her hand, offered that very [food] directly to the Pratyekabuddha who had arrived.
Then, having bathed, her son returned quickly, hungry,
and at the start of the meal, he begged his mother for his own root.
"Rejoice in this merit, my son; it has been offered by me to a guest.
Hearing these words of his mother, he felt as if he had been pierced by an arrow.
May my abundant root immediately burst open the belly of that guest who is afflicted by cholera and depart along with his life-breaths.
Thus, due to the excessive anger at his words,
that man who had committed the sin met his end through cholera in his subsequent birth.
Through the ripening of another former merit, that very same Prasenajit,
having attained a vast kingdom, met his end by that very same [means] at the conclusion.
For those traveling on the path of saṃsāra, thus their karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
becomes available for their enjoyment, just like provisions held in one's hand.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, which were both true and beneficial,
and reflecting that it was indeed so, the king bowed to him and departed.
In the meantime, Virūḍhaka, having obtained the kingdom, was approached by the son of the family priest; reminded of his enmity toward the Śākyas, he prepared for their destruction.
He set out for the city of the Śākyas, raising clouds of dust from his elephants, horses, and chariots,
as if creating a delusion that rendered the directions indistinguishable, like the confusion of the intellects.
The omniscient Blessed One, having understood that wicked conduct of his,
went to the vicinity of the Śākya city and stood beneath a withered tree.
Seeing him standing there from a distance, Virūḍhaka approached;
having descended from his chariot and come forward, he bowed and said: ||| KAvk_11.92 |||
O Blessed One, while there are trees here with glossy leaves and dense shade,
why indeed would one seek rest beneath a withered tree?
Thus addressed by the protector of the earth, the Blessed Jina said to him:
"O King, the shadow of one's kinsmen is cooler even than sandalwood."
There is no wealth equal to kinsmen; there is no steadfastness equal to kinsmen;
there is no shade equal to kinsmen; there is no beloved equal to kinsmen.
"O King, these Śākyas are my kinsmen; this beloved one was born near their city.
Out of affection for him, even this tree with its withered branches [is dear to me]."
Having heard this, Virūḍhaka’s indignation subsided; realizing that the Blessed One was indeed a partisan of the Śākyas, he turned back.
The Blessed One, having perceived the impending danger for the Śākyas,
then delivered a teaching of the Dharma for the welfare of those pure beings.
By some the fruit of stream-entry was attained, by others the fruit of once-returning,
and by yet others the fruit of non-returning, through his teaching.
But the remaining Śākyas, of deluded intellect, did not attain that state;
for there are certain birds for whom darkness arises even during the day.
Then, after the king had retired,
the son of the domestic priest awakened the sleeping serpent of enmity.
Urged by him, he set his mind upon the destruction of the Śākya clan;
for the wind of a slanderer stirs up the blazing fire of enmity.
Whose life would not be snatched away by wicked men and vetalas, who are like kings, suddenly raised up by the incantation of a terrible villain? (KAvk 11.103)
Then, as that army, towering with elephants and chariots, advanced,
there arose a great agitation within the city of the Śākyas, whose paths were now blocked.
There, for the sake of protecting the Śākyas,
the Blessed One spoke to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was prepared to take their side.
"This fault of the Śākyas' karma has arisen in every way;
therefore, you must provide protection there by constructing a bridge in the sky."
For a person, auspicious and inauspicious fortunes of inconceivable power come and go repeatedly and without restraint;
yet the syllables of one's karma, inscribed by one's own hand upon the station of one's birth, do not indeed become meaningless.
When the Blessed One had spoken these words and departed, the Śākyas bowed to him and held a consultation as Virūḍhaka drew near.
"We must not commit violence against any living being whatsoever;
let the arrows discharged by our enemies enter only our own bodies."
Having thus reached an agreement, those wise men, with their hands joined in the *viyaṣṭika* gesture and their bows set aside, stood firm for the sake of the great undertaking.
In the meantime, due to his engagement in ritual action,
the Śākya Śampāka, not remaining in his own country and unaware of the news, arrived there.
Seeing the lord of the earth with his army arrayed in the city, he alone,
out of anger, wrought a slaughter of the great warriors in battle.
Slain in battle by that lion among men,
those elephants among heroes attained a state of enviable renown through their glories, as if through white lotuses.
The sword of that king, provoked by his enemies, blazed forth with some inexplicable power;
by its majesty, he advanced against the vast host of his foes.
The Śākyas did not grant entrance to Śampāka because he had slain his enemies;
even though he was their own kinsman, he was abandoned by them for his merciless deed.
Even close kinsmen turn their faces away from one who is cruel, yet they cling closely to a virtuous man;
even from a stranger, generosity is better than wealth, and good deeds are dearer than one's own kin. Fame is more beloved than life itself for those who are ever devoted to propriety.
Exiled by them, he gradually reached the presence of the Blessed One;
for the sake of his own prosperity, he requested from him some personal token.
The Blessed One gave him his own hair, nails, and a piece of cloth;
taking these, he went to the district named Vākuḍa.
There, by the power of his wisdom and through the quality of his valor and enthusiasm, he attained a kingdom; for prosperity is easily obtained everywhere by the steadfast.
Fortune is the innate characteristic of the skillful, fame is that of the learned,
and all successes are the wife of those who have perseverance as their companion.
Remaining there, he then established for the Blessed One a stūpa adorned with various jewels upon a fragment of his hair and nails.
Virūḍhaka also, desiring to cross over the enmity of the Śākyas,
suddenly entered once more by means of a stratagem through the breaking open of a city gate.
Having slain seventy-seven thousand Śākyas there,
he bound a thousand maidens and youths and then carried them away.
Having utterly crushed five hundred Śākyas with elephants and iron maces,
he made the city resemble the city of Death.
The Blessed One, too, having perceived that the Śākyas' enmity had been incited by the persistence of past karma, became despondent for a moment.
Approaching him, the monks, overwhelmed with compassion, asked:
"What terrible deed was committed by the Śākyas, the fruit of which is such as this?"
Thus questioned by them, the Blessed One, the Omniscient, spoke to them:
"This destruction of the Śākyas is due to the ripening of their own karma."
Formerly, when two great fish were caught by fishermen from within a river,
they were then pierced with a hook and, being held fast, caused no further pain.
In another birth, by those very same [beings] who had attained beauty through time,
those two householders were killed and burned after their wealth had been carried off.
Those two fish and those two householders, Virūḍhaka and the priest,
both met their deaths at the hands of the Śākyas— some by the slaves and some by the thieves.
Having heard this account of the succession of the fruits of the Blessed One’s deeds,
all the monks considered it to be entirely non-contradictory.
Then Virūḍhaka, having reached his own city and being intoxicated with the pride of victory, was addressed by his son named Jetā out of affection during their childhood play: ||| KAvk_11.133 |||
"O King, why have you slain the Śākyas? They have committed no offense against us.
Speaking thus, Virūḍhaka killed his own son.
What does a wicked person not trample, destroy, or fail to do?
Like an elephant intoxicated with rut, he crushes everything in his path.
Seated in the assembly and looking down at his own arms, he said:
"Alas! By my enemies, I have been treated like a moth in the fire of my own suffering."
These two abundant arms of mine have become the gateway-arch pillars at the end of time,
attaining the dignity of officiants in the initiation for the total slaughter of the Śākyas.
Hearing of that praiseworthy valor of his, those Śākya maidens who had been carried off spoke with intense agitation, their faces cast down.
For embodied beings bound by the noose of karma,
there is no power to transcend death, even for those possessing wings like birds.
That water by which the submarine fire (Vāḍava) is indeed fully pacified,
that very water the sun seizes at the proper time;
it is beyond the scope of the path of reflection and is the locus of wondrous conduct.
In this entire system of ritual action, who is capable of performing what for whom?
Having heard this, the king,
fierce with the poison of terrible indignation, ordered the cutting off of their hands as swiftly as a horse moves to another step.
On its bank was committed that slaughter of their hands being cut off;
even today, that lotus pond is known on earth as Hastagaṅbhī.
Even upon the creepers they cast the fire of burning chaff; even upon the lotus-stalks, the saw;
and even upon the garlands, the pitiless ones indeed rain down showers of stones.
With their lotus-like hands severed and tormented by intense pain,
they meditated upon the Blessed One in their minds and went to him for refuge, for refuge.
Having understood their intense suffering from being struck in their vital organs,
the Omniscient One thought of the goddess Śacī, who was suitable for comforting them.
With their lotus-like hands born from that touch, clothed in divine garments,
they abandoned their bodies and went to heaven through the clarity of their minds.
Having approached him who was like a god, those women, adorned with divine lotuses and water-lilies,
attained the vast state through the Teacher’s teaching of the Dharma.
When the Blessed One was questioned by the monks regarding the fruit of that karma, he declared:
"These women committed the fault of fickle hands in their mockery of the monks."
Through the ripening of that karma, you were previously devoured by me;
yet, through the clarity of your hearts toward me, you have now attained this auspicious rebirth.
Having spoken thus regarding the variety of the ripening of the fruits of karma, the Blessed One,
in connection with that subject, gave a teaching on the Dharma for those whose [suffering] was exhausted.
In the meantime, a secret agent dispatched by the king,
having learned of the Blessed One’s conduct, approached Virūḍhaka.
He said: "O King, this was told to me by the monks previously;
I see that the fruit of his own karma is imminent for that monarch."
Burned by fire for seven days,
that evil-souled domestic priest shall fall into the unbearable hell named Avīci.
Having heard those words, the king, together with his domestic priest,
stayed with great effort for seven days within a house provided with water.
When only one moment remained of that week and he had entered the inner apartments,
fire blazed forth through the contact with the heat of the sun-gem.
Swiftly consumed by the blazing fire that arose with the speed of the ocean's whirlpools at the time of dissolution, he was instantly incinerated and reached the hellish flames;
for in this world, the passions of the wicked become like hair of fire after death.
Everywhere, for those who possess merit, there are cool lands of steadfast happiness.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Legend of Virūḍhaka," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

12. The Avadāna of the Subduing of Hārītī: The virtuous, with faces moist as nectar, and the rays of the moon, both dispel suffering and point the way to the attainment of happiness; they revive the people and remove the darkness of ignorance; they cause the blossoming smile of the noble mind to unfold. (KAvk 12.1)
In the city named Rājagṛha, the very essence of the earth, there was Bimbisāra,
a lord of the land who was the most excellent among all kings.
He whose arm was the foundation of forbearance and whose mind was the foundation of forbearance— before him,
all other beings quickly cast down their hands.
While he fulfilled the hopes of others through his generosity and heroism,
the grasping for a sword became firmly established in his hand even as he released a flood of jewels.
Once, there occurred in that city a great upheaval,
as turbulent as the time when pride is born from a new rise to power.
To him, who was seated upon his throne and finding leisure in the contemplation of his subjects—
like a father to his people— he made known the welfare of the realm.
O Lord, by your command,
this ocean of people, possessing divine power, always remains within its bounds and never oversteps them.
Why has this sudden onset of obstacles come upon him, who has established his conduct and is proceeding along the path of the righteous?
For when men abide by their own duty and act with peace under a good king,
calamities do not befall even those things that are secret.
By what means are our children being carried away from the homes of us married women, like fruits from trees that have not been properly tended? KAvk 12.10.
But we do not know those beings, O lord of the earth, nor even the illusion by whose power families are reduced to childlessness. (KAvk 12.11)
Thus, by their words, the king became transfused with their distress;
for the supreme suffering of the virtuous enters within like water into a field.
Enveloped for a moment by that intense suffering of the people which pervaded his entire body,
as if by poison, his heart became bewildered.
He said: "What can I do here when it is not within the power of my arms and devoid of human effort?
Indeed, how can countermeasures be applied against things that are so difficult to perceive?"
"Go today, sirs, each to his own abode for one day;
with my vows intact, I myself shall provide for your protection until the end of your own lives."
Having heard these words of the king, the eminent citizens were delighted;
bowing before him with their hands joined in a gesture of worship, they spoke to him.
"O King, because of your attentive listening and your sympathetic hearing,
we who have entrusted our concerns to you no longer experience any weariness."
This very gaze of yours, serene and noble,
rains down as it were the very life-force of these people.
But why is this speech of yours so dear to you—resembling nectar, dispelling heat, gentle, and sweet? What does it not bestow upon us?
Accomplished, grateful, a treasury of compassion, and easy to behold— that lord,
straightforward in his goodness, is obtained only through the enjoyment of great fortune.

Familiarity with her is more exquisite than nectar; her speech is as pleasant to hear as the fifth note [of the scale]; and her conduct bestows a mass of bliss, possessing the splendor of a multitude of autumnal moons.
For the virtuous who dwell in pure hearts, what else need be said? Even the mind is tenderer than a flower.
His kindness is even more cooling than yellow sandalwood in extinguishing the heat of suffering.
Having spoken thus, the citizens, bowing to him who was full of grace,
departed while scattering a garland of flowers in the form of his noble virtues throughout the quarters.
The king also, having performed the sequence of rites for the worship of the spirits within the city,
prepared the requisites for peace and well-being, remaining firm in his vows.
He heard it proclaimed by the tutelary deity of the city that there was a yakṣī named Hārītikā who lived in the city and carried off children.
Then the lord of the earth, together with his ministers and the citizens,
went to the bamboo grove hermitage situated in the place called Kalandakanivāsa.
He went to see the Blessed One, the Sugata, for the sake of pacifying his faults—
the unharsh medicine for those afflicted by the fever and exhaustion of all suffering.
Seeing that pleasant sight from afar, the king bowed to him and,
sitting before him, reported the suffering of the citizens.
The Blessed One, having understood the destruction of the citizens' lineage,
and being restless with anxiety, the treasury of compassion quickly spoke.
Having bid farewell to the circle of citizens along with the king,
that friend of the world took up his bowl and robe and went to the abode of the Yakṣī.
Having reached that house bereft of her, the Blessed Jina caused his son,
named Priyaṅkara, to vanish from sight.
When the Blessed One had departed, the yakṣī quickly returned to her own home;
though she had many sons, she did not see her beloved son Priyaṃkara.
Gazing at him, she wandered among the people, helpless and bewildered by agitation like a cow whose calf has been stolen.
"Alas, Priyaṃkara! Alas, my son! Where indeed shall I see your face?"—thus lamenting loudly, she wandered through all directions until she was gone.
Having quickly searched all directions and become hopeless of seeing her son,
she went crying out toward the mountain-island within the circle of the ocean.
Having transcended the realm of mortals,
she [dwelt] in all the regions of heaven— within formidable cities and amidst celestial palaces, gardens, and fields.
Exhausted and finding no rest, the Yakṣiṇī Praṇighātinī searched for her son, but did not see him even in the cities of the world-protectors.
Then, at the word of Kubera, she went to the hermitage of the Sugata and,
pained by separation, sought refuge with the Blessed One, the protector.
Having heard that account of her suffering as it was reported by her, he,
his lips whitened by a slight smile, spoke to her as she was grieving.
"O Hārītī, you have five hundred sons, alas!
Having heard this said by him, the Yakṣī, wounded by grief, replied: KAvk_12.39.
"O Blessed One, even among a hundred thousand sons, the loss of a single son cannot be endured;
there is nothing dearer than a son—what sorrow could be greater than his destruction? (KAvk 12.40)

Only one who has a son knows the pain caused by the poison of affection for a son; innate love for a child is a bond that requires no external cause. To whom is a son not like the moon—though he may be soiled, deformed, or wasted away?
Having heard these words of the yakṣa’s wife, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward all beings, spoke to her with a smile, overwhelmed by affection.
If this is the grief of a woman with many sons at the loss of even one,
what kind of agony must there be for those who have lost their only son?
Entering the house constantly, you eat the sons of women unobserved;
even the mother of her own son, like a tigress toward the fawns of a deer.
Whatever causes suffering to one's own body should not be inflicted upon another, for the experience of pain is the same for all.
If you indeed take up the three precepts of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
turning away from violence, you will regain your beloved son.
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, she then received the precepts;
by desisting from violence, she went to him and obtained her beloved son, Priyaṅkara.
When the Blessed One was questioned by the monks regarding her history in a previous birth and the sequence of the fruits of her karma, he related that account to them.
Formerly, in this very city, certain citizens who were devoted to pleasure amused themselves with dancing and other diversions in a series of mountain gardens.
Then, along that very path, a certain cowherd’s beloved,
thick-breasted and deer-eyed, arrived carrying her merchandise of churned butter.
With her gait languid from the weight of her womb, walking with the majestic stride of an elephant,
she approached them slowly and gazed at them with longing.
Even the forest deer, unaccustomed to her glances that were innocent yet moist with grace,
fell into a state of longing.
Invited by them there, she fell into a state of intoxication from passion;
being heedless, she did not realize that her virtue had been suddenly lost.
Then, as they had departed,
her fetus— due to the exhaustion from sexual union— fell along with her fortitude, like the sun [the offspring of Aruṇa] falling out of anger.
In the meantime, by virtue of that merit,
she beheld a Pratyekabuddha approaching, which brought serenity to her body and mind.
Bowing from afar with her mind alone, she offered him five hundred mangoes purchased for their price by means of churning.
Then, having been born now in this family of Yakṣas which possesses the power of merit,
she gave five hundred mangoes to her sons as soon as they were born.
Due to her abandonment of evil, her failure to forget her moral conduct (*śīla*),
and her prostration before a *pratyekabuddha*, she attained the precepts and other virtues at that time.
Having thus related this manifold and wondrous system of karma with its various ripenings,
the Teacher of all the world established a bridge of merit for people in the ocean of existence and inspired virtuous thoughts in everyone there, including the female yakṣa.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Subduing of Hārītikā," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
13. The Avadāna of the Miraculous Display (Pratihārya)

He who always moves upon the path of thought, whose unfolding wonder is such that there is no association with dreams and no prior acquaintance with him; he in whom the sequence of events is unprecedented,
and where the speech of men is as if silent, yet he is the guest of their ears and eyes.
We pay homage to that delightful one, whose majesty consists of the power of guileless people.
Having seen the Jina staying in the Veṇuvana hermitage, being honored by King Bimbisāra in the city known as Rājagṛha, [he stood there].
Burning with the poison of envy, those fools who considered themselves omniscient could not endure his excellence, just as owls cannot endure the light.
The nocturnal masses of darkness, ever rising in the opposite quarter and soiled by their own destruction,
constantly vie with the day.
Maskarī Saṃjayin Vairaṭīputra, Kakuda,
as well as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others— these and other ascetics are fools.
Deluded by the magic of Māra and blinded as if by smoke through the fault of rivalry and hatred, they approached the king and spoke.
"This ascetic who dwells in the forest, claiming to possess omniscience—
let the miraculous power of him and of ourselves be seen by you."
Whatever great wonder is seen, whether through the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) or other means, which is forceful in attracting people— that is called a miracle (*prātihārya*).
O King, let there be honor for him, or for us, in the three worlds— whosoever possesses the power to perform a miracle in this assembly.
Having heard these words of theirs, the king, turning away from their pride, said:
"What desire is this of yours—to leap over mountains like cripples?"
"This is utterly improper; what rivalry can there be between fire and moths?
This must not be said again, for I shall have this disputant cast out from the city."
Thus, their efforts rejected by the king who knew their virtues,
those wicked men departed like figures suspended in the supportless sky.
"King Bimbisāra is partial toward foolishness;
let us go to another ruler," they thought together.
In the meantime, when the Blessed One had reached the Gabled Hall Monastery near the city of Śrāvastī,
they departed for the very ends of the earth.
Having reached Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, there,
they reported to him that very same competition regarding the performance of miracles.
The king, who knew their various qualities, desiring to humble their pride and with the intent to display his supernatural power and inspire them, went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having approached him with humility and prostrated, he said to him:
"O Blessed One, you ought to subdue the pride and power of the heretics."
"Due to their persistent rivalry in supernatural powers, their desire to see your majesty,
and their boasting of their own virtues, our ears have been deafened by them."
O Lord, manifest your own splendor which wins over the virtuous;
let all the darkness known as the heretics go to its destruction.
Having heard these words of the king, the noble-minded Blessed One, remaining unchanged and free from resentment, spoke to him with joy.

O King, this collection of virtues is not intended for the purpose of crushing others, for disputation, or for intoxication; rather, it is made so that you may be worthy of the ornament of discernment.
Of what use are those qualities, sullied by envy and deficient in discernment, which,
extended through the bonds of rivalry, seek only to diminish the excellence of others?
He who conceals the virtues of another by means of his own virtue is himself destroyed by that very unwholesome act.
The mere examination of good qualities alone brings about distinction from others;
for those who are pure, the mockery of being placed upon a scale is not appropriate.
He who, though possessed of virtue, does not show favor toward others,
is like one holding a lamp whose light is obscured by the shadow of his own vessel.
We know only those who are omniscient; what more could we know?
To be bold enough to overcome the pride of others is one's own defeat.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, which were intent upon tranquility,
the king made a fervent request regarding the sight of the wonder.
Then, having been granted his request by the Blessed One,
the king returned to the capital rejoicing, under the agreement of a seven-day limit.
At this juncture, the king’s half-brother wandered near the inner apartments along the path on the palace roof.
As he was walking gracefully, a flower garland, fallen from the hand of the king’s wife, dropped upon his shoulder as if impelled by the winds of his own past actions.
When his fault had been recognized, the informers, anticipating that very offense through the testimony of witnesses,
spread that rumor which reached the king's ears.
Having found even a slight opening, petty,
double-tongued people who cause harm to all quickly enter the empty hearts of their masters.
The king, a ghost among men, intensely inflamed by the poison of envy toward his brother,
fell into a swoon and immediately ordered the amputation of [the brother's] hands and feet.
With his hands and feet cut off due to the failure of his ritual acts,
the prince lay upon the ground where he was to be executed and entered into a perilous calamity.
The mendicants beheld him for a moment as he was writhing in intense agony, while his mother and kinsmen lamented, their eyes darting about.
Approaching them, those kinsmen of the prince, afflicted with grief and intent on rescuing him,
spoke to all the living beings.
"This prince named Kāla has been subdued by Doṣa;
you who profess omniscience—let your favor be bestowed upon him."
Thus, being entreated by those who were lamenting with spreading tears,
they remained silent and speechless, and out of embarrassment, departed elsewhere.
Then, by means of a truthful prayer, Ānanda, the monk who had come there according to his destination, restored the limbs of that man through the teaching of the Sugata.
But the prince, having regained his hands and feet and with a serene mind,
went for refuge to the Jina and became his attendant.
Then, when seven nights had passed, the lord of the earth had a great palace constructed for the removal of fatigue,
in order to behold the miraculous power of the Blessed One.
When the king was seated there together with the mendicants and others,
by the will of the Sugata, the ground became like a wish-fulfilling tree.
Then, when the gods had arrived to behold the splendor of the Blessed One,
the Blessed One ascended the great lion-throne which was illuminated by jewel-lamps.
For him who had entered the fire element,
the circle of the world became pervaded by masses of flames emerging from his cheeks.
When the fire, resembling a grove of lotuses, had gradually subsided out of fear that the stability of the entire world might be destroyed,
then from the body of the Blessed One— an ocean of compassion— radiated pure splendors like waves of full-blown nectar.

The eyes of the multitude of serpent lords drank with affection that one who was the essence of loveliness, possessing a radiance exceeding a thousand moons, whose expanding splendor had rendered the solar orb fruitless— a sight obtained through merit and filled with unprecedented joy.

Then, near him, lotuses rose from the surface of the earth, their stalks made of beryl, their broad cups of radiant red jewels, and their filaments and pericarps shimmering with gold; they were drawn toward by bees attracted to the weight of their fragrance.
Then, as they sat down, the Sugata was seen from afar, possessing the lovely luster of gold and eyes as gentle as those of a deer;
by his sudden appearance, which was as cooling as the light of the moon—delicate with nectar—the world attained happiness.
The Blessed One bore their majesty and splendor more fully than they did in his midst, like Mount Meru among the immovable mountains;
he was tall, with a well-proportioned trunk and a dense arrangement of radiant luster, like the Pārijāta tree among the celestial trees.
With their heads adorned by unfading garlands and bracelets scattered by the lotus-hands of celestial nymphs,
even mortals attained for a moment the state of immortals through their unblinking gazing upon her lotus-face.
In the courtyards of the sky, filled with the sounds of celestial drums, conchs, and trumpets, and accompanied by the great laughter of showers of flowers,
there resounded the swelling sound of the praises and hymns of the Blessed One, sung by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, lords of sages, and Cāraṇas.

There, the fortunate ones drank the honey of the Blessed One’s sweet speech, produced from his own essence and endowed with true fragrance—from that lotus of a face whose lower petal was his reddish lip, white with the rays of his teeth, and strewn with the filaments of his hair. KAvk 13.52.
Cast off evil and sow the seeds of merit; abandon enmity and partake in the happiness of equanimity.
Drink the nectar of wisdom, which removes the poison of death; for this body is not a long-lasting companion to virtuous deeds.
Fortune is fickle, youth is followed by old age, and the body is merely an abode for a multitude of calamities;
life-breaths are but momentary travelers in the huts of these little bodies. Therefore, exert yourselves in the Dharma, which is ever-arising.
By means of such skillful instructions of the Blessed One— radiant with discernment, pure through discrimination, and distinguished by wisdom—
the mountain of the twenty peaks of the view of a self-identity among people was swiftly shattered, as if by thunderbolts.
Having clearly perceived the Blessed One’s splendor of supernatural power, the heretics—like venomous serpents struck down by spells—had their pride shattered;
like lamps overwhelmed by the brilliance of the sun’s rays, they became as motionless as figures in a painting.

In the meantime, the Kṣapaṇaka, the perpetual adversary of the Blessed One who by all means sought to destroy the New Dharma, was driven away from the earth by Vajrapāṇi; having been repelled by the excellent gatekeepers and attendants, he took refuge in a hole.
Then, having pointed them out, the Blessed One—compassionate, fearing for their safety, and a refuge for all who seek instruction—spoke:
"The mountains, forests, the earth, jewels, and even the underworld—all these are indeed said to be the refuge of the cowardly in times of fear."
Having awakened my intellect and established it in the light of truth,
those who have taken refuge in the Dharma along with its Saṅgha—
may they remain fearless even amidst the terrors of the world's destruction.
There is no acceptance of the wretchedness of seeking refuge from anyone else.
In the difficult-to-cross, intense darkness of the next world, Dharma is the risen sun;
in the emergence of the calamities of unbearable sin and heat, generosity is the rain-cloud;
and in the treacherous abyss of the great precipice of delusion, wisdom is the hand-hold.
For men everywhere, merit alone is the refuge for those who are not overcome by wretchedness.

Thus, having established— as it were— a firm foundation for the instruction of the pure Dharma, which was worthy of opening the eyes of those whose vision was shrouded by darkness and whose light was manifested by the rays from his jewel-like teeth, the Moon of the Sugata departed for his own forest from that assembly.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Story of the Miraculous Display," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

14. The Legend of the Descent of the Gods. Victorious is the power of the Great Ones, which exists both behind and before, serving as a path for the wholesome deeds of people—a radiant jewel-lamp for you all.
Long ago, in the city of the gods, upon a stone slab named Pāṇḍukambala,
near the Pārijāta and the radiant Kovidāra tree.
Having delivered a teaching of the Dharma to the hosts of the thirty-three gods,
the Blessed One descended to Jambudvīpa for the sake of favoring mortals.
As he descended to earth followed by the immortals,
the courtyard of the world became filled with groves of celestial chariots.
With the streams of light from his teeth,
the Four-faced One (Brahmā) took up a moon-bright fly-whisk that seemed as if it were covered with his own instructions.
Puraṃdara took from him a parasol marked with a hundred ribs, stainless and pale like a streak of saffron, as if it were a graceful edifice embodied in form.
At the edge of the city of Sāṃkāśya, near an udumbara tree in the forest,
the virtuous ones bowed with joy to him who had descended.
In that gathering of people, a female mendicant named Utpalavarṇā,
finding no opportunity to see him, assumed the form of a king.
Upon seeing his new form— with a crown blazing with jewels and earrings swaying as he performed the *gaṇḍatāṇḍava* dance— the one with the sprout-like *uṣṇīṣa* laughed.
She reflected: "Who might this man be, who stands before me without a gap among the people?
Having seen my royal form, he will respectfully grant me an audience."
Otherwise, however, my prostration before the Blessed One would be difficult to obtain;
for people who are devoted to power do not value virtue, which is the true ground of respect.

Alas! By means of wealth—which is as fleeting as blades of grass and straw, and which is essence-less and tasteless—people are carried away from the practice of mental impressions through a lack of discernment.
Suddenly granted an opening by the people out of respect for the king,
she made a prostration before the Blessed One, her necklace swaying.
At this moment, a monk named Udayin, beholding her in such a state within the assembly, spoke with a smiling face: KAvk_14.14.
This nun named Utpalavarṇā, who has assumed the form of a king,
bows at the feet of the Blessed One through her supernatural power, she who is honored by the people.
"Having previously recognized her by her complexion, which was like the fragrance of a blue lotus,"—
when he had finished speaking thus, the Blessed One also spoke.
It is indeed improper for a nun to display supernatural power out of pride;
for such arrogance causes the fever of passion to bring about the wasting away of tranquility.
Having spoken thus and having given various auspicious instructions,
the Blessed One dismissed the gods and departed for his own abode together with the monks.
Seated there, the Omniscient One was asked by those who had bowed down about the story of the female mendicant; he related it to them, connecting it with the karma of her previous birth.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a caravan leader of great wealth;
he had a wife named Dhanavatī, who was as dear to him as his own life.
Her hands were like tender leaves, her slender form was a blossoming cluster in the garden of youth;
in due time, she conceived a child, becoming as if laden with fruit and flowers.
In the meantime, as her beloved was preparing to follow him to the islands of the ocean,
she, pained by the approaching separation, spoke to him:
How vast must that accumulation of wealth be, which even today continues to increase,
for the sake of which this unfathomable ocean is crossed?
The acquisition of wealth is fraught with many dangers, whereas the cultivation of virtue is free from danger;
indeed, those seeking riches travel from their own country to foreign lands.
Some turn back from suffering even after having gone far, while others remain motionless despite their wealth; such is the certainty of karmic actions.
Having heard these affectionate words, the caravan leader then replied:
"O charming one, one who is intent on wealth indeed becomes an object of such esteem."
For those devoid of the means to acquire wealth,
there is today or tomorrow the total exhaustion of their enjoyments along with their happiness, as they subsist on roots like mere men.
Even in their own homes, people are as harsh as saws toward the poor;
yet for the wealthy, even the next world is filled with people affectionate with love, as if they were on this very earth.
Even when diminished, people do not bind a bamboo pole that is striving for growth;
yet that which is already near exhaustion does not reach fullness.
Even a fool is worthy of homage by the learned; even an old man is beloved by women;
even a eunuch is to be served by the brave—a person for whom prosperity is imminent is honored by all.
Who else, having eaten or drunk the nectars of poetry,
could for even a moment dispel hunger and thirst, even if they were a person of discernment?
For whom wealth exists, he is praised by those exalted by their virtues; what quality does wealth not bestow upon those whose luster is marred by the defect of rising poverty?
Virtues are like withered flower-garlands to those whose splendor is tarnished by the onset of destitution.

Through wealth alone one is virtuous, but a man of virtue is not necessarily wealthy; the wealthy man is blessed, but the virtuous man is not wealthy. Wealth is the life-force of virtues, for it pacifies the accumulation of misdeeds within the body.
Having heard these words of her husband, who was intent on saving her life, she—
with tears mixed with collyrium streaming down— became like a creeper covered by bees.
Then the caravan leader embarked upon the ship together with her;
for those seized by intense thirst, the great ocean is a vessel held in the hand.
The ship of that man, who was accompanied by his wife and driven by the winds of karma, broke apart along with his hopes and his life.
Then, having reached a raft and due to the remainder of his past karma,
he arrived at Kaśerudvīpa, where its ruler met with calamity.
There, a bird in human form, born of a noble golden lineage, approached her as she grieved for her protectorless state, her hopes shattered.
That handsome one named Sumukha, whose form was radiant, said to that beloved woman:
"Take heart, O tremulous-eyed one; this refuge of yours is free from fear."
"This is a divine and auspicious land, and we are seekers of your affection;
you have come for the sake of merit, O blessed lady, yet this ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, is terrible."
Having spoken thus, she was led slowly by him to his house, the repository of jewels;
there, with her pregnancy fully matured, she gave birth to a son of beautiful form.
As that child grew, she was gradually made inclined toward sexual union by that clever man with his sweet speech, though she herself was innocent.
Because of his straightforwardness and gentleness, people who were close to him embraced him of their own accord,
just as women embrace a tree or as creepers cling to it.
Sporting with him in divine gardens,
that woman of full breasts gave birth to a son of beautiful form who resembled his father.
In that king of birds, named Padmamukha, whose form was adorned with youth,
the one of beautiful countenance passed away to another world in the course of time.
Then the illustrious Padmamukha returned to his father’s presence;
for the prosperity of noble families remains under one's own control when there is no dispute among the virtuous.
In a secluded place, his mother spoke to her son who had attained sovereignty,
having recognized that his power would grant him mastery everywhere.
"My son, you have obtained this fortune worthy of your own lineage;
however, this son born to me from the merchant caravan leader is one who shall receive no inheritance."
"O King, let this be done by you in Vārāṇasī with a sharp spear:
let there be the savor of joyful conversation; enjoy those very riches in your own land."
Thus, at his mother’s word, the bird, out of great partiality,
placed his brother upon his shoulder and traveled through the sky to Vārāṇasī.
There, upon that very day, he struck King Brahmadatta, who was seated upon his lion-throne,
with his harsh claws that were like thunderbolts.
Having consecrated his eldest son, Pūrṇa, upon that very royal throne,
he of supreme valor spoke to all his terrified ministers.
O Lord, that very king who was consecrated by me and whom I once caused to tremble has now passed away;
yet out of devotion, he shall follow him alone.
Having spoken thus to his chief ministers at his own will, the eminent bird took leave of his brother with the agreement to meet again, and departed.
Addressed by his ministers as "this very [man] is Brahmadatta," that king attained renown among both his own people and others.
In the meantime, a pregnant female elephant was brought from the forest;
she did not give birth, as if held back within by her fetus that had only half emerged.
"The touch of the tips of her virtuous hands causes her to deliver the fetus," thus the minister reported to the king what had been foretold by the astrologers and others.
Then, at the command of the king,
the women of the inner apartments touched the female elephant with their hands and performed a solemn oath of truth there.
When the female elephant did not abandon her fetus because of their truthful words,
everyone in the king’s inner apartments was filled with astonishment.
Then a cowherd woman approached, made a supplication based on her virtue and truthfulness,
and touched the female elephant, whereby she cast off the fetus.
Having learned of the lack of virtue among his own wives,
he considered Gopā alone to be a faithful wife, as if she were present in his mind throughout the three worlds.
Out of greed for the Satī lineage, he married her daughter named Sośumbā and led her to the foremost position worthy of the title of queen.
Reflecting upon her beauty and the fickleness of women,
he became apprehensive and abandoned even his all-pervading sleep.
At this moment, Padmamukha, the lord of birds, went there out of affection and with great longing to see his brother.
The king also, having embraced him with affection and performed the rites of hospitality,
related his own story to him in private and spoke again:
Because of my aversion to women due to the perceived faults of their character, and because I had ascended the scale of the truth of moral conduct,
I entered into a new marriage by turning away from my former harem.
I have no steadfastness even toward her who possesses beauty and youth;
for the mind of those who have perceived faults in one place suspects them everywhere.
Therefore, O brother, let this [man] be placed in a non-human state within your city;
casting aside my suspicion regarding his conduct, may I be free from my feverish distress.
"Therefore, it is my heart's desire that every night this bird shall, by your command,
bring her to my house at will."
Having heard these words of his brother, the bird said to him:
"O King, do not falsely stain yourself with the blemish of suspicion born of envy."
He finds no pleasure in what is delightful, he knows no taste in food;
he neither sees nor sleeps, being perpetually afflicted by the power of envy.

What kind of talk can there be regarding a eunuch who is lustful, a happy man who is learned, a wealthy man who is humble, a master who is patient, a petitioner who is honorable, a villain who is affectionate, or a woman who is chaste? (KAvk 14.71)
Though straight, they are crooked; though stable, they are exceedingly fickle;
and though of noble birth, these women—like creepers—embrace whatever stands beside them.
A tremulous lower lip, a passionate gaze, arched eyebrows, and firm breasts—
among these very limbs of women, not even one is seen that is entirely faultless.
The dark lotuses are enjoyed by the virtuous, who possess the grace of wandering bees;
yet the seeker of the lotus-root is smeared only by the mud.
The minds of beautiful women— whose smiles are the ground of wonder, who are self-restrained, and whose virtuous conduct is pure— do not find delight in union with a single man.
Nevertheless, let her be placed in my private garden, in a secluded spot.
Thus addressed by the bird, the king, his brother,
respectfully honored him and dismissed that beloved woman to the island of Kaśeruka.
She too came every night from the sky, mounted upon a bird,
bringing with her a garland produced on that island and filled with divine fragrance.
She obtained those flowers from the tree belonging to the lineage of the Pārijāta;
they were renowned as if they were darkness, due to the gloom created by the hovering bees.
Then, once upon a time, a young twice-born man residing in Vārāṇasī, a scholar among men, went to the forest to gather sacrificial fuel.
There, he was seen by a Kinnara maiden whose passion was manifest;
at the mere sight of him, she lost her mindfulness.
Like a daughter tenderly offered by her father out of new affection,
that lovely woman named Kāntimatī dwelt in the interior of a cave-dwelling.
There, amidst a mass of familiar darkness illuminated by the rays of her jeweled ornaments,
she took delight with him for a long time and in that period gave birth to a son.
When that powerful son of Marut was still a child in his infancy,
his mother gave him the name Śīghraga (the Swift).
She too, having enjoyed the pleasures of Nivāghna and being satisfied with happiness, would always go into the interior of the cave,
taking her beloved with her and closing the entrance to the dwelling with a rock.
Then, on one occasion, having heard the account related by his own father,
Śīghraga, overwhelmed with anxiety and wonder, said:
"Alas, father! Even this affection of yours has become a bond for me, like that of a blind man within a house whose door is secured by stone."
"Come, let us go to Vārāṇasī itself, our own home;
I shall remove even this mountain of Viśālā without effort."
How can you endure the suffering of separation from your own country?
No land can be abandoned as easily as one's own body.
A person separated from his own country perceives a burden as a collection of wealth, sees knots as virtues and lack of knots as faults, and regards enjoyment as being without enjoyment.
Having spoken thus, he uprooted a massive rock from his hiding place in the cave and quickly departed together with his father, who had readily given his consent.
Then, as they had quickly departed, the Kinnarī approached and, seeing the cave-dwelling empty, reflected thus out of despondency: KAvk_14.92 //
"Alas! That wicked man has gone away somewhere, having forgotten his affection for me;
what is so wonderful about the crookedness of double-tongued serpents?"
Those who crave pleasure do not find delight at the end but flee from it;
though they may remain for a long time, they are devoid of affection, like twice-born parrots.
Having reflected thus, she abandoned her affection for her husband because of his humiliation;
for loves that are like flowers cannot endure being treated with contempt.
"By what quality of learning does this son of mine excel on earth?"—
having reflected thus, she placed a lute into the hand of her friend to give it to him.
For women, affection toward their husbands is like a commodity for the pleasure of sensual enjoyment;
however, a mother's love for her son is unwaning and steadfast.
As the two of them were traveling swiftly with great speed,
Vegagāminī, their companion, out of shame for her own wickedness, gave the lute to the one who was moving faster.
"This is the primary string; it must not be touched, for it causes obstacles"—having spoken thus, he took the lute given by her and departed.
Then, having settled his father in his own home in his native land, he,
being highly skilled in the vīṇā, obtained profit and honor everywhere.
Then, on one occasion, a merchant who was traveling to an island in the ocean and who was fond of divine lutes placed him upon his ship.
By the resonance of his lute, which was a stream of nectar for the ears,
even the ocean became as if waveless moment by moment.
Then, when the ship was shattered by the impact of the first wave and overwhelmed by the resulting calamity,
the destruction of all the merchants occurred.
Then, having obtained Balāhaka, he was carried by him in an instant;
swift-moving, he reached Kaśerudvīpa due to the remainder of his karma.
There, having entered a divine garden situated on the shore of the ocean,
he beheld Śyāmā, who was accompanied by Uśumbha and whose breasts were like clusters of flowers upon her head.
She was weaving a bright garland of flowers called *timira* from the ends of large books,
binding them together with the fine threads of her own intellect, even though they were devoid of consciousness.
She too, seeing him of such lovely form—
steadfast, having reached the midpoint between childhood and youth— was filled with wonder.
With her sprout-like hands trembling from the agitation of the wind of Māra,
she bowed down before him like a creeper whose flowers of virtuous conduct have withered.
A mature affection, as if long-established, suddenly arose between the two;
for the mind, merged with the affection of a previous birth, does not abandon the [other] mind.
While she was sporting with him by day and with the king at night, her lover,
who was secretly in love with her, considered her to be practicing deceitful conduct.
Having learned that he intended to go to Vārāṇasī, she prepared herself;
then, at his word, she mounted a bird and carried him there with his eyes closed.
Although she then restrained him from opening his eyes in the sky, he,
being blind, suddenly opened his eyes out of restlessness.
Having placed him in the palace garden, she, trembling with fear and tormented by grief,
entered the king's bedchamber.
Having passed that night with a tormented mind,
at dawn she was unable either to go or to stay, being overwhelmed by anxiety.
In the meantime, there arose the month of Madhu, overflowing with fallen fragrance—
the youth of the flower-bowed god of love for all amorous delights.
The dark season, unbearable for those separated from their lovers, is seen in full bloom; it is marked by swarms of cuckoos and bees, and by fresh *aśoka* trees whose old blossoms have fallen away.
The king also, his longing unabated, prepared to go to the garden;
deluded by passion, he did not leave Uśumbā for even a single day.
Together with her, he went to the flower grove— a place of rest for passion, intoxication, and love— as if it were the very realm of *saṃsāra*.
There, seeing her who caused embarrassment even to the creepers shaken by the gentle breeze,
the king attained great joy.
Overcome by the poison of passion for another, her mindfulness became clouded;
even pleasure she experienced as pain, for her mind was agitated by the thorn of anxiety.
