Enamored men, possessing excessive passion, dance while being embraced around the necks by women who have slithering serpents within them,
as if they were garlands that had enchanted them.
There, staying hidden within a secluded bower of creepers,
that blind man, having smelled the fragrance, drank in the garlands of darkness along with the wine.
Suddenly, through a transformation brought on by passion, he forgot all social conventions;
intoxicated by love, he began to sing—for how can those who are mad with desire regard what is external?

Scattered by the playful movements of the gentle breeze, that very fragrance of the dark-blue flowers— the essence of the abundant perfume from the lotus-like face of my beloved in her state of intoxication— approaches from afar.
It was delightful with the charming sounds of bees and lutes.
Having heard that song which resonated with his own heart,
the king searched the garden and beheld him within a bower of creepers.
Intoxicated by the intense joy of his passion, he questioned him with apprehension:
"Do you know Śuṃbhā, or the description of her body?"
He said: "How could I not know Sośumbā, whose lips are as crimson as the bimba fruit, upon which the Mind-born God resides in his sovereignty of passion?"
Upon the base of her thighs, there is a lovely svastika mark as if drawn by the God of Love;
or rather, upon the circle of her breasts, there is the beauty of a whirlpool, resembling a wave of loveliness.
Having heard this, the king immediately cast away the flower of passion— which had withered from his grief— as a discarded garland from his mind.
He said: "The preservation of virtue by women does not exist even in a hundred lifetimes;
like a garland of sky-flowers, it simply never comes to pass."
Having spoken thus, the blind king quickly abandoned her outside the city, mounted upon a donkey, in the forest of the cremation ground.
As she walked shamelessly with him at the close of day,
she was encountered in the forest by the leader of the bandits together with his entire retinue.
While that band of thieves was suddenly being pursued by the people,
an innocent man, though blind, was struck down through the mistaken belief that he was a thief.
The thief also, having spent the night with Sośumbā,
took her ornaments and departed after crossing the river.
On the bank of that river Kāraṇḍavā,
naked and with her breasts soiled, she wept, staining them with streams of tears mixed with collyrium.
At that moment, O jackal, having abandoned the meat clinging to its mouth,
the bird seized the fish which had leapt into the water as it departed.
When the fish suddenly sank and its flesh was snatched away by a bird,
he stood with eyes motionless in anxiety due to the loss of both.
Seeing her even in distress, a smile was observed upon her face;
for laughter arises at the blunder of another, even when one is oneself in a miserable state.
Enraged by her embarrassment, he spoke to her who was smiling inappropriately:
"Aha! You laugh at me, who have become an object of ridicule in this world."
"Having abandoned the king, I have indeed come to one who is blind; having abandoned the blind man, I have resorted to a thief.
Thus, I am fallen from both, yet I am the object of your smile, O you who have fallen from three [supports]."
"Let this jest of yours rest; I shall bring it about for you by means of a stratagem.
Those wicked men who are experts in mockery are themselves in a precarious position."
Having spoken thus, he went to the city and reported to the king:
"It is my opinion that she, along with Aśumbha, is engaged in ascetic penance on the bank of that river."
Then the king led her away, having stripped her of her ornaments and garments;
for passion and hatred merely conceal the faults of embodied beings.
She was that very Utpalavarṇā, and he was Udāyin, though swift of foot;
by virtue of merit from a previous birth, they both entered upon the vows of a monk.

In that moment, because of her union with passion, her heart— which was subject to the dictates of love and filled with longing— became exceedingly moist with intense emotion, and she ceased from her tranquility and detachment.
She paid homage to me, who was gladdened by having assumed the form of a king.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Descent as a Deva," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

15. The Legend of the Throwing of the Stone (Śilānikṣepāvadāna). The strength, majesty, fortitude, and heroism of those possessed of power become truly wondrous; for through union with a great refuge, all their greatness comes to be manifested. (KAvk 15.1)
In the past, the Blessed One, the Sugata, wandering at his own will, set out for himself toward the beautiful city of Kuśī, belonging to the powerful Mallas.
Having heard of his arrival, those seekers of virtue, desiring what was auspicious,
cleared the path, being diligent in the performance of hospitable rites.
As they adorned the land, it was sprinkled with sandalwood water and cleared of grass,
thorns, stones, pebbles, and dust.
In the midst [of the procession], a massive stone, sunken into the earth, arrived;
it was like the bride of Mount Vindhya, exhausted and despondent.
As they tore it up with their shovels as arms and ropes for hands,
a month passed away, yet not even a thousandth part of it was damaged.
Then the Blessed One arrived, the moonlight of the nectar that quells the heat of saṃsāra, the kinsman who brings joy to the minds of all.
Having clearly perceived the excellent fruit through his cessation of dense darkness,
and having distributed his quarters with serenity, he was like the autumnal light.

Seeing them exhausted, tormented by the fruitlessness of their efforts, and hearing of their resolve, he spoke to them as they stood with bowed heads: sa tān dṛṣṭvā pariśrāntān viphalakleśapiḍārditān / śrutvā ca tadvyavasitaṃ tānūce praṇatānanān // KAvk_15.9 //
"Oh, how the undertaking of the fruits of affliction for those who exert themselves with such toil!
Your exertion in this enterprise is like that of one engaged in the activities of cyclic existence."
The wise do not undertake an action that involves hardship at its outset, is fraught with uncertainty while being performed, and is unworthy of being adopted even if it should succeed.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One placed the massive rock upon his right hand, having pressed it with his left hand using his big toe.
Having released [his power] as far as the world of Brahmā, he of boundless prowess roamed through the three worlds like a messenger, engaged in wondrous conduct.
When she was suddenly hurled down by him, the performer of such a wondrous deed,
a sound arose that pervaded the people, like a roar emerging from the sky.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent"—thus they establish the non-deluded [view];
"all dharmas are selfless," and that is indeed the peace of Nirvana.
When these words had been clearly uttered, the rock in the Blessed One’s hand was seen once again,
standing there with the shape of the peak of the king of mountains.
In an instant, she was scattered by the Blessed One with the breath from his mouth,
and turned into a spreading succession of atoms throughout the directions.
Furthermore, the Blessed One placed that very same stone, now composed of atoms,
elsewhere, causing wonder throughout the three worlds.
Then the wrestlers, their eyes motionless with wonder, beheld the Blessed One’s prowess which had conquered Bali; bowing down, they spoke to him.
Oh, how great is this power of yours, arising from strength and heroism,
such that even the gods do not venture to challenge you in the attainment of certainty!
By your powerful force, which is intent on bestowing grace,
this stone— like a people submerged in a downward course— has been held up.
Does anyone know the limit or measure of your powers of vigor, wisdom, and so forth,
which perform such exceedingly wondrous deeds?
Seeing them speaking thus, motionless with wonder,
the Blessed Jina, seated upon that stone, spoke.
Indeed, whatever combined strength belongs to all beings in the three worlds,
that strength is not equal to the strength of a single Sugata in this world.
The waters of the ocean can be surpassed by means of jars, and the worlds by means of atoms;
however, the power of the Buddha cannot be overcome.
Even he who knows the true number of Mount Sumeru by means of weighing and measuring does not know the weight of the excellent qualities of the Sugatas.
Having spoken thus, when the assembly of gods had arrived at the abode of Śakra and Padma, the Blessed One gave a discourse on virtue.
Through that instruction and by relying on those various forms of awakening,
the Mallas attained the state of Pratyekabuddhas and Samyaksambuddhas, along with those known as Śrāvakas.
By some the fruit of stream-entry was attained, by others the state of once-returner;
by yet others the fruit of non-returning, and by others the rank of arhatship.

Having thus observed and understood their latent dispositions, underlying tendencies, elements, and destinies, as well as their respective natures, the Blessed One delivered an incomparable instruction—
a clear and perfect illumination of the Four Noble Truths— for the sake of the arising of virtue in them.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Story of the Casting Down of the Stone, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
16. The Avadāna of the Prophecy of Maitreya.
The dwelling of purity named Asaṅgama gives birth to excellences for one who desires virtue;
it is averse to cyclic existence, delighted by well-performed deeds, and a cessation of the dust of enmity through the impurities of the mind.
Long ago, having crossed the Gaṅgā by means of a bridge of serpent-hoods,
the Blessed Sugata reached the further shore and addressed the monks:
"Formerly, there was a sacrificial post here made of jewels and possessing wondrous luster;
I shall show it to you right here, if you have the curiosity to see it."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One touched with his hand, marked with divine signs, the ground where the heap of jewels had been lifted up by the hosts of nāgas, and showed the jeweled sacrificial pillar.
Upon seeing him, all the monks remained for a long time with unblinking eyes,
their bodies motionless as if they were figures painted in a picture.
Then, questioned by them regarding that story, the Blessed One spoke once more,
as if scattering the light of his teeth, [revealing] his knowledge of the past and the future.
Formerly, at a certain time, a certain son of the gods,
having fallen from heaven by the command of Śakra, became a king named Mahāpraṇāda.
On this earth, he requested from Śatakratu some appropriate mark for the purpose of remembering the practice of dharma.
Then, at the command of the Lord of the Gods, Viśvakarman fashioned in his palace a radiant jeweled pillar, lofty as if it were merit itself.
Then, while the people remained motionless with curiosity, intent on beholding him,
the activities such as agriculture were abandoned, and the king’s treasury began to dwindle.
Then, having been cast by that king into the waters of the Ganges,
he remains even today in Pātāla, strewn with jewels like suns.
In time, his destruction will be brought about by its own limits;
for in this world, there exists no name whatsoever that remains inexhaustible in the face of transformation.
In a future time, when the lifespan of men is eighty thousand years,
there will be a king named Śaṅkha, whose fame shall be as white as a conch shell.
The king, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree, will bestow this sacrificial post obtained through merit upon Maitreya,
the son of his domestic priest.
Maitreya, too, having taken this [treasure] and instantly broken it into pieces,
will make the world free from poverty, like a wish-fulfilling gem for those who seek.
Then, having given a sacrificial post, Maitreya attained the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
he will become a treasury of unsurpassed knowledge, honored by the gods.
King Śaṅkha, surrounded by eighty thousand [attendants],
along with his harem and the assembly of his ministers, will likewise go forth into the religious life.
Through the power of his vow in a previous birth, Śaṅkha’s arising of merit—
because what has been done must necessarily be experienced— will bear fruit upon its transformation.
In ancient times, in the Middle Country, there was a king named Vāsava who was like Indra;
and in the northern region, there was a king named Dhanasaṃmata.
Between those two, who were inflamed by the fire of enmity born from their rivalry for power,
there arose a mind impetuous with the preparations for the commencement of battle.
Then, having entered the city and assembled his forces,
Dhanasammata made the banks of the Ganges completely filled with his armies of horses and chariots.
There, he attained the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha named Ratnaśikhin;
he was seen with his feet being worshipped by the gods, including Brahmā and Śakra.
He thought: "Aha! King Vāsava is possessed of great merit;
for he dwells at the edge of his domain, he who is honored by the thirty gods."
Then, through the power of that [teaching],
the dust of enmity between those two kings was laid to rest through peace, resulting in the complete destruction of their false delusion.
Then King Vāsava,
having formed an alliance with his enemy, approached the Blessed One and honored him with all kinds of enjoyments.
And at the conclusion of the worship, he made this aspiration: "I bow down to him;
by this root of merit, may I become great."
At this terrible moment, when the sound of conch shells had arisen,
Ratnaśikhin spoke to him who stood bowed before him.
"You shall become a universal monarch named Śaṅkha, O protector of the earth;
and in the end, endowed with enlightenment, you will attain the auspicious state."
Thus, through his true aspiration and by the arising of merit, the lord of the earth named Śaṅkha shall attain sovereignty as directed by Ratnaśikhin;
and Maitreya, out of affection, will likewise cause him to apply his pure intellect toward awakening.
For association with the virtuous is indeed a sun that causes one to cross over through the merit of devotion to what is auspicious.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Prophecy of Maitreya," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
17. The Avadāna of Ādarśamukha:

Even by a mere fraction of the fruit of a tiny flower-gift, radiant with a pure affection born from clarity of mind, the excellence of the fruits of giving mountains of gold, Mount Rohaṇa, the lord of mountains, and the ocean of nectar cannot even approach comparison.
Long ago, the omniscient one of noble intent dwelt in the beautiful Jeta Grove,
the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, at Śrāvastī.
The noble one named Mahākāśyapa, a storehouse of compassion and his disciple,
went to the edge of the city grove while wandering among the people.
There, Sudurgati, a woman afflicted with leprosy who hung from a city wall, happened by chance to see that Kāśyapa.
Seeing him, she reflected with serene faith:
"By virtue of my merit, have I not become worthy of alms-food in this vessel?"
Perceiving her aspiration, which was endowed with marvelous faith, he,
overwhelmed with compassion, extended his bowl and accepted that alms-food.
With intense clarity of mind as she remembered the essence of her devotion,
the leper woman, whose fingers were withered, dropped [the food] into her bowl.
Then, as if casting off a sinful and impermanent body,
she was reborn in the abode of the gods known as the Tuṣitas.
Śakra, recognizing that wonder and filled with reverence for the merit of the gift,
diligently filled the noble vessel of Kāśyapa with nectar.
Even when offered nectar, that monk, free from desire as if it were a blade of grass,
turned his bowl face down, being filled with the nectar of tranquility.
Overcome with compassion for the wretched, the virtuous cultivate affectionate love;
yet they close their eyes to such regard when the faces of others are swollen with the pride of wealth.
Having heard that she was devoted to the Tuṣita host of gods,
King Prasenajit made a formal invitation for the Blessed One to a meal.
Having seen the wondrous prosperity in that king's house,
the Blessed One was questioned by the Venerable Ānanda and explained its source of merit.
Long ago, the son of a householder fell into servitude due to poverty;
occupied with field labor, he became emaciated by hunger and reached a state of exhaustion.
Having finally obtained a lump of sour gruel brought by his own mother— though it was devoid of affection and salt—
he approached respectfully to eat it.
At that moment, having washed his hands,
he gave it with a serene mind to a Pratyekabuddha who had arrived there by chance.
In time, he was born as this very King Prasenajit;
such is the first fruit of the splendor of that single grain of his gift.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, the monks were filled with wonder;
the king, too, performed extensive worship in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having offered all enjoyments worthy of a king as a token of devotion,
he arranged a garland of lamps consisting of ten million jars of oil.
There, a woman of low birth gave a single small lamp,
which did not go out even when all the others had gone out due to the exhaustion of their oil.
Having reflected upon her future state as Śākyamuni through that pure-minded vow, the Omniscient One declared to her: "You shall become him."
Having offered a row of jewel-lamps before the Blessed One, the king sat down, prostrated himself, and with affection addressed him.
Through the Blessed One’s vow and by the power of those various merits,
supreme perfect enlightenment has not been withheld from anyone.
Out of affection for your grace, I desire to obtain that [state];
indeed, the wish-fulfilling trees are cultivated for the sake of attaining the fruit of non-conceptualization.
Having heard these words of the king, the Blessed One replied:
"O Lord of the Earth, unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is difficult to attain."
Subtler than lotus fibers, heavier even than mountains,
and deeper even than the oceans— that [state] is not easily attained.
"Even through many gifts, this knowledge—clear and pure due to the serenity of mind—was not obtained by me in other births; they say that its cause was that very [serenity]."
During my birth as Māndhātṛ, by virtue of my sovereignty over the four continents, I enjoyed for a long time the fruit of my giving; yet, that awakening was not attained.
Through that gift, the supreme glory of a universal monarch was enjoyed by me at the time of my birth as Sudarśana;
yet, that enlightenment was not attained.
In the past, by giving eight elephants at the proper time to those of non-twice-born birth, I acquired great merit;
yet, that awakening was not attained by me.
"In former times I was a prince of handsome form and virtuous soul;
yet, because I was called a *piśāca*, I was abandoned by my own wife."
How could he whose shoulder is for glory and whose delight always resides in the renunciation of prosperity be miserable due to a deficiency of beauty? Where, indeed, is the arising of all virtues?
When he had abandoned his body due to the loss of his beauty, the Lord of Śacī gave him a divine crest-jewel and made him equal to the five-arrowed god of love.
In the sacrifices of that performer of rites, sixty thousand cities,
adorned with golden sacrificial posts, attained the splendor and strength of Mount Meru.
In that birth of merit, which was rendered a mountain by my excessive giving,
those merits were indeed acquired, yet that enlightenment was not attained.
By the power of my truth, during the birth of King Triśaṅku, I brought about rain that ended a severe famine; yet, I did not attain that awakening.
When Mahādeva was born as a king in Mithilā, I, though performing sacrifices,
attained an abundance of merit, yet I did not attain that awakening.
Long ago in Mithilā, at the birth of King Nimi, merit was acquired through gifts,
austerities, and sacrifices, yet that awakening was not attained.
Long ago, King Nanda had four wicked sons,
and the fifth was Guṇādhika, whose face was like a mirror.
When his term had come to an end, that king reflected:
"These four harsh men do not deserve the kingdom in my place."
The glory of sovereignty, reflected in my son Ādarśamukha—
who is of excellent conduct and endowed with the purity of wisdom— attains its full splendor.
Having reflected thus, he said to his ministers:
"That lord of men whom you honor with rising from your seats has been treated by the women of the harem as if he were one of them."
He whose head does not tremble even when touched by jeweled sandals [upon entering] sees the six treasures at the gates, trees, mountains, ponds, and wells.
When the king had spoken thus and departed for heaven, the ministers, following his instructions,
gradually established Īśvara Ādarśamukha as their sovereign according to those very characteristics.

In matters concerning the determination of the Dharma, upon merely looking at him, the plaintiff and the defendant would stand by themselves, their victory or defeat being settled through principles of justice.
Long ago, having incurred the sin of slaughter by the Nirbhaya king,
the compassionate [king] went before a Brahmin named Daṇḍin.
For the sake of his wife, the householder was struck by a mare while he was dead;
the carpenter was accused of striking his wife with the fall of an axe.
Having declared that the vintner had been initiated for the execution of his own son— a punishment equal to that which he himself deserved—
and having done so out of fear of his enemies, the king released him once the vintner had abandoned that intent.
Due to the particularity of the resolute intentions of those non-human beings,
he performed the purification of his mind through the resolution of each respective doubt.
During that twelve-year drought and famine,
he provided food and sustenance for the lives of all sentient beings.
Thus, through these [deeds], my attainment of merit occurred during the birth as Ādarśamukha;
yet that Great Awakening, which brings supreme exaltation, was not fully realized.
"O Lute, today I have attained the purity of knowledge through the great power of practice cultivated over hundreds of previous births."
This perfect enlightenment is a certain, supreme, and unsurpassed realization of truth accessible through knowledge and wisdom; indeed, O King, it is not attained by the merit of giving alone.
It belongs to those who possess the manifest purity of a cloudless sky when the darkness of delusion has come to rest.
That splendor of the day becomes a ground of unfeigned bliss, cutting asunder the cycle of worldly existence.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Legend of Ādarśamukha," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
18. The Avadāna of Śāriputra’s Renunciation.
Neither a kinsman nor a friend, nor a brother, nor a mother, nor a father performs this;
rather, it is some noble teacher of wisdom, a cause of auspiciousness, who constructs a bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Long ago, while the Blessed Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, he stayed at the delightful Bamboo Grove hermitage known as Kalandakanivāsa.
In former times, two wandering mendicants, Kilita and Upayiṣya,
having entered the state of monks, he brought them to the restraint of tranquility.
Then, the instruction of the monk Śāriputra was accomplished,
by which he realized arhatship and became fit for the state of liberation.
Having seen that wonderful thing worthy of wealth, all the monks asked him about his previous history, and he related it to them.
The wife of the Brahmin Agnimitra was Guṇavarā,
who bore the playful name Śūrpikā given to her by her father.
His elder brother, named Prathamaśīla, who had attained the state of a pratyekabuddha, once came to his house; he was known by the name Śūrpa.
Impregnated by her devotion to the householder through her husband’s command, he was gratified by her service,
her humble entreaties, and her respectful conduct.
Once, while he was making a patch for his robe,
seeing the labor involved in the work of the needle, he made a solemn vow.
"May I possess such another wisdom as this knife—so sharp and so penetrating," she thought with devotion. (KAvk 18.10)
Through that vow and by means of the discipline of a Pratyekabuddha,
she attained in this very birth the state of being Śāriputra, endowed with wisdom.
This very Śāriputra, O noble-minded one, having today attained the state of a monk with the sharpest and most excellent intellect,
has become a vessel of excellence, like a wish-fulfilling creeper.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, the monks asked again:
"Why was Śāriputra born into a family of actors, among the lowest of men?"
Then the Blessed One said to them: "In a previous birth, he was a prince named Mahāmati, esteemed by the virtuous."
Even though he was prosperous, his mind turned toward the life of renunciation;
for those whose minds are clear through ripening, wealth does not lead to turbidity.
"Renunciation is not at all suitable for the family of young princes," having said this,
his father affectionately tried to dissuade him with great effort.

Once, while traveling on the public road mounted upon an elephant, he saw a poor old man and, out of compassion, spoke these words: KAvk_18.17: "Once, while traveling on the public road mounted upon an elephant, he saw a poor old man and, out of compassion, spoke this."
In this world, those who are unfortunate and destitute, being constrained by the bonds of kinship, do not attain the life of renunciation at all; but by whom were you prevented?
He informed me that for one as poor as I, there was neither a bowl nor a robe;
yet even the requisites for wealth were present, as were the requisites for tranquility.
Having heard that he was the king’s son, he went to the sage’s penance grove,
caused him to take up the life of a renunciant, and gave him a bowl and robes.
In a very short time, he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
approaching the prince, he displayed his divine supernatural powers.
Beholding his power, the prince reflected:
"Alas! Because of my great good fortune, the life of a renunciant has become difficult for me to attain."
Because of poverty and lack of discernment, even for the lowly this birth in a base family is difficult to obtain; therefore, I am possessed of discernment.
It is this very Śāriputra who is known by virtue of that former vow;
he was ordained by the Blessed One Kāśyapa in another lifetime.
Therefore, this man, disciplined by his commitment to the precepts and his modesty, having attained perfect clarity,
was designated for spiritual welfare by the Treasure of Truth as the foremost among the wise;
in time, he shall be esteemed as an excellent disciple through his union with Śākyamuni.
O Maudgalyāyana, this discourse on those filled with spiritual awakening was spoken here by me.

In another birth, having been poor and a laborer, he was given a bowl and robes by a certain great sage out of compassion; having been shown miraculous power, he became possessed of incomparable majesty.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Avadāna of Śāriputra’s Ordination," from the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

19. The Legend of Śroṇakoṭikarṇa. That certain supreme and most inexhaustible power, arising from an abundance of merit, which is directly perceptible and witnessed by the side of virtue, attains the state of a physical mark in another birth. KAvk 19.1.
Long ago, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the delightful Jeta’s Grove,
the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī, the Tathāgata resided there.
In Vāsavagrāma there was a householder named Balasena,
who fulfilled the hopes of supplicants like a shady tree laden with fruit.
In due time, a lotus-eyed son was born to his wife Jayasenā;
through his merits, he was like a festival incarnate.
It was like the flame of a jewel-lamp upon the ear-ornament of Karṇa;
its value could not be equaled even by hundreds of millions of gold pieces.
Born under the asterism Śravaṇā, he was worthy of millions of jewels for his ear-ornaments;
thus that prince became known as Śroṇakoṭikarṇa, a name befitting his virtues.
Possessing stainless luster, lovely, and perfected in all his arts,
who did he not become like the moon, overflowing with intense bliss?
Although that youth was being restrained by his father, who possessed the wealth of Kubera,
his mother, with tearful eyes, spoke to him in a most piteous voice.
Though Priyaṃvada was pleasant-spoken, he was to be censured like the moon that showers poison;
seeking jewels with a great caravan, he went to a distant foreign island.
As he was traveling through a desolate region after crossing the ocean, the source of sea-monsters,
he was separated from his own caravan on the road by the upheaval of the waves of karma.
The caravan also, failing to find him, turned back slowly out of grief;
having accumulated suffering, it entered its own country without restraint.
Exhausted and seeking rest, he too plunged into a pool in the southern direction, which was characterized by rows of parched desert sands.
He thought: "Alas!
This effort of mine to acquire wealth in exchange for my own person has resulted in a painful outcome through nothing but misconduct."
Oh, how the obsession with acquiring wealth, due to the lack of contentment in men,
is a convergence of all reproaches and the very seat of censurable calamities!
Even when Hemācala was reached, there was no end to the effort of killing;
for embodied beings in this world, hatred and delusion persist through the habituation of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Like a vast and blazing fortune that has become tasteless through excessive exertion,
this [desire] extends thirst ever further across the great earth.
Alas! Even these mirages in the desert, which at every step produce delusion in the deer blinded by thirst, produce delusion in me as well.
"This is thirst, and this is toil; these are lands devoid of water.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? I see all directions ablaze."
Having reflected thus, as he slowly crept along seeking water,
he beheld an iron city that was like exertion itself given form.
There he saw a man standing at the door, terrible and as formidable as Time itself, with blood-red eyes, appearing as if he were a brother to terror.
When he was asked by him for water and did not say anything at all,
then he himself entered and beheld the world of the departed spirits (pretas).
Seeing the pretas— who resembled burnt wood, smeared with dust and filth, naked,
and whose limbs consisted of nothing but dry bones and sinews— he was deeply pained.
Requested by them for water while himself tormented by the lack of drink,
he set aside his own suffering and became distressed by their misery.
To those who were afflicted by intense thirst and uttering piteous lamentations, he said:
"How could there be water for me, pitiless as I am, in this desert wilderness?"
"Who are you that have been cast into this unbearable hardship, and by what karma?
Because of your lack of cooperation, I too am enduring this suffering."
For him who was as if free from all thorns, his sleep was like one steeped in bliss;
yet, seeing those who were afflicted, he was unable to endure it and strove for the destruction of their suffering.
They said to him: "Due to a mass of delusion, we have been cast into the peril of calamity by this contrary action;
we are mortals who cannot turn back."

By us— who, through insults, the wounds inflicted by those who insult, lack of fortitude, the weight of pride, ignoble vices, and jealousies that bring about unavoidable calamities— have constantly and mercilessly inflicted the pain of arrows upon the heart of our dear friend with words smeared with poison. (KAvk 19.28)
No gift was ever given; wealth was indeed only plundered; the mind was directed solely toward violence;
and with these very limbs of ours, we committed acts of perversion such as the abduction of another's wife. (KAvk 19.29)
We, who were devoted to deception and skilled in base deeds,
have gone to this terrible city of the dead to become vessels for suffering.
Having heard these words of theirs and having seen other such undesirable pretas elsewhere as well, he was overcome with compassion.
Having emerged from that inaccessible fortress by the power of his merit,
he reached a forest region that was pure and possessed cool shade.
Then, scorched by the long journey and utterly exhausted,
the blind man slowly descended from the mountain like the sun, distressed by thirst and heat.
When the day, like merit, had waned and all hope for light had vanished,
a darkness as foul as sin and turbid with delusion rose up over the world.
The seal of closing, which accompanied the lotus ponds whose bees and birds had departed,
arose like sleep.
Then, as if out of compassion, the moon, with a probe of nectar-like moonlight,
made the world— its stars wide open— free from distress.
The reversal of destruction and arising,
which dispels the manifold delusions of the day and night of saṃsāra, is like the moon that causes laughter.
In the moon, which was a rain of nectar for the eyes, a source of pleasant touch, a mirror for the faces of the quarters like brides, and which had arisen as if joy personified— KAvk_19.38.
Śroṇakoṭi first beheld a celestial palace, radiant with the splendor of its face,
which, out of curiosity, seemed like heaven itself descended to earth in another form.
There he saw four celestial women in a state of rapture,
as if they had gathered together for the pleasure of sporting in the joy of the moon's rising.
In their midst, he beheld one of beautiful form sporting there,
appearing as if the very abundance of youthful love had taken on a physical shape.
With the rays of light from his jeweled bracelets, armlets, crown,
and garments, he seemed to paint a wondrous and boundless marvel across the faces of the directions.
Having witnessed that wondrous abundance of the bliss of sensual enjoyment,
he considered it to be the flourishing glory of the fruit of the tree known as "well-performed deeds."
Having been hospitably received by him with affection through sweet drinks, food, and other comforts,
Śroṇakoṭikarṇa then spent that night in happiness.
Then, the morning light of the stars, flowers,
and bees brought about the destruction of the moon's splendor, just as impermanence brings about the exhaustion of fortune.
When the night had come to an end and the sun, the eye of the world and the sole witness to the happiness and suffering of all beings, had risen; KAvk_19.46.
In an instant, the celestial chariot and the divine women vanished from sight,
and a man, his facial luster destroyed, fell to the earth.
Then, a most terrifying pack of dogs fell upon his back,
like the entire mass of suffering arising from the sin of the curse of the three worlds.
Being devoured by them as they tore at the morsels of flesh beginning from his neck and mouth, and by his own cries,
blood, and tears, he went to his destruction.
At the end of the day, he beheld that celestial chariot returning,
along with those four apsarases, that man, and the radiant youth.
Then Śroṇakoṭikarṇa, filled with great wonder, asked him:
"Friend, what is this marvel that is seen? Let it be told."
Questioned by him, he said: "Friend, listen to this:
I know you as Śroṇakoṭikarṇa, one who is worthy of his well-performed deeds."
In the village of Vāsava, I was a wicked cattle-herder;
constantly cutting off the flesh of animals, I sold it. (KAvk 19.53)
"The noble one named Kātyāyana, a treasury of compassion, arrived for alms and said to me: 'Desist from this evil deed.'"
For this affliction consisting of violence is indeed unbearable for those who seek reckless deeds;
it falls upon one's own body just like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Although I was thus being restrained by that noble-souled man, I, being ignoble, did not desist from my evil deed; then he spoke to me again.
"O merciless one, if you indeed commit violence by day in every way,
then at night take up the observance of moral conduct according to my agreement."
Having spoken thus with great effort, he who desires the welfare of all beings bestowed upon me the merit-mindedness consisting of the undertaking of ethical discipline.
Subject to the power of time, I have reached this state at last;
day and night I am as if strewn with showers of hot coals and rain of nectar.
For at night the fruit of his undertaking of moral discipline [accrues], while during the day the fruit of violence [accrues];
thus, by virtue of my own merit and demerit, he has fallen into states of happiness and suffering.
O friend, show compassion for me, who have acted so defilement;
having gone to your own country, speak to my son in private according to my words.
"I have a golden vessel buried at the edge of my house;
having dug it up, you who have abandoned sinful conduct may take possession of it."
"Let the noble Kātyāyana be constantly honored with alms-food.
Having been addressed thus, he said "So be it" out of discipline and departed.
As he proceeded, he beheld another divine celestial chariot,
lovely with creepers of jewel-lotuses, like a second Nandana grove.
At the beginning of the day, he saw that man adorned with jewels, united with a celestial woman as if the bodiless god of love were possessed of limbs.
Having been thus received as a guest with that hospitable display of affection,
he spent that long day as if it were composed of nectar, even in the midst of his suffering.
Then, when the lord of the lotuses had fallen from the summit of the celestial chariot,
the world was filled with masses of darkness as if with terrible sorrows.
Then the Lord of the Night, sluggish with the night,
appeared gradually with a pale luster, as if vomiting moonlight, like one suffering from jaundice.
When the delicate light of day had faded and she was devoured at night by a female rākṣasa,
the moon appeared like the strength of a skull.
When the world was pervaded by moonlight— anointing with the ointment of the moon of the [proper] time—
the celestial chariot departed for some unknown place, and that fawn-eyed woman ascended to heaven.
That man, having fallen from his celestial chariot, was slowly enveloped by Sarvarūpā with seven coils of a centipede.
Having made an opening in his head,
she slowly drank the brain and blood, making the skull hollow.
Then, as the day— its surface marked by labored breaths—
was shrouded by the rays of the dawn, its pupils seemed to close as if from the pain of beholding such a loathsome sight.
Once again, a divine celestial chariot appeared,
as did that lovely woman and the youth of wondrous form, adorned with divine ornaments.
Questioned by him out of great wonder, he related his own story:
"I am a brahmin named Manasa, a resident of Vāsavagrāma."
The young wife of my neighbor, Malayamañjarī,
was a wanton woman who was exceedingly dear to me, a libertine.
My mind, once distracted by delighting in the wives of others in the village,
has now become entirely focused on the village of sense-objects and has reached its destruction.

The noble Kātyāyana, having recognized that I was a thief and a lecher, and being constrained by compassion, spoke softly and privately out of pity: *āryakātyāyanaḥ pāpaṃ jñātvā mām cauryakāmukam / dayāvidheyaḥ kāruṇyāt provāca vijane śanaiḥ //* KAvk_19.78 *//

Do not go to your destruction like a moth falling into the fire of the bodiless god (Anaṅga), through the agitation of your passion for form caused by the pleasure of contact with the body of another's wife.
Alas! The devotion to the wives of others among those who are intensely attached, intoxicated by passion, heedless in their falling [into ruin], lustful, and violent, is truly supreme.
For those overwhelmed by the exhaustion of sleep and intense trembling, whose bodies are scarred by the claws of female vultures pecking at their faces,
and who harbor a longing for the wives of others— there is indeed a supreme passion for hell, which causes the hair to stand on end and induces a state of delusion.
Therefore, my child, turn away from this despicable deed;
sin is born from such contact, for delight in impurity is like that of dogs.
Thus, although I was forbidden by him out of compassion, I— being of impure intellect and bound by unceasing passion—
did not abandon her.
Then, having recognized my constant [devotion], Kātyāyana,
intent on promoting my daily conduct, bestowed upon me the formal undertaking of the ethical precepts (śīla-samādāna).
"From my undertaking of daily vows and from my going to another's wife at night,
this state of mine, consisting of pleasure and pain, has arisen from merit and sin."
"Once you have gone to Vāsavagrāma, my son must be told by you:
'There is gold hidden and kept by me in the fire-chamber. (KAvk 19.86)
"Having extracted that [work], a commentary must be composed, and that Kātyāyana should be honored out of affection"; having been addressed thus by him, Śroṇakoṭi departed from there.
He beheld a divine woman seated before him in a jeweled celestial chariot,
appearing like the goddess Lakṣmī herself, effortlessly emerged from the milk-ocean of loveliness.
At the four feet of that celestial chariot,
he beheld four pretas, bound together by sinews, most difficult to behold.
She too, having recognized him and addressed him with affectionate words,
gave him delicious and flavorful food and drink.
While he was eating, he was piteously entreated from afar by hungry ghosts;
out of compassion, he gave them morsels of food as if they were crows.
The lump of food became fodder for one, iron for another,
human flesh for the third, and pus for the fourth.
Beholding their miserable plight, he was overcome with compassion and questioned them regarding the luster of their faces, which had been made to look like faded lotuses.
Questioned about that marvel by him, the deer-eyed woman said:
"Not even the tip of Śroṇakoṭīṣa's finger, when given, would suffice for their satisfaction."
"I am the wife of this Brāhmaṇa, who formerly supported himself on his forefeet;
I am named Sunandā, the daughter of one called Nanda, and I dwell in Vāsavagrāma."
My son named Niṣṭhura is clinging to my second foot, and this maidservant and my daughter-in-law are hanging from my hind legs. (KAvk 19.96)
Previously, while I was preparing an offering of alms for the worship of the conjunction of the constellations,
the noble Kātyāyana entered my house.
Honored by me with alms-food, he whose mind was filled with serene faith departed,
his very radiance bestowing grace upon the quarters of the sky through its stainless purity.
Then, having bathed, this husband of mine returned quickly;
hearing the sound of my footsteps, he was delighted by what I said.
In anger he said to me: "Why has this deceitful ascetic, who is worthy of chaff among those who deserve honor, been honored by you instead of those who truly deserve honor? (KAvk 19.100)
When he had spoken thus out of delusion, this son also said to me:
"Is he not fit for eating even before cooking; why then would he eat iron balls?"
"This is my daughter-in-law; she constantly consumed the food before me.
When I said this, she made an oath, asserting that she was an eater of her own flesh.
And this slave girl, who used to consume the alms-food and cause its depletion,
being reproached, spoke the truth regarding the pus and blood.
There, they became hungry ghosts, whose food corresponded to their own words;
but I, through the grace of my noble husband, am now an enjoyer of divine pleasures.
"O noble Śama, having attained [this state], you must say to my daughter:
'In your father's house there are four treasures of gold.'"
Having extracted those [qualities] as appropriate, maintain your status as one not born of your own kin;
O Kātyāyana, the brother of your father is always to be honored by name.
"O Śroṇakoṭikarṇ, you are he; go now and abandon your weariness.
Twelve years of the rainy season have been completed since you departed from your own home."
Having spoken thus and commanded his four *preta* companions,
he caused him to reach his own country in a mere moment while he was still asleep.
Having suddenly risen from the garden grove of his own country,
he heard that his parents had become blind due to the grief of separation.
While the assembly of monks, brahmins, and guests was being honored in the temple of the gods,
he beheld his own ancestral home and was struck with great astonishment.
Having ascertained the impermanence of all things due to their momentariness,
and having completely cast off affection and passion, he remained there and reflected with equanimity.
Ah! This sleep of delusion continues incessantly day and night;
through the play of dreams and illusions, it creates a wondrous confusion.
The mother provides the path of birth, the father sows the seed, and the body is a resting place for the traveler; what purpose, then, is there in this adherence to religious observances?
Riches, familiar with the wandering of the clouds of saṃsāra, possess a golden luster yet are as untainted and fickle as lightning flashes;
the body is encompassed by all manner of calamities, which are the very abodes of the fear of decay.
Yet, even because of the anxieties caused by old age and disease, embodied beings do not attain dispassion.
This salutation with joined palms is offered for the welfare and success of my own kin;
may you grant me your favor out of courtesy, for renunciation alone is dear to me.
Having reflected thus, he comforted his parents, whose eyes were filled with tears,
and established them on the pure path of the Dharma, the abode of tranquility.
Though long lost from his caravan and emaciated,
he did not become an object of pity for his own people, because his wealth of courage remained undiminished.
Have compassion for this one who is overwhelmed by the afflictions of saṃsāra;
for whom among the virtuous would you have compassion, when they are devoid of longing due to contact with prosperity?

that great monastery was completed in the Tuṣita heaven, the abode of the gods.
Having heard this, his inner joy redoubled through the arising of faith,
he had a monastery constructed with a magnificent storehouse of gold and jewels.
Then, by means of the riches worthy of kings provided for him along the way,
the Blessed One, the Jina, arrived together with the gods of the triple heaven.
When the three worlds were gladdened by the joy of his arrival,
Anāthapiṇḍada poured forth a stream of water upon him.
When that stream of water did not fall upon that spot, then,
by the word of the Blessed One, it quickly fell elsewhere.
Having seen this, the Blessed One was questioned again by the monks out of curiosity; he said:
"Listen to this cause of the pillar of water."
"By this, it has been demonstrated that this very foundation was established for the sake of former Buddhas;
thus, this stream of water has fallen from another source."
In the past, this very site of the excellent grove was offered by him to the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin.
Furthermore, at the time of his birth under the Puṣya constellation, he gave [the gift] to the Buddha Śikhin;
then, at the time of his birth under the Ragu constellation, he gave it to the Jina Viśvabhū.
Having become Bhavadatta, he gave [the gift] to Kakucchanda;
having become Bṛhaspati, he gave it to the Protector named Kanaka.
Furthermore, he gave this to Kāśyapa at the birth of Āṣāḍha;
by him alone has this country now been bestowed upon me.
In due time, this virtuous youth named Sudhana, by virtue of his patience and moral discipline, will bestow [the wealth] upon Maitreya and behold the treasures.
Furthermore, having become a householder named Hemaprabha,
he performed the funeral rites for a Pratyekabuddha upon his final nirvāṇa.
Having placed his bones in a jewel-jar by virtue of that aspiration,
this Suvarṇabhāsa has now become worthy of a treasury of jewels.
Having heard this utterance of the Teacher’s words, which was like the very essence of nectar, those monks rejoiced intensely,
perfumed by the abundant flowers of merit acquired through their steadfast devotion to the Creator.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Acceptance of the Jetavana," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
22. The Acceptance of Father and Son: "Aha! Like a precious jewel, greatness is possessed by the worthy through the weight of their virtues;
for that heaviness of bodies which exists without virtue is as fruitless as that of massive stones."

In former times, the illustrious King Śuddhodana in the city of the Śākyas—a treasury of the nectar of purity—attained the state of a Sugata through the practice of dispassion; remembering his son, he was filled with great longing.
He thought: "When shall I behold the face of my son—a dwelling-place for the fragrance of merit and virtue, a lotus-bloom upon the Sarasvatī, and a pleasure-palace for the play of a serene mind?"
"Come!"— thus, by those who were sent by me to the Jeta Grove out of longing to see him,
they remain right there with unblinking eyes beholding him, drinking the nectar of immortality.
That Udāyin, whom I had sent to him out of affection because he was equal to myself,
went to that very place which delights the inhabitants of heaven, and having become a messenger with the letter in his hand, he attained the state of a letter.
Surely he has forgotten the message sent by me through his own mouth;
for indeed, everyone desires their own welfare and remains indifferent toward the interests of others.
"Come by means of your glance and quickly drench my limbs with a flood of nectar;
resting for a moment without attachment, you who are subject to compassion, perform the duty of a kinsman."
Having heard this story, he would delay for a moment even in coming to see me;
for it is not the nature of a heart as tender as a young leaf to break a bond of affection.
When the lord of the earth had set out before him with the thought, "May he see me," Udāyin arrived,
manifesting his favor through his renunciation, out of a surge of joyful emotion.
Seeing him, his mind overflowing with joy and possessing a majesty equal to that of renunciation, the king became filled with longing;
his steadfastness faltering, he fell into a swoon of delusion.
Having regained consciousness through the cool waters, he asked him, "Will she indeed come to me?
He replied, "O King, she will come to you with respect in a few days, before the provisions are exhausted."
Then, after some days had passed,
the Blessed Youth Sarvārthasiddha, followed by a multitude of mendicants, slowly traveled through the sky accompanied by hosts of celestial beings.
Adorned with a garland of mandāra flowers released from the lotus-like hands of celestial beauties,
he shone like the mountain of the immortals (Mount Meru), whose body is graced by the playful smiles of the clearly visible masses of foam upon the heavenly Gaṅgā.
The faces of the quarters shone with celestial chariots that resembled clouds shattered by collision, stumbling along with the sound of golden bells;
they appeared as if offering hymns of praise to the Teacher out of devotion.

The sky reached its limit, pervaded by gods together with hosts of Vidyādharas and Siddhas who were as if without intervals, appearing as if they were the sun’s rays, and crowded with white parasols held closely together.
Then, in an instant, everyone beheld him— intent on benefiting the entire world, possessing every form and appearing as everything— descending from the sky, from the quarters, and from the earth.
Beholding that treasure-house of vision, a mass of joy for the eyes of the people and a measure of merit for festivals of good deeds, the world leaped up, surging with waves of wonder.
Having perceived that wondrous and radiant power indicated by Udāyin,
the lord of the earth bowed from afar with palms joined in reverence to the prince, the teacher of the world.
Then, having descended, followed by noble men and being honored with affection by the king,
he entered the jeweled ground beneath the banyan tree, which illuminated the quarters of the sky with its vast radiance.
There he sat upon a golden throne provided with footstools, which supported the three worlds established in his teaching;
it was adorned with variegated leaves and sprouts of jewels, and his radiant body was like Mount Meru.
Beholding that flood of nectar for his eyes— the moon of her mind— arrived through the prayer of his heart's desire,
the lord of the earth, gazing with unblinking satisfaction, attained for a moment the state of a god.
With his throat choked with tears, he spoke to the prince, who was overwhelmed by intense joy;
as the prince entered, his gaze fixed upon the reflection of the central gem in the necklace, the king seemed to vomit forth the very essence of affection from within.
By their very nature, like the cool mountain of contentment, all beings delight in wholesome states;
why then have you given us this instruction on separation, which acts as a cruel adversary?
Out of affection, joy, and respect for your virtues, this mind of mine runs toward you irresistibly,
equally eager for an embrace, for a lasting union, and for prostrating at your feet.
Whatever matter has been spoken by me must certainly be heard out of consideration for our affection;
whether it be devoid of merit or of a harsh sequence, nothing is unfit to be said to one deluded by love.
Why do you abandon these golden palaces, which are covered by the intense radiance of the sun reflected in every single jewel, and plunge instead into the depths of empty forests?
Having been consecrated with excellent, fragrant water from golden jars offered by beloved women,
how is it that you alone bathe in desert lands where the waters are heated by the parched dust?
Do you perceive only the ornament—the radiance of the jewels in your earrings—hanging from your cheeks?
Why is it that, though devoid of pleasure, sandalwood as white as the moon does not delight you?
Why do you lie upon a bed of *kuśa* grass when you deserve a royal couch with a great canopy, as white as Śeṣa himself?
How can your body, fit for the enjoyment of embracing the fresh Lakṣmī, endure such a bed?

This limb of yours, worthy of fine garments and resembling the waves of a beloved’s smile— how has it become fond of this alms-bowl today, while your hand remains the resting place for a playful lotus?
This neck of yours, a dwelling-place worthy of the embrace of the arms of a longing beloved,
now causes the sudden breaking of affection, its joy exhausted by the splendor of worldly enjoyment.
Beauty has rendered the god of love powerless; prosperity consists of breasts as high as the frontal globes of rutting elephants;
and youth is a pleasure-grove for Rati—by whom has dispassion been conceived toward these peerless things?
Having heard this, that treasury of virtue replied with a smile as charming as the crescent moon,
making the royal splendor appear as if it were invisible, for its various colors had been transferred to the jewels of the kings.
O King, if the activity of living beings were not as fickle as a wave, like one stricken by old age and disease,
then whose longing for sense objects would not incessantly rain down the nectar of intense joy?
For those who are firmly established in the tasting of the nectar of tranquility, the grounds of the forest depths of emptiness are not places of downfall;
for those who are overwhelmed by the intoxication of the play of supernatural powers, palatial mansions are sites of ultimate ruin.
Kings who bathe with saffron-infused waters constantly fall into a state of passion;
however, those whose nature is contentment become stainless, purified by the pure water of mental clarity.

The ear of those filled with compassion shines through learning alone, not by an earring; the hand shines through giving, not by a bracelet; and the body shines through service to others, not by sandalwood paste.

These ornaments, whose beloveds have been struck down by delusion, which possess smiles as white as clinging rays of pearl-light, are not to be enjoyed by the virtuous; they are the leavings of a king.
For those afflicted by passion or tormented by the seasons, sleep indeed does not exist, nor for those possessed by thoughts of wealth;
yet upon beds of exquisite touch, the King, tranquil in every way, sleeps in peace alone.
His mode of life is that of a serpent, not because of his robe, but because of his excellent garment which is as beautiful as a snake’s slough;
he carries a bowl filled with purifying things, which produces food consisting of the nectar of loving-kindness.
The parasols are excessively crooked and dim, the gusts of wind from the fans are agitated by gems,
and the pearl necklaces, moist with yellow sandalwood paste, make the hearts of the kings heavy with clinging dejection.
Prosperity is accompanied by the disease of separation; beloveds end in a moment; pleasure is devoid of flavor;
and in this world, misfortune is ever-present—who, then, can truly enjoy such fortune? It is merely a beautiful deception.

The forceful indulgence in sensual pleasures constantly produces lethargy accompanied by yawning; it spreads thirst, delusion, infatuation, and fainting, and renders even the very essence of life unbearable.
When the splendor of happiness was like the crescent of the new moon, and even the flowers of dawn were not to be found,
then this passion of mine was cast into the grasp of the waves of karma.
Royal fortunes, with their fly-whisks, clusters of banners and silken streamers, the manes of horses, and the flapping ears of elephants—
though they are indeed fickle by nature, all such displays of luxury are subject to momentary destruction.
Having spoken thus for the sake of the king's various virtues and having established in him a supreme clarity of mind,
he gazed upon his retinue with a glance that scattered a stream of nectar from the waves of peace.
Having established the Dharma for seventy thousand wise ones born of the Śākya clan,
he there brought seven thousand others to the attainment of full and distinguished realization.
Then, through white rice and other wholesome foods provided by a multitude numbering a thousand equal to himself,
as well as through *droṇa*-measures of rice and ambrosial food, a truly great clarity of mind was attained.
Some went forth toward the awakening of the disciples, while others were devoted to the awakening of the solitary buddhas;
still others became firmly attached to the perfect, unsurpassed awakening, their minds as clear as the sky.
Some attained the fruit of stream-entry, others the fruit of once-returning, and likewise others the fruit of non-returning;
still others attained the fruit of arhatship, while others achieved liberation from the afflictions.

But there, one man named Devadatta— whose delusion was intensified by a mass of darkness consisting of the curse of accumulated sins— laughed and said to the people in the assembly, "This is an illusion," while he himself remained established in truth.

The monk Maudgalya, by means of the Jina’s teaching and through his great supernatural powers, stripped of pride that king who was previously immersed in affection for his son and had become arrogant due to the birth of a son.
Even after seeing the power of the Blessed One, the king did not consider it particularly marvelous;
he thought it was merely human prowess, for surely the superior deeds of people who are absorbed in practice do not cause astonishment.

Then, on the following day, the Blessed One sat upon a jeweled lion-throne, possessing an equal splendor like the summit of Mount Sumeru, within a great golden celestial palace prepared by the Lord of the Gods.
Then, while the gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, were seated there with their vast radiance,
the quarters of the sky shone as if garlanded with matted locks of moonbeams due to the playful movements of the crests of his uṣṇīṣa.

Having arrived at that city, which was crowded with gods entering through its four gates— gods who brought wealth and whose necklaces swayed as they jostled one another— the king could not find a path through them.
There, his desired entry being forbidden by Kuvera and the other lords with frowns and the movement of eyebrows,
the king became utterly speechless, his face pale and his words faltering.
Having been introduced by them to the teaching of the Jina and having at one time attained its highest stage,
Śuddhodana stood before him with a serene mind, yet without bowing his head in prostration.
The Teacher, however, taught him a discourse on the Dharma that awakens one to the Four Noble Truths—
a discourse by which his knowledge shattered even the mountain of the view of a self-identity, with its twenty peaks.
Then, having gone there and fulfilled the purpose of his birth, he reached Śuklodana and said: "Accept the kingdom; it is your own hereditary right.
That teaching ordained by the Blessed One is for the sake of joy, not for the sake of kingship."
Then, although Droṇodana had turned his back on the kingdom and Amṛtodana was devoted to renunciation,
the one named Bhadra assumed that royal fortune bestowed by Śuddhodana.
Then, having honored the Conqueror, the Lord of Men, with enjoyments worthy of a king that were pure and well-prepared,
and having presented him with the Nyagrodha grove, Śuddhodana’s pure aspirations were fulfilled.
The two sons of Droṇodana were also young; by the command of the king and the urging of their mother, one became the renunciant Aniruddha, while the other became a householder named Mahān.
Then, in the mind of King Bhadraka, who was dispassionate, there arose a longing for the forest;
for even new wealth does not obstruct the minds of those who dwell in solitude and are devoted to tranquility.
Then, having summoned Devadatta, whose mind was intent upon the consecration to the kingdom, he said:
"The time for my renunciation has arrived; what is to be done by you?"
To him, Devadatta, whose hypocrisy was concealed by a pretense of discernment, replied in that assembly:
"O King, I have no desire for the kingdom; rather, through the life of a wandering mendicant, I shall become like you."
Having heard these contemptuous words spoken by that deceitful and falsely humble man,
the king laughed and said, "This assembly of Śākyas is the witness to your resolve."
Then Devadatta, afflicted by the heat of his desire for wealth, reflected thus out of attachment to sensual enjoyments:
"Why did I utter this ill-omened word? Might even a renunciant take up the kingdom? (KAvk 22.68)
Abandoning their own kingdom, the Śākya princes, headed by Bhadra, departed together with Śuddhodana—
who felt joy at their departure— traveling in chariots and on elephants.
Then, as they were all departing, Devadatta seized the ruby from the crown that was fixed upon the head—
the sun whose rays made the sky blossom with light— just as a hawk, seeking meat, seizes a bird smeared with blood.
Then, having observed that fierce birthmark of his, the prognosticators declared that it portended a journey to hell;
for a bad omen indeed indicates a mind possessed of fault, while any other sign was said to be merely a repetition.

There, many characteristics of those who were excessively intoxicated with pride— such as Kokālika, Khaṇḍa, Utkaṭa, Mora, and Kāṇa, whose names corresponded to the lunar days and other such markers— were clearly indicated by their various corresponding signs.
Then, out of joy for the king, Bhadraka also, together with Devadatta and the others,
through his renunciation and his possession of the robe and bowl, made the earth as if composed of dispassion.
Having tearfully removed the hair of the king and the princes— who were adorned with discarded necklaces, armlets, and earrings— the barber Upālī, it is said, became disenchanted.
Though he was a fool and even low-born, by the very command of the Jina he became most worthy of honor through his renunciation;
I consider that neither scholarship nor birth is the cause for such supreme clarity of mind.
Then, even Bhadraka, having learned from his attendant that this was the king,
remained motionless, thinking, "How can I, a lord of the earth, bow at the feet of one so lowly?"
The Blessed One, smiling, spoke to him whose pride was unshaken and who was free from conceptual construction:
"By means of the life of renunciation, the pride consisting of birth, which is followed by great delusion, is completely abandoned."
When he had heard this and the king, together with the princes, had prostrated themselves, the earth trembled;
yet Devadatta, speaking harsh words, did not bow his feet at the words of the Blessed One.
Then, when the Teacher was questioned by the assembly of monks whose minds were filled with wonder because of the trembling of the earth, he said:
"It is said that even in another birth in a previous eon, this king offered him obeisance."
Long ago, in the city of Kāśī, a poor man named Sundaraka, having seen a courtesan named Bhadrā, performed service for her; for passion is indeed the instructor of all calamities.
Sent by her to gather flowers, like a bee repeatedly seeking more nectar,
he wandered through the forest depths, exhausted by his longing for union with her, which was like a desire of the god of love.
In the meantime, the king, exceedingly weary from his passion for hunting, reached the edge of the forest;
there Brahmadatta, beholding him, heard that song while his own body was hidden by the creepers.
"O bee, why are you thus tormented by heat, longing for ever-new flowers? Go quickly!
For that lotus-pond, with its faces of blooming lotuses, becomes closed at the end of the day."
Having heard her song, the king—the brilliance of his smile striking against the luster of his necklace—spoke to him:
"Friend, who is this person whose absorption in the essence of the song is so intense, even as he is scorched by the heat of the sun with its fierce rays?"
He too replied, "O Lord of the Earth, it is not that the sun does not scorch; rather, desire is even more scorching.
In this world, the sufferings of one's own actions destroy [all else], but the desert lands are not scorched by the summer heat."
Thus, by imparting the excellence of meaningful speech, he attained the favor of the king;
for to whom does well-spoken advice, when touched by its correspondence to reality, not become a source of honor?
Then the grateful king, weary from his journey, having had his heat dispelled by cooling treatments in that secluded place,
took him with affection and returned together with him to his own capital.

There, his mental state filled with the satisfaction of hearing the words "giver of life," he stood ready to offer half his kingdom; for what could be given to one who follows the inclinations of the heart?
Then, as he was prepared to offer half his kingdom, Sundaraka did not think of compassion;
for what use have I for the pleasures of kingship without Bhadrā? Indeed, blessed is he who is sprinkled with the nectar of her affection.
Even sovereignty and such do not please me; for even a small portion of fortune, when undivided, shines with splendor.
For when two share a single object, there is constant strife; indeed, with enjoyments shared between two, it is discord itself incarnate.
"Therefore, having struck down this dull-witted king, I shall become complete with the entire kingdom.
Having reflected thus for a moment, tormented by remorse, he again applied his mind intensely to his own state.
"What was this thought of mine, so intent on the censurable? What indeed is this manner of cruelty?
Alas! From the stain of a thought so ungrateful, there is shame even for my own heart."

May there be well-being for the kingdom; homage to pleasures! May the Mother of Delusion and the Goddess Lakṣmī forgive [this], for those whose very first nature is an intellect such as this, which has never tasted even contemplated [worldly things].
It causes delusion, it brings about fainting, it indeed strikes one down, and it spreads darkness;
alas, the creeper of Fortune, at the mere moment of being smelled, brings about the destruction of men!
Having reflected for a long time, Vimalaprabha, whose mind was set on the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha,
did not accept the kingdom at dawn, even though he was entreated by the lord of men, for his thirst [for worldly things] had ceased.

Seeing that he had attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha in due time, the king of great supernatural power observed him with a mind full of serene faith, his own crown-garland falling at the lotus-feet of the sage.
That certain discernment, born from the ripening of virtuous deeds, is worthy of homage— a consecration of tranquility—
by whose power the earth, girdled by the oceans, becomes as something to be abandoned for those whose desires have ceased.
Having heard this, and having carried out that entire matter at the king’s request, Gaṅgapāla—the barber, his intimate confidant—attained a state of peace. || KAvk_22.98 ||

Having attained through supreme application of action that state worthy of worship by the virtuous by means of renunciation, the king bowed down upon the earth and paid him homage; at that moment, the earth shook in six ways.
"Behold, Upāli, this King Brahmadatta, who is well-disposed and has offered his salutations; that artisan Gaṅgapāla is indeed doing well.
Having heard these words of wonder spoken by the Blessed One, those monks were amazed.
They considered the very cause—the pure mind—to be the refuge for well-performed deeds.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Acceptance by Father and Son," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
23. The Legend of Viśvantara:
Those rare jewels among men, whose desires have been stilled by reflection, who are beyond reproach in all worlds, and who possess unprecedented power, are worthy of being honored by others.
For those who, even by giving away their most beloved children, wives, and so forth for the sake of sentient beings, experience no withering of the face— that messenger of dejection.
In former times, when the Blessed One, the Victor, was questioned by the monks in the city of the Śākyas,
he related this past account in the course of the story of Devadatta.
The city named Viśvā became the abode of universal prosperity and the birthplace of merit,
as if it were the very source of virtue devoted to the welfare of all.
In that city there was a king named Sañjaya, who was a sun to the darkness of his enemies,
a source of nectar for the eyes, and possessed of wondrous deeds.
He had a son named Viśvantara,
a generous man, by whom the fame of the two Kalpas was surpassed through his unprecedented renunciation.
Free from envy, they were equally adorned by that wise man,
through whom eloquence was won by truth, prosperity by generosity, and intellect by sacred learning.
Even today, his fame— white as the inner petals of the ketaka flower— shines forth, having become an ear-ornament for the beauties of the quarters.
Once, he gave divine jeweled ornaments to a petitioner—
ornaments that surpassed even the desire for universal sovereignty with their brilliance.
When that excellent chariot was given, O Lord of Men, the hearts of all the people were overcome with wonder,
while the king was seized by anxious thought.
Then, having summoned his great ministers, the lord of the earth, devoid of joy and with his heart's desires overcome by mounting agitation and anxiety, spoke:
That victorious chariot, the crusher of enemies, was given by Kumāra;
it is through its power that this great army of great car-warriors was acquired.
Fortune, seated comfortably upon me,
attained stability through her presence in that chariot on the path of valor and in that elephant named Jayakuñja.
Having heard these words of the king, the ministers said to him:
"O King, this fault is yours alone, for you have become negligent through your affection."
To whom would Dharma not bring joy? To whom would giving not be agreeable?
Yet, those seeking leaves turn away from a tree whose roots have been destroyed.
"And that chariot was sold abroad by that twice-born man.
Having said this, all the ministers became as if pierced by arrows.
Then, when the time had arrived, during the spring festival of Madana,
which bestowed joy upon the heart like the ripening of one's own good deeds.
The world, seeking honey from the bees that subsist on what they gather themselves,
has been rendered white by his glories, as if by groves of blossoming flowers.
The world has become like a *kalikāla* tree— free from sorrow, providing cool shade for the people, and intent on doing good—
wherein the honey has been shaken down as the conflict is resolved.
The prince, having mounted the royal elephant Rājavardhana,
went to see the blossoming trees in the forest, which were like wish-fulfilling trees for those in need.
As he was proceeding along the road, the twice-born men employed by the neighboring king approached him and spoke,
preceded by words of blessing.
You are celebrated as the wish-fulfilling gem, the praiseworthy moving being in this world;
by the mere sight of you, the seeker is firmly embraced by Prosperity.
In this auspicious birth, there are only two renowned for their excellence yet possessed of enmity:
you in the world, whose trunk is moistened by generosity, and this elephant, whose height is firm.
"O giver of well-earned merit, let this elephant be given to us;
it cannot be given by any donor other than you."
Thus entreated by them, he, full of enthusiasm, gave them the elephant—
which, with its conch, banner, and chowrie, was like a living empire— KAvk_23.24.
Having given away the chariot-jewel and the lordly elephant with a vow centered on awakening, he of pure intellect became filled with overflowing joy.
As soon as the king heard that the world-renowned elephant Jayakuñjara had been given away,
he considered his royal fortune to be devoid of all protection.
Then the prince, having been dismissed by the enraged king who feared the loss of his kingdom,
bowed down to him and set forth.
Taking with him his son named Jālina and a daughter named Kṛṣṇā, he went to the forest together with his beloved Mādrī.
Even in the forest, he gave the remainder of his mounts and other possessions to those who requested them;
for the courage of the great remains equal in both prosperity and adversity.
Once, when Mādrī had gone out to obtain flowers, roots, and fruits,
a certain Brāhmaṇa approached and spoke to the prince.
"O Great Being, give these two clever boys to me, for you are renowned as one who gives everything, even when deprived of attendants."
Having heard this, and without even reflecting upon it, he immediately gave away his two most beloved children to him,
and thus suddenly endured the agony of separation from them.
In this world, what is not dear to anyone—wealth, sons, wife, and so forth?
For those who are generous and compassionate, nothing is more beloved than giving.
Then Mādrī, tender toward her children, approached and,
not seeing the two boys before her husband, fell down, overcome by fainting.
Having regained consciousness, she was pervaded by the blazing fire of grief;
as soon as she heard the account of the giving away of her child, she began to lament.
In her heart, the fire of grief— unbearable due to her affection for her offspring—
attained the intensity of a *puṭapāka* (hermetic cooking) as it followed the path of her love for her beloved.
In the meantime, the Lord of the Gods, having approached in the form of a brahmin,
requested the beloved wife as a servant from the prince.
Suddenly entreated by him [to give up his wife],
that ocean of courage, steadying himself with his intellect, bestowed upon him the grief born of separation from his wife.
Like a terrified doe trembling from an immediate threat,
he spoke to his beloved, inwardly cherishing the latent impression of awakening.
Take heart, O auspicious lady; you ought not to grieve.
This union with a beloved is unreal, resembling a dream or a lover's fancy.
Through service to this twice-born man, may your mind delight in dharma;
for in the fickle course of worldly existence, dharma is the steadfast friend of the virtuous.
Having seen all one's own people, good friends, and kinsmen pass away,
and having placed upon one's neck the *mitrā* flower— fragrant for a moment but withering in an instant—
one has spent youth and life incessantly for the sake of wife and son.
There is no one else who has attained [this state] except for the Dharma; it is unattainable and unfamiliar to anyone other than through the Dharma.
Having spoken thus, out of his renunciation of greed,
he carried away his beloved with the lotus of his face and with a mind characterized by fortitude.
Seeing Mādrī overwhelmed by the grief of separation, the Lord of Śacī, filled with compassion, assumed his own form and spoke to her: KAvk_23.44.
"Do not despair, my daughter; I am a god, the lord of the thirty-three.
He gives you to those who seek you, and therefore you have been requested by me."
"Now you, who were entrusted to me as a deposit, have become my husband's;
he gives you to him, not to another—how could you be given away? (KAvk 23.46)
"I shall certainly bring about your reunion with your two children," having thus spoken,
the Thousand-eyed One suddenly vanished.
Then the brahmin, taking those two boys with him out of a desire for wealth,
went to the city of Viśvāmitra and, driven by greed, prepared to sell them.
Viśvāmitra, having recognized the two children as the prince's sons,
took them with great affection, his eyes choked with tears.
When King Viśvāmitra had gone to the third heaven in due course,
Viśvantara took charge of the kingdom at the request of the citizens and the assembly of ministers.
Although he was detached from his kingdom and excessively addicted to giving,
no beggar ever failed to find success, for his prosperity increased through his very virtue.
That Brāhmaṇa Jambuka, whose wealth was filled with that very [gold], being ungrateful, declared to the people: "This prosperity is due to my own power. (KAvk 23.52)
"I am that very Viśvantara, and that twice-born man was Devadatta," having said this,
the Blessed One gave a teaching on generosity to the monks.
Giving is a support for one falling into a hundred abysses, a long-lasting light in terrible darkness, a consolation in times of unbearable suffering; it is the kinsman of men in the world beyond.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Legend of Viśvantara," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
24. The Legend of the Great Departure (Abhiniṣkramaṇāvadāna).
The sun rises to create a world filled with all manner of restless beings; the moon reaches its fullness for the sake of a supreme rain of nectar.

Yet, in this vast world, only someone rare takes birth as one worthy of veneration—a bridge of immense merit—for the purpose of ferrying sentient beings across the ocean of existence. *Kāvyālaṃkāravṛtti*, 24.1.
In former times, there was a glorious King Śuddhodana in the city of the Śākyas;
he was the progenitor of the moon of fame, like another ocean of nectar.
Fortune, who by her very nature clings to the wicked,
