was made by him— who performs wonders— to be devoted to the virtuous, having been bestowed upon the multitude of the meritorious.
Even today, by the pure glories of his fame, which cling to the forests at the ends of all directions, the life of a sage is carried forth as it were by the wise.
"May I be born of a pure mother," he had indeed vowed in the past;
thus, the son of Viśvakarman, possessing stainless luster, came to the mortal world.
Fame was exceedingly dear to him, as it is to a virtuous man;
yet there was a queen named Mahāmāyā who was as beloved to him as Kumudvatī is to the moon.
In a dream, she saw a white elephant entering her womb through the air,
ascending a mountain, and receiving homage from a great multitude of people.
In the meantime, the Bodhisattva himself, out of compassion for the world, entered her womb from Tuṣita, the abode of the Thirty-three gods.
Carrying within her womb the Bodhisattva, the delight of the world,
she became white-complexioned like the shore of the ocean of milk carrying the moon.
By him, a scion of the royal lineage of Ikṣvāku, while still dwelling in the womb,
that earth became as if possessed of hidden treasures, marked by the signs of prosperity.
A pregnancy longing arose in her, consisting of the emergence of merit from giving;
it was like the fragrance of a mango tree, which is non-deceptive even at the stage of the sprout.
In due time, having reached full term, that queen stayed in the Lumbinī grove and gave birth to a son,
just as Aditi gave birth to the Sun.
Having pierced his mother’s womb, he emerged unsullied by the impurities of the fetus;
then, by his very nature, he restored her so that her limbs were healthy and her pain had vanished.
Even as he was departing, he was blocked for a moment by Śakra, who desired to test his strength; though his limbs were as solid as adamant, he became impossible to overcome.

As soon as he was born, the infant went himself seven steps, and looking toward the directions, he spoke with words of perfectly clear syllables: KAvk_24.15: "As soon as he was born, the infant went himself seven steps, and looking toward the directions, he spoke with words of perfectly clear syllables."
This is cessation (nirvṛti), and it is the eastern direction among the worlds;
this birth is the southern, and this saṃsāra is the northern.
As he was speaking thus, the earth trembled,
as if unable to support that teacher of the world who possessed inexhaustible strength.

The deities took up for him— whose body was washed by the streams from the clouds of the sky— the white parasol of his glory, which was bright with the smiles of living beings and accompanied by fly-whisks.
At this juncture,
having seen her radiance while stationed on Mount Kiṣkindhā, the sage named Asita was questioned by Nārada, the son of his maternal uncle.
Why is this light seen like the radiance of a hundred suns,
by which the mountains, along with their caves and houses, are impoverished of darkness?
When he spoke thus out of wonder, that one with divine vision replied:
"This Puṇyaprabhāsa was born at the time of the Bodhisattva's birth."
"O child, we shall see you before long for the attainment of well-being.
Having said this, the sage, out of joy, became happy with the bliss of rest.
Upon the birth of his son, Śuddhodana, seeing the supreme accomplishment of all aims, bestowed upon him the name Sarvārthasiddha, meaning "He by whom all aims are accomplished."
There was a yakṣa named Śākyavardhana who resided in the city of the Śākyas;
by bowing down to him, the children of the Śākyas remained free from harm.
Sent by his father to offer salutations while staying there, he, together with the Guhyakas,
beheld that Bodhisattva and fell at his feet.
Then, having taken him onto his lap, the delighted lord of the earth had the marks on his body examined by those skilled in interpreting signs.
Then all those experts in the science of marks, filled with wonder, said to the king:
"Your Majesty, this divine youth is distinguished by his auspicious marks."
By these characteristics, he is born as one whose teaching brings rest to the entire world:
as Śakra, the lord of gods, as a universal monarch, or as the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.
His feet were long-fingered, marked with wheels,
well-set, ruddy, beautiful, and as soft as lotuses.
Tall like a royal swan, with webbed fingers like sprouts,
this glorious one possesses a pair of knees adorned by arms reaching down to his knees.
His private parts are concealed within a sheath, his body is well-proportioned like a banyan tree,
his body hair curls to the right, and his girth is equal to his height.
Untouched by the slightest speck of dust or impurity, he possessed the luster of refined gold;
on his hands, feet, shoulders, neck, and forehead, he bore the distinct marks of the seven-leaved tree.
With the upper half of his body like that of a lion, he possessed a large and well-defined physical form;
he had forty even white teeth and a beautiful nose.
His tongue was long and slender, his voice was like the sound of clouds or a drum;
his eyes were deep blue, his eyelashes were like those of a cow, and his head was naturally adorned with a protuberance.
This child has a mark like a crescent moon on his forehead, a chest radiant with the svastika sign,
hands marked with lines, a conch, and a lotus, and a head shaped like a parasol.
"O King, this son of yours will become a universal monarch (cakravartin),
or he will become a perfectly awakened Buddha, omniscient."
Having spoken thus, when they had been born, the lord of the earth attained great joy;
after seven days, the Teacher’s mother went to the third heaven.
At his birth, because the Śākyas possessed a tranquility like that of sages,
when they saw him, that infant then received the name Śākyamuni.
Having determined by his splendor that "he is even a god among the gods," the lord of the earth gave him the name Devātideva.
Then, accompanied by Nārada, the sage Asita, who perceives the truth,
respectfully approached that place from the penance grove in order to see him.
Beholding the Bodhisattva, who was like the rising sun illuminating the eon, she—
her own beauty blooming with joy— attained a resemblance to a lotus.
To the king who had offered hospitality and was bowing before him, the sage said:
"O King, you are as desirable through your multitude of virtues as you are by your son."
"These marks of his announce the attainment of the fortune of liberation;
the fruit of the glory of a universal monarch is not their perishable end."
By the power of this Perfectly Awakened One’s enlightenment, his lotus-like face will become a vessel for the eyes,
like a blessed lotus pond.
Fortunate will be the wise ones who, subsisting on the nectar of his speech, shall live upon the milk-ocean of enlightenment belonging to him whose nature is pure.
In this world of meritorious beings, I alone am deceived,
for the sight of one such as you is difficult to obtain even when one's time has reached its full measure.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, he went through the air to the penance grove;
making his mind perfectly serene, he contemplated the abandonment of his body.
Urged by Nārada to provide a final instruction,
the Kumāra said to him, "My child, Amṛta will tell you."
"Having attained from that prince the deathless state free from all ailment, you shall cross the ocean of existence"; having spoken thus, he cast off his body.
Having immediately performed an improper reception for him, Śrī departed for Vārāṇasī; there, through spiritual perfection, she obtained the name Kātyāyanī.
Then the prince Vardhamāna, having mastered all branches of knowledge,
became proficient in writing and devised the novel Brāhmī script.
To him, who was renowned throughout the world for possessing strength equal to ten thousand elephants,
the people of Vaiśālī sent a rutting elephant as a gift for his beloved.
Thinking, "He will become a universal monarch," Devadatta,
out of malice, killed that great elephant which was his morning gift.
Nanda dragged the two-toothed calf that had fallen away for seven steps;
but the prince, lifting it up, threw it outside the wall.
Having pierced the surface of the earth with seven palm trees with a single arrow,
he attained supreme excellence in the use of all weapons and missiles capable of cutting and piercing.
Then the prince obtained Yaśodharā as his wife, who was equal to him in virtue and renowned throughout the world, just as one of pure character attains exaltation.
In the meantime, a massive tree seven yojanas in height, uprooted by a great wind,
brought about a blockage of the river's current.
That river named Rohikā, obstructed by its vast expanse of trees,
flowed in a contrary direction, like a woman fallen from her virtuous conduct.
The prince, having uprooted that tree, broken it, and cast it aside,
warded off the flood caused by the waves of water and the fish-devouring populace.
Then once, in a garden,
the prince restored to life a swan that had been struck down by Devadatta with a sharp trap.
Devadatta experienced even greater anguish because of that dispute;
for the crooked cannot endure the rising prosperity of those from their own family.
Once, a princess named Gopikā,
upon beholding the prince whose form was like that of Kandarpa, experienced an indescribable longing.
Śuddhodana, having learned that his son had found a bride worthy of his heart,
fulfilled the desire of the God of Love with their marriage.
Then the soothsayers, having approached with great certainty, said to the king:
"On the seventh day, your son will become either a universal monarch or a sage."
Having heard that, the king, terrified by his son’s intention to go forth for the sake of attaining the state of a Cakravartin,
fell into reflection concerning the number of days [remaining].
Everyone knows that fickle fortune brings only distress, even when it is peaceful, stable, and pleasant;
nevertheless, for those addicted to enjoyments, their supreme regard is directed toward riches alone.
Then, on one occasion, the prince mounted a chariot drawn by spirited and noble horses and set out for a stroll in the pleasure garden.
On the road, he saw a man who was discolored and worn out by old age, with hair that was scattered and decayed, and whose appearance was extremely withered and harsh.
Having seen that and gazed upon his own body, he reflected for a long time: "Aha!
This loathsome body has reached its full maturity."
Although he has reached the fullness of age, he does not rely upon that fullness;
under the guise of excessive grey hair, this old age mocks the aged man.
In this body—a cage of bones strung together by the continuous snares of sinews—the old man nourishes it; alas, I believe he is merely feeding the bird of delusion.
"Charioteer, what is he doing? Why does he not go to the forest of asceticism?
With the body of an old man, his intellect likewise shrinks."
The old man leans upon a staff, yet not upon an intellect consisting of the Dharma;
for one whose body is bent by age, the very nature is a lack of discernment.
This old man produces loathing with his words, whose syllables falter,
whose teeth have fallen out, and which are drenched in trickling saliva.
His vision was lost, his body was emaciated, his strength was vanished, and his hearing was destroyed;
yet, out of delusion, the old man still gazed upon the beloved of his youth.
Does this old man maintain such utterly contemptible whiteness [of hair],
even though his body— though fickle and deeply loathsome— is so exceedingly dear to him?
As he reflected thus, a sense of world-weariness arose within him,
for he regarded his body as fraught with calamity and a mere accumulation of misfortunes.
And again, at another time, he saw a diseased man,
whose body was mostly putrefied and festering, pale as if covered in pus.
Beholding him and directing his gaze toward his own body, he reflected:
"Alas! Indeed, within this very body, there is the natural emergence of a multitude of diseases."
This alone is truly marvelous: that this body, composed of flesh, does not succumb to putrefaction even for a moment, though it has been dead for some time.
Having reflected thus, he became agitated by anxiety for his body and lost all interest in the passion for the enjoyment of sovereignty.
Then, at another moment, he beheld the corpse, its body draped in garlands and garments,
while its kinsmen were busily engaged in performing the funeral rites for the body.
Seeing him, he was suddenly overwhelmed by agitation, compassion, sorrow, and revulsion;
for a long time, he contemplated abandoning this essence-less cycle of existence.
Carrying her closely embraced in his heart, he goes to the forest of the departed spirits.
Alas! How painful is the state of being like wood or stone at the final moment for those men who are intent on the playful indulgence of sensory objects!
In this bubble of the ocean of existence, which is filled with the waters of agitation; in this flower at the tip of the creeper of karma, tossed by the wind of time;
in this mere sharing of the playful glances of the illusory wife—what is this conceit of stability that men have toward the body?
Nothing beneficial to others has been spoken; nothing endowed with Dharma has been heard; the flower of virtue, which is the very form of truth, has never been smelled;
and the state of tranquility has certainly not been touched—thus it is clear that my thoughts are obsessed.
Having come to rest, this [body] suddenly carries [the breath], having reached a state of immobility as its life-force has departed.
Having thus reflected upon his body overwhelmed by calamity,
the prince attained the highest degree of affection for us, who are attached to all worldly objects.
Then, he beheld a manifestation created before him by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm,
who had gone forth as a renunciant, bearing an alms-bowl and wearing saffron robes.
Upon seeing him, his mind became inclined toward the life of renunciation;
for one's true nature is revealed by the joy of beholding what is desired.
Having observed at every step the cause of dispassion in the prince, the charioteer reported everything to the king.
Then, out of curiosity to see the villages, the prince, traveling along the road at his father's command,
beheld treasures that had been uncovered.
When he did not accept those [treasures] which had risen up with hands extended by his ancestors,
they entered the ocean.
Then he [beheld] those farmers, their hair white and covered with dust,
their hands and feet cracked, and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.
Seeing those who were tormented by wounds to their wings caused by the harsh scratching of iron claws,
and rendered helpless by suffering, he became overwhelmed with compassion.
Having, out of compassion, brought about for them the poverty of their lack of wealth,
that bull among men, devoted to virtue, caused them to be released from suffering.
Then the prince, together with his younger brother,
turned back at midday, when the heat was intense and the radiance of the sun was shimmering.
The intervals between the quarters were darkened by peacocks looking up at the sound of the chariot;
covered with droplets of perspiration, he [beheld] the forest floor, glossy with radiance.
Having descended from his chariot there, with earrings slipping from his cheeks,
he of world-renowned fame sought the shade of a rose-apple tree for rest.
Upon his chest, he bore a manifest succession of sweat-drops,
like the mistress of a necklace that had become lovely through the embrace of his body.
As the shadows of all the trees gradually shifted,
the shadow of that rose-apple tree did not move from the slender-bodied woman.
Her cool shade dispelled his exhaustion from the heat,
just as the latent impression of intense dispassion wards off the fatigue of suffering for one who has turned away from cyclic existence.
Then the king, longing to see his son, arrived at that place,
fanned by chowries whose bees were startled by the spray from the elephant's trunk.
Seeing the prince’s shadow remain motionless through his supernatural power,
he was overcome with reverence and wonder, and he bowed down low before him who was already prostrate.
Then, accompanied by his father and intent on going to the city,
he saw at the edge of the town a cemetery crowded with corpses.
Having seen the inauspicious Śivakānana forest strewn with corpses,
he halted his chariot for a moment and spoke to the charioteer with agitation.
"O charioteer, behold the state of beings whose bodies are in decay;
having seen this, even the mind of those deluded by ignorance remains moist with passion."
Behold! His tongue, which was once satiated by respectfully tasting the sight of another's wife, is now being torn away by a crow.
The vulture, finding a state of pleasure from scratching his claws upon the surface of her breasts, tears at her lower lip like a lover overflowing with passion.

These trees, from which crows have spat out their excrement upon seeing them, seem to faint as if from the smell of the ripening pus and corpses, their leaves withered; having seen the corpse being repeatedly torn apart by vultures, its moist entrails scattered about.
Or again, she seemed to be covering him with hands of wind-swayed sprouts.
Like a female jackal clinging to the neck of a drunken elephant, her heart swiftly captivated, her passion made manifest by her redness, she inflicts some scratch with her claws;
repeatedly tasting the young man’s petal-like lip, marked by the wounds of her teeth, she remains intent upon the act of love and displays the height of her impetuous passion.
Having spoken thus, having conceived a sense of detachment through his loathing and revulsion for worldly existence,
and perceiving the extinction of the afflictions, he entered the interior of the city.
There, from her palace, a maiden named Mṛgajā— resplendent with noble lineage, gladdening the hearts of deer, and possessing eyes like those of a deer— beheld him.
Trembling with passion at the sight of him, her gaze, which had been wandering toward his ears,
suddenly became fixed upon him alone.
At the mere sight of him, that young woman, unable to endure her bashfulness,
was as if drawn forward by the God of Love and spoke to her friend standing before her.
What fortunate woman in this world shall, by the touch of this moon-like one,
find her body— burning with passion— attain its final cooling?
Upon hearing the word "Nirvana," the prince,
with his face upturned, beheld his desired object, as if opening the quarters of the sky with his gaze like a forest of lotuses.
Pleased by her words and her beauty,
he gave her a well-fashioned necklace and a mind radiant with virtues, free from distraction.
Having understood her disposition through her favorable reception of the light,
the king took her and established her in the position of his son’s inner apartments.
Then the prince entered the inner apartments, which were surrounded by six thousand beloved women, while reflecting upon his dear Śānti.
In the meantime, the prognosticators clearly said to the king:
"Tomorrow morning, a son will be born to you who will be either a sage or a universal monarch."
Then, having reflected deeply and being greatly alarmed by the prospect of renunciation,
the king had the city gates secured so that all coming and going was blocked.
Having stationed his brothers, headed by Droṇodana, at the gates of the city,
he himself remained at the main crossroads together with his ministers and soldiers.
Then Queen Yaśodharā, having conceived a child from the prince,
shone like the autumnal sky whitened by the approaching moon.
Then, with only one night remaining until the closing of the city gates,
the day arrived for him to turn toward the life of renunciation, while the sun had set in tranquility.
After wandering for a long time through saṃsāra, when the Lord of Heaven had attained peace,
he donned the saffron robe and became invisible like the twilight.
Gradually, the moon arose and made the earth— previously stainless due to the cessation of the darkness and delusion of all quarters— behold the full light.
When the sun of his mind had vanished into the heat of passion, there arose in him,
whose heart was like the pure moon, a certain unshakable serenity.
Now, in the meantime, within the interior of the harem crowded with beloved women,
which laughed with the mass of splendor from the moonlight entering through the jeweled palaces—
Observing everything as essence-less and tasteless, the prince’s memory surged forth freely and clearly, like the sky.
This host of women, a collection of torches for the fire of passion and an assistant in the torment of hundreds of intense misfortunes, must be abandoned;
now it is fitting for me to dwell beneath the trees, cooled by the creepers.
The transformation occurred toward the essence of the bliss of tranquility resulting from the abandonment of the household life.
These women in this forest, whose splendor is like the moon yet filled with intoxication, lie with their eyes constrained by the seal of sleep, their garments fallen from their seats,
uttering improper words born of dreams, and their shoulders covered by their hair.
Quickly, as if putting to shame the lamps flickering in the gentle breeze.
For embodied beings with limbs relaxed and drooping, devoid of shame and naked,
what indeed is the difference between those who are asleep and those who are dead?
While he was speaking thus and making preparations for his departure,
a conversation arose among the guards of the city gates.
"O, who is awake here? For one who is awake, there is no calamity.
All are indeed awake, intent on capturing the mind of their lord."
The wise man remains awake in the house of worldly existence, while the heedless man sleeps in the darkness of delusion;
for one who is merely living in this world but is as if dead or asleep, what difference is there?
Having heard these stories while seated on the horse during the night,
the prince felt as if his own heart’s desire had set out upon the right path.
Having seen the sign of his liberation in a dream during a momentary sleep, he [awoke].
Then Queen Yaśodharā, having suddenly awakened in terror,
related the dream that had occurred at that moment to her beloved husband.
"O Lord, in my dream the limbs of my couch and ornaments were broken;
I saw Fortune departing, and the moon and sun were eclipsed."
Having heard this, he said to her:
"O simple-minded one, this very cycle of existence is devoid of reality; it is but a dream. What kind of dream, moreover, can there be within a dream?"
Today in a dream, a creeper not yet grown has spread over the monastery,
reaching from the eastern to the western ocean with its head resting upon Mount Meru as its pillow.
"The southern ocean has been supported by me with both my arms and my two feet;
O blessed lady, this dream of yours is auspicious, for it portends great good fortune for your husband."
When the Bodhisattva had spoken thus, Yaśodharā said nothing at all;
once more she turned toward sleep with her eyes closed.
Then all the gods who consume nectar, headed by Śakra and Brahmā,
assembled together and performed an act to fill the Bodhisattva with courage for the sake of sentient beings.
Those four sons of gods, endowed with great speed and capable of supporting the earth,
its mountains, and the oceans, were appointed by them as his companions for the journey.
Commanded by Śakra, he descended and went forth, using staircases attached to the palace that had been fashioned by the yakṣa named Pāñcika.
Having awakened his sleeping charioteer named Chandaka,
he took hold of the horse named Kaṇṭhaka, as if grasping a source of despondency.
Touching with his hand that Hari, who was sharp and radiant and tremulous with the side-glances of Lakṣmī, he placed him upon his head, bound there by restraint.
With a well-disposed mind toward the exertion for tranquility, he was equal both within and without;
by his power, even children abandoned their restlessness.
Then, as he placed his foot upon the ground with the desire to test his strength,
the sons of the gods, filled with wonder, were unable to shake it.
Having mounted the waveless horse together with Chandaka,
he plunged into the vast, stainless sky as if into his own pure intention.
He departed, his sprout-like turban dancing with trembling swirls,
like a sigh of grief from Śrī as it quivered under the spreading breeze.
The sky, variegated by the streaks of light from the jewels of his ornaments,
took on the appearance of a monastic robe adorned with rows of painted floral patterns.
Covered with falling teardrops and with their lotus-eyes trembling,
the goddesses of the inner apartments beheld him as he was departing, a sight to be seen.
Having circumambulated from afar that city—which was as vast as saṃsāra and filled with kings and kinsmen—he spoke: "May you forgive me."
When the night had only a moment remaining and the people were sealed in sleep,
the one named Mahān, a kinsman of the king, woke up and saw him.
Having seen him moving in the sky and seized by the suspicion that he was the moon, he spoke after reflecting for a long time, his eyes filled with tears: KAvk_24.158.
"O Prince of beautiful form, this dispassion of yours is extraordinary; it is not fitting for one who resembles the *bandhujīva* flower, nor is it consistent with the reasons that befit you."
Your father has fixed his hopes upon you for the sake of the extraordinary excellence of his lineage;
why, O ornament of all hopes, are those hopes rendered hopeless by you?
Having heard these words of the great Śākya, the prince said to him:
"O friend, affection for kinsmen is but a chain of bondage."
This body, which is fond of the pleasures of a false home, goes to destruction;
the forest is the abode of nectar for those who have escaped the fierce poison of the sense-objects.
Dragged by the hand, with death placed upon the head of the three-hooded serpent, and wearing a dangling garland of sprouts from the fierce poison-vines bound around his neck,
he plunges into a treacherous path thick with heaps of glowing embers.
In this saṃsāra, which is a collection of sense objects, he was full of joy and negligent.
Having spoken thus, traveling through the sky and crossing over the city in an instant,
he reached the ground outside and proceeded swiftly on his horse.
Then, when the king was awakened by the great leader of the Śākyas,
a piteous cry arose from the beloved women within the inner apartments.
Then, surrounded by the thirty gods headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Kubera,
the prince reached the forest after traveling twelve yojanas.
Then, having dismounted from his horse and cast off his ornaments, he, with the radiance of his face betraying his joy, spoke to Chandaka: KAvk_24.167.
"Taking these weapons and the horse, go to your home;
for now I have no further use for these bonds of illusion."
In this forest, I am alone, with tranquility and contentment as my only kinsmen;
for a living being is born alone and perishes alone.
O friend, having abandoned enjoyment that consists of union with perilous sense-objects—who would now engage in the specific affliction of passionate desire?
In this world of humiliation, this is our station; with the splendor of passion extinguished, I take refuge in peace alone.
Having spoken thus, he cast his radiant ornaments onto his lap,
as if they were shedding their grief and falling into a heap of pearls at a settlement of outcasts.
Having drawn out his topknot with a sword, he cast it into the expanse of the sky;
and Śakra, taking it up with reverence, led it to heaven.
Where those locks of hair were cut off by that Great-Souled One as if they were afflictions,
there the virtuous established the Keśapratigraha Caitya.
Chandaka also, taking the horse, set out and after seven days reached the outskirts of the city;
afflicted with grief, he reflected slowly:
Having taken the empty horse and abandoned the prince,
how can I face the king who will be lamenting for his son?
Having reflected thus, he abandoned the horse and remained right there;
the horse, its seat now empty, entered like grief personified.
Upon seeing him, the women of the inner apartments and the king, together with his ministers,
filled all directions with the sound of their wailing.
With throats emitting cries of distress, full of longing and despondency,
and with all their eyes filled with streaming tears, that horse gave up its life.
Purified by the attainment of merit from contact with that Bodhisattva,
he took birth in a brahmin family for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra.
But at the place where the prince accepted the saffron robe given by Śakra,
the great multitude of people erected a shrine for that acceptance of the saffron robe.
Wealth for the sake of non-existence, birth for the sake of liberation from birth,
and even solitude for the sake of turning people away from the pit of delusion—
thus, desiring what is wholesome, he abandoned desire and took up [these goals].
One who has abandoned passion deserves praise, whereas the passion created by [worldly] qualities leads to attachment in people.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the *Abhiniṣkramaṇāvadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

25. The Legend of the Dispelling of Māra Victorious are those who are liberated from the fear of birth and intent upon overcoming the power of existence— those by whom Māra, the world-conqueror with eyes as beautiful as Sundarī’s, was brought under the sway of the Teaching.
Then, while the Bodhisattva was engaged in asceticism in this forest of penance,
his five attendants went forth into the religious life in Vārāṇasī.
Then Śākyamuni, who is envied by the lords of sages,
gradually proceeded himself on a tour among the people to the village of Senāyanī.
There, the two daughters of the householder named Senābhidhāna,
Nandā and she called Nandabalā, were both of beautiful conduct.
Having heard that he was the renowned son of King Śuddhodana,
they undertook a twelve-year vow for the sake of his marriage.
Like a thread always situated within the hearts of fragrant flowers,
desire is innate to children, like a string upon garlands.
Having repeatedly taken the milk from those cows whose milk had turned yellow,
he prepared auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa) in a crystal vessel at the conclusion of his vow.
When the milk-rice had been prepared according to the rules, the Lord of the Gods in the form of a Brahmin,
as well as the lotus-seated Deity, approached that place.
Then, when the two maidens had joyfully set aside their portions for the guests, Śakra said: "Let this be given first to one in whom all virtues arise."
When the king of the gods said, "This one is even superior to me, and he was the very first Brahmā," the four-faced god replied:
"There is a god superior to me who belongs to the Śuddhāvāsa realm," when this was said by Brahmā, they too, remaining in the sky, spoke.
That Bodhisattva, preeminent among all, emaciated by his ascetic penances,
entered the river named Nirājanā and stood within its waters.
Having heard this, the two maidens summoned him; descending [from their chariot], they devotedly offered him that honeyed milk-rice in jeweled vessels.
The Bodhisattva took that jewel-bowl and gave it to them;
saying, "This has been given away and must not be taken back," they two did not accept it.
She was cast by him into a river and carried off by the nāgas;
yet Prabhāvatī was recovered from them by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Indra), who had assumed the form of Tārkṣya.
Then the Bodhisattva Prasādin said to the pair of maidens:
"By virtue of your vow for this gift, what is it that you desire?"
They said to him: "The son of Śuddhodana, the treasury of bliss, the prince Sarvārthasiddha, is our desired husband."
Their spirited speech,
an exertion of Māra’s wiles, did not stain his mind, just as a lotus petal remains unstained by water.
The prince said: "Have you not heard that he has gone forth as a renunciant?
His beloved women, with their restless eyes, are like his glories."
Having heard this which they did not desire, the two maidens sighed deeply and said:
"This is the duty of giving; may its fruit accrue to him alone."
Though he had entered within, turned away from his former self, and was no longer embraced by the affection he had previously seen,
that partiality practiced for so long did not indeed cease.
Having heard those words, the Bodhisattva, with a serene mind,
took leave of Prayāta and proceeded to another forest for the sake of rest.
Having attained the arising of divine power through a portion of the nectar-like milk-rice,
he ascended the mountain, which offered the excellent shade of its dense trees.
Having assumed the cross-legged posture and remaining there in comfort,
that mountain collapsed like a towering head of egoism.
When that mountain had crumbled, he, dejected in mind, reflected:
"Alas, what deeds accompanied by their own consequences have been committed by me!"
To him, whose hundred sighs were born of such anxiety, the deities of the sky said:
"O virtuous one, you have not performed any improper deed whatsoever."
The earth is unable to support uncut and unrefined merit;
but you possess refined merit, being heavier than hundreds of lofty mountains.
Having crossed the river Nirañjanī,
proceed steadily to the region named Vajrāsana, which bestows spiritual perfection upon Bodhisattvas.
As he set out upon the earth along the path indicated by the deity,
a succession of golden lotuses appeared at every step he took.
As he proceeded, the earth, filled with shimmering waters,
rose up and bowed down like a resounding bronze vessel.
He beheld various signs appearing,
the fruit of which is the accomplishment of the treasury of unsurpassed knowledge.
In the world of Nirañjana, a blind serpent named Kālikā emerged upon hearing a sound from the ground where a Buddha had manifested his vision.
Beholding that Bodhisattva, endowed with all the marks of perfection and possessing the brilliance of glowing Jāmbūnada gold, he spoke with his hands joined in reverence.
O lotus-eyed one, you who are beloved, having bestowed the pain of separation upon [your consorts] during this youth while sporting in the forest,
you are the cause of contentment through the awakening of the distinction between the cessation of unrest and peace.
In the ocean of existence, you are the bridge of truth for embodied beings.
Now, these deer no longer release their trembling with fear here,
as the flocks of birds sport nearby like a wheel of play;
it is some indescribable abode of consolation for the hearts of both sentient and insentient beings.
Thus I think this Buddhist body grants happiness without effort.
Out of love for the lotus, the young elephant-kalabha caresses the trunk of the elephant;
the peacock pleases him with soft cries from the breeze of its tail-feathers;
and before him, the doe stands with restless sidelong glances, longing for his affection.
This state, consisting of merit and serene clarity, belongs to the time of tranquility.
Having attained pure Buddhahood this very day, you shall reach the seat of awakening for the entire three worlds,
just as the full moon makes the night-lotus bed— brightened by the joy of its immediate clarity— blossom with nectar.
From the hearts of people touched by divine light— who possess the power of awakening from the darkness of their sleep through the immediate sight of you, whose splendor is like that of the sun—
there issues forth, as if bound by a swarm of bees, a connection [to the world].
Trembling within, the series of blind darknesses of delusion shall never again set foot there.
To her who was speaking thus with humility, the King of Nāgas, his mind pleased,
addressed the Bodhisattva, crossed the river, and departed.
Having reached the unagitated foot of the Bodhi tree, the seat of the Vajra,
he prepared a mat of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing southward, which had been offered by Śakra.
Sitting there, bound in the paryanka posture with unwavering resolve,
he shone like the ocean of milk at rest after the churning has ceased.
That steadfast one, whose form was upright and who possessed a unique foundation of forbearance,
shone with a golden luster like the supreme, immovable Mount Meru.
"Until my imperishable goal is reached, this cross-legged posture of mine shall remain firm";
having formed this resolve, he established mindfulness directed toward the front.
In the meantime, Māra, envious of his self-restraint,
arrived there swiftly as a messenger and addressed the Bodhisattva.
What is this desire for the unattainable that is considered a bond in the world?
What desire can he have, whose mind takes the form of a discordant strife against the [proper] time?
Your city was seized by Devadatta, who had cast off all fear;
the ranks of the inner apartments were confined, and King Śuddhodana was bound.
Having heard these words, he was cast out by the poison of grief and indignation; with a mind free from any artificial transformation, he reflected thus: KAvk_25.47.
"Alas! Mara has indeed prepared himself to create an obstacle for me;
this evil-doer makes the world dance like a game of top-spinning. (KAvk 25.48)
O Māra, O Māra, your wickedness knows no rest;
for by means of this single sacrifice of violence, you have attained this state of sensual indulgence.
I do not venture to boast of my own sacrifices, gifts, or austerities;
for the flower of merit, once withered by the proclamation of one's own virtues, perishes.
Thus rebuked by him, Māra, the thief of the hearts of embodied beings, departed full of resentment; his efforts frustrated, he withdrew from his undertaking.
Then there appeared lovely women, their eyes curved with grace,
resembling beautiful mango creepers with hovering bees for their swaying tresses.
Unsatisfied by his charming conduct, those three celestial maidens of desire made the penance grove impassioned with the placement of their lotus-like feet.
There, by their eyes she surpassed the doe, by the graceful movements of their gait the female elephant,
and by their lotus-faces the lotus-pond was eclipsed.
Through their limbs adorned with youth, their bodies anointed with passion,
and their garments of loveliness, desire arose even in those who were otherwise mindless.
Beholding him, whose eyes were motionless in meditation through his absorption in the vajrāsana posture,
they were struck with wonder and entered into a state of meditative concentration.
Abandoning their youth, which was filled with intoxicating passion, those women suddenly took on old age as if out of shame for their bodhisattva-like intentions.
Then, his desires frustrated by their movement in the opposite direction,
Manmatha, whose undertakings are renowned, marshaled his entire army.
His vast army of thirty-six crores marched forth, filled with all kinds of weapons and terrifying with the faces of various creatures.
Drawing his bow of wrath back to his ear himself,
Māra rushed toward the Bodhisattva with a display of vast agitation.
The shower of weapons released by him, together with dust, poison, and stones,
became like mandāra flowers and lotuses before the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, O one who is patient as the earth, the gods created for him a protection equal to a thunderbolt against the rain of weapons released by the power of Māra.
Smara too, his resolve destroyed, fashioned from crystal wood a tree that was a thorn to the ear of his meditation, its leaves jingling with the sharp ringing of bells.
Having hurled that tree, noisy with its crows, and Māra along with his army and weapons onto the Cakravāḍa mountain range,
the deities of the sky cast them down.
Then the Blessed One, having attained stainless and serene wisdom,
became all-knowing, all-pervading, and supreme in his recollection of all births.
Having attained unexcelled wisdom and perfect enlightenment there,
he beheld all living beings whose destinies are fashioned by the waves of karma.
Then, in the city of the Śākyas, Māra spread a rumor from heaven, saying:
"The Bodhisattva has gone to his destruction because of the hardships of his asceticism."
There, King Śuddhodana, afflicted by the poison of affection for his son,
fell to the ground upon hearing that, as if struck by a thunderbolt.
While the king, together with his harem, was on the verge of giving up his life,
the deities of the sky, who were partial to those of virtuous conduct, spoke to him.
Your son, having drunk the nectar of immortality, has attained the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha;
since he gazes upon him with compassion, how could there be any fear of death even for his servant?
Having heard these words, the king, together with his harem and ministers,
felt as if his life had returned to him in an instant, like one sprinkled with nectar.
During that joy of the great festival, the Bodhisattva’s bride gave birth to a beloved son, Yaśodhara,
at the very moment the moon was seized by Rāhu.

Although he was but a child named Rāhula, he floated upon the water when his mother, along with a stone, cast him into the water for the sake of purification from the king's suspicion regarding his birth.
The Blessed One also remained for seven days with his body motionless;
by means of the vajraparyaṅka posture, he caused wonder among the gods.
Opposed by two deities known as Brahmakāyika, he—
who was beautiful with a mass of the nectar of supreme bliss— spoke.
"Aha! This state of yours has been known by me from the very beginning, by which the bliss of sovereignty over gods and asuras appears as a mere mass of suffering."
Young women whose limbs are bathed in the waters of loveliness, and the host of celestial enjoyments moist with nectar—
these are utterly worthless dust in comparison to the contest for the bliss of effortless renunciation of everything.
I, a traveler in the cycle of existence—a world of afflictions as treacherous as poison—was scorched and weary; yet, like the shade of a sandalwood tree, I have now attained a refuge in peace.
This state of total bliss has arisen, pervading all my faculties.
For those who have found rest in the Himalaya of tranquility, what can serve as a comparison for their happiness?
At this juncture, through the ripening of merit,
the two merchants Trapusa and Bhallika arrived at that forest with a vast caravan.
Having approached the Blessed One with devotion as they were intent upon the deities, the two of them bowed down and said,
"Please accept this alms-food."
Having heard that, the Omniscient One, who is subject to compassion, reflected:
"This was accepted by my predecessors as a vessel; it is not for hands devoid of a vessel."
While he was reflecting thus, the gods known as the Mahārājas gave him four crystal bowls and departed for the third heaven.
Then, having received the alms-food into his bowl,
the Blessed One bestowed his grace upon them by teaching the three refuges.
Association with the virtuous— witness to widespread good deeds, skilled in depositing merit, the destroyer of all remaining calamities, and a wish-fulfilling tree for prayers—
becomes available through roots of virtue to some fortunate person as a master in the initiation of auspicious transformation.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Subduing of Māra’s Army," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
26. The Birth of the Śākyas. There was a certain vast lineage, continuous with merit, whose conduct was beautiful and appropriate for the accumulation of virtues;
it produced a jewel of pure luster indicating true radiance, made of pearls, an ornament for the world.
Formerly, when [the Blessed One] was dwelling in a grove of *nyagrodha* trees in Kapilavastu,
the Śākyas questioned the Blessed Tathāgata concerning his own lineage.
Questioned by them regarding the origin of his own lineage, he appointed Maudgalyāyana—
who possessed pure insight and vision— to speak before him.
Having observed the past exactly as it truly is with the eye of knowledge, he recalled it and said to them: "Listen to the origin of the Śākyas."
In the past, when this entire world consisting of water stood as a single ocean,
the water became like water [itself] through contact with the wind.
When that water gradually attained solidity through its density,
the earth came into being, composed of color, taste, touch, sound, and smell.
From that [lake], the Ābhāsvara gods, having passed away due to the exhaustion of their karma,
were reborn as beings possessing a color identical to theirs and endowed with superior strength.
Tasting the flavor with their fingers, they were intensely deluded by that craving;
due to the defect of such food, they became heavy, coarse, and discolored.
The earth gradually became the provider of food for them,
even though their fields were obscured by darkness.
Then, because he protected them from injury (kṣata-trāṇa), he became a Kṣatriya through the protection of the earth;
he was named Mahāsaṃmata, being esteemed by the great multitude of people.
In his great lineage there was a glorious king named Upoṣadha,
whose unfading flower of fame was like the Pārijāta tree in the ocean.
His son was Māndhātṛ, a universal monarch born not from a womb;
his lineage became great, under whose single parasol the entire world was ruled.
In the lineage of Sahasravaṃśa, there was a king named Kṛki,
for whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa produced a clarity of mind.
In his lineage of the Ikṣvākus, there was Virūḍhaka;
out of affection for his youngest son, the elder sons were banished by him.
Then, having united and become free from all desire for their own country,
all the princes named Kapila went to the hermitage of that great seer.
Because they were children who cried out loudly, creating obstacles during his time of meditation,
he fashioned for them elsewhere a city called Kapilavastu.
Out of affection for his sons and with remorse, the king spoke thus to his ministers: "Let those princes be brought here at once."
All the ministers, having reached that excellent city, said to him:
"O King, they cannot be brought back, for they have now attained great prosperity through their offspring."
Thus, as they deliberated there upon what was possible and impossible for their father, they became known as Śākyas; among them, he was the founder of the lineage.
When five thousand times five hundred kings of that lineage had passed away,
the illustrious monarch Daśaratha ruled the earth.
In his lineage there was a lord of the earth named Siṃhahanu,
whom the elephant-like kings could not withstand in battle, as if they were lions.
The eldest was Śuddhodana; his son was the next, Śuklodana;
Droṇodana was his younger brother, and the youngest was Amṛtodana.
There were four daughters named Śuddhā, Śuklā, Droṇā, and Amṛtā;
and the Blessed One’s son was Śuddhodana, while another was Nanda.
Śuklodana had two sons, named Tiṣya and Bhadrika;
Droṇodana likewise had two sons, Aniruddha and Mahān.
Ānanda and Devadatta, Amṛtodana and Saṃbahu;
Śuddhāsuta, Supraśuddha, and Mālika, the son of Śuklā.
And Droṇāputra, Bhadrāṇi known as Vaiśālya, Amṛtāsuta, and Rāhula,
the son of the Blessed One, in whom the lineage was established.
Having heard this lineage as it was correctly described by him, who consists of radiant wisdom,
the Śākyas became purified by the distinguished excellence of their honored status through the powers of the Blessed One.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Birth of the Śākyas," in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

27. The Avadāna of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. Such is the great power of that certain being, who is bound to solitude and devoted to merit; it does not depart from the man even through hundreds of bodies, just as the fragrance of musk does not leave a fine cloth.
When the Jina, a lake of compassion that cools the suffering of all living beings in the world,
was dwelling within the Bamboo Grove at the city of Rājagṛha.
In Campā there was a glorious lord of the earth named Potala,
who by his wealth eclipsed the blindness born of pride in wealth that belongs even to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
To him was born a son who fulfilled hundreds of his desires;
through the attainment of his wished-for wealth, his riches became companions to his happiness.
At the birth of that son, who was born under the asterism of Śravaṇā,
he then joyfully gave twenty crores to that poor man.
Then that youth known as Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa became famous;
he was wealthy solely through his own merit, by which his lineage was adorned.
Having acquired knowledge and attained growth along with all his worldly interests, he,
upholding the affairs of state, brought his father restful happiness.
Once, as Maudgalyāyana was descending from the solar disc, which was like a mass of radiance, he reached the city and spoke to him.
"Who are you, resembling the sun and illuminating the quarters of the sky?
Are you the Lord of the Thirty-three, or the Moon, or perhaps the divine Lord of Wealth?"
He said to him: "I am not a god, but a disciple of the Blessed One, the Buddha, whose glory of qualities is venerated by the lords of the gods."
He offered to that Great Sage a pure alms-meal,
obtained through the arising of purity of being— a worthy object of enjoyment dear to the Blessed One.
Thus, O Blessed One, by hearing the name of Śroṇa as it reached his ears,
the hair on the body of Ravibhadraka stood on end, even though he was of low birth.
Whatever nature remains in someone, joined with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of previous births,
that very nature is clearly manifested even by its arousal.
With a mind imbued with faith and devoted by affection, he sent him twenty shares of sacrificial vessels, fit for those born in heaven.
Then the Blessed One, intent upon bestowing grace, personally accepted in its entirety that [offering] which had been sent by him with a multitude of devotions.
At this moment, King Bimbisāra himself arrived, bringing with devotion a portion of the food from the cooking pot, worthy of a king.
There, the king, having smelled the fragrance of the garments cast off by Śroṇa—
which had been sent by Śakra— considered it all to be divine.
Having tasted the remnants of the alms-bowl given by the Blessed One,
and hearing that it had been sent by Śroṇa, the king was thereafter filled with wonder.
Then, having bowed to the Blessed One, the lord of men entered his flourishing royal capital and reflected upon the divine prosperity of Śroṇa.
"I shall go there myself; that man of ill-repute must be seen by me.
Having thus resolved, he ordered his ministers to prepare for the expedition.
Potalaka, having learned that the king was himself preparing to come,
spoke in private to his son Śroṇakoṭi, who was skilled in statecraft.
"My son, the king—the preceptor of the social orders and stages of life—is coming to see you.
To me, this appears to be an excessive display of honor that is fraught with fault.
The lords of the earth, as if intent on partiality, strike him down without delay once he has attained a hundred thousand [in value],
like arrows released from a bowstring.
Excessive advancement makes one hated even by servants;
how much more so by kings, for whom pride is the sole essence?
In youth, beauty, power, wealth, and learning,
people cannot endure the excellence even of their own son when it is accompanied by rivalry.
O son, in a world filled with hatred, one lives by concealing one's virtues;
for even the sun finds a lotus pleasing when its beauty is concealed.
To whom is the arrogant not hateful, and to whom is the humble not dear?
The wind brings down the stiff tree, but it protects the one that is bent low.
And if that king, who is worthy of being approached, comes to you of his own accord,
then this pride and delusion of yours will not lead to much benefit.
Therefore, go from here yourself and, having presented a necklace as a gift, bow down to the Lord who is worthy of salutation, who resembles a constellation amidst the stars.
Having heard these words of his father, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
adorned with jewels, set out by ascending a ship to see the lord of the earth.
Having reached the capital and seen the king,
he offered him a necklace that was like the very laughter of joy belonging to the Goddess of Fortune herself.
Seeing him approach of his own accord, the king, with an affectionate gaze, spoke thus in wonder to Hemaromaṅkacaraṇa: KAvk_27.32.
"Aha! You are some great lord of merit, a kinsman to all beings, for by the mere sight of you my state of mind becomes serene."
Supreme sovereignty arises from virtues; from sovereignty comes the highest happiness;
from all forms of happiness comes supreme health; and from health comes association with the virtuous.
"O virtuous one, has the Blessed One been seen by you in the Veṇukā forest?
In my opinion, you ought to behold his pair of lotus feet."
When this had been said by the lord of the earth, who was partial [to him] out of kindness, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa also replied to him with affection: KAvk_27.36.
O God of gods, through this incomparable grace of yours,
I have now attained the fitness to behold the Blessed One.
When this was said, the king, who was skilled in remaining steadfast, set out together with him on foot alone to behold the Tathāgata with devotion.
From the day of his birth until his departure,
the earth was covered by his servants with costly garments so that his feet did not touch the ground.
Out of devotion, humility, and respect for the Lord,
he restrained the king's attendants from taking the garments, as if they were falling upon the earth.
Then, when the ordinary garments were set aside, the earth was covered with divine raiment;
for the prosperity of those endowed with merit requires no effortful means.
When he had removed his divine garments and set his feet upon the ground,
the earth, including its mountains, forests, and oceans, trembled.
Then, having reached the hermitage of the Jina together with the lord of the earth,
he beheld the Blessed One and performed a prostration at his feet.
As Śamaviveka sat before him, the Blessed One performed for him an inauguration with the nectar of his joyful glances.
Having examined his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature,
he gave a teaching of the Dharma to him for the purpose of perceiving the truths.
The mountain of his view of a self-identity, possessing twenty peaks,
was shattered by the vajra of knowledge as he touched the state of stream-entry.
Then, once his renunciation had suddenly occurred of its own accord,
the king, filled with wonder, bowed down to the Blessed One and departed.
Even while Śroṇa was engaged in intense ascetic observances,
at times there arose in him a recollection of the pleasures of his former bonds and enjoyments, due to the residual impressions of his latent tendencies.
Having summoned him, the Blessed One, smiling, said to that embarrassed man:
"What is this reflection of yours, when your mind is withdrawn in meditation?"
A string that is either too loose or excessively tight produces many discordant notes;
it attains sweetness when it is even. Therefore, one should rely upon evenness.
By virtue of this instruction from the Blessed One, having attained complete equanimity and being freed from remorse, he subsequently attained stainless knowledge.
Beholding that wondrous accomplishment of his, all the monks, filled with great amazement,
questioned the Blessed One, and he replied:
"Listen, Śroṇa, to the meritorious deed performed in a previous birth;
for wondrous riches do not arise for those who lack the power of merit."
In former times, the Blessed One Vipaśyin, the perfectly enlightened one, the Sugata,
went to the city named Bandhumatī on a journey among the people.
There, invited by those virtuous devotees out of devotion for their patron,
he went daily to their houses in turn, accompanied by his followers.
Then that poor Brahmin boy,
named Indrasoma, having obtained his turn, prepared with great effort a meal suitable for him.
With great effort, he covered the earth with garments and, bowing low, offered him food purified by devotion.
Through the power of his vow for that enjoyment, he was born as this man of great wealth,
with golden hair upon his feet, a lord of ten million villages, and like a god.
Never has the earth been touched by him without his garments;
therefore, trembling occurred from the ground due to the touch of his feet.
Thus, having drunk deeply of the Sugata’s speech— which was as pure as nectar and whose nature was like the radiance of emerging rays from his teeth—
the community of monks, with hearts set upon it, became established in steadfast virtue.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Avadāna of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

28. The Legend of Dhanapāla The noble-minded do not undergo any change of heart despite the unbearable injuries inflicted by vast and wicked villains; even when agitated by the surging waves of turbulent mountains, the ocean never relinquishes its nectarine nature from its heart.
Long ago, in Rājagṛha, the Blessed One dwelt in the charming Veṇukā forest,
in the place known as Kalandakanivāsa.
There, the son of Bimbisāra, a king named Ajātaśatru, became the one who terrified many hundreds of enemies and their sword-bearing kinsmen.
He had a friend born of the Śākya clan named Devadatta, who,
by means of a base mantra, became as fierce as a Vetāla.
Once, while the lord of the earth was seated comfortably in private, he said to him:
"O King, even now my taking refuge in you has not yet borne fruit for me."
The word "friend" (mitra) is applied to two things— happiness and an unimpeded mechanism—
because they mutually protect one's desires and are free from deceitful conduct.
"This Śākya ascetic who dwells in the Veṇu grove of bliss—
I wish to slay him and attain that state honored by the gods."
What is the use of that wealth of friends by which no enemy is destroyed, no fame is gained,
and no honor does not increase?
Invited by a citizen of that city named Mahādhanā,
that hypocrite, together with his monks, was to arrive in the city in the morning.
As he was entering the royal highway, that rogue elephant Dhanapālaka,
blinded by rage, was released right in front of him.
When Devadatta had spoken thus, the king, who was affectionate toward his friends,
reflected upon the power of the Buddha and said nothing, with his face cast downward.
Devadatta also, having gone out, intoxicated by his pride in the king's friendship,
spoke to the elephant-keeper, giving him a necklace as a gratuity.
"The ascetic will arrive at the city in the morning surrounded by hundreds of monks;
you must send the elephant for him," the king said.
Having heard Devadatta’s words, the lord of elephants said, "So be it";
for the row of foolish rams follows the one who goes first.
Even though he knew the intention of those evil-minded ones,
the Omniscient One arrived in the morning together with five hundred monks.
Then, released by the elephant-keeper,
the fierce elephant— blind with rage, having uprooted the palace-trees like arrows— rushed toward him.
Independent of even a heavy goad through familiarity,
he was as hostile as one pierced by a thorn, and was defiled by intoxication.
Due to their constant fickleness of ear toward those addicted to the vices of service,
a wicked master is as life-destroying to his servants as a bee is to the bees that attend it.
When that Mandara mountain, the enemy of trees, had been assailed and rushed upon, and the world suddenly fled in terror, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.

On that royal highway, filled with dense streams of vermilion powder tossed by the wind from the flapping of his ears— which resembled the falling red garments of terrified women— and where the quarters of the horizon were struck with terror by the sound of his upraised, fiercely whirling trunk, he [advanced].
There arose a flurry of agitation, possessing the beauty of bees clustering around the swaying curls of her hair.
While the people were distressed by the destruction of the city and filled with clamor,
Devadatta, his mind intoxicated, ascended the great palace.
He became intensely eager to see the Blessed One;
for an elephant finds satisfaction only in uprooting those possessed of virtue.
When all those monks had fled out of fear of the elephant,
Ānanda alone remained as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, five lions emerged from the hand of the Blessed One,
their manes and tufts formidable, as if white with the luster of his claws.
Upon catching that scent, the elephant, overcome by terror like one possessed by epilepsy,
suddenly turned his back and discharged both dung and urine.
Having fled there with speed, the elephant, having fallen into a state of poverty regarding his pride,
beheld the ten directions filled with the flames of lamps.
Beholding the world filled with the blazing flames of the fire from his net,
he approached the cool vicinity of the Teacher’s lotus feet.

For him— who was averse to contraction, whose mind was filled with anxiety, whose facial luster was destroyed, and who sighed with the heat of distress as if it were a festival of great expenditure for one blinded by greed— his hand became a burden, its movement slackened by torment, while the bees of beggars, deprived of gifts due to his fallen state, raised a clamor.
As he approached the Teacher’s feet in fear, the Teacher, an ocean of compassion,
touched him with his hand marked by the wheel and the svastika.
Placing his hand upon the water-jar, the Blessed Jina said to him:
"Son, you have reached this state through your own karma."
This body, a mountain of flesh, is the source of the light of discernment;
yet this other burden, a mass of delusion brought about by evil, is yours.
When this was said by the Blessed One, who was moist with compassion, the elephant became terrified;
once captured, he clung to the edge of the mountain and attained a state of immobility.
When Devadatta’s resolve and his exceedingly fierce elephant were broken,
the people experienced a joy free from obstacles, filled with a sense of wonder that had arisen within them.
Then, having accepted an offering of food at the householder's home,
the Blessed One set out for the forest together with the monks.
Having approached and touched the lotus-feet of the Jina with his trunk, even the lordly elephant cast off his elephantine body.
Possessing brilliant radiance, he was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings;
having been born there, he suddenly went to see the Sugata.
Having approached the Blessed One who had arrived at his own hermitage, he,
wearing blazing jewel earrings, bowed down before him who resembled the sun.
Filled with the sprout-like radiance of his armlets and crown,
the rows of clouds shone as if covered by rainbows.
Having sat down before the Teacher with his defilements cast off according to the discipline, he scattered divine, pure flowers over him and spoke: KAvk_28.39.
"O Blessed One, by the touch of your lotus feet,
the torment of my miserable state has been stilled for me, who am now filled with contentment."
Ah, the Lord’s glance— soothing, sweet, and affectionate— is a certain praiseworthy rain of nectar that quenches the feverish poison of calamities;
by it, whatever it touches, even the most violent outburst of transformation is stilled.
Even a beast, when its delusion is destroyed, takes refuge in inner peace through liberation.
As he was speaking thus, the Blessed One, for the sake of his peace from existence,
performed a teaching of the Dharma purified by the vision of truth.
Having bowed with his head— brightened by the rays of the pearls in his crown—
to the feet of the Teacher, he departed as if laughing at the wandering of existence.
When he had departed, the sky illuminated by his moon-like face,
the Blessed One was questioned by the monks and related that account.
In another previous eon, during the teaching of the Teacher named Kāśyapa,
he had also become a renunciant, yet was disrespectful toward the precepts.
Due to his lack of respect, he experienced the state of an elephant; through serving the Saṅgha and by the power of the vision of truth, he finally attained the grasp of the Teaching.
The karma ordained in a previous birth does not cease for anyone, even for one possessed of consciousness,
until its connection, as taught by karma itself, is fulfilled through devotion and experience.
In that terrible calamity, I was abandoned by all the monks, yet not by Ānanda;
even there, let this former connection be heard.
Long ago, in a lake as cool as the moon, there were two beautiful royal swans,
brothers named Pūrṇamukha and Śukla.
Once, Pūrṇamukha went to the beautiful Puṣkariṇī pond named Brahmanatī in Vārāṇasī, belonging to King Brahmadatta.
Tawny with the pollen of trembling lotus filaments,
he sported upon that lotus pond together with five hundred swans.
Abandoning their tasks, people gazed with unblinking eyes at him, who was radiant with the excellence of his form through the power of his past merit.
Having heard that, the king, eager for a sight of him while he remained there,
dispatched fishermen skilled in capturing him.
When he, whose white radiance was like the playful smile of a lotus, had been seized,
five hundred swans abandoned him and fled with speed.
But one man, because of his kindness, though unbound, remained as if firmly bound;
overcome by the snare of love, he stayed there distressed for his sake.
Then, having seen that royal swan brought by them,
the king was amazed as he gazed upon both of them, including the second one who was bound by affection.
"I am that Haṃsa with the full face, and Ānanda is his follower;
today those monks have departed, having abandoned me, and they shall surely go."
In former times, not long ago, there was a lord of the earth in Vārāṇasī named Tutura,
whose fame was inscribed by others upon the tablet of their minds.
He had a thousand warriors, a faultless man from the south,
renowned as Karadaṇḍin, a beloved leader in battle.
Once, in a terrible battle, five hundred ministers abandoned that king out of fear and fled; yet Karadaṇḍin did not desert him.
"I myself was that king, and those ministers were these very monks;
Karadaṇḍin was this very Ānanda, who has never left me."
"In another birth as well, I was a lion who fell into a well for a month;
I was abandoned in an instant by my servants, those jackals who are today these monks."
And by one who dug with his claws and made a long tunnel, I was liberated;
that very jackal is today this Ānanda, my follower.
In the past, when the leader of a herd of deer was bound by a snare set in a trap,
his followers fled at the very moment the hunter approached.
Devoted to him, that doe did not abandon him, her eyes filled with tears;
bound by the chain of affection, she seemed as if she had become motionless.
Then, seeing the hunter approaching, intent on killing the deer, she said:
"First, take my life with your arrow."
Thus, at her clear words and out of affection, the hunter was amazed;
with love, he released the deer together with his doe-companion.
"I am that leader of the deer herd, Ānanda, and she is that doe; thus this bond of affection continues from our former lives. (KAvk 28.68)
Having heard these words of the Sugata, all those monks, as if hidden by shame,
gazed with longing and moistened hearts upon Ānanda’s lotus-face, which was radiant with joy and beautiful with its splendor.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the Legend of Dhanapāla, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

29. The Avadāna of Kāśīsundara. Victorious is that preeminent being among those endowed with courage, the cause of happiness for all beings, who, even when his body is being torn asunder, extinguishes the fire of anger and exalts tranquility.
During a discourse on the Dharma, while speaking in the course of conversation with the monk Kauṇḍinya, who was foremost among his followers, the Blessed One was questioned by the monks and replied.
The son of King Brahmadatta, the lord of Vārāṇasī,
was named Kāśisundara, and there were also two others named Kālabhū.
The prince Kāśīsundara, who was uniquely worthy of bearing the burden of the crown prince,
reflected for a long time upon the kingdom composed of both dharma and adharma.
My mind finds no delight in youth that perishes in an instant, in life as flickering as a wave, or in this kingdom which is like a marriage in a dream and rooted in delusion.
In this saṃsāra, which abounds in the lamentations of passion, is constantly filled with deceit and hypocrisy, and is as essence-less as the weeping of a courtesan, there is no truth whatsoever.
Therefore, O sinless one, go forth from the home to the homeless state;
for what is the use of worldly splendors that are attached to a cruel way of life?
Having reflected thus, the prince, whose mind was purified by discernment and who was eager to depart for the forest, approached the king and spoke.
"O King, this circle of my enjoyments is of no use to me;
let this undertaking intended for the consecration of the crown prince be desisted."
O dear one, these riches of passion (rājasa-sampad), which produce the fear and exhaustion of bound attachments and are intensely heated by the fire of anger, are not at all pleasing to me.
Whom do the flames of royal splendor— not pervaded by most cruel conduct and already ablaze— not terrify, like the crests of fire in a cremation ground?
Shaded by parasols and fanned by the breeze of yak-tail whisks,
lords of the earth, intoxicated with pride, fall into the abyss of sin.
Upon the body of kings, which has become exceedingly tender through the habitual use of soft enjoyments and fine garments,
affliction falls at last, as terrible as a thunderbolt.
For these people, who lament with intense thirst due to the continuous torment of anxiety and who are afflicted by the fever of sovereignty,
this swoon of delusion does not cease.
The activity of kings— who are crooked, radiant with jewels, double-tongued, and who reveal vulnerabilities at every step— is supreme murder.
"Thinking, 'He considers me, who has been enjoyed by hundreds of royal dynasties,
as his exclusive possession,' the Goddess of Fortune, smiling with her necklace and chowrie, [deserts] the lords of the earth."
The royal fortune, its sighs manifested by the waving of fans, shed a continuous stream of pearl-like tears,
as if remembering former kings who had passed away due to the burden of delusion.
Therefore, I shall go to the forest— a place devoid of the company of those who have not renounced—
which provides the cool shade of contentment and allays the heat of suffering.
For this traveler on the path of saṃsāra who finds no rest, even this body is difficult to bear since it is constantly subject to ruin; how much more so, then, the burden of the earth?

Having heard these words of his son, which were extremely unpleasant, the king—startled by the word "renunciation" and filled with agitation—spoke to him: iti putravacaḥ śrutvā bhūptirbhṛśamapriyam / pravrajyāśabdacakitaḥ sodvegastamabhāṣataḥ // KAvk_29.20 //
O son, for the sake of increasing this great lineage and empire, I, whose hopes are fixed upon you, have placed my highest trust in you.
"My child, you ought not to frustrate my resolve at this time;
this great splendor of your youth is not suited for the forest."
For kings who are devoted to the practice of mantras, capable of beholding holy men,
and have conquered their senses, penance consists in the protection of all beings everywhere.
Even in its own natural state, the lotus dwells in water without attachment;
even in the forest, the aśoka tree receives the kicks from the feet of beautiful women.
As long as one has not yet experienced the "poisoning by sight" through enjoyments easily available in one's own home,
these sense objects can be abandoned for a moment.
Having happily abandoned his own kin and departed from his home,
a person cannot endure the suffering of long separation from the pleasures he has grown accustomed to.
In the home, Dharma is heard, remembered, and practiced with ease;
in the forest, for those who are withered, the acts of hearing, remembering, and practicing it all wither away.
For one whose feet are wounded by the blades of the darbha grass as it is being trampled,
what further suffering will there be for one who craves the next world?
As they eat, people behold them reduced to mere skin and bone;
they always consume what is given by others, like wretched pretas.
O son, dwelling in the forest and clothing oneself in dust are equal to the preservation of celibacy,
which is like drying up the ocean.
With faces contorted by frowns like the smoke of forest fires, with caves for houses thick with the scent of cow-dung liquor and owls,
and stained crimson by the blood of elephants slain by lions— whose heart could find steadiness in such forests after abandoning home?
The lustful man desires self-restraint and remembers the pleasure of dark-complexioned women; the self-restrained man, satisfied, delights in most rigorous vows; the hungry man longs for food;
the solitary man seeks company, while he who is distressed by the world desires the forest.
Having abandoned [their wealth], people intent on searching for it once again encounter humiliation.
"O son, you ought not to abandon me and go into the thicket;
let the desire for forest-dwelling belong to your enemies."
Like creepers of swords that possess the laughter of manifest pearls,
proud women who are the wealth of kings, once abandoned, do not return again.
Although addressed thus repeatedly by his father, he did not waver from his resolve;
for the determination of great-souled ones is like a crest-jewel of adamant.
Although he was entreated by his mothers, ministers, kinsmen, and the leading citizens,
he remained silent and abstained from food for three days.
"Whether he be a king’s enjoyer or an ascetic, let him live according to his own will;
for this fickle man follows his desires," thus spoke the ministers to the king.
Having been permitted with some difficulty by the king, whose eyes were filled with tears,
he departed for the hermitage of the sages, observing silence while the city folk wailed around him.
Through the ripening of dispassion,
he cultivated toward all beings a compassion purified by loving-kindness and cherished for its solitude.
By its power, the mental dispositions of all the forest-dwellers there became cooled by the abandonment of innate enmity.
When the Pulindas had abandoned the slaughter of life and were intent on herds of does,
and when the lions had ceased their tearing of elephants and were clinging to every limb [of the women],
the women with slender hips cast aside their peacock-feather veils and were divested of their strings of pearls.
There, the Kirāta women became such that their lips were parched by the cessation of their breath.
Having abandoned patience toward the earth-garmented ocean and having taken refuge in patience toward all beings,
that Kāśisundara became renowned as Kṣāntivādin.
In the meantime, when Brahmadatta, the joy of the earth, had departed for heaven,
there arose a king who was the very embodiment of the Kali age, like a source of agitation for all living beings.
Then, with his face darkened by the frowning arches of bees wandering in great numbers,
Spring appeared, hating the self-restraint of the sages.
The splendor of the springtime, which had arisen as a messenger for the destruction of pride and was like a magical spell causing the intoxication of love in the fawn-eyed women, shone forth.
Suspecting that the red aśoka tree was embracing the creeper at its side,
the Malaya breeze, as if out of jealousy, carried away its flowers.
At that time, during the youth of spring in the garden filled with the cries of cuckoos,
the king, accompanied by his harem, set out, eager to behold the forest.
Beholding the delightful forests strewn with various kinds of falling flowers of many colors, he gradually reached the ascetic grove.
Having wandered for a long time in those lovely forest glades with his maiden companion, he,
rested from his amorous play, fell asleep for a moment.
Smiling with unprecedented blossoms as they gathered flower clusters there,
the women of the inner apartments moved about like walking creepers.
In the meantime, Kṣāntivādin, finding rest in a secluded place,
stood motionless in solitude, contemplating inner peace.
Flowing with an abundance of bliss, worthy of homage by the wise,
though slender, he possessed no small beauty, like the moon at its first rising.
Her form was by no means empty, possessing the appearance of an ancient painting, beautiful with its lines and contours, yet charming through its transformation.
Upon seeing him, who was like a mirror for the minds [of women],
the royal ladies stood motionless right there, as if they were painted in a picture.
Then the king, having quickly awakened, did not see his beloveds before him;
searching through the forest, he saw them standing surrounding the sage.
Upon merely seeing them, the serpent, hissing and overwhelmed by the poison of jealousy,
emitted a fierce venom like the *hālāhala* poison of the *vāra-cūpa*.
"Who are you, who, by means of this mere artificial and painted guise of a sage, rob the hearts of the simple-minded? You are surely a deceiver of women!"
In the abduction of another's wife, meditation and recitation serve to ward off obstacles;
for rogues, the supreme means is the ascetic practice of consoling the simple-minded.
The conduct of you, who are a rogue with a sweet mouth yet clothed in bark,
produces delusion— alas!— like that of a poisonous tree in the forest.
Who, moreover, knows the inner truth of such conduct, which is like that of a sage even in its outward appearance,
or even of its highly esteemed spiritual accomplishment?
When the king had spoken thus out of anger, the Proponent of Forbearance, whose disposition was sweet with non-anger, addressed him with an unchanging mind: KAvk_29.61.
"I am a sage who preaches forbearance; you ought not to suspect me.
To me, these women and those stones are without distinction."
Having heard what he said, the king, saying, "I shall now see if you have attained patience," cut off his two hands with a sword.
Even as he was being torn apart, seeing that the man remained patient and unchanging,
the jealous king cut off his feet for the sake of his own tranquility.
Wicked men, like dogs, indicate misfortune on the path, defile with their tongues,
and finally tear apart one's limbs.
Devoted to forbearance even when struck, remaining silent even when their shoulders are severed,
and cool even amidst intense heat, they are as upright as the *sarala* tree.
With his hands and feet cut off, he steadied himself against the intense pain; guarding his anger and mental agitation through patience, he reflected thus: KAvk_29.67.
"Just as my limbs were severed by him who has abandoned all other actions,
so shall I effect the severing of the harsh afflictions of saṃsāra."
When the king had departed for the city, having treated his brother, the sage, with contempt out of anger and delusion,
the earth became as if withered by grief due to the dust.
Then, provoked by that suffering, the deity of Patience caused a calamity of famine,
pestilence, and drought to afflict the king’s city.
