Having learned from the omens that the defeat of the sage was due to an offense against the deity, the king went to appease him.
Having fallen at his feet and said,
"Forgive me," he became as if unconscious from the despair of remorse.
To him the Preacher of Forbearance said: "O King, I have not even the slightest anger;
such is the destiny that must come to pass, determined by the lines of one's karma."
Destiny acts according to its own will and takes no account of anything—
not fortitude, nor virtue, nor wealth, nor austerity, nor even honor.

A living being reaps the fruits of his own karma-tree, which has its roots firmly established in the place of birth; it possesses a succession of seeds produced within its intestines, and its branches are divided and made variegated by the ripening of time.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, no transformation has occurred within me;
by this truth, behold this blood turned into milk.
"If my mind remained unpolluted even when my limbs were being severed,
by this truth let those very limbs be restored to me."
Thus, through the fervent supplication of that pure-minded one,
those very limbs, though entangled, suddenly regained their natural health.
Then the king, whose feet were touched by the crown, said to him:
"O Sage, you possess great power through your asceticism; therefore, what do you desire?"
O ocean of compassion, you ought to lift me up, who have fallen at the end of my evil deeds, by taking hold of me with your hand of merit.
Thus entreated by the lord of the earth,
the sage replied to him for the sake of delivering those who are submerged and for the liberation even of those who are bound.
For the consolation of the frightened and for the nirvāṇa of those who are deluded.
But when you attain that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
I shall then cut through your delusion with the sword of wisdom.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, the sage departed for his own hermitage;
the king also returned to the capital, meditating upon that very person in his mind.
"I am that very Kauṇḍinya, the teacher of patience, who has now become Kālabhū;
having attained perfect enlightenment, I have now rescued him."
Thus, having drunk in the clear and sweet words— which were like honey produced from the lotus-face of the Sugata—
the assembly of monks experienced an indescribable joy, as if they had become bees themselves.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Avadāna of Kāśīsundara," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

30. The Legend of Suvarṇapārśva. Praiseworthy is that certain essence of beings, straightforward and established in the merit of benevolence; blameworthy is that supreme ungrateful one, who is an obstacle to traveling upon the path of Dharma.
Having reflected for a very long time upon his wondrous deeds, a person, covered with horripilation,
becomes simultaneously speechless and tearful when beholding him.
Long ago, on account of Devadatta, the Blessed One was questioned by the monks;
he then related a narrative based on past events.
In Vārāṇasī there was a lord of men named Mahendrasena,
by whose splendor all other sovereigns were rendered lusterless.
Candraprabhā became his beloved, like a divine glory;
by the power of her husband, even her dreams attained the state of reality.
At that time, there was in the forest a leader of a herd who had died;
he was known by the fitting name Suvarṇapārśva, and his complexion was like gold.
The radiance of his glance, resembling a pearl necklace shimmering from the interior of a blue gem,
became the ornament of the beauty of the forest.
The radiance of that [palace], which possessed sprouts of coral creepers and a bark-like surface inlaid with variegated gems,
shone like a wave from the wondrous ocean of nectar.
The body of that Bodhisattvāvatāra became beautiful;
for physical beauty is indeed the mark of one who has previously performed virtuous deeds.
An old crow, his long-sighted friend,
became alarmed at the search for Labdhaka and was intent on scanning the directions.
The two of them took their pleasure in conversation with one another in secluded places;
for through former merits, even the speech of animals becomes human-like.
Once, while searching for water, that leader of the Yādavas arrived with his followers upon the sandy bank of the river Veṇumālinī.
Hearing his increasingly piercing and long-drawn-out cry of lamentation,
all the lions fled with their necks twisting in confusion.
Then Suvarṇapārśva, overcome by the noose of compassion,
stood motionless right there, as if pierced in his vital organ by an arrow.
Seeing him prepared for its extraction and possessed of far-sighted vision, the crow said: "Friend, this exertion of yours is not appropriate."

In times of adversity, these wicked ones who claim to be friends of their own bodies are like flowers; yet when their purpose is achieved, they are like thunderbolts—they do not acknowledge what has been done for them.
Thus, although being dissuaded by the crow, Sarala, overwhelmed with compassion,
quickly descended into the river and ferried him across.
Having released him from his bonds, the deer, free from apprehension,
spoke to that wretched man who had fallen at his feet and was preparing to depart.
"O friend, you must not tell anyone that I am staying here;
for greedy hunters, craving skin, will seek me out for my gold."
Having been addressed thus by him, he, named Kuṭila, replied with humility, "So be it," and after bowing to him and offering the praise at hand, he departed.
In the meantime, at night, the king’s wife Candraprabhā saw in a dream a deer seated upon a throne, preaching the true Dharma.
Then, having had a true dream, that queen woke up and said to the king:
"O King, a wondrous golden deer was seen by me in a dream."
I wish to see him in person,
appearing like a deer that has emerged from the lap of the moon out of fear of Rāhu.
Thus addressed with affection by the queen, the lord of the earth was pleased and,
bestowing wealth, dispatched hunters to capture the deer.
Then those hunters, having returned from searching the forest,
spoke with trembling to the king, who was enraged at their fruitless journey.
"O Lord, we have traversed this entire world, searching everywhere among the gathered mountains;
yet we have wandered on without rest, for such a deer as that cannot be found."
With eyes drawn by a wondrous creation, that beautiful-eyed one—
whose form was as perfect as a dream— whence did this golden deer come?
O King, if you are pleased with this diversion of the mind,
let some skilled artisans fashion a golden deer.
Having heard this, the king, bestowing even greater wealth,
became intent upon his resolve to search for the deer.
Then Kuṭilaka, having approached the king and heard that he was a generous giver, spoke—his mind as greedy as that of hunters—in his desire for the acquisition of wealth: KAvk_30.29.
"O Lord, grant me your favor; I shall show you the deer.
That golden-limbed antelope was seen by me just now in the forest."
Having heard this, the lord of the earth, his eyes blossoming with great joy, said repeatedly: "My good man, show me where he is! Where is he? (KAvk 30.31)
Placing that very person at the head as his guide to the path of the deer,
he went forth with his army, appearing like the mountain of the rising moon with its clear umbrella.
Then the crow, perched upon the top of a tree, cast his far-reaching gaze upon the forest,
which was being cleared of the clouds of dust raised by the throngs of elephants and horses.
Approaching Suvarṇapārśva, he said to the leader of the deer herd:
"What was spoken by me for your benefit previously was neither heard nor acted upon by you."
This very man has arrived with his bowmen ready for battle;
even though I have restrained him, he is not satisfied with mere withdrawal.
Now that fear has arisen, where should we go, what should be done,
what beneficial course should be followed, or is it simply that we must all die together?
This ungrateful man, of cruel conduct and base nature, is a defiler of the Saṃgha;
you yourself have nurtured this poisonous tree for your own destruction.
Even by the destruction of those who offer their own bodies, he is not satisfied;
the submarine fire is ungrateful, swallowing the entire ocean of living beings.
Benefiting the ungrateful, placing trust in those with deceitful souls, and giving instruction to the foolish result only in harm to the doer. (KAvk 30.39)
When the crow had spoken thus and the king was drawing near,
the leader of the herd reflected upon what would be beneficial for his troop at that moment.
"Let this army of excellent warriors plunge into the great forest;
through my assistance, it shall, in a mere moment, leave it devoid of deer."
Therefore, I shall go myself into the presence of the army commander;
let there be the death of this one alone, while all these deer remain alive.
Having thus resolved, the deer went into the presence of the king;
for to great-souled ones, their own lives are as a blade of grass when it comes to protecting the lives of others.
Seeing him approaching swiftly, Kuṭūhalaka was delighted;
"This is he! he quickly exclaimed, pointing him out from afar to the king with both hands.
At that moment, by Drona’s curse— which fell like a thunderbolt—
the two sprouts of his tree of sin were cast down.
Having heard that account related by the deer, the king was struck with amazement;
his face became vocal with cries of "Shame! at the conduct of the ungrateful man.
Then the lord of the earth,
with supreme affection and profound respect, led that deer to his own city.
Then, having reached the capital, the king gave him a jeweled throne and sat down before him together with his harem and ministers.
That Bodhisattva Hariṇa, possessing divine intellect,
taught the Dharma in that assembly, by which the people became endowed with the precepts.
I myself was formerly that Sāraṅga with golden flanks;
and he who was the crooked and cruel Devadatta has now become this one.

Thus, having heard this account of the noble being’s life— composed of tranquility and told by the Blessed One for the sake of shattering the fear of worldly existence— that assembly of monks was inspired toward virtue.
Something occurred that was beautiful through the discernment born from the ripening of merit.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the *Suvarṇapārśvāvadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
31. The Avadāna of the Good Deed. This distinction between the virtuous and the wicked is perceived in the world through the examination of the characteristics of direct perception:
the sun renders the universe clear with its light, while darkness makes the entire world blind.
The Blessed One, the omniscient one, surveying the entirety of past events even at the very commencement of this narrative,
spoke once more:
In the city named Pāṭaliputra, there was a king, a Indra among rulers, named Purandara,
whose palace was a treasury of merit.
He had a son named Kalyāṇakārī who was exalted by a multitude of virtues,
and a second son named Akalyāṇa who was devoid of merit.
Performing virtuous deeds, a wish-fulfilling tree of compassion for all who seek his aid,
and possessing the virtues of generosity and ethical conduct, he reduced his father’s royal fortune to nothing but the royal parasol.
To him, King Puṇyasena dispatched a messenger named Manorama with a letter and gave his daughter in marriage by word alone.
Then, with his wedding imminent, the prince said to the king:
"Father, the marriage has arrived; in my opinion, this is not appropriate for me at present."
"Out of affection and gentleness,
I have emptied your treasury, for I am addicted to giving away my natural splendors that were once swollen with pride."
Therefore, having crossed the great ocean by means of a ship,
I shall indeed go to the Island of Jewels, intent on acquiring divine gems.
"Having attained divine fortune, I shall take a wife;
for a wife is a source of terror to one who has not yet achieved his purpose, even amidst an abundance of pleasures."
Having spoken thus and received his father’s command, he bowed at his feet and entered the ocean,
which embraced the sky with its restless waves.
His younger brother, a younger sibling whose outward kindness was merely a mask for his inner malice, followed him,
though devoid of virtue, while inwardly contemplating hatred and enmity toward those possessed of merit.
The elder brother said to him, "O child, when the ship is destroyed due to a failure in our task at sea,
I must be taken up by you upon your shoulder once I am born."
Thus reassured by his brother, that rogue said "So be it" to him;
for a wicked man, intent on finding fault, resorts to a display of affection.
Then, having boarded the ship and reached Ratnadvīpa by means of favorable winds that seemed like his own merits, the prince— *KAvk_31.15*.
Then, as the prince was slowly returning after having obtained the two jewels,
a violent wind suddenly shattered his ship.
When that carriage was wrecked, that deceitful younger brother seized his brother by the neck according to their prior agreement, like a serpent.
Driven swiftly by the wind of karma, the prince reached the shore and suddenly fell into sleep, the first messenger of blindness.
Seeing his jewels bound up while he was asleep,
his cruel younger brother proceeded to strike him at that moment of vulnerability caused by his misfortune.
Having plucked out the lotus-eye of that [rival] who was firmly bound,
he rendered that very Tāraka devoid of stars within the ocean of fear.
When he who was his own jewel had departed, the son of Vāja lost his luster;
he became like a lotus pond whose blossoms have been uprooted by an elephant.
He became devoid of light, enveloped by the intense darkness of grief,
like the beginning of a night in the dark fortnight when both sun and moon have vanished.
In the meantime, the lord of Gokula arrived at that place;
seeing the prince blind, he was overcome by the same distress that had befallen him.
Having led him to his own abode, the king became devoted to serving him,
captivated by the power of his virtues, kindness, and affection.
There, skilled in musical notes, he played the lute— which always delights the mind and serves to pacify the grief of the virtuous— just as he had practiced before.
Association with the virtuous, the enjoyment of extensive discourses on discernment, the practice of yoga, the wine of poetry, intimacy with dear friends,
and dwelling in forest groves lovely with flowers and the sound of the lute.
It is an immersion in nectar for those whose minds are scorched by the fire of grief.
The wife of that lord of cowherds, Tīgavīṇā, who was skilled in discernment,
beheld the prince and became filled with longing.
Constantly instructed like a lute, she, being crooked and fainting with fresh passion, thought longingly: KAvk_31.28.
"This fortunate man is exceedingly dear to my sight and dwells within my heart;
yet my fever of longing does not cease unless love itself proceeds toward him."
Blessed is this lute of his, which, jingling repeatedly with the strikes of his fingernails,
has attained through his merits the fitness to rest upon his lap.
Having reflected thus, she spoke to him freely and with agitation,
touching his lotus-like hand with her own trembling sprout-like hand.
O giver of honor, this mind of mine, which has gone out to you, does not remember its affection for you as one ungrateful forgets a favor, due to that shame so easily found by women.
Cast away by passion and devoid of shame, women take no account of morality, family conduct, pride, or doubt.
Out of affection for me, you ought to make my resolve fruitful;
for women, when honored, bring pleasure just like the deities.
Having heard these words of his, uttered in a broken and uncontrolled tone, the prince spoke to that fickle woman, his heart filled with terror: KAvk_31.35.
"O mother, this lapse from virtuous conduct is not fitting for one who is good.
Fie upon the life of one whose virtue is destroyed and who is touched by the poison of sin!"
He who embraces the body of another's wife with his own limbs will,
in turn, embrace the flames of the fires of hell like a moth.
Those who are devoted to helping others, who show no regard for the wives of others,
and who are dedicated to non-violence— they truly live, while others are dead.
Having heard what he said, her hopes were shattered;
for to women, the denial of affection is more grievous than death.
Then, approaching her husband when her desire had met with failure,
that female serpent spoke as if vomiting the poison of her wrath.
"O virtuous one, this affection for others is a source of trouble for you who are so simple-hearted;
for who would allow those of unknown character to take possession of his home? (KAvk 31.41)
For you who touch upon intense confidence in others, this is not fitting; for whom does which person truly know one's guarded mind and wealth? KAvk 31.42.
The thousand-eyed Indra, who was an adulterer, has been kept blind by you in your home out of compassion for the wretched and the blind; behold now the fitting fruit of that act.
Today, in that secluded encounter, I was ardently entreated by him;
were his eyes still there, how could I have fled?
Thus addressed by her, the lord of the cowherds, greatly tormented by anger,
cast him out at the door and made both his house and his heart cool.
That a father abandons his son, or that a friend slays a companion—
that is the manifestation of those wives who are like the edge of a sword for the severing of kinsmen.
Whatever crookedness there is in the eyebrows and eyes, whatever sharpness and whatever fickleness,
and whatever hardness there is in the breasts— all that resides in the hearts of women.
Slowly escorted by the caravan of the doer of good deeds across the path,
he heard that his father had gone to the third heaven and that his brother had become king.
In due time, he reached the city of his father-in-law, King Puṇyasena—
a kinsman who was the remedy for the exhaustion of the long journey.
In the meantime, it was heard that the charming daughter of the king had previously been promised in marriage by word to one who had fallen into the ocean.
When the lords of men had been summoned and seated in their respective order,
she ascended a jeweled palanquin and went to the site of the self-choice ceremony.
Gazing at the kings with her slowly moving eyes,
she beheld that prince who had arrived there by chance.
Even though he was blind, he suddenly became the beloved object of her eyes;
even though the moon was obscured by clouds, it remained dear to the night-lily amidst the darkness.
When the kings had departed, embarrassed by the failure of their efforts,
the daughter of the monarch chose him, whose excellence was manifest through his virtues.
Having cast the necklace around his neck, that large-eyed woman,
speaking slowly and sweetly, said to him, "I am under your power."
Trembling at the conduct of women, he spoke to her in that secluded place:
"This which you have done is not fitting for a woman so impoverished in wisdom."
"While there remain lotus-eyed kings who are friends through the affection of love,
why have you chosen me, one whose birth is barren and who am blind?"
Even the wives of those who possess sight turn their gaze toward other men;
how much more so the wife of a blind man, who goes to meet another even during the day?
I have no business with women; I have no confidence in them.
Women are crooked rivers that cause one to fall from family to family.
Having been addressed thus harshly by him, the king’s daughter, trembling with shame, said to him:
"O Lord, you ought not to entertain any suspicion regarding me in any matter."
If you are so excessively suspicious that you perceive fault in some noble woman, then how can she,
though herself faultless, be tainted by you?
"If my love is for you alone, and my mind has no other refuge,
by that truth may one of your eyes become stainless."
As soon as Sudṛśī had spoken thus, by the power of her truth, his right eye became like a blossoming lotus.
Then the prince, delighted and astonished by the qualities of the beauty of that lotus-face, propitiated Śilocanā and spoke to her.
"I am that very same prince, the doer of good deeds and the fortunate one,
to whom you were formerly betrothed by my father with these words."
"If I am indeed that very same person, now free from enmity toward the tearing out of my eye,
by that truth may my other eye become healthy."
"By this truthful supplication," [he said]; and instantly his second eye also attained clarity, together with his mind.
Then, having been granted assistance by King Puṇyasena, who had learned of his conduct,
he regained his own kingdom accompanied by his beloved.
"I am that Devadatta who performed virtuous deeds, and he was my younger brother;
by the power of that former experience, even today he remains just as he was."
Having heard this noble and stainless account of the Bodhisattva’s conduct,
as well as his corresponding deeds, those monks were indeed struck with incomparable wonder.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the *Kalyāṇākārya-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
32. The Legend of Viśākhā.
Generally, those who are perverse toward the virtuous remain free from disease;
yet at twilight, the passionate one, turning away from the darkness, casts the sun down from the mountain.
Even though Devadatta’s life story, which spanned many previous births,
had already been told, the Blessed One, an ocean of wisdom, spoke once more.
Long ago, in the land of Kaliṅga, there was a glorious king named Aśoka, the destroyer of his enemies,
whose immeasurable valor was renowned.
He had four sons of equal status:
Śākha, Praśākha, Anuśākha, and Viśākha, who became renowned throughout the world.
Intoxicated by their youth, they were banished by their father along with their wives;
even affection for one's sons perishes when accompanied by such resentment and humiliation.
Having gradually reached that formidable forest, which was like an unbearable state of misfortune, they— emaciated by hunger and with their provisions exhausted— reflected together.
In times of calamity, these women are like shackles binding our ankles;
yet they remain as sisters to us even when we subsist on mere leaves, obtained with great difficulty.
As they reflected thus, the resolve to kill their wife arose;
for the minds of those whose fortunes are scorched by misfortune become terrible.
Among them, however, Viśākha, apprehensive due to his wicked intentions,
took his wife and fled separately out of compassion.
That woman named Kalaṅkavatī, having fallen into a state of extreme distress and being exhausted from running the long distance, fainted and fell to the ground.
Then, at the moment her life was ebbing away, she was made to drink her own blood, produced by the wound from the arrowhead, by her husband who was moistened with compassion.
The ocean of beings, having cut off his own limb, provided sustenance for life with his flesh to her, whose life had been restored by drinking his blood.
Having gradually crossed that waterless and terrible wilderness,
the two of them reached the bank of a mountain river, shaded by dense trees.
While the two of them were resting there, a man with his feet and hands cut off arrived,
crying out in intense agony as he was being carried away by the current of the river.
Upon seeing him fallen into such dire calamity, Viśākha was embraced by compassion;
plunging into the river with his two arms, he ferried him across.
Then, having restored her life with water, roots, fruits, and other provisions,
he made her free from the pain of her wounds within just a few days.
Although healthy, he was unable to go anywhere due to his lack of mobility;
there he remained, taking his meals at the proper time with his wife.
The prince, however, had little union with his wife;
for heroes, being generally intent on lions, are mostly desirous of conquest.
Her body gradually filled with the essence of divine herbs as her nourishment,
his wife, though frail, conceived a longing for sexual union.
Women, who find pleasure in the touch of their own will, are not smeared by affection nor bound by virtue; they do not cling to their elders.
That woman of full breasts, enjoying herself with him in silence during the night,
felt her husband to be an obstacle because she was not yet satiated by their fearless lovemaking.
That unfaithful wife made an agreement for her husband's execution with him;
for indeed, wicked women are skilled in punishing those who commit sins.
Claiming an incomparable headache as a pretext for herself, she—
who had inscribed her sins upon her face— bound a cloth bandage across her forehead.
When the prince had recovered from her intense headache,
he reflected upon various means for its remedy out of compassion.
To him, who was motionless with dejection and anxiety and sighing deeply, she spoke,
like a lotus withered by frost whose bees hum in distress from the cold.
"In the past, my daughter suffered from such a headache that it was cured by physicians with a plaster made from *pāṣāṇabheda*."
"This front slope of the mountain is covered with *pāṣāṇabheda* stones;
having descended by means of a rope, you should take them if it is possible."
"I will support you with my two hands as a prop," said the king's son when thus addressed out of affection by his wife; "So be it," he replied.
Then, taking hold of a rope held by his hand,
he slowly descended to the bank of a mountain river that was roaring as it struck against the rocks.
Devoted to the giving of medicine and having abandoned all other supports,
he fell into a great abyss, into the waters as fickle as a woman’s mind.
Due to the remainder of his auspicious karma, his body remained unbroken;
being carried along by the current, the steadfast man reflected thus: KAvk_32.31.
"By showing me this whirlpool that reflects the mind of a woman,
she has surely given me instruction regarding my vow of celibacy toward women."

Difficult to be understood even by those of expansive intellect, resembling dreams and mental constructions, they are addicted to the deployment of the uneven exertions of passion, hatred, and calamity;
through desire, these objects of desire have been set forth for the delusion of all people.
And even for a woman who has been known for a moment, she is but an illusion destined for downfall.
While he was thus reflecting,
he was carried by the great force of the river to the city of Puṣkarāvatī, as if by his own merit.
At that moment, when the sonless king had passed away,
he who possessed auspicious marks was taken up by the great ministers who were experts in omens.
There he was consecrated by them according to the prescribed rite with auspicious waters;
having witnessed the wonders of women's conduct, he became an adversary to marriage.
Even on Mount Kalaṅkavatī, though devoid of Bodhisattvas,
the medicinal herbs possessed little potency at that time, and the people became distressed by the interruption of their livelihoods.
Placing him with his limbs broken upon her shoulder, she went along the paths of villages and towns and begged for alms,
crying out with the words, "I am a devoted wife!"
Out of respect for her ascetic life, everyone gave him much;
even a false report of one's conduct can produce prosperity in times of adversity.
Wandering slowly, she reached the city of Puṣkarāvatī;
hailed as "The Virtuous One" by everyone, she went to the vicinity of Vṛṣadvāra.

"The king detests the conduct of women, yet he pays homage to a devoted wife. Having reflected thus, the family priest spoke to the king out of devotion for her: KAvk_32.41: "The king detests the conduct of women, yet he pays homage to a devoted wife. Having reflected thus, the family priest spoke to the king out of devotion for her.
"O King, some woman of devoted virtue has arrived from a distant foreign land,
by whose footsteps this earth has been purified."
"O King, behold that virtuous woman who has placed her husband upon her shoulder;
by bowing before a wife devoted to her husband, the lifespan of men increases."
Thus requested by the domestic priest to have an audience with him, the king said to him:
"O simple Brahmin, you do not know [who he is]."
The popular saying that "a woman is affectionate" is a delusion of the mind, as devoid of substance as the attainment of a flower in the sky; there is no doubt that a woman is sinful.
Women who ascend to the fire [of passion] without fruit are as straight in their conduct as they are in social gatherings;
like reed-creepers, they lack firm roots and bonds.
Homage to women, homage to women, homage to women—homage, homage! To those who by their very nature are ill-behaved and whose sole character is treachery and divisiveness.
To me, whose mind is tormented by anxiety over the faults in the conduct of the woman I have seen,
even this earth filled with jewels does not please me.
Deceptive as female mountain deer, yet exceedingly sharp at deceiving others, they are intent on bestowing their own bodies and snatch away the very lives of men;
they inspire fear when spring has arrived, and they drink even fire.
Women are neither straightforward nor crooked; they cannot be understood even through hundreds of reflections.
"Nevertheless, if you are insistent, I shall show you that woman.
Having said this, the lord of men ascended the palace and beheld her.
Having recognized that very wicked woman clinging to his body,
the lord of the earth informed his ministers of the entire incident.
Having recognized the king, that wicked woman, her face cast downward for a moment,
was rejected and quickly departed while the people covered their ears.
Hearing this account related by the Jina— that "I am that son of the lord of men named Viśākha, and Devadatta is his bride"— the assembly of monks censured his conduct.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Legend of Viśākhā, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

33. The Legend of Nandī and Panandā. There exists a certain power of merit and tranquility belonging to those of pure soul, whose very nature is like nectar; by its influence, even the cruel are instantly freed from the poison of their wrath.
Long ago, when the Tathāgata was dwelling in the Jetavana monastery,
and by his command the community of monks was wandering through the mountain forests;
Standing upon the terraces of Mount Sumeru, intent on meditation,
the monks arrived with faces pale and lusterless, and emaciated.
Then, having paid homage at the lotus-feet of the Blessed One,
they were questioned by the monks regarding the cause of their physical frailty and spoke.
Having encircled Mount Sumeru with a triple winding,
the two nāgas Nanda and Upanandaka remained stationed there, invisible even to Vainateya.
Those two constantly emit a threefold exhalation that scatters fire;
by its mere touch, even stones are instantly turned to ash.
We, practitioners of meditative yoga, have been scorched by the poisonous breaths of that [serpent];
with the luster of our faces turned pale, we have come to nothing but emaciation.
When they had spoken thus, the Teacher, requested by the community of monks before him,
appointed Maudgalyāyana as the one fit for the subduing of the two nāgas.
Having reached Sumeru, which embraces the sky with its peaks, he,
his form concealed through yogic power, beheld the two sleeping lords of the nāgas.
When those two, being struck by him, did not wake up even slowly,
he then assumed the body of a great serpent and coiled around them.
Having seen him of terrifying form, the two, though awakened, were tormented;
they fled in human guise and stood there overwhelmed by fear.
Then, having abandoned their serpent forms and assumed their own original shapes,
as they were fleeing from one another, Maudgalyāyana said to them:
"O two nāgas, where are you going so quickly? Abandon this fear! That nāga who routed you both is not present there. (KAvk 33.13)
If, in every way, you possess no steadfastness because of that fear,
why do you not offer salutations to the Buddha, who is the refuge?
Having heard what he said, the two of them spoke to him with humility: "O Noble One, please show us favor by granting us an audience with the Blessed One."
Having thus spoken, the two lords of the nāgas led [the king] into the presence of the Blessed One;
having reported that account to him and bowed down, he sat down.
Then the Blessed One spoke to the two lords of the nāgas who had come for refuge;
they prostrated themselves, their bodies adorning the ground with the radiance of jewels.
Having received the precepts that grant fearlessness to all beings,
you two are now free from fear due to the commitment of having taken refuge.
By the mere sight of him, they were made by the Blessed One to be completely free from fault and hatred; having bowed to him, the two departed.
By the mere sight of those great-souled ones, and by the instruction of their splendor clinging to their bodies,
even enemies scorched by the heat of the poison of hatred attain coolness through the nectar of peace.
When the monks asked the Blessed One, the Conqueror, out of wonder at his power, the All-Seeing One recounted to them that account of his previous birth.
In former times, there was a glorious lord of men named Kṛki in Vārāṇasī;
he received the teaching of the Dharma from the Blessed One known as Kāśyapa.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his two ministers, Nanda and Upananda,
he became intent upon awakening, finding fulfillment in the vision of truth.
Having ruled the kingdom with both dharma and adharma, those two ministers of his built for Kāśyapa a monastery equipped with all necessary provisions.
These two lords of nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, were born at the proper time;
through the merit of having offered a monastery, Mount Meru became their abode.
Thus, when the assembly of sages who had heard the life of the serpent-king as proclaimed by the Jina— a life well-known for its meritorious deeds through the transformation of his own body—
there arose a hymn of praise for the virtue of subduing the venomous serpents.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the *Nandopananda-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

34. The Avadāna of the Householder Sudatta: Whatever small fraction of wealth remains after being given away through the cultivation of the welfare of others, it becomes a distinguished and supreme merit by virtue of its inexhaustible quality.
Then, after some time had passed, he came into the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dharma teaching of Nanda and Upananda.
King Prasenajit, having approached to see the Blessed One,
departed without having performed an act of hospitality or prostration toward those two.
Having bowed to the Jina and departed, he resolved upon their suppression;
meanwhile, those two arrived through the sky, discharging a rain of weapons.
Sent by the Omniscient One, Maudgalyāyana quickly arrived there and turned that shower of weapons from the king into a row of lotuses and water-lilies.
Having returned to the presence of the Blessed One, the lord of the earth, at his command,
asked forgiveness from the two lords of the serpents who had arrived there.
Then, requested by the king,
the Blessed One went with a company of mendicants to the royal palace to eat the food purified by devotion.
While the foods were being cooked there at night, a fire broke out;
by the power of the Jina, it was suddenly extinguished.
When the Blessed One had departed after eating, the king, in his own city,
issued a decree by means of a legal ordinance to prohibit the kindling of fires at night.
In the meantime, the householder Sudatta’s young son,
named Mithyādoṣaddhivala, was struck down by the king.
Formerly, through the grace of the teaching of the Blessed One, the Teacher,
he had attained wisdom and fortitude, and thus remained unpained even by the suffering caused by his son.
Having bestowed his abundant wealth upon the wretched, he, being childless,
gradually reduced his fortune to a single coin out of excessive devotion.
Then there was a householder named Sudatta, who had acquired all his wealth through gambling and gave away very little; for indeed, a house is said to be one's own prison.
Once, when he had come to see the Blessed One and was standing before him,
the Blessed One spoke out of compassion to him, who was ashamed because of his name, "Svalpadāna" (Little-Giver).
O householder, you ought not feel shame for a small gift;
a single grain of an offering bestowed with faith attains the stature of a mountain of gold.
In former times, a great deal was given by the twice-born Velama;
yet, due to the common absence of faith, it did not increase in that manner.
If one were to feed with devotion all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa,
and another were to feed a single person endowed with the thought of awakening, the merit of the latter would be greater than that of the former.
Having heard these true words of the Blessed One and having rejoiced in them,
the householder bowed down to him and departed for his own home.
Having offered a lamp and recited the Buddha’s instruction during the night,
he was led away by the king’s men on a stake because of his act of setting fire [to the palace].
Because of the possibility of punishment,
Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods came at night to see him, who was bound and held in the prison.
When he did not accept the wealth when they entreated him, saying,
"Take it," then this instruction on the Dharma was delivered in his palace.
The king also, having seen the city set ablaze by its power,
was released from that prison-house, yet he did not see water anywhere.
Having gone to see the Sugata,
he once stood before him and observed the king who had arrived behind him to pay homage to the Jina.
He did not show affection toward the king at the outset;
for no one else deserves worship in the presence of the Blessed One, who is honored by the entire world.
Having addressed the Jina, the king bowed and returned to his own city;
he then ordered the expulsion of the householder from his realm.
Then the deity who was well-disposed toward Sudatta made the king frantic with the venom of stings from small creatures that she had released.
Terrified by them, the king, accompanied by his ministers and the women of the inner apartments,
approached Sudatta and, having gone to him, sought to propitiate him through the teaching of the Jina.
Thus, through constant proximity, Sudatta, the lord of the householder, attained the peace proclaimed by the Blessed One, which is filled with the supreme nectar;
he obtained it as if it were his own, free from the separation caused by obstacles.
The disciple of those with pure minds [attains] the great treasure of solitude.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Avadāna of the Householder Sudatta, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

35. The Legend of Ghoṣilā. He who assists in the act of giving shares in the donor’s equal fruit; for one whose nature is intent on helping others does not become a minister to those engaged in unmeritorious deeds. (KAvk 35.1)
Long ago, in the beautiful and blessed city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove,
the Conqueror took delight in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada’s park.
In Kauśāmbī there was a king of the Vatsas named Udayana,
whose fame even today is sung by the women of the Vidyādharas.
In his kingdom there was a householder named Sudhana, who lived by working in mines and was expert in lending and receiving money.
Once, having recognized that petitioner who had come to the assembly hall by his speech alone, the king spoke to him with due respect.
"I know, householder,
that you possess a vast store of gold, with its sound enhanced by the accumulation of bullion."
Thus addressed by the king, he replied to him with a smile and joined palms:
"O King, it is indeed true that there is a hoard of gold in my house."
When you, the king, who are devoted to reflecting on virtuous conduct and are tender with affection,
are the protector of these people, what indeed is there that they lack?
The wealthy fall into poverty, and the poor meet their end;
even a king becomes like a tiger, merciless in its craving for the scent of prey.
When the king’s wealth is righteousness, people acquire riches without hesitation, they share what has been acquired, and they clearly enjoy what has been shared. (KAvk 35.10)
Having heard those well-founded words of that wise man, the king spoke to him,
as if showing his favor with the radiance of his teeth.
"O wise one, you ought to become my minister for affairs;
for it is only by those like you, preeminent in intellect, that the burden of the earth is sustained."
Having heard these words of the king, Śuddhana addressed him:
"We are not experts in the circles of assemblies or in the service of kings."
Service indeed brings about the destruction of the garden of freedom, the sale of the happiness of sound sleep,
and strikes fear with the wretchedness of worldly suffering for men.
With the feet of the lords placed upon my head,
I, their servant, always remain as if I have achieved my life's purpose, serving as a footstool for them.
Even for those who have attained prosperity through the toil and exertion of service,
its enjoyment is marred by association with backbiters and is as fragile as the frown of a master.
And these royal fortunes do not remain stable, even when held with great effort; they are seized by the fierce crocodiles of pride, which are difficult to restrain.
For a moment, the splendors were delightful with silent women who were intent on the special affection of ever-new embraces.
Thus addressed, that minister was also forbidden by the king;
for who indeed can transgress the will of one who possesses power?
Having attained a position of great maturity, he was appointed by the king to the office of chief minister;
yet all the other ministers, corrupted by envy, could not tolerate him.
Though repeatedly appointed to that ignoble task by the king— who, out of a desire to investigate the Dharma, had been incited by a slanderer— he did not perform it at all.
Then, though looked upon with hostility by the king out of false anger,
he nevertheless did not issue any command joined with unrighteousness.
"I shall not perform an action censured by the virtuous for the sake of happiness in a single lifetime, which would cause suffering for hundreds of future births," he declared.
Purified by his integrity even in the face of fear,
he was released by the king and established an uninterrupted feast of giving for all seekers.
During that glorious man’s world-renowned festival of giving,
his reverence for the wish-fulfilling tree reached its highest point among all people.
In the meantime, groups of sages coming from the southern region for the sake of visiting sacred fords entered a desolate forest, a wilderness difficult to traverse.
There, all those afflicted by thirst, lying unconscious upon their beds,
out of delusion cried out loudly for water— even though they were senseless.
"Among the gods, gandharvas, and nāgas, whoever here is an ocean of compassion,
let him stand and grant us water," they said.
Then he, with the resonant sound of his jeweled armlets and bracelets,
emerged from the midst of the trees, carrying a golden pitcher in his hand.
Having drunk the water up to their throats from that [lotus] which was lowered by his lotus-like hands— water possessing the taste of nectar— they rejoiced as if they had regained their very lives.
Requested once more, they returned and, filled with wonder, asked him who had emerged from his dwelling in the invisible tree: "Who are you?"
He, whose fame was widely renowned and whose heart was set upon prosperity, said: "In Śrāvastī there is a master of the household named Anāthapiṇḍada, who gives to all."
Formerly, as a tailor living near that house,
I would constantly raise my arm and point toward that residence for those who came seeking alms.
By that merit, I attained the state of a god and dwell here;
this right arm of mine shines, for it was the giver of gifts to those in need.
Having taken leave of him, those sages set out once more into the forest;
being hungry, they beheld an extraordinary tree of lush and beautiful shade.

"Right here on the bank of the lotus pond, in a hollow, there is a full supply of divine food;
go there and eat whatever you desire."
Having been thus instructed by him and having eaten that divine food, they asked him, who was resting beneath the celestial tree, "Who are you? (KAvk 35.38).
He also related: "In Śrāvastī there was a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada;
I was his brahmin priest for the communal feeding of the Saṅgha."
He was diligent in his service as the distributor of the curd-pots;
when their meal was finished, he himself ate what little food remained.
Seeing the respectful offering of food to the monks, I became distressed in mind; the king’s meal was for me like non-saline food.
At the word of Anāthapiṇḍada, out of a respectful disposition toward the meal,
I then undertook the eightfold Poṣadha vow.
Then, because I ate at night out of greed while my vow was still incomplete,
I became known in the world as Khaṇḍapoṣadha (the one with broken fasts).
"Even by means of a partial vow, I have attained the state of a son of the gods.
Having heard those words of his, the sages departed in amazement.
Reflecting thus as they traveled, they said: "By means of our intense asceticism, we have been afflicted for a very long time, yet even now we have not touched the state of spiritual well-being."
Now we shall strive for the very vow to observe the Poṣadha;
for who would not have respect for their own welfare, which is a means to happiness free from calamity?
Reflecting thus, they went toward Kauśāmbī and reached the renowned house of Sudhana, the householder.
There, having been offered hospitality by him and having reported that marvel to him,
they went together with him to see Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having reached Śrāvastī, they were respectfully honored by him;
they reported everything to him exactly as it had been seen and heard.
That minister of dharma, being pleased, led all those friends who desired to take vows, as well as Sudhana, into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One also, out of those words, bestowed his grace upon them;
having realized the vision of truth, they went to a happy rebirth.
When they had departed, the Blessed One, beholding Sudhana with a glance full of partiality, duly made him a vessel of wisdom.
Having attained a distinguished excellence through the vision of the truth,
he went to Kauśāmbī and had a monastery built for the Jina.
Because he was commanded by the Blessed One to go there and provide assistance,
the monk named Cunda became the resident of the Cunda Monastery.
Then the Blessed One, out of compassion, took up the tattered garment of this maidservant named Rādhā, who was an attendant in the pleasure grove.
"May I not be a slave," with these words of faith and aspiration, she offered that robe to the Blessed One; it then became of a single color.
Having seen Sudhana’s wondrous and radiant accumulation of merit,
the Blessed One, questioned by the monks, explained its prior origin.
In ancient times, there was a householder named Sundhāna in Vārāṇasī,
for whom there was no exhaustion of his generosity despite his noble elephant.
During that twelve-year period when the land was struck by drought,
his umbrella of protection remained unobstructed and food was provided without interruption to those in need.
In his house, a treasurer named Padmākara provided assistance for his giving, for prosperity indeed accompanies its own source.
The wise minister named Dharmadūta was present, serving as the announcer of the mealtime for the community of Pratyekabuddhas.
When his time had passed due to the distraction of his duties,
at one point his dog announced the hour of death to them.
I, who was that very Sundhāna, am now this Koṣṭhika Anāthapiṇḍada;
and he who was the Dharma-messenger of the Saṅgha is none other than King Udayana.
He who was the dog named Saṃjñānideśaka was also Sudhana;
he was recognized by King Ghoṣa as being one who bore the other name Ghoṣila.
"O monks, this 'Life' (carita) was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, the destroyer of worldly existence;
with their cupped hands of ears, those of noble mind drank it in, as if it were the essence of the fragrance of well-performed deeds and the nectar of immortality."
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the Legend of Ghoṣila, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.

36. The Legend of Pūrṇa In a lake of the wise, beautified by lotuses and a bed of water-lilies, a lotus born on the pure bank is not touched [by the water]. For those whose virtues are white, innate and ever-present within, it is their nature that is the cause, and not their birth. (KAvk 36.1)
Long ago, in Śrāvastī, while the Victor’s wish-fulfilling tree— the Jetavana grove— stood there, dedicated to the welfare and meditative absorption of all sentient beings.
In the city named Śūrpāraka, there was a man named Bhava, an ocean of accumulated jewels, a leader of caravans, and the best among the wise.
Bhavila, Bhavabhadra, and the renowned Bhavanandin were his three sons,
born of his wife Ketakī.
Due to the onset of disease, he once fell into a state of near-death;
because of his harshness, he was utterly neglected by his wife and sons, who were deeply distressed.
One of his female servants, named Mallikā, was devoted to him with supreme dedication to service; through her attendance, he regained his health.
Devoted to her through his service and affection, and grateful for her kindness,
he united with her during her fertile season and begot a son.
When, at his birth, all the father's goals reached fulfillment,
that boy— beautiful as the full moon— then became known by the name Pūrṇa.
The three elder sons, seeking wealth, went to the ocean;
Pūrṇa, however, earned his fortune in his father’s warehouse.
Then, having returned from the ocean with their objective achieved,
they calculated the hundreds of thousands of gold pieces and entered their own city.
Whatever wealth they had acquired from their sea voyage,
Pūrṇa’s own gain from his merchandise in his home was even greater than that.
Having seen that, his aged father Janaka said to them on the final day:
"This desire for the future is not satisfied by the destruction of one thing or the arising of another."
"You have seen that by those who exerted themselves in seeking oceanic treasures,
great wealth was acquired by Pūrṇa without any excessive hardship."
Through the ripening of virtuous karma, wealth comes to those who seek riches;
from the hand of one it flees away, while another obtains what has fallen.
Through not abandoning the true path, through discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate,
and through a thorough knowledge of place and time, the virtuous possess prosperity everywhere.
The wise who partake of the Dharma remain empty-handed in their own homes;
others, having gone to the ocean of jewels, meet with the danger of losing their lives.
The supreme secret of wealth must be understood with effort by the virtuous:
for those whose minds are pure and free from malice, prosperity flows from their own wealth as if it were already within their grasp.
And you must constantly guard against dissension within this united assembly;
for from a divided family, prosperity slips away like water from a broken jar.
Just as the similar flames of a fire whose fuel is not distinct perish,
so too do the prosperities of one from a vast lineage perish when the family line is broken.
How indeed can the persistent division among brothers be turned back,
when they have been constantly taught the science of hatred by their wives at night?
No division arises among those who are exalted and self-controlled as long as a woman does not enter between them, like the edge of an axe.
By repeating the faults of their brother, by harshness and contempt toward their teacher,
and by their longing for a single friend, women lead men to a state of division.
Even when laughing, women speak with such playful arching of their brows that it becomes the cause for uprooting the very foundation of friendship and affection.
Having thus spoken what was beneficial and desired for the welfare of his sons,
Bhava, overcome by impermanence, met his death in due time.
While the wealth was undivided, the elder brothers were capable of acquiring riches in other lands,
but Pūrṇa, however, thought only of the wealth in his own home.
When they returned home at the appointed time, disputes arose over clothing and food;
their ears were captivated by the counsel of women, and thus dissension broke out among them.
Then, while the wealth was being divided, those who were under the sway of hatred said,
"This is the son of a slave-girl," and thus Pūrṇa was deprived of his share.
Even he, though accustomed to eating his fill, saw on the road at that time a helpless load of wood, which had shriveled up from the cold despite the heat of summer.
Having taken that load of wood from him for the price of timber,
he beheld divine sandalwood that brought coolness even to fire.
Having obtained great wealth through that very same great merit,
he became worthy of service by caravan leaders and honored by the lord of the earth.
Having traveled six times to Ratnākara, he, who gave to all seekers,
bestowed favors such as the remission of ferry-tolls upon all merchants.
Requested once more by the merchant caravan-leaders residing in Śrāvastī,
he quickly departed for the island in the ocean, having mounted his ship.
Then, as the carriage was returning, he heard the merchants singing ancient mountain songs dedicated to the Sugata.
When he asked them, "To whom do these belong? they all replied:
"These verses were sung by the Blessed One, the wise Buddha."
Having heard these very words concerning the Buddha, he attained joy;
for that which is rooted in one's own latent impressions manifests clearly when it is uttered to men.
Having heard the story of the Blessed One related at length by them,
his mind became fixed upon it, and he grew eager for a vision of him.
Having returned home slowly and abandoned all his belongings,
he went to Śrāvastī to see his friend Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having declared his desire for renunciation to him, he who had conquered his senses went together with him out of devotion into the presence of the Blessed One.
Upon seeing there the Omniscient One, the sun that dispels the darkness of delusion,
he considered his purpose fulfilled simply by the sight of His feet.
Having understood his intention, the Blessed One spoke to him,
illuminating the quarters with the stainless purity of discernment by means of the moonlight of his teeth.
"Come, O monk, free from fear, free from adversaries, having abandoned [all] decay;
practice the desired holy life within the Dharma and Vinaya that have been proclaimed."
When this had been uttered before him by the Jina, whose nature is serenity,
his renunciation suddenly fell upon his body, unnoticed [by others].
Then, having attained equanimity through tranquility toward both enemy and friend,
and having received the Teacher’s instruction, he bowed down to him and departed.
He went there himself to personally examine the patience of the people in the land named Śroṇāparāntaka, which was a refuge for brave men.
Then, seeing him approaching— an ill omen for his hunt—
the hunter drew his bow and rushed forward in a rage to kill him.
Upon seeing him— who was free from agitation, devoid of fear,
and who spoke thus, "Strike!"— he immediately attained tranquility.
As he was pacifying him, that hunter suddenly became serene;
[the Bodhisattva] taught him the Dharma by which he, along with his followers, attained awakening.
There he caused five hundred delightful monasteries to be built for the Sugatas and Arhats, complete with every kind of necessary equipment.
Pūrṇa, too, was perfected in knowledge; he attained the state of being honored by the gods of the three realms and became endowed with the splendor of dispassion, which is envied even by sages.
Then his elder brother, Bhavila, having reached a state where his wealth was exhausted,
set out for Sandūra in the hope of acquiring riches.
Then, having boarded a ship, he was carried by favorable winds to the forest of Gośīrṣa sandalwood in just a few days.
Five hundred woodcutters were prepared to cut down that divine sandalwood grove, which was teeming with swarms of serpents.
The lord of those yakṣa armies, known as Maheśvara,
released in anger a terrible and great wind called Kālikā.
Threatened with a great danger to their lives by that mighty Maruta,
all the merchants cried out to the gods, headed by Śarva and Śakra.
After reflecting for a long time, Bhavila, the leader of the caravan, overcome with remorse, spoke to those who were crying out in distress.
His younger brother Pūrṇa, who desired my welfare, spoke to me as before:
"The ocean is full of great suffering and offers little joy; where are you going, to that sea?"
Having failed to follow the words of that wise man who perceives the truth,
I have fallen through greed for wealth into this terrible ocean of calamity.
Having heard this world-renowned power of Pūrṇa, all the merchants meditated upon him in their minds and went to him alone for refuge.
Homage to you, who remove the poisonous defects of the world's afflictions,
whose mind is filled with the overflowing nectar of perfected compassion.
When the sky was filled with their single-syllable cry,
Pūrṇa went in an instant and reported that event to his own deities.
Having heard of their disaster while staying in Śroṇāparāntaka, he,
armored with meditative concentration, reached the ship in an instant by traveling through the sky.
Seated there in the paryanka posture, as immovable as Mount Meru, he checked the movement of his arms,
which possessed the violent force of the cosmic dissolution.
Knowing that his breath was obstructed by Pūrṇa, the leader of the hosts of Yakṣas appeased him and departed,
leaving the sandalwood forest to them.
Having received sandalwood trees through the king's full favor, Bhavila,
filled with joy, went together with him to his own city, Śūrpāra.
Then, with his brother’s consent, Pūrṇa constructed there for the Sugata a temple named Candanamālā, adorned with gośīrṣa sandalwood.
There, having been meditated upon by Pūrṇa, the Blessed One quickly departed from his residence and arrived at Jetavana,
traversing a distance of one hundred yojanas.
As the Blessed One approached, the entire world,
reddened by the radiance of his body spreading before him, became like snow.
Seeing him from their dwellings on the outskirts of the city, the women of the houses attained a state of being inclined toward tranquility through the intense clarity of their hearts.
The Blessed One delivered a teaching on the truths to those women who had accumulated merit;
they, who were devoted to existence, became enamored of it, attained [the fruits], and went toward the wholesome.
By means of his supernatural power, the Blessed One [caused] a shrine there named after the city women, which was constructed by them;
even today, those who worship shrines pay homage to it.
Having thus granted the pure favor of ordination to the sage clad in bark garments, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, delivered a teaching on the Dharma.
Then the Blessed Jina, having entered the crystal palace named Candanamālā, made it capable of supporting the weight of the multitude of people.
Then, seated there upon a jeweled throne, that treasury of compassion delivered a teaching on nirvāṇa for the peace of all sentient beings.
In the meantime, the two lords of sages, Kṛṣṇā and Gautama, together with their followers,
approached and received the teaching of the Lord from whom they were to hear the Dharma.
Having there accepted the gift of the palace,
the Blessed One then set out with the monks, returning once more to the Jetavana.
Vraha established Maudgalyāyana’s mother, who resided in the world of Mārīci,
in the noble truths and settled her upon the path of Dharma.
Then, having arrived at Jetavana, the monks, filled with wonder, asked the Blessed One about the merit of Pūrṇa; he too spoke.
In a previous birth, during the time of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa,
Pūrṇa was an official in charge of monasteries and an attendant to the Saṅgha.
Once, seeing that the pleasure-ground had not been swept,
he spoke with intense anger to the monk who was in charge of the monastery's requisites.
"Whose monastery is this, where today an impudent man has stayed without paying the fee for his lodging?"—
saying this, he rebuked him, calling him "the son of a slave-girl."
Having experienced the miserable state of hell due to that sin of harsh speech,
Pūrṇa became the son of a slave for five hundred births.
For him, the very service of the Saṅgha became a source of even greater merit,
by which he attained Arhatship, having cast off all the afflictions of existence.
Thus the Victor described the power of Pūrṇa, which was produced by the accumulation of merit;
having heard this marvel in the assembly, the community of monks became devoted to the praise of merit.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Legend of Pūrṇa, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
37. The Story of the Mute and the Lame:

Free from desire for the bliss of nothingness, those virtuous ones who enjoy the splendor of dispassion abandon everything—including their bodies as companions—and go to the forest for the sake of tranquility.
Even in that display of religious observances, if there is an accumulation of resources for the sake of undertaking a retinue,
what offense has been committed against the household by means of treasuries, attendants, and utensils?
In former times, when the Jina was delighting in his residence at the Jetavana monastery,
he stood before the Śākya princes who had already embraced the life of renunciation.
Having observed the vast accumulation of variegated robes, excellent alms-bowls, meditation bands, and other such items,
the Blessed One reflected:
Alas! Even now, the cause of their bondage has not ceased:
this attachment to the body, consisting of conceit, which clings so fondly to its own possessions.
The body’s requisites are its series of accessories;
alas, the gathering of those very things is indeed a chain of bondage!
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, whose conduct is not restricted to solitude,
exerted himself for the welfare of those who had approached him out of compassion.
He made an agreement that attendance should be performed by whomever for three months,
so as not to be seen by the monks.
While that rule was being observed, a monk named Upasena, who followed the forest-dweller's vow and wore but a single robe, arrived for the sake of some business.
Having been invited and having obtained the sight of the Sugata, that fortunate man,
his task accomplished, stood for a moment and then departed after bowing down to him.
As he was walking along, the monks approached him, surrounding him, and asked:
"O Noble One, how is it that you have been granted the sight of the Blessed One?"
How was that rule of three months for his audience, established by the Teacher’s ordinance,
broken by you, who have led the Saṅgha onto a wrong path?
Having heard those words of theirs, Upasena replied with a smile:
"No violation of our agreement has been committed by me."
"I was personally told by the Blessed One at the time of his appearance:
'There is no prohibition for me against seeing a forest-dwelling monk.'"
Having severed their bonds by renouncing all personal belongings and requisites,
they dwell at the roots of trees, wearing robes made of rags from dust-heaps, and possessing a vision that cannot be obstructed.
"For those who are intent on accumulation,
thinking 'this is today' or 'it will be tomorrow,' there is no vision of the truth here among the circles of those who wander with begging bowls."
Afflicted by thirst, they long for waters cool with spreading frost;
yet those miserable ones remain perpetually destitute, even though the treasury of the ocean is ever open. For them, the fire produced from the sandalwood tree becomes a source of torment.
By whomsoever this stubborn obsession with pride has been bound to the equipment for the vow of tranquility.
Having heard what was said by Upasena, those Śākya monks,
their enthusiasm shattered by embarrassment, suddenly reflected:
This was commanded by the Blessed One specifically for us and not for others,
since we alone are those who wear garments fashioned from various kinds of robes.
Those who have renounced desire are dear to the Teacher, while we, who possess great desire, are not dear;
therefore, having abandoned desire, let us become agreeable to him.
Having reflected thus, they all put on their collection of beautiful robes,
cast away their surplus, and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
When their desire had ceased, the Blessed One bestowed his grace upon them—
he who shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity with the thunderbolt of wisdom.
When asked by the monks about the former history of the Śākya princes who had attained the fruit of stream-entry, the Tathāgata spoke as follows.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a lord of the earth named Brahmadatta,
whose arm— its hand moistened by the act of giving— supported the world like a world-elephant of the quarters.
To him there was a wife named Brahmāvatī, renowned for her virtues like a pearl necklace;
she was as celebrated as the fame of a virtuous man.
At the proper time, that woman of pure intent, having gone for water-sports, gave birth to a son who possessed divine marks and was like a reflection of her husband.
That boy, known as Udaka, was born within the water;
as he grew, he attained the aspirations of the crown prince, equal to his father.
On the same day as his birth, five hundred ministers obtained five hundred sons who were equal in appearance to him.
Remembering his own past lives and his former history, that child slowly reflected upon what was beneficial for himself and what he ought to do at that time.
Having previously held the position of crown prince for sixty years,
I was long tormented by hardship in the perils of hell.
Even in this life, the position of crown prince has once again presented itself;
yet, even if entreated in every way, I shall not commit a sinful act.
Having reflected thus for a long time, he turned his back on royal pleasures and assumed the state of being lame and mute,
which caused distress to his father.
Although he possessed all the auspicious marks, he was unfit for the life of a king;
known by the name Mūkapangu, he became a source of increasing sorrow for his kinsmen.
When the sons of the ministers arrived, who had brought forth the power of weapons, scriptures, and strength,
the prince, though grown up, neither rose nor spoke.
Then, questioned by the lord of the earth, the physicians declared the remedy for that ailment:
"O King, no physical deformity is seen in the prince."
If, through habituation, even a fault has arisen in him who indulges in pleasure, then,
