This armor, capable of protecting everything and expressive of deep affection, has been sent to me by that king as if it were his very kindness.
I see no gift that would be equal to this, nor even superior;
for a small recompense is like a thorn in both a favor and an injury.
"Let something appropriate be considered;
let more than this be sent," said all the ministers, whereupon the king became overwhelmed with anxiety.
Then the wise great minister, having reflected for a long time, said to him:
"There is a brahmin named Varṣākāra who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge."
Therefore, there is only one means that possesses manifold virtues;
let an effort be made to dispatch him, if it is possible.
This Blessed Buddha, who resides near your domain,
together with his image on a cloth painting, is an object of veneration for the gods.
He, the wish-fulfilling tree for the budding welfare of the entire world,
is beheld through vast merits in a wondrous dream or even in a mental conception.
Having heard these words of the minister, the lord of the earth said, "So be it," and having gone before the Blessed One, he bowed and reported that very matter to him.
Then, having been authorized by him, the king quickly commanded excellent painters for the task of sketching the image of the Blessed One.
Gazing upon the form of the Jina, they were captivated by its beauty;
though previously confident in their ability to measure things, they became powerless to do so.
Then, they gradually completed the reflection of the Blessed One, which had been transferred onto a stainless cloth,
as it bore the splendor of a golden hue.
Then the protector of the earth sent forth that cloth-painting of the Buddha,
which was like a personified accumulation of the merits of the eyes of the world.
King Yaśodharman, delighted, personally read the hand-lettering seal of Bimbisāra which had been obtained before the cloth painting.
From the noble land of Magadha— a region distinguished by the excellence of the city of the Thirty-three and by the vicinity of the merit arising from the Sugata’s placement of his lotus-like feet—
there arose King Bimbisāra, whose form was fashioned from roots of virtue.
Your kinsman in dharma addresses you, the ornament of the earth's surface.

This image of the Blessed One, possessing the luster of the moon, has been sent to you as a beneficial medicine for the great disease of delusion regarding existence; it removes the poison of hatred for kings,
quenches the thirst of craving, and— being clear and sweet— is now placed within the vessel of your eyes.
O fortunate one, being filled with longing, drink the elixir of merit to your heart's content, even to the throat, by force!
To establish one on the true path, to constantly instruct in the acquisition of a multitude of virtues, to ward off evil conduct, to urge toward the attainment of firm happiness,
and to act with one's whole being and without interruption for the sake of sincere assistance— this is [the nature of a friend].
What more than this should be done for the welfare and benefit of the virtuous by their spiritual friends?
Having thus savored the meaning of the letter, which was worthy of the nectar of a friend’s affection,
the king went before the cloth-scroll mounted upon the elephant.
Rejoicing with joy, he, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, welcomed him and,
having spread out a golden lion-throne, seated him upon its lap.
Beholding that body of the Sugata, an abode of beauty and merit, the people of the world exclaimed: "Homage, homage to the Awakened One!"
Upon merely hearing the name "Buddha," his body was adorned with horripilation;
when a rain of flowers was released by the gods, the lord of the earth was filled with wonder.
Having heard of the Blessed One’s merit and having tasted the nectar of his conduct there,
he attained a likeness to the blue-throated Śiva, who yearns for the gift of water from the clouds.
Having beheld the twelvefold dependent origination depicted on the lower part of the cloth-painting, both in its forward and reverse order, he abandoned his delusion.
Then the king, having seen the truth through the very fruit of stream-entry,
dispatched a reply to his friend by means of dismissing the monks.
Then Bimbisāra, having performed his duties for the Blessed One,
dispatched Kātyāyana and the nun named Śailā.
Then the noble Kātyāyana gave a teaching on the Dharma there to King Udrāyaṇa, who was performing acts of worship.
Through his teaching of the Dharma, a very great multitude of people gathered together and attained the stages of stream-entry,
once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
In that city, two renowned householders named Tiṣya and Puṣya went forth into homelessness for the sake of peace and,
in his presence, attained final nirvāṇa.
At the end of their lives, their kinsmen erected two stupas at the appropriate time, marked with their names; even today, those who pay homage to shrines revere them.
That nun named Śailā also constantly gave Dharma teachings in the inner apartments of Queen Candraprabhā in due course.

Then once, the king, who was skilled in interpreting omens, learned that his beloved, while in her pleasure chamber, had only seven days remaining to live. Having understood the nature of worldly existence, the lord of the earth then [addressed] her.
He granted permission for him to attain the auspicious state through renunciation first.
On the seventh day, at the king's word, the queen went forth as a nun within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and cast off her body.
Suddenly, among the gods of the Cāturmahārājika realm,
she attained the state of a celestial maiden and went to the grove of the Victor.
There, a woman with a face like the full moon, adorned with divine ornaments,
seeing Śākyamuni, was filled with joy and fell at his feet.
The Tathāgata bestowed upon her, who was strewn with divine flowers,
an instruction in the Dharma by which she attained the vision of the Truths and departed.
Having gone through the air to her husband’s city like the lunar form itself,
she awakened him as he slept at night and brought about the illumination of enlightenment.
When she had departed for her own abode, at dawn the lord of the earth,
intent upon the life of a wandering mendicant, consecrated his son Śikhaṇḍin.
Then, having entrusted him to two great ministers for the protection of the subjects,
he went to the city of King Bimbisāra, his friend.
When he arrived, stripped of his parasol and fly-whisk,
Bimbisāra bowed down and honored him with royal offerings purified by joy.
To him, who was seated at ease upon his throne, he spoke with wonder,
both delighted by the sight of him and pained by his separation from Śrī.
O King, whose commands rest upon the crests of infinite vassals and who are equal to Indra,
how have you come to such a state?
O hero, the seizure of your kingdom by another is not possible for you, who are of unswerving and upright nature, whose counsel is secret, and who are wise.
Thus questioned by his friend, he spoke to him with a smile:
"O King, this all-pervading increase of my wealth is not dear to me."
Out of aversion to the taste of sense objects, I myself, being free from craving,
have renounced and utterly abandoned sovereignty, which is but a vessel for enjoyments.
By you, my spiritual friend, that painting of the Sugata’s image,
which was sent for my benefit, has become for me a teacher of dispassion.
Now, by your grace, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One,
I wish to obtain the going-forth from the home to the homeless state.
Having heard these words of his friend and reflecting, "So be it," Bimbisāra spoke to him with respect, through the discernment of that [truth].
"You are blessed and highly esteemed by the virtuous, O Lord of the Earth;
how has your mind become thus averse to the cycle of existence?"
With contentment as your wealth and the enjoyment of pleasures as your fortune, you shine most brilliantly;
for this is the characteristic of pure beings: a mind adorned by sovereign self-restraint.
What is the use of a universal sovereignty of great power accompanied by its dust, or of means of accomplishment that are difficult to achieve;

what is the use of enjoyments that are but momentary feasts, or of pleasures that dwell within the family of existence; for the sake of bringing an end to saṃsāra, [the merit] earned by the virtuous in other births [is dedicated] to the mind?
If one establishes detachment, which destroys the sprouts of great delusion, [then one attains the state].

He by whom the earth, though it provides life, breath, and pleasure, is abandoned with ease; he who is a master of initiation into aversion toward the pleasures of love, even those esteemed throughout the three worlds;
and by whom this world, afflicted by the calamity of delusion, was made an object of compassion.
Through merits, someone among the wise is born as a tranquility that is contrary to the flow of worldly existence.
Having said this, Bimbisāra led him to the Veṇuvana hermitage and,
after prostrating before the Blessed One, reported the entire account to him.
Udrāyaṇa, too, beholding the form of the Sugata which he had long contemplated,
considered himself to have accomplished his purpose out of joy.
With his head bowed and focused upon the body that cuts through the cycle of existence,
the Blessed One’s gaze fell upon him along with the initiation into the wandering life.
Then, having attained the state of a monk, with bowl in hand and clad in his robe,
he caused wonder among the people as he wandered for alms in the city.

Having protected his subjects according to dharma, Śikhaṇḍin, with a serene mind, passed away in the course of time; however, [his son] became turbid in character and took great delight in unrighteousness.
Whose mind does Fortune not agitate— she who is turbid yet flashes with the brilliance of lightning against a golden glow, like a row of clouds?
The two great ministers,
Hiruka and Bhiruka, being angry, abandoned that lord who was addicted to unrighteous actions and was no longer under their control.
The two ministers, Daṇḍa and Mugdara, who were skilled in following the king's will and had been appointed to his position by the monarch,
spoke freely to him as he remained attached [to his vice].
Devoted solely to pleasing the subjects and proclaiming the king's wickedness,
these rogue ministers are born only for the purpose of broadcasting their own fame.
They do not account for dharma, nor happiness, nor wealth, nor fame, nor even their own lives;
those servants of noble devotion act for the sake of their master.
Subjects who are not mutilated, not exhausted, not tormented, and not oppressed,
indeed perform their duties for the king like sesame seeds.
Though they spoke thus, those two, appointed by the king to attend to the affairs of the kingdom,
became wicked through greed and set out to destroy the defenseless subjects.
When the lord of the earth is devoid of reflection, of evil conduct, and of wicked intellect;
and when the great minister has lost all truth—whence can there be life for the subjects?
Then, after a short time, while on a merchant's journey,
Udrāyaṇa once inquired about news concerning his own country, the king, and the kingdom.
He said, "O King, your son, the lord of the earth, is well;
however, being deprived of good ministers, he has fallen under the influence of evil counselors."
There, by the command of the sovereign, a certain widespread affliction has befallen the subjects,
because of which the city-dwellers grieve day and night over their birth in that despicable land today.
Where the sun creates darkness, where the moon rains fire,
where the Kālakūṭa poison— more virulent than nectar— manifests itself,
and where the king as protector seizes away the livelihood of his subjects; [there, O Lord, you are the refuge].
Who there shall hear that cry, amidst the spreading and vast calamity?
Having heard these words, full of distress, from the merchant who was exhausted by the fatigue of his attachment to the king, that treasure-house of compassion spoke to him: KAvk_40.80.
"Go from here quickly and comfort the subjects;
I myself shall come and establish Śikhaṇḍin in the Dharma."
Having been addressed thus by him, the merchant, filled with joy, went slowly to his own country and freely offered consolation to the people before them.
When that rumor had spread, the two ministers Daṇḍa and Mudgara, terrified by the arrival of the deceased king, spoke to the current monarch: ||| KAvk_40.83 |||
O King, everywhere is heard this report, censured by the virtuous:
"The aged king has become a renunciant, yet he is striving for the sake of the kingdom."
Having been tormented by his severe vows and longing for sensual enjoyments,
he will cast aside his shame along with his renunciation and return once more.
O King, that which those whose dispassion is yet unripened abandon all at once returns to their state of endearment even more intensely than before.
A longing for objects that are contrary to the stability of the world arises especially in a living being, just as a craving for unwholesome food arises in a sick person.
Abandoned due to his arrogance regarding his own happiness, Prahasta approached him;
for generally, everything becomes as dear to a fool as a mango tree.
Therefore, having driven you away from your throne—
the very treasury of majesty— that elder, like a waning moon, now desires to enjoy the kingdom.
With his body distressed by the monastic robe and longing for fine garments,
a desire for a jeweled crown arose in him whose head was shaven.
Who could endure dwelling in the forest, having abandoned the effortless luxury arising from the abundance of new enjoyments in jeweled palaces?
How can those who are worthy of the comfort of soft beds lie upon ground strewn with sharp thorns raised by the hooves of deer?
How can those by whom honey as cool as moonbeams was drunk [now endure this]?
They drink bitter water that possesses the heat of the forest-born fire.
O Prince, at this very moment, as you stand in a precarious position on the verge of entering [the city], the first doctrine of the logicians is your downfall.
Therefore, O Lord, the future king must first be slain by you;
for a moth destroys the lamp only if it falls upon it before being burnt.
At those words, "Of the two," the king immediately became agitated;
for whose mind does turbidity not arise when it is brought about by wicked clouds? (KAvk 40.95)
Filled with apprehension and having become as cruel as a saw, he said to the two of them:
"This danger is common to both you and me here before me."
Having deliberated upon the essential purpose of the matter with your minds resting in the skillful means of discipline, let that which is appropriate be carried out by you two alone.
Thus, having been encouraged by the king, they quickly dispatched assassins and set out upon Udrāyaṇa’s main path solely for the purpose of killing him.
He, too, intent on enjoining his son to the protection of wisdom,
approached the Blessed One and respectfully requested, "I am going."
Permitted by the Omniscient One with the words, "Enjoy what you yourself have done," he,
drawn by the noose of karma, went to the city of Roruka.
Therefore, as he was walking along the road with guileless conduct like that of a holy man,
assassins dispatched by wicked ministers struck him down.
And taking his robes, alms-bowl, and other belongings from him as he lay slain,
those two— the king and the minister— exulted, saying, "A pleasing deed has been done by us."
Then, seeing his father’s robe smeared with blood, which had been pointed out to him by those two who rejoiced in evil, the king suddenly fell into a swoon.
Having regained consciousness, he slowly grieved not so much for his teacher as for himself,
fallen into the terrible abyss of hell.
He said: "My dear child, I have reaped this fruit from wicked people;
greedy for the honey of power, I failed to see the fall of sin."
Alas!
Association with the wicked brings immediate downfall to those who have risen high, even in this supportless and terrible abyss of hell.
"This great sin was committed by me through the intellect of wicked ministers;
now that I have fallen, even fire is no longer purifying for me."
The killing of my father, who was an Arhat, is equal [to other heinous crimes]; what atonement can there be for me, in that I once drank burning poison from the same vessel?
While my aged father, free from attachment, had retired to peace through the life of a renunciant,
I, out of greed, brandished the sharp weapon of my own mind against him.
That which is merely contemplated causes trembling and cannot be endured to hear;
that which, when seen, produces a pang of grief even in insentient things;
and wherein even cruelty becomes softened by the fire of intense remorse—[that is the heart].
Even there, the cruel deeds of those with merciless minds spread forth, sharpened by their ruthlessness.
Having spoken thus, tormented by grief and his face made clamorous with lamentation,
he forbade the entry of those two wicked ministers out of anger.
Having recognized their other virtues,
he quickly appeased Bhīruka and Hiruka and brought those two ancient ministers of his father back.
Then, while the king was emaciated by anxiety and had turned pale from grief,
those two wicked ministers approached his mother in private and said:
"O Queen, your son is illustrious and naturally upright in disposition;
he does not understand the protection of a kingdom, which is harsh due to the destruction of one's own kin."
Even though his father had gone forth as a renunciant, he came to seize the kingdom;
since we brought him to peace, what blame can there possibly be in that?
If this sequence is one that arises from base tantras and is an inauspicious method,
how could such a method apply even to that monk who desires sovereignty?
"Since we two were forbidden by the king because of our patricide,
why do you now falsely wither yourself away in grief?"
"We two have performed a good deed; the Lord’s body has become emaciated by suffering.
In all circumstances, it is only the offenders who suffer."
The king grieves for what is past; once it is done, it is simply done. O Queen, why do you neglect him, when your son is so wasted by anxiety?
Having heard what was said by those two, the queen-mother,
showing respect for their words, slowly spoke to the one named Taralikā.
This is an act of immediate retribution, a fall into hell for both of you—
whether brought about by your own opinion or by the king's prior deed.
I, however, am warding off his grief arising from the murder of his father;
may you two also ward off the suffering arising from the murder of an Arhat.
Having thus instructed them at her leisure, she went into the presence of the king and spoke to him,
who was overcome with grief like the waning moon.
"Son, the kingdom of kings consists of both dharma and adharma and is full of many deceptions;
why do you wither away in grief over it, fearing the sins of others?"
"If you are indeed distressed because of the killing of your father, even though you are dear to your guru,
then cast aside shame and speak regarding this crisis of your sorrow."
"You were born by another of your own accord; he is not your father according to dharma.
For women, who take pleasure in eating as they wish, are indeed shameless."
Having heard those words in private, even though they were unpleasant,
the king cast off the intense torment of suffering caused by the sin of patricide.
These [rays] instantly undergo the affliction of being joined with the mountain of sunrise from the mountain of setting; they provide the fresh amusement of shattering the kings of the earth;
and they suddenly produce fire from water, and that [fire] from burning.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is impossible for women to accomplish.
Then, tormented by that very act of killing an Arhat, which was like a thorn piercing him,
the king questioned those who knew the Dharma regarding the atonement for that deed.
Then those two wicked ministers, having caught two kittens inside the shrines known as Tiṣya and Puṣya, held them fast with a bait of meat.
Although they were forbidden, they entered the king’s assembly out of audacity and spoke to him,
who was seeking relief from the intense heat of his ascetic penance.
"O King, you are causing your mind to be greatly deluded in vain;
in this world, it is your opinion that there are no Arhats who are auspicious in every respect."
If they were truly possessed of supernatural power like royal swans in the sky,
how could their slaughter by another have been possible?
Therefore, Arhats do not exist; how then can there be the sin of killing them?
What dispute over boundaries can there be where no village exists?
The two householders Tiṣya and Puṣya, who had attained the state of Arhat, were born in the interval as two cats;
they are those very ones today in the two self-caityas.
Those two are clearly visible; who could have any doubt about this being a matter of direct perception?
If there is no conviction, why do you not look for yourself?
Having spoken thus and having made the king's mind wavering with doubt,
those two wicked men went together with him to behold the shrine.
While the people gathered there were seized by an unprecedented curiosity,
and the king along with his ministers were intent on looking on, two wicked ministers [acted].
The two rogues, Tiṣya and Puṣya, who were bound by their addiction to material gain,
slowly called out to the cat and the young boy.
"If you two are indeed the Arhats Tiṣya and Puṣya in the form of cats, then let a circumambulation be performed by you around these two shrines; by that truth [may this be so]."
At the moment when the gift of their flesh was being offered,
those two cats emerged quickly and circumambulated them, uttering these words.
Seeing that, as the king along with his followers departed with sudden confidence restored,
the very illusion of the wicked man went forth to conquer the world.

Is it not merely a magical illusion (indrajāla) for the delusion of those with the intellect of a beast or a child— to perceive wind in the fist, a lotus on a stone, or variegated patterns in the expanse of space, and to perform the playful acts of creating and dissolving vast arrays of forms upon the tip of the tongue?
Scoundrels display a personified form that inspires confidence through a momentary acquaintance.
Then the king, devoted to the doctrine of no-cause,
offered an act of faithful worship before the noble Kātyāyana in the Buddhist system.
Then, having been forbidden from entering the capital, he remained outside with his followers out of compassion for those to be converted; and there Śailā, the nun, also stayed.
Then, once, seeing the king approaching before him from the throng of people, Kātyāyana departed out of fear of being insulted.
Seeing him departing as he had been previously dispatched by the two ministers, the two wicked ministers, harboring long-standing enmity, spoke to the king: KAvk_40.147 //
"O King, today we saw on the road this shaven-headed monk, a headless vessel of inauspiciousness; we do not know what will happen."
"I shall not look upon the face of that wicked king," he said;
for indeed, having gone to a secluded spot, he stood far away from here for a moment.
Hearing this, the king, out of indignation toward the wicked man, said to his attendants:
"Let this man, while standing at a distance, be filled with handfuls of dust!"
Being filled with those handfuls of dust by the wicked servants,
he constructed a divine hut for the sake of providing relief through his entry into it.
Serpents provoked by indignation, or tigers of yellow and red hue, attain gentleness through pacification; but the servants of a king do not.
Then, as the king had departed, Hiruka and Bhiruka approached him, who was covered by hundreds of heaps of dust, and spoke out of sorrow: KAvk_40.153.
"Noble sir, you have fallen into distress because of the cruel king's evil deeds; fie upon our eyes, by which this is seen before us! (KAvk 40.154)
Blinded by delusion, the king has been cast by wicked men into the pit of sin;
we too shall share in his guilt simply by witnessing this deed.
O you of expansive intellect, this earth, afflicted by manifold evils, must be abandoned by you;
for to whom is the company of the wicked unbearable, and to whom is renunciation not agreeable?
Peace does not attain tranquility, forbearance does not reach its consummation, and the intellects of the virtuous do not become touched by the defect of harsh anger;
nor do insults, which are like thorns, dwell in the minds of the good.
In this world, there is no happiness greater than the avoidance of wicked people.
For those possessed of virtues, sovereignty brings only the exhaustion and toil of falling downward;
their profundity appears like darkness, snatching away the life-breath of those who enter it;
and even that worthiness of theirs is lost amidst base, wicked, and crooked serpents.
Alas, there is no such thing as a well that is not joined with a multitude of faults; such is the case with a wicked person.
Having heard these words of theirs, Mahākātyāyana said:
"I have no anger even at this humiliation; such is the course of karma."
"This alone is my sorrow: that because of the fault of associating with the wicked, a great danger has befallen this foolish king."
For in the first [moment], a great wind shall fall upon his city;
in the second, a rain of flowers; and after that, a rain of garments.
In the fourth [dream] there was a rain of silver, and in the fifth a rain of gold;
then in the sixth a rain of jewels, and in the seventh a rain of dust.
"Because of her, the king, along with his kinsmen and his kingdom, will cease to exist.
Therefore, you two must depart, taking the jewels for your own great welfare."
Having heard those words and having resolved, "So be it," Hiruka appointed his son Śyāmaka as his attendant.

And Bhiruka, taking his daughter Śyāmāvatī by the hand, approached the mendicant woman Śailā and spoke these words out of affection: KAvk_40.165: "And Bhiruka, taking his daughter Śyāmāvatī by the hand, approached the mendicant woman Śailā and spoke this out of affection."
"Noble lady,
as you have approached the end of your life, this daughter of mine must be entrusted by you to the house of the householder Ghoṣila."
Having spoken thus and handed over those two ministers, they both went home;
Śailā also, taking her daughter, set out for Ghoṣila’s abode.
Then, in due course, it happened in the city exactly as the monk had described:
Prajñā Jñānadīpavatī beheld reality according to its true nature.
Then, on the sixth day, when a rain of jewels had fallen,
those two ministers, remaining unobserved, set out taking a boat filled with jewels.
Having gone to the southern direction, those two built two cities:
one named Hiruka, and the other named Bhiruka.
On the following day, as a great rain of dust fell, the king,
along with his kinsmen and his kingdom, went to his destruction and became a guest of hell.
When the king had departed with his staff and mallet, leaving only his guilt behind,
Kātyāyana took that minister’s son and traveled through the sky.
Following him with affection through the sky,
the city deity established her residence at Khavaṇīkarvaṭa by his command.
Through the power of the merit of the monks, by the good fortune of the minister’s son,
and through the empowerment of the queen, that city became exceedingly magnificent.
Then, at that place, the deity of Suravatī erected a shrine for Kātyāyana,
which even today those who worship shrines pay homage to.
Then, taking the minister’s son by the corner of his robe,
Kātyāyana went through the air to a supreme region where he could hang him.
When people asked in amazement, "Who is this hanging down?
as he hung there, those people became known in that place as the Lambakas.
In the meantime, when that sonless monarch had ascended to heaven,
Śyāmaka was made king by the command of the one who knew the marks [of royalty].
Then, having gone to the region called Bhokkānaka,
Kātyāyana established a pure teaching of the Dharma there for his mother.
Having seen the truth, she respectfully took her son's staff and, though herself venerable,
had a great staff-caitya constructed.
Then, having reached Śrāvastī with longing, Kātyāyana slowly beheld the Jina and, filled with joy, performed prostration at his feet.
Having heard the story of Udrāyaṇa’s son related there by him, the All-Knowing One was questioned by the monks and spoke to them: KAvk_40.182.
In the forest near the outskirts of Karvaṭa, a hunter named Kālapāśa set down a snare with a trap ahead of him to capture deer.
Having set down a mechanical device encircled by nooses, he departed by chance;
a Pratyekabuddha, arriving at that place, found rest there.
By the power of his merit, wild animals did not enter his enclosure;
for no evil person can prevail in the presence of those whose souls are pure.
The hunter, having approached from there and seeing that the snares were empty of deer,
blinded by rage, struck the Pratyekabuddha with a poison-smeared arrow.
Seeing the wondrous power of that man, who was pierced by arrows yet possessed a radiance like a blazing fire, he fell at his feet.
Then, distressed by the agony of having committed an unworthy deed, the hunter,
lamenting and blaming himself, cast aside his arrows and snares.
Having enshrined the relics of him who had attained final nirvāṇa,
he constructed a stūpa adorned with parasols, banners, and other offerings, which was constantly venerated.
By that merit, the hunter became King Udrāyaṇa;
yet because of the killing of a Pratyekabuddha, he underwent many deaths.
The householder named Nandana, a resident of a small town, had a daughter called Madalekhā,
who was the very manifestation of wealth, grain, and other riches.
Once,
intoxicated with pride, she out of delusion scattered the dust from her house-cleaning over a Pratyekabuddha who was approaching on the road.
On that very day, the suitor she had long desired through her constant reflections arrived,
seeking her hand, while she was oppressed by the weight of her breasts.
Because she had thrown a handful of dust upon the head of a Pratyekabuddha,
she said to her brother, "My marriage is imminent."
Then, because of her reputation, mature maidens cast dust upon the head of a Pratyekabuddha in order to obtain him as a husband.
Deluded by a cognition that functions through the appearance of qualities,
they act without investigation even toward contradictory objects.
When he had set about practicing sinful conduct, the two householders named Buddhabuddha and Abhidha restrained him from that deed.
That very maiden became King Śikhaṇḍin, who partook of sin;
and his brother, the author of that scandal, was this very monk Katyāyana.
Born as householders, because they had warded off established evil conduct and were liberated from the torments of the city, those two were named Hiruka and Bhiruka.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One and having reflected upon them, the monks understood the diverse ripening of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma;
they regarded the speech of the wicked as equal to an enemy and the teacher as equal to their own discernment.
They considered nothing in this world to be a kinsman equal to one's own good deeds.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the Avadāna of Udāyana, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
41. The Legend of Kapila:
Even one who is destitute obtains a full burden of excellent fruit from a very meager gift, provided it surpasses in merit the abundant wealth of the vast gifts bestowed by kings.
For one who is pure, endowed with the flourishing abundance of faith white with the Dharma,
there is that which is appropriate for the mind and wealth— a manifestation free from saṃsāra.
Long ago, in Śrāvastī, there lived a wealthy householder named Dhīra who resided in the Jeta Grove monastery belonging to the Victor.
He had a son named Paṇḍita, who was truly wise;
he was adorned with the ornament of unimpaired fame, merit, and generosity.
Even as a child, he performed the rites of hospitality for the monks, headed by Śāriputra, providing them with garments and food fit for a king.
Then, at one time, when the people had been exhausted by a famine that showed no sign of ending,
the breaking off of alms for supplicants became equal to begging from a beggar.
At that time of extreme hardship for the monks, most terrible,
the wise one, summoned by the Sugata, set out for the Jetavana grove.
As he was proceeding on horseback, adorned with a golden necklace,
certain parasites, unable to endure his excellence and energy, approached him and said:
"You are renowned in all directions as a wish-fulfilling tree for the petitions of the needy;
we five hundred have arrived before you with hope."
"Ornaments and a pair of garments—each one is our desired object;
let them be given right now without delay, if it is possible."
Thus addressed by them, that wise Sadācāra dismounted from his horse,
performed a respectful salutation for them, and reflected for a moment.
If I were to go to my own home without even seeing the Blessed One,
how could that be anything other than an obstacle for one who is close to drinking the nectar of immortality?
If I, shameless as I am, depart without giving what is dear to those who seek it,
how can I myself commit that violation of the vow of generosity?
As he was thinking thus, the Naga king Śeṣa himself emerged, having burst through the earth, and granted the desired object to the supplicant.
The Naga king gave him garments and ornaments;
having quickly bestowed these upon them, he attained, as it were, a state free from all thorns.
Having seen that marvel, they too considered the meritorious cultivation of the Sugata to be the very mother of all accomplishments and the attainment of every goal.
With their hearts filled with serene faith, they then departed together with him to see the Blessed One, their defilement of hatred having been destroyed.
Then, beholding the Blessed One with his face bowed in prostration, the prince,
rendered fortunate by the dust of his lotus feet, made a tilaka-mark upon his forehead.
Then, placing a necklace as radiant as moonbeams at the feet of the Teacher,
he prostrated before him and presented them to him.
Through his teaching of the Dharma, the Blessed One, the bearer of the vajra of wisdom,
shattered the mountain of the view of a self-existent body and established them in the fruit of stream-entry.
When those who had seen the truth had departed,
the Blessed One himself, having bowed with affection to that wise prince, spoke.
"My child, by your merits you have attained the full measure of the splendor of well-done deeds;
even in times of famine, provide sustenance for the monks."
"I have one hundred and thirteen monks who are arhats;
you should seek out others in the city who are afflicted by hardship and share [the provisions] with them."
Having heard this from the Blessed One, the wise man was overwhelmed with joy and,
out of devotion to the Saṅgha, made a lifelong invitation.
Then, having returned to his own home, he constantly honored the Saṅgha, headed by the Perfectly Awakened One, with food fit for a king and esteemed by monks.
That compassionate king, through his generosity, made the poor wealthy, the indigent prosperous, those who were merely supplicants into true beggars, and rendered others worthy of compassion.
Seeking out the remaining multitudes of the wretched, that ocean of compassion gave them a heap of jewels that dispels the darkness of poverty.
That heap of jewels became for those men a pile of charcoal;
for jewels, gems, and varieties of precious stones are but the fortunes of men.
Approaching him like those who have seen wealth in a dream, they said to him:
"By you, under the name of 'jewel,' that heap of charcoal was given to us."
A person who has suddenly attained high status through the acquisition of great wealth does not survive when,
due to its sudden depletion, they are instantly cast down.
Having heard these words of theirs, the wise one, a treasury of compassion, said to them: "For those who are destitute of merit, even jewels turn into non-jewels."
"In the past, out of delusion, you did not accumulate a store of merit;
therefore, this heap of jewels has turned for you into a mass of charcoal."
Even jewels that were stored with great effort vanish far away through the exhaustion of merit, yet they are brought back through the conjunction of fortune;
the acquisition of wealth is merely a cause for the grief of loss, for true wealth is the mind, properly cultivated and directed toward virtuous deeds.
Therefore, may the community of monks be accepted by you for a meal;
I shall provide for you the perfection of an abundance of enjoyments.
Thus addressed by him, they honored the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, for one day with the abundance of wealth and food provided by him.
Having duly honored the Saṅgha, they made this aspiration for a moment: "May we never experience poverty."
Then, following the words of the wise man, they went and saw right before them that very heap of coals which had turned into a mass of jewels.
Then, in the palace of the wise and powerful prince,
a hundred treasures that had been hidden opened up without obstacle.
Knowing the Dharma, he gave King Prasenajit a sixth part of his treasures for the sake of protecting the established order; yet the king became like charcoal to him.
"This accumulation of treasure is to be enjoyed by the prince alone through his own merits"—
this was the voice that the king then heard from the sky.
Seeing that those treasures had been dug up again by the very word of the prince,
the king was filled with wonder and sent him back to his home.
Then, having bestowed all that wealth,
the prince of vast intent established his riches within the dwellings of the destitute.
Then, his longing for the essence-less cycle of existence having ceased through reflection on impermanence, that steadfast man spoke to his father:
"Father, please grant me leave to go now to the forest;
these worldly riches of mine have been defiled by the remnants of hundreds of births."
This vessel of life for all beings is so small that even the attainment of the prosperity of the three worlds becomes merely an object of enjoyment within it.
For whom I constantly provide an embrace with garments of soft touch in the cold, for whom I arrange anointing with cool sandalwood paste in the heat,
and for whose sake my fear of poison, weapons, fire, and the multitude of serpents is supreme— [for that person, I shall give up my life].
Even that which has been obtained perishes through misfortune; and even when protected from harm, the body goes to its destruction.
Detached from enjoyments, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant in the forest with my beloved,
I dwell there, removing the anxiety of a mind tormented by cares.
Having spoken thus and abandoned the bonds of attachment to sense-objects,
Śāriputra, having received his father’s formal permission, went to the peace of the Śramaṇas.
Having gone forth there, with bowl in hand and clad in his robes, he wandered about, self-restrained, as a follower of that very man.

Seeing the stream being diverted from field to field by the farmers as it flowed along the designated path, he reflected thus out of wonder: sa dṛṣṭvā karṣakairdhārāṃ kṣetrāt kṣetrapravartitām / nirdiṣṭena pathā yāntīṃ vismayādityacintayat // KAvk_41.49 //
"Ah! While water, though insentient, achieves its purpose by following the path prepared for it, embodied beings do not achieve such success through their actions."
Having reflected thus, as he walked ahead, the best of the wise saw an arrow that had been heated by a skilled fletcher and used as a staff; he then meditated upon it.
These insentient arrows attain straightness through heat;
but embodied beings, though tormented by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), do not become upright even when heated.
Meditating thus, he looked ahead and saw that the pieces of solid wood had been turned by a carpenter into the form of cart wheels;
then he fell once more into deep reflection.
Aha! By the conjunction of circumstances, even the insentient and formless minds of embodied beings attain flexibility in an instant.
Having reflected thus, he who was devoted to the discipline of the True Dharma approached his affectionate teacher and spoke to him as a son would to a father.
"Let the Noble One himself go today for alms on my account;
as for me, I shall attend to my own vow as directed by you."
Having thus requested the preceptor for the sake of his meal, the scholar,
once he had departed, entered the monastery hall as directed.
There, having made his body as motionless as a pillar and establishing mindfulness directed toward the front,
he meditated upon his own duty while remaining steady in the full lotus posture.
When he was thus armored with meditative concentration, the entire earth, together with its mountains and oceans,
trembled, its silken garments— the waters of the seas— swaying to and fro.
Knowing him to be devoted to meditation, Śakra commanded the guardians of the quarters, along with the moon and the sun, to protect the directions for the sake of his unimpeded success.
Then the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, knowing that his success was imminent through the ripening of his roots of merit, reflected for a moment.
If Śāriputra were to meet him while he was close to attaining the state of an Arhat and open the door, this would undoubtedly be an obstacle in his path.
Therefore, as he approaches, I shall go before him myself and engage in various conversations based on questions in order to waste his time.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One himself went in that direction and caused a delay for the monk as he was approaching by means of a discourse.
Due to the power of the gods, when the birds in the sky became silent,
the wise man attained a state comparable to a lamp in a windless place within the world.
After attaining the fruit of stream-entry, he reached the state of a once-returner;
then, having attained the fruit of non-returning, he subsequently achieved the fruit of arhatship.
Then, when the Sugata had departed for his own hermitage at the conclusion of their conversation,
Śāriputra entered and beheld his disciple, who was like the sun.
Seeing him who had suddenly emerged, his bonds of existence shattered,
he praised that perfection of his which is attained only after hundreds of ages.
Having heard of her attainment of the state of an Arhat, which was renowned throughout the world,
the Blessed One, questioned by the monks, the Victor related her story.
Formerly, the Blessed One Kāśyapa was a Tathāgata in Vārāṇasī together with twenty thousand monks who were residents of that city.
Devoted to the welfare of sentient beings, he dwelt for some time, honored with pure and excellent offerings that were pleasing to the mind and fit for all enjoyments.
While that devotion to honoring the monks was prevailing in every house,
the one named Durgata, sighing deeply and inconceivably, remained truly miserable.
"Fie on me, who am so utterly wretched due to poverty and devoid of virtuous deeds, that by my misfortune not even a single monk has been invited! (KAvk 41.73)
Those who are excluded from all the social dealings of people and are unfit for the application of words, the means of valid knowledge, and grammatical composition;
who have ceased their activities and lack the capacity for action or logical reasoning—such men become like words devoid of meaning.
To him, who was thus overcome by the fire of anxiety and censured for his lack of wealth, a certain man approached and, impelled by his own merit, spoke: KAvk_41.75.
Even though you are destitute, why have you not invited at least one monk, by any means possible, to attain merit for future lives?
Thus addressed by him, as if struck again while his arrow was still lodged within him,
he became exceedingly distressed due to the lack of food and drink.
In some way, though emaciated by hunger, he went to the merchant’s house and with great effort obtained his share of the payment through the work of splitting wood.
Having performed the husking of pure rice right there,
his wife respectfully presented to her husband what she had obtained as wages for that portion of the work.
Then, as that being of pure nature exerted himself for the sake of preparing a meal for the monk and for his own purification, Śakra became his assistant.
When Śakra had prepared food of divine color, flavor, and fragrance, he,
out of affection, appeared in disguise as a monk and said, "The scribe is not in distress."
When the assembly had been invited by the former inhabitants of the city, who were secretly deluded by worldly prosperity, the wretched man, out of grief, prepared to die.
Out of compassion, the Blessed One Kāśyapa himself approached him;
having fully understood his purity and spiritual attainment, he accepted the offering of food.
"Ah! I shall provide you with food," the king said;
yet even though he was earnestly entreated, the impoverished man did not value the wealth at all.
"May I be filled with the wealth of virtues and be a source of consolation for the poor.
Then, having worshipped the Blessed One, he made this aspiration.
When Kāśyapa had departed for his own hermitage and the Lord of the Gods had gone to heaven,
the entire house of the man in distress was filled with divine jewels.
Then, by the command of Śakra, Viśvakarman constructed for him a residence with beautiful gardens, adorned with pillars of jewels.
Having attained stainless sovereignty, he, together with all the monks,
honored Kāśyapa for seven days with wealth and enjoyments.
The other house of his became like the Raurava hell: its women were emaciated by hunger, its door was shunned by supplicants, its children were weeping,
its soot-stained walls were motionless, flies buzzed in the corners of the floor,
and a young cat slept upon the hearth.
Who would not themselves marvel at the fact that even his prosperity became an object of longing for the king?
By the power of that gift, which was purified by nectar,
he who had been destitute attained wisdom in another birth and reached the state of an Arhat.
Thus was the former life of the wise one recounted by the Omniscient One out of regard for his virtues;
having understood the merit of his pure generosity, the community of monks praised him as one worthy of wholesome deeds.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Legend of Kapilā," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
42. The Legend of Kanakavarṇa: Through courage, the rays of the sun flash forth in the darkness; through righteousness, the heaps of jewels from the sky shine;
through fortitude, all calamities come to rest; and through generosity, the quarters of the world become auspicious with enjoyments.
In the past, at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Blessed One, the Sugata,
bestowed a teaching of the Dharma upon those who had arrived for the sake of wholesome qualities.
In a previous eon, when the lifespan of people was eighty thousand years,
there was a glorious lord of the earth named Kanakavarṇa.
The city named Kanaka was his residence, just as Amarāvatī is for Śakra;
it became the beloved abode even of that lord of all the worlds.
He bore in his heart the affairs of the subjects— bright with glory, worthy of a leader, and endowed with the qualities of beauty and integrity—
just like a pearl necklace.
Due to the ripening of the karma of the people,
there occurred in that city a most terrible drought, which brought fear to all living beings.
That drought, which robbed all of them of their fortitude and caused distress to the entire world,
became the cause of mental anguish for the king.
With all remedies rendered ineffective, he, his mind paralyzed by anxiety,
reflected for a long time and then spoke to the circle of his chief ministers.
This unseasonable fall of rain upon the people is beyond remedy;
it renders my diligent efforts at protection fruitless.
The quarters of the sky cease their rains and the clouds become clear,
while the subjects shed tears like rain due to the sins of the kings.
For that king who does not provide protection for his subjects from great fear,
it is clear that his grasping for a crown and diadem is like that of an actor.
Then the Kṛta Yuga prevails in the world, when the king acts for the welfare of his subjects.
Devastated by famine, overwhelmed by vast rows of afflictions,
and unrestrained in their cries of "Alas!",
the subjects— tormented by wicked favorites and lamenting as they head toward destruction— find no refuge from the sins of kings.
Therefore, with all my resources, I must protect the subjects;
for kings, the merit of protecting their subjects is a treasure composed of jewels.
Having spoken thus and reflected upon the treasury and the storehouse of all the world,
he rendered everything his own a constant source of enjoyment and utility.
Then, in the course of time, due to a severe famine,
his store of food was exhausted through great expenditure until only enough remained for the meal of a single person.
At that moment, the Pratyekabuddha Raviprabha, having arrived through the air, then provided him with a meal.
While he was in that state of uncertainty regarding the maintenance of his own life, he,
with a serene mind, reflected upon everything and gave it all to him.
Having offered his own vital breath to that guest who was so pleased by the hospitality,
he departed through the sky, praising his virtuous character.
Then there arose a row of clouds hanging in the western quarter, like a dark line of bees upon the great elephant of the sky, or like a cluster of black aloe-wood paste upon its temple.
Then the entire expanse of the sky shone as it was being covered by clusters of fresh clouds, which resembled groves of blooming blue lotuses and appeared like swarms of bees.
Then, for seven nights, a desirable rain of all kinds of food fell upon the earth for the subjects;
immediately after that, there was a rain of grain and other crops, and thereafter, a rain of jewels in succession.

Thus King Kanakavarṇa, shining loftily like the crest-jewel of monarchs, ensured the protection of his subjects' lives, being gratified by the abundance of his own meritorious deeds; for the power of the virtuous prevails for the sake of others.
"This King Kanakavarṇa is none other than myself now, in this very body";
having spoken thus, the Blessed Jina delivered a teaching on the Dharma for the wise among the virtuous.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Legend of Kanakavarṇa," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

43. The Avadāna of Hiraṇyapāṇi: A power inclined toward helping all, a great prosperity upon which everyone depends—this is the first flower of one worthy of the sprout of merit, for it is worthy of vast foliage as its fruit.
Long ago, when the Jina had gone to his residence in the Jetavana monastery,
there was in Śrāvastī a glorious householder named Devasena.
He who considered himself a father of a true son had a son named Hiraṇyapāṇi,
whose two hands were born wonderfully fashioned out of gold.
Every morning, two lakhs of silver appeared in his two hands;
by means of that, he became a wish-fulfilling tree for those in need.
Through the ripening of his discernment of the manifest,
his devotion toward the Jina arose with increasing strength in the roots of virtue over time.
Then, having gone to the Jeta Grove and seeing the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, he,
filled with joy, performed a prostration at his feet.
The Blessed One also bestowed upon him a glance that was cooling like the moon to pacify the torments of saṃsāra,
a friend to nectar, and a protective fence for his welfare.
By the mere sight of the Teacher, he was freed from the gloom of delusion and shone like a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
Then the Blessed One bestowed upon him a teaching of the True Dharma,
by which the eye consisting of Dharma arose, its light unimpeded.
Through the maturation of his former merit, having developed the latent impression of dispassion,
he of stainless wisdom bowed down and spoke to the Omniscient One.
O Blessed One, refuge for those who have sought shelter,
grant me the going forth into homelessness, which brings an end to existence and destroys all afflictions without exception.
The lifespan of living beings is fleeting, and youthful vigor is even more so; these worldly prosperities are as unstable as the flickering play of lightning.
As he was speaking thus, the state of homelessness, arisen through the grace of the Sugata,
spontaneously descended upon his body, which was now free from all passion.
Wearing his red robes as a clear manifestation of his dispassion,
he abandoned his status as a vessel for cyclic existence by taking up the alms-bowl.
Having witnessed that miraculous accomplishment of his before their very eyes,
the monks questioned the Blessed One concerning his past history, and he spoke.
Long ago in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Kṛki when the Blessed One known as Kāśyapa was about to pass into parinirvāṇa.
Having prepared his body, he constructed a stūpa made of jewels,
lofty as if it were merit incarnate, mature enough to plunge into heaven.
While that staff was being placed upon the pedestal for worship,
a gambler named Kandala deposited two coins.
By that abundant merit arising from the purity of his serene mind,
Hiraṇyapāṇi has today attained a state envied even by the great.
One becomes noble through the renunciation of worldly existence, possessing all virtues and spreading white fame upon the earth that is like a twin to the moon;
for merit, when it reaches its fruition, transforms even that which is small into something not small.
That very thing, when the mind is stainless, is manifested as purity of faith.
Thus the Victor described the power of the merit of Hiraṇyapāṇi;
upon merely hearing it, that assembly of monks became filled with affection, joy, reverence, and wonder.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the *Hiraṇyapāṇy-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

44. The Legend of Ajātaśatru’s Patricide For those fallen into the most terrifying darkness of the unbearable venomous serpents of wicked people, the recollection of the Jina produces a support and removes the fear of cyclic existence.
Long ago, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, dwelt upon the ridge of Gṛdhrakūṭa on the slopes of the mountain known as Rājagṛha.
At that moment, King Bimbisāra, who was so fond of his son,
was there by his son Ajātaśatru, who had committed a cruel deed.
Like a friend of fire,
he was cast into the terrible, dark prison of Devadatta, which was devoid of any passage for movement.
Knowing that his wife had brought secret food into his confinement,
he, desiring its exhaustion, forbade it to him who was emaciated by hunger.
That lord of the earth became coarse, emaciated, and exceedingly soiled,
like the moon in the dark fortnight afflicted by an untimely black cloud.
For those of tender hearts,
calamity— when it is mature and deeply affectionate— generally brings about an embrace out of the distress caused by living in close proximity.
Aiming toward the direction where the Sugata had dwelt, he, afflicted by grief,
with palms joined and head bowed, spoke in a feeble voice:
Homage to you, the Blessed One, the most worthy, the great Arhat,
whose mind is intent upon perfect enlightenment and is armored for the upliftment of the wretched.
Homage to you, the Victor, who are the shore for those drowning in the ocean of the terrible saṃsāra,
and the cause for pacifying the birth and afflictions of living beings.
Homage to the one who is eternally awakened, the sole kinsman of all sentient beings,
the Buddha of pure nature, an ocean of the nectar of compassion.
Thus, having sprinkled the nectar of devotion worthy of being heard by the Sugata,
he composed this cluster of praises that brings forth the flowers of merit.
The Omniscient One, perceiving his state of physical exhaustion,
brought him nourishment through the light of the openings of the prison cell.
Ajātaśatru, having learned of that conduct and being filled with suspicion toward his father,
had even the most minute crevices in the prison cell closed up.
Then, at his command, the prison guards performed the cutting off of his feet with a razor while they were firmly bound.
Afflicted by the intense pain of that slaughter, the king uttered a cry of distress, exclaiming repeatedly:
"Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha!"
Then the Blessed One, the omniscient one, appeared before him in person;
seated upon the throne offered by Śakra, he spoke to him out of compassion.
"O King, what can be done? Such is the destiny of those who commit cruel deeds;
the fruit arising from good and evil is not exhausted until it has been experienced."
In this essence-less saṃsāra, which is addicted to the poisons of passion and hatred and is unbearable with its various calamities,
the very core is nothing but suffering.
In this time mired in affliction, fraught with the perils of both misfortune and prosperity,
steadfastness alone is protection, as is untroubled dispassion.
Drenched by the spreading conflagration of suffering growing within the terrifying depths of saṃsāra,
the eyes of those accustomed to virtuous deeds become clouded with teardrops, as if by rising columns of smoke.
"O King, resort to fortitude in this sorrow and abandon the hope for enjoyments;
all the activities of worldly existence are inherently opposed to their own final outcome."
"Your physical well-being is now close at hand," having said this and comforted him, the Blessed One departed for his own abode.
At the end of his life, at that very moment,
Bimbisāra was born in heaven as the illustrious Jinarṣabha, the son of Vaiśravaṇa.
Ajātaśatru, realizing that Janaka was dead,
honored his body and lamented his own misdeeds.
His mind, afflicted by exceedingly intense sin and defiled by evil conduct,
acted like a penance, falling into the fire of remorse.
He said: "Alas! Through delusion, my mind greedy for the intoxication of power, I have fallen headlong into the pit of the sins of wicked conduct."
For those impoverished in learning and wisdom who follow the counsel of the wicked, anxiety— stealing away the comfort of their own sleep— consumes their very limbs.
For me, who have fallen and despaired in the mire of sin, who am negligent and without support,
the recollection of the Jina is my refuge.
Having reflected thus for a very long time, he went into the presence of the Sugata;
loathing his evil deed, he fell into a state of extreme despondency.
There, considering himself impure and filled with shame,
he bowed from afar to the Jina, as if out of fear of being touched by sin.
With tearful eyes and trembling, he entreated the Omniscient One for protection,
as if shaking off his misdeeds clinging to his body.
O Blessed One, I am one who has committed evil deeds and am close to the fires of hell;
scorched by suffering, I have come to you alone, the ocean of compassion, for refuge.
This gaze of yours, with its lotus-like radiance, reaches as far as the Śoṇa river.
"By me— wicked, negligent,
and sinful, driven by evil counsel and greedy for power— my father was slain."
Having heard these lamentations of his, the Tathāgata uttered the *Puṇyasarasvatī* for the sake of purifying the dust of that man's sins.
O King, like a wicked man who has not anticipated his own deed,
you have been impelled by your own action toward the murder of your father and have fallen into this calamity of sin.
That suffering must be experienced by him, and that guilt must be incurred by you;
O King, this destiny is equal for both you and him.
Fate is immovable for human beings, like an inscription carved upon one's own throat or situated upon the surface of the forehead, as if etched in a fragment of stone.
By performing a defiled deed at the instigation of the wicked, you have,
with your own hand, cast aside the supreme bliss of immortality that was near at hand.
Even now, if you desire to destroy your evil and attain prosperity,
then direct your mind toward merit, which brings an end to sin.
Like the function of a lamp, it produces happiness and makes one's fame blaze;
this association with the virtuous is a form of nectar, well-rounded in its conduct.
Through the onset of the fire of remorse, through association with the virtuous,
through the recitation [of the Buddha's names], and through giving, the sin of embodied beings is destroyed.
It purifies the vessel, does not diminish virtues, does not destroy affection, and does not produce impurity;
beautiful until its faults are exhausted and never subject to flickering—association with the good is an incomparable lamp in the abode of merit.
Skilled in initiating the misfortune of the multitude of virtuous men, resembling a moment of the night, he obstructs the operations of all eyes among people;
he is an abode of uneven and unequal suffering due to the total destruction of light.
For association with the wicked produces a dense darkness born of great delusion.
O King, in due time you shall become a Pratyekabuddha, your defilements exhausted,
having gradually made solitude your delight through seclusion.
Thus the Blessed Jina bestowed consolation upon him with compassion;
for the virtuous, whose eyes are moist with pity, feel it even more intensely toward those who have fallen.
Then, having bowed to the Sugata, the king departed for his own abode;
he felt as though the great burden of his sin had become lightened.
When he had departed, the Omniscient One, being questioned out of curiosity about that deed by the monks,
related the former history of the protector of the earth.
In Vārāṇasī, there were four sons of merchants who were unrestrained in their fortune and devoted to effortless luxury and enterprise.
Once, while intoxicated with pleasure and engaged in mutual quarrelsome talk, they,
arrogant in their youth, saw a Pratyekabuddha approaching.
Seeing him, those who had conceived hatred and were revilers of tranquility and self-restraint, the eldest brother named Sundaraka, spoke to his brothers with a smile: KAvk_44.52.
"This monk, marked by his robe and bowl, has lost his life through drink;
that he be made intoxicated—this is my desire."
When this was said, out of impetuosity, a second one named Kundara spoke to the monk:
"I wish to cast him into the water and kill him."
Then the third wicked one, named Sundaraka, also said:
"Let this monk be cast down that street with speed; that would be best."
The fourth, named Kandarakā, of cruel mind, also spoke:
"Let the two feet of the monk be made skinless with a razor."
As they were speaking thus, their resolve became turbid;
by that [resolve], they obtained in another birth a fruit corresponding to their own desire.
One blinded by greed sees only wealth; one blinded by anger sees only an enemy;
one blinded by desire sees only a woman; but one blinded by pride sees nothing at all.
For those whose transformations have become like wealth, whose minds are unstable,
and whose discernment is dulled by intoxication, joy turns into the bondage of affliction.
They become angry without cause and they fall in love without cause;
struck by delusion and lacking discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful, these human beasts, being utterly satisfied, remain in a state of total indifference.
That very same eldest son of the merchant, due to his evil deeds,
was reborn in another life as a Śākya named Śāriryāna, who perished after drinking liquor.
The second great Śākya, named Mahān, perished in the water;
and the third, King Prasenajit, was overthrown by his own son.
This Bimbisāra, the fourth, was held in prison by his son;
for an action performed with wealth is experienced along with its interest.
For here, by the virtuous who are struck down by delusion and by the wicked alike, this fruitless action is performed with sudden mockery;
it is experienced here by those rendered helpless by abundant grief, their eyes filled with the water of tears.

Having clearly heard in the assembly of the wise this account of Bimbisāra— told by the Sugata concerning his previous life and its harsh, poisonous ripening— the monk reflected that his own mind alone was corrupted, being the cause of hundreds of calamities.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Avadāna of Ajātaśatru’s Patricide," from the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

45. The Story of Gratitude (*Kṛtajñāvadāna*) Even when blinded by the darkness of his own vision and cast down by a wicked man during the absence of the goddess Lakṣmī’s play, the lotus— rich in its virtues— passes through the night as if it were a state of misery, and returns once more to its own prosperity.
While the Sugata was dwelling in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī,
Devadatta, overcome by the malady of intense hatred, reflected:
My brother, a human born of the Śākya clan, is my equal and peer;
yet through the power of his merit, he has become a Jina, worthy of worship by the three worlds.
Therefore, I shall make an effort for the sake of his survival;
for when the sun has not yet set, the light of another does not shine.
Through discernment, experience, knowledge, austerity, and prosperity, one may endure the excellence of others;
for a mind exalted by pride does not indeed tolerate it.
Holding poison on the tips of my own nails, I prostrate before him and, drawing near,
transfer it onto his body by pressing against his feet.
Having reflected thus, that wicked man, overcome by malice and filled with turbid thoughts,
approached his kinsmen headed by Tiṣya and spoke as follows.
Cruel and having committed an offense, I, burdened by heavy sins, today prostrate at the feet of the Sugata,
who is upright and gracious.
Speaking thus, he, whose mind was wicked, went together with all of them who were approved by Sudatta to see the Jina seated in the Jetavana.
Upon seeing the Blessed One there in his entirety, he cried out loudly, "I am burnt! while raising his foot.
Struck as if by a thunderbolt by the sin of his intention to harm,
he fell at that very moment, body and soul, into the fire of hell.
The Omniscient One, seeing that he had suddenly fallen into a terrible hell,
spoke to the assembly of monks, who were astonished upon hearing his story.
"Fallen into the straits of affliction through the fault of sin, he indeed produces intense darkness; for the mind is in every way defiled."
In the city of Atighoṣā,
King Ratisoma formerly had two sons, Kṛtajña and Akṛtajña.
Grateful and compassionate toward those who sought his aid, like a wish-fulfilling tree,
he incessantly gave away his own collection of jeweled ornaments, having relinquished them himself.
"All the father's property, being undivided, belongs in common to both of us";
by speaking thus, although he was ungrateful, he did not give it up, even as she was abandoning it.
Then, with words of praise, the king bestowed his daughter, named Janakalyāṇikā, upon that grateful man whose intellect was as profound as the ocean.
Then the grateful man, his heart filled with the desire to give away the wealth he had earned by his own efforts,
boarded a ship upon the great ocean.
As he was departing, intent on acquiring jewels, that wicked man— though ungrateful— followed him out of greed, driven by a competitive envy born of hatred.
Then, filled with caravans of merchants, that ship slowly reached the desired island by way of a favorable wind.
Then, when he had returned and was intent on going to his own country,
his preparations being fully completed with heaps of jewels, he set out for his native land.
Grateful, he took five hundred jewels— the very price of the earth—
and tied them with a knotted cloth to the hem of his silken garment.
Then the great ship, exhausted by its heavy load of jewels,
was shattered by mighty winds, just as prosperity is destroyed by misconduct.
Then, having regained his life, the grateful man carried the ungrateful one on his back across the water, using a wooden plank as an oar.
Rescued by his brother out of compassion from that terrible ocean filled with sea-monsters,
he beheld a beautiful heap of jewels upon the edge of his garment.
Overpowered by greed for that jewel and by hatred,
he conceived a treacherous intent toward his brother, who was exhausted on the shore of the ocean.
While he was fast asleep, that ungrateful man gouged out his eye with a weapon,
seized the heap of jewels, and fled swiftly.
Accepted by that cruel man, like the sun by Rāhu, he too, his benefit to the world thwarted, became distressed and reflected: KAvk_45.28.
Now that my desire for the purpose of giving to supplicants has become futile,
what use have I, a blind man, for this barren life?
If the vital breaths do not depart because their objects have not yet been reached,
then those unions, being unable to endure separation, cause torment.
When wealth, people, hatred, pride, and infirmity are all equally fleeting for men,
the only thing that remains is the loss of one's reputation.
Having reflected thus, traveling slowly,
he was escorted by a caravan and reached the outskirts of the city of King Matighoṣa.
He remained there in the cowherd’s dwelling for some time,
until he was noticed by the princess who had come on a trip to the garden.
Upon seeing him, though he was blind, marked by the distinct characteristics of royalty,
she became filled with longing due to the bond of affection from a previous birth.
Then, having performed the ritual of the *svayaṃvara* at her father’s command,
she chose the sightless man from among the honorable kings.
"Having abandoned the protectors of the earth, you have chosen a blind man, O wicked woman!
Having spoken thus, she was cast out by her father in anger, and she did not shine.
Having placed him, who was blind, in the garden, she would always bring food with great effort and give it to him,
her respect augmented by love and affection.
Once, when the time for food had passed and she had not returned for a long while,
the prince, his face withered by hunger, spoke to her.
"By you, acting without due reflection and out of mere fickleness,
I have been chosen as a blind man, having abandoned kings with wide-open eyes."
Surely, having now grown weary of your regard for me due to remorse,
you are now intent on displaying a wild dance of passion.
Distressed by the sight of the blind man and longing for the sight of one with beautiful form,
you have arrived here only after a long time, even though the hour for taking food has passed.
Having been addressed thus harshly by him, she, trembling like a creeper,
spoke with a voice as sweet as a swarm of humming bees.
O Lord, you ought not to harbor my suspicion as something false out of anger;
for my heart, tender with affection, cannot endure the falling of the arrows of your words.
"I know you alone to be the deity, if my mind is pure;
by that truth, let one of your eyes become possessed of light."
When she, endowed with great goodness, had spoken thus, one of her eyes immediately attained a stainless clarity, taking on the appearance of a full-blown lotus.

Filled with great wonder by the power of her truth, and grateful, he spoke to her with confidence born of that truth and with renewed vigor: *The King said:* "O lady of pure conduct, you have truly performed a most difficult task.
