When that ungrateful brother tore out both my eyes,
neither did any transformation of mind, nor enmity, nor even injury arise within me.
"By that truth, let my second eye also become clear!
As soon as he had spoken, a distinct eye appeared before him in that very instant.
Therefore, having approached her father, the virtuous Janakalyāṇī, being delighted, reported the news as it had been told by her husband, who was grateful and worthy.
Then, honored by his father-in-law with jewels, elephants, and horses,
he went to his father’s city together with Śrī, as if with a beloved wife.
There, with his crest bowed at his father’s feet, he was established by his joyful father in the station of sovereignty,
a realm made auspicious by the people's affection.
Though ungrateful, shameless, and deceitful, he reflected on how to win him over;
then, while prostrating at his feet, he plotted treachery against him.
With crooked intentions, he came there intending to kill him;
crying out, "Alas! I am burnt! I am burnt!", he fell right then into hell.
That very Devadatta is he, and I am indeed the one who was grateful;
yet, due to the continuity from a previous birth, his hatred does not cease.
"Spoken by the Omniscient One," [they thought], yet that life-story of Devadatta was of great consequence and caused deep distress.
Upon hearing it—resembling the accumulation of sins gathered over many lifetimes—the community of monks became as if dejected.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the *Kṛtajñāvadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
46. The Avadāna of the Rice-Stalk.

For those whose minds are single-pointedly intent on generosity and who are vessels for great beings, the wish-fulfilling tree—purified by the abundance of its fruits, which consist of the qualities of energy, honor, and enjoyments, and composed of a store of merit—is said to bear fruit in its entirety at the proper time.
In the past, the Blessed One, the Jina, dwelt together with a multitude of monks in the grove of Vārāṇasī in Śrāvastī, belonging to the lord of Kosala, the ruler of the earth.
Exerting himself for the welfare of the three worlds, he entrusted the True Dharma— which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end, and which accomplishes the overcoming of many oppressions.
In the meantime, four sons of the Naga kings dwelling in the ocean [heard] the supreme nectar of the True Dharma proclaimed by the Sugata.
Urged by their sister named Abhirati,
those known as Bala, Atibala, Śvāsa, and Mahāśvāsa arrived together to listen.
In the presence of the Blessed One Krakucchanda, the wise one;
and with great effort before the sage named Kanaka and before Kāśyapa.
Attached to glorious happiness, they came even though uninvited to hear [the teaching],
having arrived there in former times through the ripening of that merit of Śākyamuni.
Having bowed to the Teacher among them, with their heads touching his feet,
they assumed human forms and sat down in the assembly.
King Prasenajit, the lord of Kosala, went to hear the True Dharma,
setting aside his royal parasol and fly-whisks which bore the luster of his gentle smile.
As he entered the assembly to prostrate at the feet of the Teacher,
everyone bowed down and made way for him out of respect for the king.
As he was being greeted by men as the venerable preceptor of the hermitage of Varṣā,
the daughters of the Naga king offered him neither space nor honor.
While that teacher of the castes and stages of life was being welcomed by the people,
the daughters of the Naga king gave him neither space nor honor.
Having instructed his own attendants standing before him with a gesture,
he remained as if devoid of emotion regarding their detention during the journey.
The Blessed One, the omniscient one, having understood his resolve,
smiled and spoke at the conclusion of his instruction on the Dharma:
In the tarnished mirror of a mind filled with the dust of hatred,
the reception of the reflection of the instruction of the Dharma does not shine.
Instruction does not restore even a slight portion of virtue in those who lack equanimity and are struck down by anger and delusion;
for medicine does not function as medicine for those of ruined intellects when their bodies are filled with many defects and devoid of purity.
Although the lord of the earth heard these beneficial words spoken by the Blessed One, he did not abandon his dejection regarding the nāgas.
Then, after the king had bowed to the Blessed One and departed for his own abode,
the nāgas traveled by way of the sky along the path blocked by his soldiers.
Having reflected thus in their own abodes, they— having seized the opportunity to destroy the earth and having swallowed the world with masses of clouds and terrible thunderclaps— arrived.
Knowing the resolve of those partisans, the Omniscient One appointed Maudgalyāyana, who was capable of protecting the king, [to guard him].
Then, by the power of the lord of the earth, the rain of thunderbolts released by the hosts of nāgas turned into a rain of flowers upon the monarch.
Then, the unbearable rain of weapons and missiles hurled densely by them was,
through the resolve of Maudgalyāyana, transformed into food fit for a king.
When the serpents had departed, their desire for enjoyment extinguished by his power,
the king, freed from all distress, went and paid homage to the Sugata.
By the command of Jina, he offered Maudgalyāyana the customary water of honor, made beautiful by the refinement of his devotion and the excellence of his wealth.
Then, having beheld the sovereign’s splendor worthy of heaven, the mendicant,
out of curiosity, questioned the omniscient one with his palms joined in reverence.
"Blessed One, by the power of what merit did Prasenajit obtain a vast kingdom,
resplendent with all enjoyments?"
From this, stalks of sugarcane and stalks of rice grow;
such an abundance of divine food and drink—of what karma is that the fruit?
Thus questioned by the affectionate monk, the Blessed One, the Victor, said:
"Listen to the cause of the king’s abundance of enjoyments."
In this kingdom of Kosala, a sugar-cane farmer named Khaṇḍa formerly gave sugarcane juice and boiled rice to a Pratyekabuddha.
Having eaten that meal of sugarcane juice, the Pratyekabuddha, who had been afflicted by a wind-disorder, became clear and attained well-being through those merits.
This very King Prasenajit is that meritorious maker of sugar-cakes;
by the power of that merit, he shines, partaking in great enjoyments.
A favor rendered to the grateful, an injury to those of cruel mind, and even a small portion of merit for the virtuous—each of these attains no small magnitude. (KAvk 46.32)
When the All-Knowing One had thus described the former merit of the lord of the earth,
the monk became motionless with wonder at the excellence of his virtuous deeds.
Then, having performed the consecration ceremony for the Blessed One with devotion,
the king personally presented each of those various riches worthy of the gods.
When the Tathāgata was seated comfortably upon a golden throne, beautifully adorned with various offerings, the lord of men addressed him.
O Blessed One, for me, whose glory of merit has been distributed through devotion to you,
this accumulation of roots of virtue will lead to non-liberation.
When asked by Pārthiva—who prided himself on his full store of merit—"From whom did you receive the Vinaya? the Sugata, casting a smile and a white radiance, spoke.
O King, how can this path of saṃsāra— which arises without beginning or end—
be easily traversed by men without first attaining the destruction of their afflictions?
With its long-habituated whirlpools of rebirth, this cycle of existence— naturally profound and characterized by effortless coming and going— is not easily traversed; for indeed,
in the absence of the practice of yoga, there is no destruction of karma.
Even the Dharma, which consists of a series of manifest fruits, has become a basis for this [work].
For me too, who had turned away from everything through the extensive practice of giving,
there arose a cycle of existence for the sake of the Dharma, spanning many births.
In former times, there was a wealthy man named Dhanika in Vārāṇasī;
he was like a shady tree for those in need, removing their distress and abundant with fruit.
When the world was ravaged by famine and distressed by the afflictions of adversity,
he requested food for five hundred Pratyekabuddhas.
Possessing no small fortune and free from pride, the steward of the granaries provided them with food fit for the enjoyment of others, sufficient until the end of the famine.
Then, in order to eat at his house, two thousand pratyekabuddhas arrived there one after another, in groups of five hundred each.
Through the dwelling power of that merit, born from the glory of his attained fruit,
there arose for him an inexhaustible treasury of jewels produced by his gifts during the famine.
Through his aspiration, he attained eternal bliss and the state of enjoying merit;
thereafter, he was led by the Teacher to perfect enlightenment.
Enveloped by merit and sin, this engagement with the fruits of action belongs to those in the cycle of existence;
this rope of bondage is white and black, and they say that upon its exhaustion, one enters the path of liberation.
Having heard this account of liberation as taught by the Jina for the removal of delusion, the lord of the earth,
considering that tranquility alone is worthy of destroying the afflictions, relaxed his pride in merit.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Avadāna of the Rice-Stalk," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

47. The Legend of Sarvārthasiddha: For those who are free from longing while acting for their own welfare, who are constantly exerted in helping others, and who are neither terrified by afflictions nor led astray by calamities, success comes without causing pain even through obstacles.

In Śrāvastī, the Blessed One, the former Victor, residing in the Jeta Grove, spoke to the community of monks during the course of a discourse on the Dharma: śrāvastyāṃ bhagavān pūrvaṃ jino jetavanasthitaḥ / dharmākhyānaprasaṅgena bhikṣusaṃghamabhāṣata // KAvk_47.2 //
There was a virtuous sovereign of the whole earth named Siddhārtha, whose edicts were cherished by the crowns of all kings.
The son of the nāga named Sāgara, who dwells in the ocean,
became the son of that king as Sarvārthasiddha.
That Bodhisattva of the Fortunate Aeon, whose radiance brilliantly illumines all beings,
as soon as he was born, filled the surface of the earth with his own miraculous powers.
As he grew, his fame— which pervaded all the worlds and was honored by the gods— increased like the Dharma itself.
Once, while traveling in a chariot through a magnificent garden,
that youth saw before him an old man created by a deity.
Beholding him, worn out by old age, he— his latent tendencies of world-weariness having arisen—
regarded that body as being as devoid of essence as cyclic existence itself.
Having gradually returned from his excursion to the pleasure garden,
he beheld on the road wretched people whose radiance had been scattered by poverty.
Seeing them afflicted by suffering, his mind drawn by compassion, he thought: "Alas! These miserable beings on earth endure such pain."
Those who say that suffering arises from not giving are inconsistent;
for even on a earth filled with jewels, they subsist on the alms of others.
This indeed is the infallible mark of those who have committed foul deeds:
that these wretched men beg from another man.
"Alas! These men have acted wickedly;
they are spurned at every step, for though they beg, they remain hungry, distressed by their search for alms."
Having reflected thus for a very long time, he who was intent on the destruction of all afflictions went to the ocean seeking jewels in order to make the world free from poverty.
As if somehow permitted by his father, he, firm in resolve,
boarded a ship and reached Ratnadvīpa.
There he spoke to the merchants who had boarded the ship as his traveling companions: "Let the collection of jewels be carried out by you as you desire."
"I have no need for these common jewels;
in my treasury there are great, radiant, and most excellent gems."
However, this great effort of mine is for the sake of obtaining the wish-fulfilling gem;
by means of it, I desire to make the earth free from poverty through joy.
"I have heard that there dwells in the great ocean a Naga king named Sāgara;
in his house is a jewel that grants whatever object one desires."
Having traversed that difficult path, I shall go to fetch him;
for those who possess fortitude as their companion and are resolute, nothing is inaccessible.
"And no misfortune shall befall you during my absence,
provided that this effort of mine toward virtuous deeds is truly for the sake of others."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of them, the courageous prince, firm in his resolve, set forth,
relying upon great fortitude.
Having traveled for seven days by a pathless route through the Ganges at knee-deep,
he proceeded for seven days at thigh-deep, and for seven days at waist-deep.
After four weeks,
he then went to the waters of a lotus pond and beheld before him terrible hooded serpents whose very glance was poisonous.
Then, having rendered them poisonless with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
he reached Yakṣadvīpa, which was surrounded by yakṣas possessed of cruel wrath.
There, having made them free from anger with a mind of loving-kindness, he heard what was said by them, who were filled with great enthusiasm and wonder: KAvk_47.26.
O Prince, by means of this abundant courage and such vigor,
he reached that abode of the Naga king while remaining in meditative concentration.
"In time you shall become a perfectly awakened one, omniscient;
and we shall become your disciples, following in your wake."
Having welcomed their words with "So be it," the prince reached the formidable Rākṣasa Island, which was surrounded by lords of the Rākṣasas.
In that very manner, honored by those who were free from cruel transformations,
he was cast in an instant by the raising of their arms into the abodes of the lords of the nāgas.
There, amidst that blazing splendor, accustomed as he was to celestial splendor and happiness,
he heard the sound of weeping that signaled the agony of long-standing suffering.
Hearing that, he became agitated; for his mind was by nature moist with compassion, and seeing the Naga maiden before him, he asked, "What is this?"
She spoke to him, her radiance of the bimba-fruit lip being repeatedly withered by her sighs, which betrayed the heat of her clinging grief.
The virtuous, lotus-eyed son of the Naga king,
the eldest named Sarvārthasiddha, who was so beloved, has met his death.
Therefore, since joy has departed and the festival of happiness has ceased,
there can be no staying in this house with wealth that is accompanied by weeping.
Having heard these words of hers, he, carrying within him his long-cherished longing and having reached his own country, went into the presence of the King of the Nāgas.
Recognizing him as he approached, the Naga king, accompanied by his beloved wife, cried out, "Come, come, my son! and became overwhelmed with joy.
Having heard from him the account of his mortal birth and the reason for his own arrival as reported,
the Naga embraced him and said:
"My son, take this wish-fulfilling gem which is the ornament of my crown;
I cannot bear to let your resolve go unfulfilled."
"Having already performed his duty for the world, he must now be given back to me by you.
Having said this, he released the jewel from his divine crest and gave it to him.
Joyful, he bowed to the lord of serpents and went to the vicinity of the ship.
There, the goddess of the ocean, having seen him and heard his story, said:
"O virtuous one, what kind of wish-fulfilling gem have you obtained?"
Seeing the jewel, acquired with such great hardship, fallen into the ocean,
he spoke, rendered motionless by the agitation of his firm exertion having come to naught.
"Ah! You whose form is so worthy of virtue, who speaks so softly out of affection—having committed an act defiled by hatred, do you not feel shame?"
For one who experiences the distress of rivalry and grief regarding the excellence of others,
even these cool directions become encircled by flames.
The fame of that ocean of being, who is beloved by those he protects,
bears the tilaka of the three worlds, white as camphor.
"O Queen, give me the jewel; desist from this sinful act.
The creeper of slander does not climb upon the virtuous."
If, out of greed, negligence, or hatred, you do not grant me the jewel,
then I shall dry up this ocean, which is your refuge.
When she did not give him the jewel despite his having spoken thus repeatedly,
he then set out to dry up the ocean by means of his own supernatural power.
As soon as it was meditated upon by Viśvakarman at the word of the Thousand-eyed One,
a leaf fashioned by him suddenly appeared in his hand.
With that [hand] shaped like Agastya’s cup, he lifted up water from the ocean and,
intent on consuming it, cast it into the sky.
When the ocean had been reduced to nothing but a portion of land by that performer of most wondrous deeds,

Who truly understands the guileless audacity and brilliance of the great— their power being like that of jewels— as well as the efficacy of their mantras and ascetic penances?
First, the ocean is renowned as vast, by the power of its effortless activity amidst boundless and insipid waters, its expanse of sky constrained by rows of surging waves;
yet, the profound majesty of the virtuous is some other kind of influence, whose greatness is truly immeasurable.
In that abode of wonder, the method of contemplation wherein the intellects float to their end.
Then, having recognized the wish-fulfilling gem and reunited with his own caravan,
the prince reached his own city with his desires fulfilled.
Having accomplished his purpose and being honored there by his father with great joy,
he placed a jewel upon the tip of a banner and spoke in the assembly of people:
If this effort of mine is solely for the sake of others and never for my own sake,
by that truth may this entire world attain freedom from poverty.
When this was said by that compassionate treasury of beings,
an endless rain of jewels fell upon the surface of the earth.
By that mass of jewels shining in all directions,
the darkness consisting of the people's poverty was brought to total extinction.
Bound by the fetters of hope, entering the outer courtyard with force, struck by the gatekeepers, repeatedly stumbling within the interior of the doorway,
sinking down in despair, falling with long sighs of grief, and longing for the destruction of the body— [This is the state of those who seek wealth.]
A certain extraordinary union with prosperity occurred for the wretched, variegated by the rays from heaps of jewels.
When that leader of serpents had departed for his own realm and the wish-fulfilling gem had gone, and when the people were free from misery,
the hearts of those everywhere devoted to the joy of giving became agitated by the ceaseless arrival of crowds seeking every kind of object.
"I am that very same Sarvārthasiddha, the son of the protector of the earth, who has appeared here in another body.
Having heard this account related by the Jina, those monks attained a state of identification with him.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the *Sarvārthasiddha-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.

48. The Legend of Hastaka Mature young women, delightful with breasts as high as the frontal globes of rutting elephants, their laughter radiant with the shimmering rays of camphor necklaces—both these and worldly riches bring joy to those possessed of merit. (KAvk 48.1)
Long ago, while the Blessed Tathāgata was wandering in the forest near Śrāvastī,
there lived a glorious householder named Suprabuddha.
He had a son named Hastaka who was exceedingly dear to him,
appearing like the personified accumulation of merits acquired in former lives.
On his day of birth, there appeared a great elephant made of gold,
like a multitude of wonders gathered into one.
That lordly elephant, the prince, his father’s desire,
and the treasury of the world’s curiosity— all simultaneously reached their fulfillment.
Like the infant moon, having in due time attained the state of being the abode of its digits, he,
radiant and the kinsman of the eyes of all the world, shone forth.
Gradually, he attained fresh youth, which served as the dwelling place for the onset of the god of love and was adorned by the pillar-like arms whose fullness had been completed.
Then once, [he saw] the daughter of King Prasenajit,
who was resplendent with her innate mark of a thin monastic robe.
He beheld a maiden known as Cīvarakanyā, whose face was graced with beauty,
whose eyes were long, and who had come to visit a garden.
Beholding her, whose form was unstained and whose radiance was unfading,
he suddenly fell equally under the power of wonder and love.
He thought: "Oh, how lovely and most wonderful is this form, in which the moon, pure and free from blemish, shines under the guise of her face!"
The slender woman possesses an incomparable loveliness; her lower lip, as beautiful as the *bandhūka* flower, is sweet by nature.
It vies with the sprouts of succulent coral, yet it renders their deceptive resemblance to the radiance of a bimba fruit utterly futile.
The moon cannot endure its own crookedness; its beauty causes pain to the nectar of the blossoming lotus grove; its gaze robs the light of the stars.
I think that for one whose body is accustomed to union with the God of Love, it brings about the fear of rivalry.
Her playful grace suddenly causes the drying up of the waves of Rati’s amorous charms.
Alas, even though her pair of firm, protruding, and fault-ridden lips had long since lost their discernment, they remained bound by a necklace that was itself full of defects; and furthermore,
a swarm of bees clings to her face with the mistaken notion that it is a lotus.
The minds of the sages are somehow absorbed in the tranquil eyes of the tremulous-eyed woman.
As he was thinking thus, the princess, beholding his body which resembled the god of the flower-arrows, became motionless with wonder.
When the garment of modesty was stolen from her by Smara, who brought forth a smile,
her body, covered with fresh thrills of horripilation, became clearly visible.
Hindered by fresh longing and turned back by embarrassment,
she went slowly as if vacant, having fixed her mind on that very spot.
Having reached the capital city, she became as if closed, as if hidden, and as if exiled by shame, wonder, and love.
The prince, too, having conceived a passion within his own palace,
repeatedly depicted that very moon-faced woman before him with his thoughts.
Remembering her as the very essence of his heart, like the lore of the god of love,
he brooded, considering her to be the daughter of a universal monarch, difficult to obtain.
Blessed is he whose body in another birth has long been familiar with austerity; he attains that very body, which is like a creeper upon the tree of merit.
The sight of him is obtained through the merit of giving delightful gifts;
I do not know what those merits are, the fruit of which is union with him.
Through the festive joy of remembering her face, which is like the cool-rayed moon, and through the fever of separation caused by her being so difficult to attain,
I know not whether this is steadfastness or whether it is delusion.
What is life, and what is the possession of vital breaths, [if there is] separation?
Defeated by the lotus of her face, the moon, the beloved of the night, forcibly undergoes waning;
and the god of love’s bow, put to shame by the playful grace of her eyebrows, bows down in submission.
Her lower lip, distressed by its own nectar which steals the beauty of tender sprouts, suffers emaciation.
Surely, having suffered defeat, she now clings to the forest ground like a fallen bimba fruit.
Thus, motionless in his meditation on the face of her whose countenance was like the full moon,
he passed the night as if abandoned by sleep out of jealousy.
Then, having heard the account of the maiden's appearance as reported by him,
his father became filled with anxiety that had taken hold of him.
He said to him: "O son, we are the city-dwellers of this king;
how will that universal monarch give you his daughter?"
The wise, who desire honor, do not do what is impossible, they do not strive for what is unattainable, and they do not speak of what is inconceivable.
Disregarding the mango and campaka vines that are at his disposal,
the bee withers away while longing for the *pārijāta* creeper.
If the connection between you and her was ordained in a previous birth,
then the arising of its fruit will certainly occur without any effort.
Destiny ordains that which is not dragged by the snares of hope, not tormented by anxieties,
and not exhausted by the burdens of effort.
Having heard his father's words and reflecting, "So be it," he was nevertheless unable to bring back the maiden who had been led away by her own heart.
Having gone there, he requested a pair of ivory tusks from Hemakuñjara as a fitting gift to please the king upon his first audience.
Then, taking the pair of tusks given by the elephant Puṇyabandha,
he went to see the lord of the earth.
Having reached the king’s palace, which was resplendent with jewels,
he entered and, bowing down out of affection, presented him with two golden tusks.
Honored with favor by the king, whose virtues were renowned,
and told, "Choose a boon," he did not accept anything at all.
The king, whose conduct was beautiful through propriety and who was himself free from desire, bestowed even greater honor upon that man of unblemished luster; for whom is such a person not dear?
Whenever he was in the king's presence, he delighted in giving golden-bodied elephants that were as if newly born with fresh limbs.
Restrained by the affection of service, the protector of the earth said to that female messenger:
"Bring peace to my mind, displaying the radiance of your face."
"I cannot endure this heavy, copper-lined vessel filled with an abundance of gold; for the wealth of kings must indeed be concealed."
What pleasure do I find in the gold brought by people after it has been shared out?
This very form of yours, with its priceless virtues, alone is dear to me.
Greed shines even among the jewels of men who are worthy of ornaments;
yet in the treasuries of kings, hoards of gold, gems, and stones perish.
"Tell me, what most desired thing shall I grant you?
Let there be no lingering regret on my part for having given away my entire treasury."
If fortunes are not obtained by becoming the object of a king's glance,
then what is the purpose of serving a monarch who has already achieved his ends?
Thus addressed by the protector of the earth, the prince, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him:
"O King, who else ought to be the giver?"
By bestowing jewels upon the gods without being asked,
you have sealed that ever-awake fame of the ocean.
Even with great effort, a person of noble mind is never filled;
that which is a source of power for the lowly is but poverty for the truly great.
However, for those people protected by your arms who live according to the path of Dharma,
there is no poverty, nor is there any wealth that needs to be sought.
We do not seek wealth, nor are we servants;
for those who prize wealth, wealth is their goal, but for the high-minded, honor alone is their treasure.
Due to their closing of virtues through service to the Supreme Lord, the flowers have suddenly reached the state of being roots;
because of their wretchedness, they have fallen from the marketplace of the base, and thus virtuous people do not grant them even a touch.
For embodied beings whose souls are dejected by wretchedness, death is better than begging; for the beggar is a dwelling place for the contempt of all people, while even a corpse is worthy of honor.
Furthermore, a virtuous jar goes downward as long as it remains at the top, but once it enters the well, it ascends.
As long as one remains helpless, having entered the darkness of delusion, one clings to the state of being a petitioner.
Wealth and prosperity are common to the wise, always attainable through trade or agriculture;
if they lack contentment, what else remains? There is the earth covered with treasures, and there are those works of gold and jewels that delight in providing extraordinary grace.
To whom is the sale of one's body for the sake of union with a beloved desired? It is the very essence of servitude.
Having heard these words of his, the king, whose intellect was limited, spoke with respect: "Let something else be taken. (KAvk 48.53)
A king finds pleasing even harsh speech if it is skillful and appropriate;
whereas a miserly man, though full of flattery, causes nothing but pain to the ears.
Greatly pleased by his magnanimity, the king was entreated by him;
he said to him, "If you are indeed pleased, let my daughter be given to me."
When he had spoken thus, the king, his mind swaying with doubt, said,
"I shall speak in the morning," and for a moment gazed at the surface of the earth.
Then, having dismissed the prince, he spoke to the chief minister:
"In my haste for favor, I have indeed committed this verbal rashness."
A maiden born into the lineage of a universal monarch is worthy of a price in merit;
how can she be given to an ordinary citizen merely for his virtues?
"Having promised 'I shall give,' how can I, later agitated by remorse, become unfaithful and leave the petitioner empty-handed? (KAvk 48.59)
How shall I see his face before me in the morning when he has arrived?
Though he was dear to me, he has become an object of aversion because of my unattainable desire.
Surely, even for embodied beings who are endowed with virtues by their very nature, one remains beloved only so long as he does not say, "Give me. (KAvk 48.61)
Having heard these words of the lord of the earth, who was swinging to and fro,
the great minister reflected and spoke to him in a manner suited to the occasion.
The intellects of masters, whose limits have not been scrutinized, possess a fresh and intense passion; they are indeed impetuous by their very nature.
By him,
who was intent on royal service, the golden elephant was destroyed through a pursuit of an impossible goal, like a greedy man seeking only the extraction of its tusks.
"You should tell him freely that he has returned seeking a maiden;
having mounted a golden elephant, he shall obtain my daughter."
Therefore, since he cut that elephant down with his own hand, how could it ever return to him?
And deprived of him, the elephant does not return again out of shame.
Thus, following the minister’s words and adopting that reasoning, the king,
on the next day, spoke directly to the prince who had arrived there.
The prince also, having gone home and performed the auspicious rites appropriate for a wedding,
mounted his ceremonial elephant and set out together with his kinsmen.
Seeing him approaching, mounted upon a golden elephant of wondrous splendor, the lord of the earth considered him the foremost among the meritorious.
Then, out of curiosity, the king, filled with great enthusiasm, mounted that elephant which was like a form of gold,
just as the wielder of the thunderbolt ascends Mount Sumeru.
When the protector of the earth had mounted, that elephant did not move;
but when the prince was seated, it moved again, its seat thus adorned.
Having recognized him as a god and being amazed by his power, the king,
saying "I am blessed," gave him the maiden Smaraśrī.
Having honored Puruṣottama with that jewel of a maiden, the king,
uplifted by a festival of joy, shone like an ocean of nectar.
Then, when the prince had taken his beloved and gone to his own home,
the labor of drawing the bow of the Bodiless One became fruitful.
In his youth, which was worthy of enjoyment and marked by union with a new beloved,
there was for him a magnificent abundance of wealth and a constant succession of ever-new festivals.
Then once, King Prasenajit, having accomplished his purpose, reflected as he contemplated the power of his son-in-law’s merit: KAvk_48.76.
"Oh, this divine power of the prince is clearly visible;
for such a ripening of merit does not belong to those of ordinary virtue."
A noble lineage is a palace of fortune; beauty is a wave that has stolen the pride of the moon; youth is fit for enjoyment; a collection of virtues is a heap of ornaments;
and fame is as beautiful as the radiant blossoming of flowers spread through a garden of merit.
We do not know whose manifestation of the ripening of wholesome karma this is.
Having reflected thus for a very long time, he, filled with curiosity,
set his heart’s desire upon beholding the Omniscient One.
Having summoned his brother-in-law and his daughter, and accompanied by his ministers,
he went to see the Blessed One, having already approached him mentally.
Having come within the range of his vision at Jetavana, the king abandoned his vehicle and,
approaching on foot, gazed upon the Blessed One.
Having bowed to him, he— whose crest-jewel was the splendor of his lotus-feet—
humbly introduced his daughter and his son-in-law to him by name.
When they had all sat down with their heads bowed in prostration,
the king, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the omniscient Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, by what karma has this prince, endowed with a multitude of virtues and the best among the illustrious, arrived here like a lordly elephant of gold?"
And this Cīvarakanyā, my daughter and his new bride—by the power of what merit has she become more dear to him than life itself? (KAvk 48.85)
Thus questioned by the lord of the earth, the Blessed One, the omniscient Jina, said to him:
"O King, the prosperities of men arise from merit."
Whatever is noble, whatever is appropriate, whatever is radiant, whatever is wonderful,
and whatever is desirable in the world— all that is brought forth by merit.
In former times, the Blessed One Vipaśyin, the Sugata, together with his monks,
wandered through the city of King Bandhumat out of compassion for the world.
At that moment, on the path where they were playing, the boy placed a wooden elephant before him along with the girl.
Beholding him approaching,
possessing the brilliance of molten gold and eyes as tender with compassion as the petals of a full-blown lotus—
Their hearts overflowing with the nectar of devotion for the Blessed One,
they presented the play-elephant to him and stood before him, bowing down.
The Blessed One, the omniscient one, having understood their desire,
out of compassion performed the touching of the feet of the wooden elephant.
Then, as the two boys were being seen by the Blessed One with a mind of perfect clarity,
they both made a mutual vow to marry one another.
"May my next birth be worthy of [my] family's power and prosperity;
and may a golden-toothed elephant be the mount for the prince"—such was his thought.
Seeing the two beautiful robes clinging to the Blessed One, she thought:
"May I too be endowed with such robes as these."
It was through that very vow that he was born here as Hastaka,
and this maiden Cīvarikā possesses the mark of wearing thin robes.
Having heard this account related by the Sugata,
the lord of the earth touched his lotus-feet with his crown and departed for his own palace.
When the queen had departed with wonder, the prince, together with his wife,
listened with a pure mind to the Dharma being expounded by the Blessed One.
Then, having developed dispassion and exhausted the latent tendencies of cyclic existence,
they conquered their afflictions through the life of renunciation and attained pure awakening.
Through the practice of the yoga of merit and well-performed deeds, those men who partake in virtue attain the perfection of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Having enjoyed that desired fruit together with their wives, they ultimately attain peace, which possesses the splendor of a cloudless sky.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the Story of Hastaka, in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā composed by Kṣemendra.
